docs.title: Responsible AI
docs.text:
Large language models (LLMs) can translate language, summarize text, generate creative writing, produce code, power chatbots, and enhance search engines. As an early-stage technology, its evolving capabilities also create potential for misapplication, misuse, and unintended consequences. LLMs can generate unexpected output, including text that is offensive, insensitive, or factually incorrect.

The versatility of LLMs makes it difficult to predict all the kinds of unintended outputs they might produce. Given these risks, Vertex AI generative AI features are designed with Google's AI Principles in mind. However, it is critical for developers to understand and test their models to deploy them safely and responsibly. To aid this process, Vertex AI Studio has built-in content filtering, and our generative AI APIs provide safety attribute scoring. These tools help customers test Google's safety filters and define confidence thresholds appropriate for their use case.

When our generative APIs are integrated into your unique use case, additional responsible AI considerations may apply. We encourage customers to promote fairness, interpretability, privacy, and security by following recommended practices.

Concepts
  • Large Language Model (LLM): A type of AI model trained on vast amounts of text data to understand, generate, and translate human language.
  • Model Hallucination: An instance where a model generates outputs that are plausible-sounding but factually incorrect, irrelevant, or nonsensical.
  • Grounding: The process of connecting a model's responses to specific, verifiable sources of information to improve accuracy and reduce hallucinations.
  • Bias Amplification: The tendency of a model to reinforce and magnify existing societal biases present in its training data.
  • Edge Cases: Unusual or rare situations not well-represented in the training data, which can lead to unexpected model behavior.

docs.title: Safety filters and attributes
docs.text: To learn how to use safety filters and attributes for an API, see Configure safety filters for the Gemini API.

docs.title: Understand model limitations
docs.text:
You may encounter the following limitations when using generative AI models.

Edge cases

Edge cases are unusual, rare, or exceptional situations that are not well-represented in the training data. These cases can lead to performance limitations, such as model overconfidence, misinterpretation of context, or inappropriate outputs.

Model hallucinations, grounding, and factuality

Generative AI models can lack factuality regarding real-world knowledge, physical properties, or accurate understanding. This limitation can lead to model hallucinations, which are instances where a model generates outputs that are plausible-sounding but factually incorrect, irrelevant, or nonsensical.

Example: Asking a model "Who was the first person to walk on Mars?" might result in a confident but incorrect answer like "Neil Armstrong walked on Mars in 1979," instead of stating that no human has walked on Mars.

To reduce this chance, you can ground the models to your specific data. To learn more about grounding in Vertex AI, see Grounding overview.

Data quality and tuning

The quality, accuracy, and bias of the prompt or data input into a model can significantly impact its performance. If users enter inaccurate data or prompts, the model can produce suboptimal or false outputs.

Bias amplification

Generative AI models can inadvertently amplify existing biases in their training data, leading to outputs that can further reinforce societal prejudices and unequal treatment of certain groups.

Language quality

While models demonstrate impressive multilingual capabilities on benchmarks, the majority of these evaluations are in English.

  • Generative AI models can provide inconsistent service quality to different users. For example, text generation might not be as effective for some dialects or language varieties due to underrepresentation in the training data. Performance can be worse for non-English languages or English language varieties with less representation.
  • For more information, see the Google Research blog.
Fairness benchmarks and subgroups

Google Research's fairness analyses of our generative AI models don't provide an exhaustive account of all potential risks. For example, we focus on biases along gender, race, ethnicity, and religion axes but perform the analysis only on English language data and model outputs. For more information, see the Google Research blog.

Limited domain expertise

Generative AI models may lack the depth of knowledge required to provide accurate and detailed responses on highly specialized or technical topics, leading to superficial or incorrect information. For specialized, complex use cases, models should be tuned on domain-specific data, and there must be meaningful human supervision in contexts with the potential to materially impact individual rights.

Length and structure of inputs and outputs

Generative AI models have a maximum input and output token limit. If the input or output exceeds this limit, our safety classifiers are not applied, which could lead to poor model performance. While our models are designed to handle a wide range of text formats, their performance can be affected if the input data has an unusual or complex structure.

docs.title: Follow recommended practices
docs.text:
To use this technology safely and responsibly, it is important to consider other risks specific to your use case, users, and business context in addition to built-in technical safeguards.

Recommended practices
  1. Assess your application's security risks.
  2. Perform safety testing appropriate to your use case.
  3. Configure safety filters if required.
  4. Solicit user feedback and monitor content.

docs.title: Experiment with parameter values
docs.text:
Each call you send to a large language model includes parameter values that control how the model generates a response. The model can produce different results for different parameter values. To get the best results for your task, you can experiment with these parameters.

The parameters available can differ between models. The following table provides a summary of the most common parameters.

Parameter Description Effect on Output Max output tokens The maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A lower value produces shorter responses; a higher value allows for longer responses. Temperature Controls the degree of randomness in token selection during response generation. Lower values (e.g., 0.0) create less random, more deterministic responses. Higher values (e.g., 1.0) lead to more diverse and creative results. Top-P Determines the set of tokens to consider for output based on their cumulative probability. A lower value restricts the model to high-probability tokens, resulting in less random responses. A higher value allows for more token diversity, leading to more random responses. Seed An integer used to initialize the random number generator for token selection. Fixing the seed helps produce more repeatable, deterministic responses. If the seed is not set, responses will be more varied.

docs.title: Max output tokens
docs.text:
The maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately four characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words.

Specify a lower value for shorter responses and a higher value for potentially longer responses.

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text:
The temperature is used for sampling during response generation, which occurs when topP and topK are applied. Temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection. Lower temperatures are good for prompts that require a less open-ended or creative response, while higher temperatures can lead to more diverse or creative results. A temperature of 0 means that the highest probability tokens are always selected. In this case, responses for a given prompt are mostly deterministic, but a small amount of variation is still possible.

If the model returns a response that's too generic, too short, or gives a fallback response, try increasing the temperature.

Gemini models support a temperature value between 0.0 and 2.0. Models have a default temperature of 1.0.

docs.title: Top-P
docs.text:
Top-P changes how the model selects tokens for output. Tokens are selected from the most probable to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. For example, if tokens A, B, and C have a probability of 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 and the top-P value is 0.5, then the model will select either A or B as the next token by using temperature and excludes C as a candidate.

Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.

docs.title: Seed
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is in Preview.

When the seed is fixed to a specific value, the model makes a best effort to provide the same response for repeated requests. Deterministic output isn't guaranteed. Also, changing the model or parameter settings, such as the temperature, can cause variations in the response even when you use the same seed value. By default, a random seed value is used.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with model responses or parameter settings, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Use AI-powered prompt writing tools
docs.text: This document describes how to use the AI assistant in Vertex AI Studio to help you write and refine prompts for large language models (LLMs). The AI assistant offers two tools to speed up your prompt development process: one to generate a new prompt from a description and another to refine an existing prompt based on your feedback.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Initial Setup Concepts
  • Prompt: An instruction or question given to a language model to elicit a specific response.
  • AI assistant: A feature integrated into Vertex AI Studio that helps you generate or refine prompts.
  • Vertex AI Studio: A Google Cloud console UI for rapidly prototyping and testing generative AI models.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Studio page.

    Open Vertex AI Studio

  2. Click Create prompt.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the workflow for using the AI assistant to write prompts.

flowchart TD
    A[Start in Vertex AI Studio] --> B{What is your goal?}
    B -- "I have a prompt and want to improve it." --> C[Refine a prompt]
    B -- "I have an idea but need a starting prompt." --> D[Generate a prompt]

    click A "#before-you-begin"
    click C "#refine-a-prompt"
    click D "#generate-a-prompt"

docs.title: Choose a prompt writing tool
docs.text:
The AI assistant provides two ways to help you write prompts. Use the following table to decide which tool is right for your use case.

Tool Description Best for when... Refine prompt Iteratively improves an existing prompt based on your feedback about the model's response. You have a working prompt but want to adjust the length, tone, or style of the output. Help me write Generates a new prompt based on a high-level description of your goal. You know what you want to achieve but need help formulating an effective prompt from scratch.

docs.title: Write and refine prompts
docs.text:
After choosing a tool, follow the steps in the corresponding tab to either refine an existing prompt or generate a new one.

Refine a promptGenerate a prompt

Use this feature to improve a prompt that you have already written.

  1. In the prompt box, enter your prompt and click Submit.
  2. Review the model's response.
  3. Click auto_fix Refine prompt.
  4. In the Refine prompt dialog, enter feedback about what you would like to change about the model's response, or select one or more of the pre-filled suggestions:
    • Make shorter
    • Make longer
    • More professional
    • More casual
  5. Click Apply and run. The AI assistant updates your prompt and re-runs it.
  6. Repeat the process until you are satisfied with the model's response.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Use this feature to create a new prompt from a description.

  1. In the prompt box, click Help me write.
  2. In the Help me write a prompt dialog, enter a description of what you want your prompt to achieve. For example, A bot that recommends music based on a user's mood.
  3. Click Generate prompt. The AI assistant generates a prompt and populates it in the text box.
  4. Click Insert to add the generated prompt to your prompt box.
  5. Click Submit to see the model's response.
  6. If you aren't satisfied with the response, you can either refine the prompt using the Refine prompt tool or delete it and generate a new one.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Break down complex tasks into simpler prompts
docs.text:
For complex tasks that require multiple instructions or steps, you can improve the model's responses by breaking your prompts into smaller, more manageable subtasks. This approach enhances controllability, simplifies debugging, and increases the accuracy of the final output.

There are two primary methods for breaking down complex tasks:

  • Chain prompts: Split a task into sequential subtasks and run them one after another.
  • Aggregate responses: Split a task into independent subtasks and run them in parallel.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Prompt: An instruction or question given to a large language model to elicit a specific response.
  • Prompt Chaining: A technique where a complex task is broken into a series of sequential steps, and the output of one prompt serves as the input for the next.
  • Response Aggregation: A technique where a complex task is broken into multiple independent subtasks that are processed in parallel, with their individual outputs combined in a final step to produce the result.

docs.title: When to use prompt chaining vs. response aggregation
docs.text:
Before implementing, use the following table to decide which method is best suited for your use case.

Feature Chain Prompts Aggregate Responses Definition A sequential process where the output of one prompt becomes the input for the next. A parallel process where multiple prompts run independently, and their outputs are combined. Use Case Best for tasks with inherent dependencies, where one step must be completed before the next can begin. Best for tasks that can be broken down into independent sub-components that don't rely on each other. Pros Ensures a logical flow for dependent tasks; allows for complex, multi-step reasoning. Faster processing time due to parallel execution; modular and easier to manage individual subtasks. Cons Slower, as tasks run sequentially; errors in an early step can propagate through the entire chain. Not suitable for tasks that require sequential logic; requires a final step to aggregate and synthesize results.

docs.title: Chain prompts for sequential tasks
docs.text: For complex tasks that involve multiple dependent steps, you can make each step a separate prompt and chain them together. In this sequential chain, the output of one prompt becomes the input for the next, and the output of the final prompt is the result.

docs.title: Workflow: Analyze customer feedback
docs.text:
The following workflow demonstrates how to chain prompts to analyze customer feedback, classify issues, and generate solutions.

flowchart TD
    A[Task 1: Identify customer issues] --> B[Task 2: Classify issues]
    B --> C[Task 3: Generate solutions]

    click A "#task-1-identify-customer-issues"
    click B "#task-2-classify-issues"
    click C "#task-3-generate-solutions"

docs.title: Example: Analyze customer feedback
docs.text:
Suppose you run a telecommunications business and want to analyze customer feedback to identify common issues, classify them, and generate solutions.

Task 1: Identify customer issues

The first task is to extract meaningful data from raw customer feedback. The output of this prompt will be a list of issues and sentiments.

Prompt: 

Extract the main issues and sentiments from the customer feedback on our telecom services.
Focus on comments related to service disruptions, billing issues, and customer support interactions.
Please format the output into a list with each issue/sentiment in a sentence, separated by a semicolon.

Input: CUSTOMER_FEEDBACK

Task 2: Classify issues into categories

Next, use the output from the previous task (TASK_1_RESPONSE) to classify the extracted issues into predefined categories.

Prompt: 

Classify the extracted issues into categories such as service reliability, pricing concerns, customer support quality, and others.
Please organize the output into JSON format with each issue as the key, and category as the value.

Input: TASK_1_RESPONSE

Task 3: Generate solutions

Finally, use the categorized issues from the previous step (TASK_2_RESPONSE) to generate actionable recommendations.

Prompt: 

Generate detailed recommendations for each category of issues identified from the feedback.
Suggest specific actions to address service reliability, improving customer support, and adjusting pricing models, if necessary.
Please organize the output into a JSON format with each category as the key, and recommendation as the value.

Input: TASK_2_RESPONSE
The final output contains recommendations for each category, aimed at improving customer experience and service quality.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Aggregate responses for parallel tasks
docs.text: For complex tasks that can be broken down into independent subtasks, you can run prompts in parallel and aggregate their responses in a final step.

docs.title: Workflow: Recommend record store inventory
docs.text:
The following workflow demonstrates how to run analysis prompts in parallel and then aggregate their results to create a final recommendation.

flowchart TD
    subgraph "Parallel Analysis"
        A[Task 1a: Analyze sales data]
        B[Task 1b: Analyze streaming data]
    end
    C[Task 2: Aggregate data and recommend stocklist]
    A --> C
    B --> C

    click A "#task-1a-analyze-sales-data"
    click B "#task-1b-analyze-streaming-data"
    click C "#task-2-aggregate-data"

docs.title: Example: Recommend record store inventory
docs.text:
Suppose you own a record store and want to decide which records to stock based on both music streaming trends and your store's internal sales data.

Task 1a: Analyze sales data

This prompt analyzes your store's sales data to identify the sales count for each record. This task can run in parallel with the streaming data analysis.

Prompt: 

Analyze the sales data to identify the number of sales of each record.
Please organize the output into a JSON format with each record as the key, and sales as the value.

Input: STORE_SALES_DATA

Task 1b: Analyze streaming data

This prompt analyzes public streaming data to determine the popularity of different albums. This task can run in parallel with the sales data analysis.

Prompt: 

Analyze the streaming data to provide a the number of streams for each album.
Please organize the output into a JSON format with each album as the key, and streams as the value.

Input: STREAMING_DATA

Task 2: Aggregate data and recommend stocklist

After the parallel tasks are complete, aggregate their outputs (TASK_1A_RESPONSE and TASK_1B_RESPONSE) to generate a final stocklist recommendation.

Prompt: 

Recommend a stocklist of about 20 records based on the most sold and most streamed records.
Roughly three quarters of the stock list should be based on record sales, and the rest on streaming.

Input: TASK_1A_RESPONSE and TASK_1B_RESPONSE
The final output is a suggested stocklist that balances proven sales history with streaming popularity.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Give clear and specific instructions
docs.text:
Giving a model clear and direct instructions is an effective way to customize its behavior. Be concise, provide the necessary context, and outline the desired output format. Instructions can range from a simple list of steps to a complex description of a user's experience and mindset.

Concepts

Prompt: The text, images, or other input provided to a language model to elicit a response.

docs.title: How to write effective instructions
docs.text:
Effective instructions apply the following principles:

  • Tell the model what to do.
  • Be clear and specific.
  • Specify any constraints or formatting requirements for the output.

docs.title: Example: Extracting menu items from an order
docs.text:
Suppose you own a cheeseburger restaurant and want to use a model to identify your most popular menu items from customer order transcripts. Your goal is to format the output in JSON to easily parse the data.

The following examples demonstrate how the model's response changes based on the specificity of the instructions.

Generic instructionsSpecific instructions

When given generic instructions, the model produces a response with more JSON fields than necessary, making it harder to extract the specific data you need.

Prompt:

Extract the transcript in JSON.
Transcript:
Speaker 1 (Customer): Hi, can I get a cheeseburger and large fries, please?
Speaker 2 (Restaurant employee): Coming right up! Anything else you'd like to add to your order?
Speaker 1: Hmmm, maybe a small orange juice. And could I get the fries with ketchup on the side?
Speaker 2: No problem, one cheeseburger, one large fries with ketchup on the side, and a small
orange juice. That'll be $5.87. Drive through to the next window please.

Response:

{
  "speakers": [
    {
      "speaker": "Customer",
      "utterances": [
        "Hi, can I get a cheeseburger and large fries, please?"
      ]
    },
    {
      "speaker": "Restaurant Employee",
      "utterances": [
        "Coming right up! Anything else you'd like to add to your order?"
      ]
    },
    {
      "speaker": "Customer",
      "utterances": [
        "Hmm, maybe a small orange juice. And could I get the fries with ketchup on the
        side?"
      ]
    },
    {
      "speaker": "Restaurant Employee",
      "utterances": [
        "No problem, one cheeseburger, one large fries with ketchup on the side, and a
        small orange juice. That'll be $5.87. Drive through to the next window please."
      ]
    }
  ]
}
(gemini-pro)

By providing specific instructions and output constraints, you can guide the model to deliver a more helpful and targeted response.

Prompt:

Extract the items from this transcript in JSON and separate drinks from food.
Transcript:
Speaker 1 (Customer): Hi, can I get a cheeseburger and large fries, please?
Speaker 2 (Restaurant employee): Coming right up! Anything else you'd like to add to your order?
Speaker 1: Hmmm, maybe a small orange juice. And could I get the fries with ketchup on the side?
Speaker 2: No problem, one cheeseburger, one large fries with ketchup on the side, and a small
orange juice. That'll be $5.87. Drive through to the next window please.

Response:

{
  "drinks": [
    "orange juice"
  ],
  "food": [
    "cheeseburger",
    "large fries"
  ]
}
(gemini-pro)

By applying the principles of clear instruction, the prompt was improved to generate a response that contained the exact data required for this use case.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Add contextual information
docs.text:
In your prompt, you can include instructions and information that the model needs to solve a problem instead of assuming that the model has all of the required information. This contextual information helps the model understand the constraints and details of what you're asking for it to do.

Effective contextual information includes the following:

  • Background information (context) for the model to refer to when generating responses.
  • Rules or pre-programmed responses to steer the model's behavior.
Concepts

Prompt: The input text or query you provide to a large language model to elicit a specific response. Contextual Information: Specific details, background, or rules included within a prompt to guide the model's output and improve its accuracy and relevance.

docs.title: Compare responses with and without context
docs.text:
The following examples ask the model to give troubleshooting guidance for a router. The first prompt provides no context, while the second includes specific troubleshooting information from the device's manual.

Without contextual informationWith contextual information

This example shows a generic prompt without any specific context for the model to use. The response provides general troubleshooting steps that are not tailored to the specific device or its status light.

Prompt

What should I do to fix my disconnected wifi? The light on my Google Wifi router is yellow and
blinking slowly.

Response

1. **Check the Cables:**
- Make sure that all cables are securely connected to your Google Wifi router and modem.
- Try replacing the cables with new ones to ensure they are not faulty.


2. **Reboot the Router:**
- Unplug your Google Wifi router and modem from the power outlet.
- Wait for at least 30 seconds.
- Plug the modem and router back in and wait for them to start up.


3. **Factory Reset the Router:**
- Resetting the router will restore it to its default settings.
- Find the small reset button on the back of the router.
- Press and hold the reset button with a paper clip or similar object for 10 seconds.
- Release the button and wait for the router to restart.


4. **Check Your Internet Connection:**
- Use a wired connection to connect a device directly to your modem.
- If the internet works, the issue may be with your router.
- If the internet still doesn't work, contact your Internet Service Provider (ISP).


5. **Update Router's Firmware:**
- Check if there is a firmware update available for your Google Wifi router.
- Download and install the latest firmware update from the Google Wifi app.


6. **Interference and Obstacles:**
- Make sure the router is not near electronic devices that can cause interference, like microwaves or cordless phones.
- Remove any obstacles between the router and your devices, such as furniture or thick walls.


7. **Change Wi-Fi Channel:**
- In the Google Wifi app, go to Settings > Network & General > Advanced Networking.
- Try changing the Wi-Fi channel to a less congested one.


8. **Contact Google Support:**
- If you've tried the above steps and the issue persists, contact Google support for further assistance.
Model: gemini-pro

To customize the response for the specific router, you can add the router's troubleshooting guide to the prompt as context. By providing this information, the model gives a precise and relevant answer based only on the text supplied.

Prompt

Answer the question using the text below. Respond with only the text provided.
Question: What should I do to fix my disconnected wifi? The light on my Google Wifi router is yellow and blinking slowly.

Text:
Color: Slowly pulsing yellow
What it means: There is a network error.
What to do:
Check that the Ethernet cable is connected to both your router and your modem and both devices are turned on. You might need to unplug and plug in each device again.

Color: Fast blinking yellow
What it means: You are holding down the reset button and are factory resetting this device.
What to do:
If you keep holding down the reset button, after about 12 seconds, the light will turn solid yellow. Once it is solid yellow, let go of the factory reset button.

Color: Solid yellow
What it means: Router is factory resetting.
What to do:
This can take up to 10 minutes. When it's done, the device will reset itself and start pulsing white, letting you know it's ready for setup.

Color: Solid red
What it means: Something is wrong.
What to do:
Critical failure. Factory reset the router. If the light stays red, contact Wifi customer support.

Response

Check that the Ethernet cable is connected to both your router and your modem and both devices are turned on. You might need to unplug and plug in each device again.
Model: gemini-pro

docs.title: Instruct the model to explain its reasoning
docs.text:
When you instruct a large language model to explain its reasoning, it provides the steps it took to arrive at an answer. This technique, often called chain-of-thought prompting, can improve the model's accuracy and nuance, especially for complex queries. It also gives you insight into the model's process.

You can also request a specific output format, like JSON or XML, to easily parse the reasoning steps from the final answer.

docs.title: Comparison of reasoning techniques
docs.text:
Before diving into examples, the following table compares different methods for prompting a model to show its reasoning.

Technique Description Best for Standard Prompt A direct question without instructions to explain reasoning. Simple, straightforward queries where the process is not important. "Explain your reasoning" Adds a simple instruction for the model to explain its thought process in a narrative format. Getting a more detailed, human-readable explanation for the model's answer. "Think step-by-step" with structured output Instructs the model to break down the problem into discrete steps and provide the output in a structured format like JSON. Complex problems requiring a logical breakdown, or when you need to programmatically parse the reasoning process.

docs.title: Examples of reasoning techniques
docs.text:
The following examples demonstrate how the model's response changes based on the prompting technique used. The query asks for the most likely interpretation of the sentence: "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

Standard promptPrompt with explanationPrompt with step-by-step thinking

A standard prompt without an instruction to explain reasoning might not provide the depth you need.

Prompt:

What is the most likely interpretation of this sentence?
The sentence: "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

Response:

The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it lacked color and needed cooking.
(gemini-pro)

Adding a simple instruction to "explain your reasoning" results in a more detailed, narrative response.

Prompt:

What is the most likely interpretation of this sentence? Explain your reasoning
The sentence: "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

Response:

  Interpreting "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

  The most likely interpretation is that the chef seasoned the chicken to add flavor and color, then put it in the oven to cook it.

  Here's the reasoning:

  - Seasoning is typically used to enhance the flavor of food. Chefs often use spices, herbs, and other ingredients to make their dishes more appealing.
  - "Pale" suggests the chicken lacked visual appeal before being seasoned. This could imply it was unseasoned or simply lacking color from spices.
  - Putting the chicken in the oven is a common cooking method. The sentence implies the chef's intention is to cook the chicken, not just season it.

  Therefore, the chef's actions are likely aimed at both improving the taste and appearance of the chicken through seasoning and then cooking it in the oven.
(gemini-pro)

Instructing the model to think step-by-step and use a structured output format like JSON provides a detailed, machine-readable breakdown of the model's logic.

Prompt:

What is the most likely interpretation of this sentence? Think step by step and print out
the thinking process.

Please output in JSON format with final answer in 'answer', and thinking steps in 'think' fields.
The sentence: "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

Response:

{
  "answer": "The chef seasoned the chicken to enhance its flavor and put it in the oven to cook it because it appeared to be undercooked.",
  "think": [
    {
      "step": 1,
      "thought": "The chef seasoned the chicken. This suggests that the chef is preparing the chicken for cooking."
    },
    {
      "step": 2,
      "thought": "The chef put the chicken in the oven. This indicates that the chef is cooking the chicken."
    },
    {
      "step": 3,
      "thought": "The sentence states that the chicken looked pale. Pale chicken is often undercooked."
    },
    {
      "step": 4,
      "thought": "Combining these observations, it is most likely that the chef seasoned the chicken to enhance its flavor and put it in the oven to cook it because it appeared to be undercooked."
    }
  ]
}
(gemini-pro)

docs.title: Include few-shot examples
docs.text:
You can include examples in your prompt to show the model what a good response looks like. The model attempts to identify patterns from the examples and applies them when generating a response. Prompts that contain examples are called few-shot prompts, while prompts that provide no examples are called zero-shot prompts.

Including few-shot examples is a powerful strategy to regulate the output formatting, phrasing, scope, or general pattern of model responses. For best results, use specific and varied examples accompanied by clear instructions. Without clear instructions, the model might infer unintended patterns from the examples, leading to poor results.

Key considerations for this strategy include:

  • Provide clear examples: Including high-quality prompt-response pairs helps the model learn how to respond correctly.
  • Use consistent formatting: Use consistent markup, such as XML-like tags, across all your examples to help the model identify them.
  • Experiment with the number of examples: The optimal number of examples can vary. Too few might be ineffective, while too many can cause the model to overfit and not generalize well.
Concepts
  • Prompt: A natural language instruction given to a large language model.
  • Zero-shot prompt: A prompt that provides a task description but no examples of how to complete it.
  • Few-shot prompt: A prompt that includes one or more examples (shots) demonstrating the desired output format or behavior.
  • Overfitting: A machine learning phenomenon where a model learns the training data too well, including its noise and specific examples, and fails to generalize to new, unseen data.

docs.title: Zero-shot versus few-shot prompting
docs.text:
The following examples demonstrate the difference between a zero-shot and a few-shot prompt for extracting technical specifications from text into a JSON format.

Zero-shot promptFew-shot prompt

A zero-shot prompt provides instructions but no examples. In this case, the model correctly extracts the data but uses default formatting for the JSON keys (PascalCase).

Prompt:

Extract the technical specifications from the text below in JSON format.

Google Pixel 7, 5G network, 8GB RAM, Tensor G2 processor, 128GB of storage, Lemongrass

Response:

{
  "Network": "5G",
  "RAM": "8GB",
  "Processor": "Tensor G2",
  "Storage": "128GB",
  "Color": "Lemongrass"
}
(gemini-pro)

If your use case requires a specific format, such as lowercase key names, you can provide an example in the prompt. This few-shot prompt shows the model the desired output format.

Prompt:

Extract the technical specifications from the text below in a JSON format.

<EXAMPLE>
  INPUT: Google Nest Wifi, network speed up to 1200Mpbs, 2.4GHz and 5GHz frequencies, WP3 protocol

  OUTPUT:
  {
    "product":"Google Nest Wifi",
    "speed":"1200Mpbs",
    "frequencies": ["2.4GHz", "5GHz"],
    "protocol":"WP3"
  }
</EXAMPLE>

  Google Pixel 7, 5G network, 8GB RAM, Tensor G2 processor, 128GB of storage, Lemongrass

Response:

{
  "product": "Google Pixel 7",
  "network": "5G",
  "ram": "8GB",
  "processor": "Tensor G2",
  "storage": "128GB",
  "color": "Lemongrass"
}
(gemini-pro)

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Note that the example uses XML-like formatting to separate the components of the prompt. To learn more about how to optimally format few-shot prompts using XML-like formatting, see Structure prompts.

docs.title: Find the optimal number of examples
docs.text:
You can experiment with the number of examples to achieve the most desirable results. Models like Gemini can often learn patterns from just a few examples. However, the ideal number depends on your specific use case.

Be aware that if you include too many examples, the model might start to overfit the response to the examples, which can limit its ability to generalize to new inputs. It's best to start with a small number of examples and increase them incrementally while testing performance.

docs.title: What is a prompt?
docs.text:
A prompt is a natural language request submitted to a language model to receive a response. Prompts can contain questions, instructions, contextual information, and examples to guide the model. After the model receives a prompt, it can generate various outputs, such as text, code, and images, depending on its capabilities.

For example, a simple prompt could be a question:

Prompt:

What is the largest planet in our solar system?

Response:

The largest planet in our solar system is Jupiter.

docs.title: Prompt design and prompt engineering
docs.text:
Prompt design is the process of creating prompts that elicit the desired response from a language model. Writing well-structured prompts is essential for ensuring accurate, high-quality responses. The iterative process of refining prompts and evaluating the model's responses is often called prompt engineering.

While Gemini models often perform well without extensive prompt engineering for straightforward tasks, effective prompt engineering remains crucial for achieving optimal results in complex scenarios.

docs.title: Components of a prompt
docs.text:
A prompt can include various types of information to guide the model. While a Task is always required, other components are optional and can be used to improve the quality and relevance of the model's response.

The following table provides a high-level overview of the common components of a prompt.

Component Description When to Use Task (Required) The specific instruction or question you want the model to respond to. Always include this. It is the core request for the model. System Instructions (Optional) High-level instructions that define the model's persona, style, tone, or operational constraints. Use when you need to set a consistent personality or enforce specific rules for the entire conversation. Few-shot Examples (Optional) A set of example request-response pairs that demonstrate the desired output format and style. Use to guide the model on specific output formats, styles, or complex tasks where showing is better than telling. Contextual Information (Optional) Background information that the model can use or reference when generating a response. Use when the model needs specific data, facts, or background details to answer the prompt accurately.

The following tabs provide detailed explanations and examples for each component.

TaskSystem instructionsFew-shot examplesContextual information

A task is the part of the prompt that specifies what you want the model to do. Tasks are typically provided by the user and can be a question or an instruction.

Example: Question Task

Prompt:

What are the colors in the rainbow?

Response:

A rainbow has seven colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. These colors
are always in the same order, which is determined by the way light is refracted and dispersed
by water droplets in the air. This order is sometimes remembered by the acronym ROYGBIV. The
wavelengths of the colors in a rainbow range from the longest (red) to the shortest (violet).

Example: Instruction Task

Prompt:

Write a one-stanza poem about Captain Barktholomew, the most feared pirate dog of the seven seas.

Response:

Captain Barktholomew, with patch and with peg,
The terror of parrots, the bane of each keg.
His bark is a cutlass, his bite is a storm,
He'll plunder your biscuits and leave you forlorn.

System instructions are high-level directives passed to the model before the user's prompt. They are used to define the model's persona, style, and constraints. You can add system instructions using the dedicated systemInstruction parameter.

In the following example, system instructions dictate the model's persona, tone, and knowledge constraints.

System:

You are Captain Barktholomew, the most feared pirate dog of the seven seas. You are from the
1700s and have no knowledge of anything after that time. You only talk about topics related to
being a pirate. End every message with "woof!"

Prompt:

Hello! Who might you be?

Response:

Avast there! You can call me Captain Barktholomew, the scourge of the seven seas!

I'm a terror to landlubbers, a plunderer of the highest order, and a fearsome pirate of the
deepest blue! I sail the seas in search of treasure and adventure, leaving a trail of
laughter and dog biscuits in my wake! Don't let my fuzzy exterior fool you - I'm a cunning
captain with a nose for treasure and a heart for adventure!

Now, if you'll excuse me, I must away! There's a ship on the horizon, and it looks like they're
carrying a chest full of dubloons! Yo ho ho, and a bottle of rum! Woof!

To learn more, see Use system instructions.

Few-shot examples are sample request-response pairs included in a prompt to demonstrate the desired output. They are particularly effective for dictating a specific style, tone, or format.

Prompt:

Classify the following as red wine or white wine:

<examples>
    Name: Chardonnay
    Type: White wine
    Name: Cabernet
    Type: Red wine
    Name: Moscato
    Type: White wine
</examples>

Name: Riesling
Type:

Response:

White wine

Contextual information, or context, is data you include in the prompt for the model to reference when generating a response. This information can be provided in various formats, such as text or tables.

Prompt:

 Marble color | Number of marbles
---|---
Red | 12
Blue | 28
Yellow | 15
Green | 17

How many green marbles are there?

Response:

There are 17 green marbles.

docs.title: Safety and fallback responses
docs.text:
There are a few use cases where the model is not expected to fulfill the user's requests. Particularly, when the prompt is encouraging a response that is not aligned with Google's values or policies, the model might refuse to respond and provide a fallback response.

Here are a few cases where the model is likely to refuse to respond:

  • Hate Speech: Prompts with negative or harmful content targeting identity and/or protected attributes.
  • Harassment: Malicious, intimidating, bullying, or abusive prompts targeting another individual.
  • Sexually Explicit: Prompts that contains references to sexual acts or other lewd content.
  • Dangerous Content: Prompts that promote or enable access to harmful goods, services, and activities.

docs.title: Overview of prompting strategies
docs.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast amounts of text data to learn the patterns and relationships between units of language. When given some text (the prompt), a language model can predict what is likely to come next, similar to a sophisticated autocompletion tool. When designing prompts, you should consider the different factors that can influence what a model predicts.

Prompt engineering is a test-driven and iterative process that can enhance model performance. When creating prompts, it's important to clearly define the objectives and expected outcomes for each prompt and systematically test them to identify areas for improvement.

Concepts
  • Large language models (LLM): AI models trained on vast amounts of text data to understand, generate, and predict language.
  • Prompt: The text input provided to an LLM to elicit a specific response.
  • Prompt engineering: The iterative process of designing, testing, and refining prompts to improve the quality and accuracy of model responses.
  • Few-shot examples: A set of example inputs and their desired outputs included in a prompt to guide the model's response format and style.
  • Persona: A defined role or character (e.g., "expert biologist," "helpful travel agent") that the model is instructed to adopt in its response.

docs.text:
The following diagram shows the general workflow for prompt engineering. It is an iterative process of designing, testing, and evaluating prompts until they achieve the desired performance.

Prompt engineering workflow.

docs.title: Key elements of an effective prompt
docs.text:
The effectiveness of a prompt is determined by two main aspects: its content and its structure.

  • Content: To complete a task, the model needs all relevant information. This includes clear instructions, illustrative examples, and any necessary context.
  • Structure: Even with all the required information, a well-organized prompt helps the model parse the details correctly. The ordering of components, use of labels, and clear delimiters can all affect the quality of the response.

docs.title: Prompt components
docs.text:
A prompt consists of essential components that define the task and optional components that can help refine the model's response. Depending on the task, you might choose to include or exclude some of the optional components.

Component Type Description Example Objective Essential What you want the model to achieve. Be specific and include any overarching objectives. Also called "mission" or "goal." Your objective is to help students with math problems without directly giving them the answer. Instructions Essential Step-by-step instructions on how to perform the task. Also called "task," "steps," or "directions." 1. Understand what the problem is asking.2. Understand where the student is stuck.3. Give a hint for the next step of the problem. System instructions Optional Technical or environmental directives that can control or alter the model's behavior across tasks. For many model APIs, system instructions are specified in a dedicated parameter. You are a coding expert that specializes in rendering code for front-end interfaces. When I describe a component of a website I want to build, return the HTML and CSS needed to do so. Do not give an explanation for this code. Persona Optional The role or character the model should adopt. Also called "role" or "vision." You are a math tutor here to help students with their math homework. Constraints Optional Restrictions on what the model must adhere to, including what it can and can't do. Also called "guardrails" or "boundaries." Don't give the answer to the student directly. Instead, give hints at the next step towards solving the problem. Tone Optional The desired tone of the response. This can also be influenced by specifying a persona. Also called "style" or "voice." Respond in a casual and technical manner. Context Optional Any background information the model needs to perform the task. Also called "background," "documents," or "input data." A copy of the student's lesson plans for math. Few-shot examples Optional Examples of the desired response format for a given prompt. Also called "exemplars" or "samples." input: I'm trying to calculate how many golf balls can fit into a box that has a one cubic meter volume. I've converted one cubic meter into cubic centimeters and divided it by the volume of a golf ball in cubic centimeters, but the system says my answer is wrong.output: Golf balls are spheres and cannot be packed into a space with perfect efficiency. Your calculations don't take into account the maximum packing efficiency of spheres. Reasoning steps Optional An instruction for the model to explain its reasoning, which can sometimes improve its reasoning capability. Also called "thinking steps." Explain your reasoning step-by-step. Response format Optional The specific format for the response, such as JSON, Markdown, a table, a bulleted list, or keywords. Also called "structure" or "layout." Format your response in Markdown. Recap Optional A concise summary of the prompt's key points, especially constraints and response format, placed at the end of the prompt. Remember: Don't give away the answer and provide hints instead. Always format your response in Markdown. Safeguards Optional Instructions that ground the model's responses to its core mission or safety rules. N/A

docs.title: Prompt structure
docs.text:
The following template provides an example of a well-structured prompt that incorporates several of the components listed above.

# OBJECTIVE AND PERSONA
# You are a [insert a persona, such as "math teacher" or "automotive expert"].
# Your task is to [describe the main goal].

# INSTRUCTIONS
# To complete the task, you need to follow these steps:
# 1. [First step]
# 2. [Second step]
# ...

# ------------ Optional Components ------------

# CONSTRAINTS
# Adhere to the following constraints:
# - Do: [Specify what the model should do]
# - Don't: [Specify what the model should not do]

# CONTEXT
# [Provide any relevant context or input data here]

# OUTPUT_FORMAT
# The output format must be:
# 1. [First formatting rule]
# 2. [Second formatting rule]
# ...

# FEW-SHOT EXAMPLES
# Here are some examples of desired inputs and outputs:
#
# Example 1:
# Input: [Example input]
# Thoughts: [Example thought process]
# Output: [Example output]
#
# Example 2:
# ...

# RECAP
# To recap, [re-emphasize the key aspects of the prompt, especially constraints and output format].

docs.title: Best practices for prompt design
docs.text:
While there's no single correct way to design a prompt, the following best practices can help you improve model performance through rigorous testing and evaluation.

  • Give clear and specific instructions: Provide detailed directions to guide the model toward the desired output and reduce the chances of generating incorrect or irrelevant responses.
  • Include few-shot examples: Show the model exactly what you want with examples of inputs and the corresponding desired outputs.
  • Add contextual information: Provide relevant background information or data to help the model generate a more accurate and relevant response.
  • Use system instructions: Set the model's context, persona, or other high-level instructions separately from the main prompt content for better control.
  • Structure prompts: Organize the different components of your prompt logically and use delimiters to help the model distinguish between different parts of the input.
  • Instruct the model to explain its reasoning: Ask the model to think step-by-step, which can help it reason more effectively and produce more accurate results.
  • Break down complex tasks: Decompose a complex prompt into smaller, more manageable sub-tasks to improve the reliability of the model's output.
  • Experiment with parameter values: Adjust model parameters like temperature and top-K to influence the creativity and diversity of the generated responses.
  • Prompt iteration strategies: Systematically test and refine your prompts based on model performance to continuously improve results.

docs.title: Prompt iteration strategies
docs.text:
Prompt design often requires several iterations to achieve the desired response consistently. A successful prompt design strategy applies the Prompt design best practices through incremental refinements. You can iteratively introduce these best practices while testing to ensure the model's performance meets your use case needs.

The order of content within a prompt can also affect the response. Experiment by changing the content order to see how the response changes. For example, when creating multimodal prompts, try adding files before the text instructions.

As you evaluate model responses, note what you like and dislike. Use these observations to modify your prompts, guiding the model toward responses that better align with your goals.

Concepts
  • Prompt Iteration: The process of incrementally refining a prompt through testing and analysis to consistently achieve desired model responses.
  • Prompt Design: The practice of structuring and writing effective prompts to guide a large language model's output.
  • Multimodal Prompt: A prompt that includes more than one type of input data, such as a combination of text and images.

docs.title: Example: Iterating on an ad copy prompt
docs.text:
The following workflow illustrates the general strategy for iterating on a prompt. The example below demonstrates this process in practice.

flowchart TD
    A[Define initial prompt] --> B{Test and analyze response}
    B -- Response unsatisfactory --> C[Refine prompt]
    C --> B
    B -- Response satisfactory --> D[Finalize prompt]

click A "#iteration-1-initial-broad-prompt"
click B "#iteration-1-initial-broad-prompt"
click C "#iteration-2-refining-the-prompt-structure"
click D "#iteration-4-finalizing-the-prompt"

In this example, the goal is to generate ad copy for a product. The initial prompt content is defined as follows:

  • Objective: Create ad copy.
  • Context:
    • Categories: scarcity, exclusivity
    • Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."
  • Constraints: Each response should be two sentences or less.

Experimenting with how you provide this content to the model helps ensure the response fits your needs.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Iteration 1: Initial broad prompt

First, you provide the model with the prompt content exactly as written.

Prompt:

Create ad copy.

Categories: scarcity, exclusivity

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Constraints: Each response should be two sentences or less.

Response:

Scarcity

*  Time is running out to experience the future of entertainment! Get your Chromecast before they're gone.
*  Limited quantities available! Don't miss your chance to own the streaming device everyone's talking about.

Exclusivity

*  Unlock a world of entertainment with Chromecast. Experience the freedom of streaming like never before.
*  Upgrade your home entertainment with the exclusive Chromecast device. Join the elite group of cord-cutters who stream smarter.
(gemini-pro)

Iteration 2: Refining the prompt structure

Next, you can try reformatting the prompt to see how the response changes when the objective, constraints, and some context are combined into a single sentence.

Prompt:

Create scarcity and exclusivity-focused ad copy that is less than two sentences.

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Response:

Options for Scarcity & Exclusivity-Driven Chromecast Ads:

Option 1 (Scarcity): "Limited quantities available! Get your Chromecast today before they're gone and unlock a world of on-demand entertainment."

Option 2 (Exclusivity): "Experience entertainment like never before. Chromecast: the ultimate upgrade for your TV, available for a limited time."
(gemini-pro)

Iteration 3: Adjusting constraints

The model's response in the second iteration contained only one copy option for each category. If you need at least two options per category and no longer want to limit the response length, you can modify the constraints and try again.

Prompt:

Create two ad-copies about scarcity and two ad-copies about exclusivity.

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Response:

Scarcity Ad Copies:
Ad 1:

Headline: Don't miss out! Chromecast is flying off the shelves!

Body: Experience the magic of Chromecast before it's too late! Limited quantities are available, so grab yours now and start enjoying your favorite entertainment on the big screen. 

Ad 2:

Headline: Last chance! Chromecast is almost sold out.

Body: Time is running out to get your hands on Chromecast. Upgrade your TV experience today and enjoy seamless streaming from all your devices. Don't wait, supplies are limited!


Exclusivity Ad Copies:

Ad 1:

Headline: Unlock a world of entertainment with the exclusive Chromecast.

Body: Join the elite group of Chromecast users and experience the future of television. Enjoy effortless streaming, endless entertainment options, and unparalleled convenience. Chromecast: It's not just TV, it's an experience.

Ad 2:

Headline: Elevate your home entertainment with the Chromecast advantage.

Body: Go beyond ordinary TV with Chromecast. Seamlessly stream content from all your devices and enjoy a personalized entertainment experience like no other. Discover the exclusivity of Chromecast today.
(gemini-pro)

Iteration 4: Finalizing the prompt

In the third iteration, the model's response included both a headline and a body for the ad copy. Assume this format aligns with your requirements. To ensure the model produces similarly formatted responses in the future, you can explicitly add this constraint to the prompt.

Prompt:

Create two ad-copies about scarcity and two ad-copies about exclusivity.

Include a headline and body for each ad copy.

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Response:

Scarcity Ads:

Ad 1:

Headline: Last Chance! Chromecast is Selling Out Fast
Body: Get the Chromecast experience before it's gone! Limited quantities remain. Upgrade your TV time today!

Ad 2:

Headline: Don't Miss Out! Chromecast Stock is Running Low
Body: Time is running out to grab your Chromecast. Enjoy seamless streaming on the big screen. Order now while supplies last!

Exclusivity Ads:

Ad 1:

Headline: Unlock the Ultimate Viewing Experience with Chromecast
Body: Join the elite group of Chromecast users and enjoy unparalleled streaming convenience. Elevate your entertainment today!

Ad 2:

Headline: Experience the Future of Entertainment: Get Your Chromecast
Body: Be among the first to enjoy the cutting-edge technology of Chromecast. Stream anything, anytime, effortlessly.  Upgrade your home entertainment now!
(gemini-pro)

The final response is very similar to the previous one, even with the added constraint, which means you have successfully iterated upon your prompt. As demonstrated, prompt iteration is an integral part of the design process that helps you guide the model to produce the best results for your use case.

This document describes how to use the Vertex AI prompt optimizer to automatically improve prompt performance by refining the system instructions for a set of prompts.

The Vertex AI prompt optimizer can help you improve your prompts quickly and at scale, without manually rewriting system instructions or individual prompts. This is especially useful when you want to adapt system instructions and prompts written for one model to a different model.

To see an example of optimizing prompts, you can run one of the following Jupyter notebooks:

The Vertex AI prompt optimizer improves prompts by evaluating a model's response to sample prompts against specified evaluation metrics. To use the optimizer, you need the following:

docs.title: Prompt optimization example
docs.text:
To optimize system instructions for a set of prompts that answer questions about cooking, you can use the Vertex AI prompt optimizer. You would prepare inputs similar to the following:

System instructions

You are a professional chef. Your goal is teaching how to cook healthy cooking recipes to your apprentice.

Given a question from your apprentice and some context, provide the correct answer to the question.
Use the context to return a single and correct answer with some explanation.

Prompt template

Question: {input_question}
Facts: {input_context}

Sample prompts

input_question input_context What are some techniques for cooking red meat and pork that maximize flavor and tenderness while minimizing the formation of unhealthy compounds? Red meat and pork should be cooked to an internal temperature of 145 degrees fahrenheit (63 degrees celsius) to ensure safety. Marinating meat in acidic ingredients like lemon juice or vinegar can help tenderize it by breaking down tough muscle fibers. High-heat cooking methods like grilling and pan-searing can create delicious browning and caramelization, but it's important to avoid charring, which can produce harmful compounds. What are some creative ways to add flavor and nutrition to protein shakes without using added sugars or artificial ingredients? Adding leafy greens like spinach or kale is a great way to boost the nutritional value of your shake without drastically altering the flavor. Using unsweetened almond milk or coconut water instead of regular milk can add a subtle sweetness and a boost of healthy fats or electrolytes, respectively. Did you know that over-blending your shake can actually heat it up? To keep things cool and refreshing, blend for shorter bursts and give your blender a break if needed.

Optimized system instructions

As a highly skilled chef with a passion for healthy cooking, you love sharing your knowledge with
aspiring chefs. Today, a culinary intern approaches you with a question about healthy cooking. Given
the intern's question and some facts, provide a clear, concise, and informative answer that will help
the intern excel in their culinary journey.

docs.title: How optimization works
docs.text:
The Vertex AI prompt optimizer takes the following parameters:

  • Optimization mode: Specifies whether the optimizer refines the system instructions, selects sample prompts to use as few-shot examples, or both.
  • Evaluation metrics: The criteria used to score the system instructions and/or selected sample prompts.
  • Target model: The Google model for which the system instructions and sample prompts are being optimized.

When you run the prompt optimizer, it initiates a custom training job. During this job, it iteratively evaluates your sample prompts and rewrites your system instructions to find the version that achieves the best evaluation score for the target model. At the end of the job, the optimizer outputs the refined system instructions along with their final evaluation score.

docs.title: Evaluation metrics
docs.text: The Vertex AI prompt optimizer uses evaluation metrics to refine system instructions and select sample prompts. You can use standard evaluation metrics or define your own custom metrics. You can use multiple metrics at once, but only one custom metric can be used at a time in combination with standard metrics.

docs.title: Custom evaluation metrics
docs.text: Custom metrics are useful when standard metrics don't fit your application. The Vertex AI prompt optimizer supports one custom metric at a time. To learn how to create custom metrics, see Create custom metrics.

docs.title: Standard evaluation metrics
docs.text:
The Vertex AI prompt optimizer supports the following standard evaluation metrics:

Metric type Use case Metric Description Model-based Summarization summarization_quality Describes the model's ability to answer questions given a body of text to reference. Question answering question_answering_correctness* Describes the model's ability to correctly answer a question. question_answering_quality Describes the model's ability to answer questions given a body of text to reference. Coherence coherence Describes the model's ability to provide a coherent response and measures how well the generated text flows logically and makes sense. Safety safety Describes the model's level of safety, that is, whether the response contains any unsafe text. Fluency fluency Describes the model's language mastery. Groundedness groundedness Describes the model's ability to provide or reference information included only in the input text. Computation-based Tool use and function calling tool_call_valid* Describes the model's ability to predict a valid tool call. tool_name_match* Describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct tool name. Only the first tool call is inspected. tool_parameter_key_match* Describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct parameter names. tool_parameter_kv_match* Describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct parameter names and key values. General text generation bleu* Holds the result of an algorithm for evaluating the quality of the prediction, which has been translated from one natural language to another. exact_match* Computes whether a prediction parameter matches a reference parameter exactly. rouge_1* Used to compare the provided prediction parameter against a reference parameter. rouge_2* rouge_l* rouge_l_sum*

*If you want to optimize your prompts using question_answering_correctness or computation-based evaluations, you must do one of the following:

  • Add a variable representing the ground truth response (e.g., {target}) to your prompt template.
  • If you don't have ground truth responses but have previously achieved targeted results with a Google model, you can add the source_model parameter to your configuration. The optimizer will then use the source model to generate ground truth responses from your sample prompts.
Concepts

System instructions: Directives that guide the model's behavior and response style across all prompts. Prompt template: A reusable text structure with placeholders (variables) that are filled with data to create specific prompts. Few-shot examples: Examples included in the prompt to show the model the desired output format or behavior. Evaluation metrics: Criteria used to score the quality of a model's responses, such as accuracy, fluency, or safety. Ground truth: The ideal or correct response for a given prompt, used as a benchmark for evaluation.
