    print(chunk)
Use advanced features

Use extra_body

The extra_body parameter allows you to pass Google-specific parameters, such as thinking_config, that are not part of the standard OpenAI specification.

Python SDKREST API (thinking_config) 
client.chat.completions.create(
  ...,
  extra_body = {
    'google': { ... }
  },
)

This example uses extra_body to enable thinking, which provides insight into the model's preliminary thoughts before generating a final response.

curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/locations/us-central1/endpoints/openapi/chat/completions \
  -d '{ \
    "model": "google/gemini-1.5-pro-preview-0409", \
    "messages": [ \
      { "role": "user", \
      "content": [ \
        { "type": "text", \
          "text": "Are there any primes number of the form n*ceil(log(n))" \
        }] }], \
    "extra_body": { \
      "google": { \
          "thinking_config": { \
          "include_thoughts": true, "thinking_budget": 10000 \
        }, \
        "thought_tag_marker": "think" } }, \
    "stream": true }'

Use extra_content

The extra_content parameter allows you to pass Google-specific data at the message, content, or tool call level. You can populate this field by using the REST API directly.

  • extra_content with string content: 

    {
  "messages": [
    { "role": "...", "content": "...", "extra_content": { "google": { ... } } }
  ]
}

  • Per-message extra_content: 

    {
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "...",
      "content": [
        { "type": "...", ..., "extra_content": { "google": { ... } } }
      ]
    }
}

  • Per-tool call extra_content: 

    {
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "...",
      "tool_calls": [
        {
          ...,
          "extra_content": { "google": { ... } }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Get structured output

You can use the response_format parameter with type="json_object" to instruct the model to return a JSON object. When using the Python SDK, you can also pass a Pydantic model to parse the output into a structured object automatically.

Python SDK (Pydantic) 
from pydantic import BaseModel
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

class CalendarEvent(BaseModel):
    name: str
    date: str
    participants: list[str]

completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
    model="google/gemini-1.5-flash-001",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Extract the event information."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Alice and Bob are going to a science fair on Friday."},
    ],
    response_format=CalendarEvent,
)

print(completion.choices[0].message.parsed)

docs.title: Using OpenAI libraries with Vertex AI
docs.text:
To see an example of using the Chat Completions API, run the "Call Gemini with the OpenAI Library" Jupyter notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab Open in Colab Enterprise Open in Vertex AI Workbench View on GitHub

The Chat Completions API is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint designed to simplify interfacing with Gemini on Vertex AI using the OpenAI libraries for Python and REST. If you already use the OpenAI libraries, you can use this API to switch between calling OpenAI models and Vertex AI-hosted models to compare output, cost, and scalability without changing your existing code. If you are not already using the OpenAI libraries, we recommend that you use the Vertex AI SDK for Python.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Chat Completions API: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Vertex AI for interacting with models using OpenAI's library structure.
  • Model Garden: A platform on Vertex AI for discovering, deploying, and managing foundation models and custom models.
  • Hugging Face Text Generation Inference (HF TGI): An open-source toolkit for deploying and serving large language models.
  • vLLM: An open-source library for fast LLM inference and serving.
  • Gemini: A family of multimodal models developed by Google.

docs.title: Supported parameters
docs.text:
The Chat Completions API supports the following OpenAI parameters for Google models. Any unsupported parameter you pass is ignored. For a description of each parameter, see OpenAI's documentation on Creating chat completions. Parameter support for third-party models varies by model. To see which parameters are supported, consult the model's documentation.

Standard parameters Parameter Description messages Supports the following message types:
  • System message
  • User message: The text and image_url types are supported. The image_url type supports images stored as a Cloud Storage URI or a base64 encoding in the form "data:<MIME-TYPE>;base64,<BASE64-ENCODED-BYTES>". To learn how to create a Cloud Storage bucket and upload a file to it, see Discover object storage. The detail option is not supported.
  • Assistant message
  • Tool message
  • Function message: This field is deprecated, but supported for backward compatibility.
model The model ID to use for the request. max_completion_tokens Alias for max_tokens. max_tokens The maximum number of tokens to generate in the chat completion. n The number of chat completion choices to generate for each input message. frequency_penalty A number between -2.0 and 2.0. Positive values penalize new tokens based on their existing frequency in the text so far, decreasing the model's likelihood to repeat the same line verbatim. presence_penalty A number between -2.0 and 2.0. Positive values penalize new tokens based on whether they appear in the text so far, increasing the model's likelihood to talk about new topics. reasoning_effort Configures how much time and how many tokens are used on a response.
  • low: 1024
  • medium: 8192
  • high: 24576
As no thoughts are included in the response, only one of reasoning_effort or extra_body.google.thinking_config may be specified. response_format An object specifying the format that the model must output.
  • json_object: Interpreted as passing "application/json" to the Gemini API.
  • json_schema: Fully recursive schemas are not supported. additional_properties is supported.
  • text: Interpreted as passing "text/plain" to the Gemini API.
  • Any other MIME type is passed as is to the model, such as passing "application/json" directly.
seed Corresponds to GenerationConfig.seed. stop Up to 4 sequences where the API will stop generating further tokens. stream If set, partial message deltas will be sent, like in ChatGPT. temperature Controls the randomness of the output. top_p The cumulative probability of tokens to consider when sampling. tools A list of tools the model may call. Currently, only functions are supported as a tool.
  • type
  • function
    • name
    • description
    • parameters: Specify parameters by using the OpenAPI specification. This differs from the OpenAI parameters field, which is described as a JSON Schema object. To learn about keyword differences between OpenAPI and JSON Schema, see the OpenAPI guide.
tool_choice Controls which (if any) function is called by the model.
  • none
  • auto
  • required: Corresponds to the mode ANY in the FunctionCallingConfig.
  • validated: Corresponds to the mode VALIDATED in the FunctionCallingConfig. This is Google-specific.
web_search_options Corresponds to the GoogleSearch tool. No sub-options are supported. function_call This field is deprecated, but supported for backward compatibility. functions This field is deprecated, but supported for backward compatibility. Multimodal input parameters

The Chat Completions API supports select multimodal inputs. In general, the data parameter can be a URI or a combination of MIME type and base64 encoded bytes in the form "data:<MIME-TYPE>;base64,<BASE64-ENCODED-BYTES>". For a full list of MIME types, see GenerateContent. For more information on OpenAI's base64 encoding, see their documentation. For usage, see our multimodal input examples.

Parameter Description input_audio
  • data: Any URI or valid blob format. We support all blob types, including image, audio, and video. Anything supported by GenerateContent is supported (HTTP, Cloud Storage, etc.).
  • format: OpenAI supports both wav (audio/wav) and mp3 (audio/mp3). Using Gemini, all valid MIME types are supported.
image_url
  • data: Like input_audio, any URI or valid blob format is supported. Note that image_url as a URL will default to the image/* MIME-type and image_url as blob data can be used as any multimodal input.
  • detail: Similar to media resolution, this determines the maximum tokens per image for the request. Note that while OpenAI's field is per-image, Gemini enforces the same detail across the request, and passing multiple detail types in one request will throw an error.
Gemini-specific parameters

Several features supported by Gemini are not available in OpenAI models. These features can still be passed in as parameters, but must be contained within an extra_content or extra_body block, or they will be ignored.

extra_body features

Feature Description safety_settings This corresponds to Gemini's SafetySetting. cached_content This corresponds to Gemini's GenerateContentRequest.cached_content. thinking_config This corresponds to Gemini's GenerationConfig.ThinkingConfig. thought_tag_marker Used to separate a model's thoughts from its responses for models with Thinking available. If not specified, no tags will be returned around the model's thoughts. If present, subsequent queries will strip the thought tags and mark the thoughts appropriately for context. This helps preserve the appropriate context for subsequent queries.

extra_part features

extra_part lets you specify additional settings at a per-Part level.

Feature Description extra_content A field for adding Gemini-specific content that shouldn't be ignored. thought This will explicitly mark if a field is a thought (and take precedence over thought_tag_marker). This should be used to specify whether a tool call is part of a thought or not.

docs.title: Models supported by Model Garden
docs.text:
Model Garden provides access to a wide variety of foundation models from Google, open-source providers, and third-party partners. These models are discoverable in the Vertex AI Model Garden and can be used for various generative AI tasks.

To help you choose the right model, the following table summarizes the different types of models available.

Model Category Description Key Characteristics Google's first-party models State-of-the-art, proprietary models developed by Google. - Fully managed and optimized for Google Cloud.- Enterprise-grade support and reliability.- Includes flagship models like Gemini and Imagen. Open-source models Popular open-source models with provided notebooks for deployment, tuning, and serving on Vertex AI. - Offers flexibility and control over the model and infrastructure.- Requires you to manage deployment and serving.- Includes models like Llama, Gemma, and Stable Diffusion. Partner models Models from leading AI companies, available as managed APIs on Vertex AI. - Billed through your Google Cloud account.- No need to manage the underlying infrastructure.- Provides access to specialized models from partners like Anthropic and Mistral AI.

docs.title: Deploy and inference Gemma using Model Garden and Vertex AI TPU-backed endpoints
docs.text:
In this tutorial, you use Model Garden to deploy the Gemma 2B open model to a TPU-backed Vertex AI endpoint. You must deploy a model to an endpoint before that model can be used to serve online predictions. Deploying a model associates physical resources with the model so it can serve online predictions with low latency.

After you deploy the Gemma 2B model, you get online predictions from the model by using the PredictionServiceClient. Online predictions are synchronous requests made to a model that is deployed to an endpoint.

Step 1: Deploy the Gemma model
docs.text:
You deploy the Gemma 2B model to a ct5lp-hightpu-1t Compute Engine machine type that is optimized for small to medium scale training. This machine has one TPU v5e accelerator. For more information on training models using TPUs, see Cloud TPU v5e training.

In this tutorial, you deploy the instruction-tuned Gemma 2B open model by using the model card in Model Garden. The specific model version is gemma2-2b-it -- -it stands for instruction-tuned.

The Gemma 2B model has a lower parameter size which means lower resource requirements and more deployment flexibility.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Model Garden page.

    Go to Model Garden

  2. Click the Gemma 2 model card.

    Go to Gemma 2

import (

    "fmt"
    "io"

    "cloud.google.com/go/aiplatform/apiv1/aiplatformpb"

    "google.golang.org/protobuf/types/known/structpb"
)

// predictTPU demonstrates how to run interference on a Gemma2 model deployed to a Vertex AI endpoint with TPU accelerators.
func predictTPU(w io.Writer, client PredictionsClient, projectID, location, endpointID string) error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    // Note: client can be initialized in the following way:
    // apiEndpoint := fmt.Sprintf("%s-aiplatform.googleapis.com:443", location)
    // client, err := aiplatform.NewPredictionClient(ctx, option.WithEndpoint(apiEndpoint))
    // if err != nil {
    //  return fmt.Errorf("unable to create prediction client: %v", err)
    // }
    // defer client.Close()

    gemma2Endpoint := fmt.Sprintf("projects/%s/locations/%s/endpoints/%s", projectID, location, endpointID)
    prompt := "Why is the sky blue?"
    parameters := map[string]interface{}{
        "temperature":     0.9,
        "maxOutputTokens": 1024,
        "topP":            1.0,
        "topK":            1,
    }

    // Encapsulate the prompt in a correct format for TPUs.
    // Example format: [{'prompt': 'Why is the sky blue?', 'temperature': 0.9}]
    promptValue, err := structpb.NewValue(map[string]interface{}{
        "prompt":     prompt,
        "parameters": parameters,
    })
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "unable to convert prompt to Value: %v", err)
        return err
    }

    req := &aiplatformpb.PredictRequest{
        Endpoint:  gemma2Endpoint,
        Instances: []*structpb.Value{promptValue},
    }

    resp, err := client.Predict(ctx, req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    prediction := resp.GetPredictions()
    value := prediction[0].GetStringValue()
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "%v", value)

    return nil
}

// predictGPU demonstrates how to run interference on a Gemma2 model deployed to a Vertex AI endpoint with GPU accelerators.
func predictGPU(w io.Writer, client PredictionsClient, projectID, location, endpointID string) error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    // Note: client can be initialized in the following way:
    // apiEndpoint := fmt.Sprintf("%s-aiplatform.googleapis.com:443", location)
    // client, err := aiplatform.NewPredictionClient(ctx, option.WithEndpoint(apiEndpoint))
    // if err != nil {
    //  return fmt.Errorf("unable to create prediction client: %v", err)
    // }
    // defer client.Close()

    gemma2Endpoint := fmt.Sprintf("projects/%s/locations/%s/endpoints/%s", projectID, location, endpointID)
    prompt := "Why is the sky blue?"
    parameters := map[string]interface{}{
        "temperature":     0.9,
        "maxOutputTokens": 1024,
        "topP":            1.0,
        "topK":            1,
    }

    // Encapsulate the prompt in a correct format for TPUs.
    // Pay attention that prompt should be set in "inputs" field.
    // Example format: [{'inputs': 'Why is the sky blue?', 'parameters': {'temperature': 0.9}}]
    promptValue, err := structpb.NewValue(map[string]interface{}{
        "inputs":     prompt,
        "parameters": parameters,
    })
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "unable to convert prompt to Value: %v", err)
        return err
    }

    req := &aiplatformpb.PredictRequest{
        Endpoint:  gemma2Endpoint,
        Instances: []*structpb.Value{promptValue},
    }

    resp, err := client.Predict(ctx, req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    prediction := resp.GetPredictions()
    value := prediction[0].GetStringValue()
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "%v", value)

    return nil
}

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
To avoid incurring charges to your Google Cloud account for the resources used in this tutorial, either delete the project that contains the resources, or keep the project and delete the individual resources.

Cleanup steps Delete the projectDelete individual resources

Deleting a project has the following effects:

  • Everything in the project is deleted. If you used an existing project for the tasks in this document, when you delete it, you also delete any other work you've done in the project.
  • Custom project IDs are lost. When you created this project, you might have created a custom project ID that you want to use in the future. To preserve the URLs that use the project ID, such as an appspot.com URL, delete selected resources inside the project instead of deleting the whole project.

If you plan to explore multiple architectures, tutorials, or quickstarts, reusing projects can help you avoid exceeding project quota limits.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Manage resources page.

    Go to Manage resources

  2. In the project list, select the project that you want to delete, and then click Delete.

  3. In the dialog, type the project ID, and then click Shut down to delete the project.

If you're keeping your project, delete the resources used in this tutorial:

  • Undeploy the model and delete the endpoint
  • Delete the model from Model Registry

Undeploy the model and delete the endpoint

Use one of the following methods to undeploy a model and delete the endpoint.

Note

You can only delete the endpoint after all models have been undeployed from it.

==== "Console"

1.  In the Google Cloud console, click **Online prediction** and then click **Endpoints**.

    [Go to the Endpoints page](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/endpoints){: .md-button}

2.  In the **Region** drop-down list, choose the region where you deployed your endpoint.

3.  Click the endpoint name to open the details page. For example: `gemma2-2b-it-mg-one-click-deploy`.

4.  On the row for the `Gemma 2 (Version 1)` model, click more_vert **Actions**, and then click **Undeploy model from endpoint**.

5.  In the **Undeploy model from endpoint** dialog, click **Undeploy**.

6.  Click the **Back** button to return to the **Endpoints** page.

    [Go to the Endpoints page](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/online-prediction/endpoints){: .md-button}

7.  At the end of the `gemma2-2b-it-mg-one-click-deploy` row, click more_vert **Actions**, and then select **Delete endpoint**.

8.  In the confirmation prompt, click **Confirm**.

==== "gcloud"

To undeploy the model and delete the endpoint using the Google Cloud CLI, follow these steps.

In these commands, replace:

*   `PROJECT_ID` with your project name
*   `LOCATION_ID` with the region where you deployed the model and endpoint
*   `ENDPOINT_ID` with the endpoint ID
*   `DEPLOYED_MODEL_NAME` with the model's display name
*   `DEPLOYED_MODEL_ID` with the model ID

1.  Get the endpoint ID by running the [`gcloud ai endpoints list`](/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/endpoints/list) command. This command lists the endpoint IDs for all endpoints in your project. Make a note of the ID of the endpoint used in this tutorial.

    ```
    gcloud ai endpoints list \
        --project=PROJECT_ID \
        --region=LOCATION_ID
    ```

    The output looks like this. In the output, the ID is called `ENDPOINT_ID`.

    ```
    Using endpoint [https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/]
    ENDPOINT_ID: 1234567891234567891
    DISPLAY_NAME: gemma2-2b-it-mg-one-click-deploy
    ```

2.  Get the model ID by running the [`gcloud ai models describe`](/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/models/describe) command. Make a note of the ID of the model you deployed in this tutorial.

    ```
    gcloud ai models describe DEPLOYED_MODEL_NAME \
        --project=PROJECT_ID \
        --region=LOCATION_ID
    ```

    The abbreviated output looks like this. In the output, the ID is called `deployedModelId`.

    ```
    Using endpoint [https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/]
    artifactUri: [URI removed]
    baseModelSource:
      modelGardenSource:
        publicModelName: publishers/google/models/gemma2
    ...
    deployedModels:
    - deployedModelId: '1234567891234567891'
      endpoint: projects/12345678912/locations/us-central1/endpoints/12345678912345
    displayName: gemma2-2b-it-12345678912345
    etag: [ETag removed]
    modelSourceInfo:
      sourceType: MODEL_GARDEN
    name: projects/123456789123/locations/us-central1/models/gemma2-2b-it-12345678912345
    ...
    ```

3.  Undeploy the model from the endpoint. You'll need the endpoint ID and model ID from the previous commands.

    ```
    gcloud ai endpoints undeploy-model ENDPOINT_ID \
        --project=PROJECT_ID \
        --region=LOCATION_ID \
        --deployed-model-id=DEPLOYED_MODEL_ID
    ```

    This command produces no output.

4.  Run the [`gcloud ai endpoints delete`](/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/endpoints/delete) command to delete the endpoint.

    ```
    gcloud ai endpoints delete ENDPOINT_ID \
        --project=PROJECT_ID \
        --region=LOCATION_ID
    ```

    When prompted, type `y` to confirm. This command produces no output.

Delete the model

==== "Console"

1.  Go to the **Model Registry** page from the Vertex AI section in the Google Cloud console.

    [Go to the Model Registry page](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/models){: .md-button}

2.  In the **Region** drop-down list, choose the region where you deployed your model.

3.  At the end of the `gemma2-2b-it-1234567891234` row, click more_vert **Actions**.

4.  Select **Delete model**.

When you delete the model, all associated model versions and evaluations are deleted from your Google Cloud project.

5.  In the confirmation prompt, click **Delete**.

==== "gcloud"

To delete the model using the Google Cloud CLI, provide the model's display name and region to the [`gcloud ai models delete`](/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/models/delete) command.

```
gcloud ai models delete DEPLOYED_MODEL_NAME \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID
```

Replace `DEPLOYED_MODEL_NAME` with the model's display name. Replace `PROJECT_ID` with your project name. Replace `LOCATION_ID` with the region where you deployed the model.

docs.title: Overview of Model Garden
docs.text:
Model Garden is an AI/ML model library that helps you discover, test, customize, and deploy models and assets from Google and Google partners.

Concepts
  • Foundation Model: A large, pre-trained model that can be adapted for various tasks.
  • Fine-tuning: The process of adapting a pre-trained model to a specific task by training it on a smaller, task-specific dataset.
  • vLLM: An open-source library for fast Large Language Model (LLM) inference and serving, optimized for high throughput on GPUs.
  • LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): A parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique that significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks.
  • TPU (Tensor Processing Unit): Google's custom-developed application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) used to accelerate machine learning workloads.

docs.title: Advantages of Model Garden
docs.text:
When you're working with AI models, Model Garden provides the following advantages:

  • Available models are all grouped in a single location.
  • Model Garden provides a consistent deployment pattern for different types of models.
  • Model Garden provides built-in integration with other parts of Vertex AI such as model tuning, evaluation, and serving.
  • Serving generative AI models can be difficult—Vertex AI handles model deployment and serving for you.

docs.title: Explore models in Model Garden
docs.text:
To view the list of available Vertex AI and open source foundation, tunable, and task-specific models, go to the Model Garden page in the Google Cloud console.

Go to Model Garden

The model categories available in Model Garden are:

  • Foundation models: Pretrained multitask large models that can be tuned or customized for specific tasks using Vertex AI Studio, Vertex AI API, and the Vertex AI SDK for Python.
  • Fine-tunable models: Models that you can fine-tune using a custom notebook or pipeline.
  • Task-specific solutions: Most of these prebuilt models are ready to use. Many can be customized using your own data.

To filter models in the filter pane, you can specify the following:

  • Tasks: The task that you want the model to perform.
  • Model collections: Models that are managed by Google, partners, or you.
  • Providers: The provider of the model.
  • Features: The features that you want in the model.

To learn more about each model, click its model card. For a list of models available in Model Garden, see Models available in Model Garden.

docs.title: Model security scanning
docs.text:
Google does thorough testing and benchmarking on the serving and tuning containers that we provide. Active vulnerability scanning is also applied to container artifacts.

Third-party models from featured partners undergo model checkpoint scans to check authenticity. Third-party models from HuggingFace Hub are scanned directly by HuggingFace and their third-party scanner for malware, pickle files, Keras Lambda layers, and secrets. Models deemed unsafe from these scans are flagged by HuggingFace and blocked from deployment in Model Garden. Models deemed suspicious or those that have the ability to potentially execute remote code are indicated in Model Garden but can still be deployed. We recommend you perform a thorough review of any suspicious model before deploying it.

  • Model deployment: You are charged for the compute resources used to deploy the model to an endpoint. See predictions pricing.
  • Colab Enterprise: See Colab Enterprise pricing.

docs.title: LoRA and QLoRA recommendations for LLMs
docs.text:
This page provides configuration recommendations for tuning large language models (LLMs) on Vertex AI using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods. Specifically, it compares Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (LoRA) and its more memory-efficient version, Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA).

Concepts
  • Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA): A parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that reduces the number of trainable parameters by freezing the original model weights and injecting smaller, trainable rank-decomposition matrices.
  • Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA): An even more memory-efficient version of LoRA that uses 4-bit quantization to compress a pretrained language model, further reducing memory usage during tuning.
  • Batch Size: The number of training examples utilized in one iteration.
  • Max Sequence Length: The maximum number of tokens in an input sequence that the model can process.

docs.title: Compare LoRA and QLoRA
docs.text:
The following table provides a high-level comparison of LoRA and QLoRA to help you decide which method best suits your needs.

Specification LoRA QLoRA GPU memory efficiency Standard High. QLoRA has about 75% smaller peak GPU memory usage. Tuning speed Fast. LoRA is about 66% faster than QLoRA. Standard Cost efficiency High. LoRA is up to 40% less expensive than QLoRA. Standard Max sequence length Standard Higher. Supports longer sequences due to lower memory usage. Accuracy improvement Similar to QLoRA Similar to LoRA Batch size support Standard Higher. Supports significantly larger batch sizes.

docs.title: When to use LoRA vs. QLoRA
docs.text:
Use the following tabs to explore the use cases and benefits of each method in more detail.

LoRAQLoRA

Choose LoRA when your primary considerations are tuning speed and cost.

  • Speed: LoRA is significantly faster for tuning, making it ideal for rapid experimentation and iteration.
  • Cost: The faster training times and efficient architecture can result in lower overall tuning costs compared to QLoRA.
  • Hardware: LoRA is well-suited for scenarios where you have access to enterprise-grade GPUs (like A100 or H100) that can accommodate its memory requirements.

Choose QLoRA when you need to maximize memory efficiency, especially when working with limited hardware resources or large models.

  • Memory Efficiency: QLoRA's main advantage is its drastically lower GPU memory footprint, which allows you to tune larger models on smaller, more accessible GPUs (e.g., L4, V100).
  • Larger Batch Sizes: Reduced memory consumption allows for much larger batch sizes, which can improve model stability and performance. For example, when tuning openLLaMA-7B, recommended batch sizes vary significantly:
    • 1 x A100 40G GPU:
      • LoRA: Batch size of 2 is recommended.
      • QLoRA: Batch size of 24 is recommended.
    • 1 x L4 GPU:
      • LoRA: Fails with an out-of-memory (OOM) error.
      • QLoRA: Batch size of 12 is recommended.
    • 1 x V100 GPU:
      • LoRA: Fails with an out-of-memory (OOM) error.
      • QLoRA: Batch size of 8 is recommended.
  • Longer Sequence Lengths: By saving memory, QLoRA enables the use of longer maximum sequence lengths, which is critical for tasks requiring more context, such as document summarization or advanced question-answering.

docs.title: Overview of self-deployed models
docs.text:
Model Garden offers both open and partner models that you can deploy and serve on your own infrastructure within Vertex AI. These are known as self-deployed models. When you self-deploy a model, it runs securely within your Google Cloud project and VPC network, giving you direct control over the hardware and configuration.

This approach differs from model-as-a-service (MaaS) offerings, which are fully managed by Google or its partners and do not require you to manage the underlying infrastructure.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Model Garden: A curated platform in Vertex AI for discovering, testing, and deploying foundation models from Google and its partners.
  • Self-deploy open models: Freely available models that you deploy and manage on your own Vertex AI infrastructure.
  • Open weight models: A type of open model where the model's trained parameters (weights) are publicly released, but the training data or code might not be.
  • Open source models: Models where not only the weights but also the source code, architecture, and often the training data are publicly available.
  • Self-deploy partner models: Proprietary models from third-party partners that you license and deploy on your own Vertex AI infrastructure.

docs.title: Compare self-deploy models
docs.text:
The following table provides a high-level comparison between self-deploying open models and partner models to help you choose the best option for your use case.

Feature Self-deploy open models Self-deploy partner models Access & Licensing Freely available under specific open licenses (e.g., Apache 2.0, Gemma). Requires purchasing a license from the partner via Google Cloud Marketplace. Cost You pay only for the Vertex AI infrastructure you use for deployment and serving. You pay for the model license (usage-based) and the Vertex AI infrastructure. Flexibility & Customization High. You can access and export model weights for fine-tuning and modification. Limited. You cannot export model weights. Customization is restricted to what the partner allows. Support Community support and standard Google Cloud support for infrastructure issues. Model-specific support is provided directly by the partner. Google Cloud supports infrastructure issues. VPC Service Controls Fully compatible. Not compatible, as model uploads are blocked by VPC Service Controls.

docs.title: Self-deploy open models
docs.text: Open models provide pretrained capabilities for various AI tasks. When you use an open model with Vertex AI, you have full control over the infrastructure. You are free to use, modify, and publish outputs from these models as long as you adhere to their licensing terms.

docs.title: Open weight vs. open source models
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers access to both open weight and open source models, and it's important to understand the distinction:

  • Open weight models provide transparency by releasing the model's weights, which are the numerical parameters learned during training. This allows you to use the model for inference and tuning without needing to know the specifics of the original dataset or training code. Many large language models (LLMs) fall into this category.

  • Open source models go a step further by providing the full source code, model architecture, and often the training data, in addition to the weights. This offers the highest level of transparency and allows for deeper customization and research.

docs.title: Self-deploy partner models
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Model Garden allows you to purchase and manage licenses for proprietary models from partners. After purchasing a model license from Cloud Marketplace, you can deploy it on on-demand hardware or use your existing Compute Engine reservations and committed use discounts. You are charged for both the model license and the Vertex AI infrastructure you use.

To request access to a self-deploy partner model, find the model in the Model Garden console, click Contact sales, and complete the form to connect with a Google Cloud sales representative.

For more information, see Deploy a partner model and make prediction requests.

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Consider the following limitations when using self-deploy partner models:

  • Unlike with open models, you cannot export model weights.
  • If you have VPC Service Controls set up for your project, you can't upload models, which prevents you from deploying partner models.
  • For endpoints, only the shared public endpoint type is supported.

Note

Support for model-specific issues is provided by the partner. To contact a partner for model performance-related issues, use the contact details in the "Support" section of their Model Garden model card.

docs.text:
Discover, test, tune, and deploy generative AI models by using Model Garden in the Google Cloud console. You can also interact with Model Garden models programmatically by using the Vertex AI SDK for Python, the Google Cloud CLI, or the REST API.

This document guides you through the common lifecycle of using a model from Model Garden, from initial discovery to final cleanup.

The following workflow shows the general steps for using a model from Model Garden.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Model Garden: A central place in Vertex AI to discover, test, tune, and deploy Google-proprietary and select open source models.
  • Model Registry: A central repository for managing the lifecycle of your ML models after they are trained or imported.
  • Endpoint: A service you deploy your model to, which serves online predictions. An endpoint has a unique URI that you send prediction requests to.
  • Tuning: The process of adjusting a pre-trained model's parameters on a specific dataset to improve its performance on a particular task.
Set up your project and environment
  1. In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.
  2. Make sure that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.
  3. Enable the Vertex AI API.
  4. If you are using the gcloud CLI or the SDK, install and initialize the Google Cloud CLI.

docs.title: Discover and test a model
docs.text:
The first step is to explore Model Garden to find a model suitable for your use case. You can then test it directly in the console using the prompt design interface or review its documentation for code samples.

Steps to discover and test a model

Send test prompts

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Model Garden page.

    Go to Model Garden

  2. Find a supported model that you want to test and click View details.

  3. Click Open prompt design. You're taken to the Prompt design page.
  4. In the Prompt field, enter the prompt that you want to test.
  5. Optional: Configure the model parameters.
  6. Click Submit.

View code samples

Most model cards for task-specific models contain code samples that you can copy and test.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Model Garden page.
  2. Find a supported model and click its model card to view details.
  3. Click the Documentation tab to find embedded code samples.

docs.title: Tune a model
docs.text:
For some models, you can fine-tune them with your own data to improve their performance on a specific task. Model Garden supports tuning through a guided pipeline or by using a Jupyter notebook for more control.

Method Best For Description Fine-tuning pipeline Users who prefer a guided, UI-based experience for tuning standard models like T5-FLAN or BERT. A structured pipeline in the Google Cloud console that walks you through the tuning process. Notebook Developers who need more flexibility and control over the tuning process and environment. Most open source and fine-tunable models provide a notebook that can be opened in Vertex AI Workbench or Colab. Tune with a fine-tuning pipelineTune in a notebook

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Model Garden page.

    Go to Model Garden

  2. In Search models, enter BERT or T5-FLAN, then click the magnifying glass to search.

  3. Click View details on the T5-FLAN or the BERT model card.
  4. Click Open fine-tuning pipeline. You're taken to the Vertex AI pipelines page.
  5. To start tuning, click Create run.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Model Garden page.

    Go to Model Garden

  2. Find a supported model that you want to tune and go to its model card.

  3. Click Open notebook.

docs.title: Deploy a model
docs.text:
After you have selected a model, deploy it to a Vertex AI endpoint to serve online predictions. You can deploy models using the Google Cloud console for a guided experience, or programmatically using the Vertex AI SDK, gcloud CLI, or REST API for automation and integration.

Method Best For Key Features Console Quick deployments and users who prefer a graphical interface. Guided, step-by-step UI for configuration and deployment. Vertex AI SDK for Python Integrating model deployment into Python applications and MLOps workflows. High-level, intuitive Python library for managing AI resources. gcloud CLI Scripting, automation, and terminal-based management. Command-line interface for managing Google Cloud resources. REST API Integrating with custom applications or services in any language. Language-agnostic interface for programmatic control over resources.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

ConsoleVertex AI SDK for PythongcloudREST API

You can deploy both open models and partner models through the Google Cloud console.

Deploy an open model

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Model Garden page.

    Go to Model Garden

  2. Find a supported model that you want to deploy, and click its model card.

  3. Click Deploy to open the Deploy model pane.
  4. In the Deploy model pane, specify details for your deployment.
    1. Use or modify the generated model and endpoint names.
    2. Select a location to create your model endpoint in.
    3. Select a machine type to use for each node of your deployment.
    4. To use a Compute Engine reservation, under the Deployment settings section, select Advanced. For the Reservation type field, select a reservation type. The reservation must match your specified machine specs.
      • Automatically use created reservation: Vertex AI automatically selects an allowed reservation with matching properties.
      • Select specific reservations: Vertex AI uses a specific reservation. If there's no capacity, an error is thrown.
      • Don't use (default): Vertex AI uses the general Google Cloud resource pool.
  5. Click Deploy.
Deploy a partner model

Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Before you begin

You must have an agreement with the partner, including terms, licensing, and pricing. To initiate contact, see the partner documentation on their Model Garden model card and click Contact sales. You must deploy on the partner's required machine types.

Note: For self-deploy partner models, if you have sufficient quotas but encounter serving quota issues during deployment, contact your Google Cloud account team for assistance.

Steps

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Model Garden page.

    Go to Model Garden

  2. To find a specific model, enter its name in the Model Garden search box.

  3. To view all models that you can self-deploy, in the Model collections section of the filter pane, select Self-deploy partner models.
  4. Click the name of the model to deploy, which opens its model card.
  5. Click Deploy options.
  6. In the Deploy on Vertex AI pane, configure your deployment such as the location and machine type.
  7. Click Deploy.

After the deployment is complete, you can request predictions by using the SDK or API. Additional instructions are available in the "Documentation" section on the model card.

For more information about setting up the SDK, see the Google Gen AI SDK overview or Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python.

Deploy an open model

1. List deployable models

List the models that you can deploy and record the model ID.

import vertexai
from vertexai.preview import model_garden

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below lines
# PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1")

# List deployable models, optionally list Hugging Face models only or filter by model name.
deployable_models = model_garden.list_deployable_models(list_hf_models=False, model_filter="gemma")
print(deployable_models)
# Example response:
# ['google/gemma2@gemma-2-27b','google/gemma2@gemma-2-27b-it', ...]

2. View deployment specifications

View the machine type, accelerator type, and container image URI for a model.

import vertexai
from vertexai.preview import model_garden

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below lines
# PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
# model = "google/gemma3@gemma-3-1b-it"
vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1")

# For Hugging Face modelsm the format is the Hugging Face model name, as in
# "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct".
# Go to https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/model-garden to find all deployable
# model names.

model = model_garden.OpenModel(model)
deploy_options = model.list_deploy_options()
print(deploy_options)
# Example response:
# [
#   dedicated_resources {
#     machine_spec {
#       machine_type: "g2-standard-12"
#       accelerator_type: NVIDIA_L4
#       accelerator_count: 1
#     }
#   }
#   container_spec {
#     ...
#   }
#   ...
# ]

3. Deploy a model to an endpoint

Model Garden uses the default deployment configuration unless you specify additional arguments.

import vertexai
from vertexai.preview import model_garden

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below lines
# PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1")

open_model = model_garden.OpenModel("google/gemma3@gemma-3-12b-it")
endpoint = open_model.deploy(
    machine_type="g2-standard-48",
    accelerator_type="NVIDIA_L4",
    accelerator_count=4,
    accept_eula=True,
)

# Optional. Run predictions on the deployed endoint.
# endpoint.predict(instances=[{"prompt": "What is Generative AI?"}])
Deploy a partner model

Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Note: The values for the machine type, accelerator type, and accelerator count, must all match one of the partner's recommended configurations. View the partner's Model Garden model card to see the recommended configurations.

In your code, replace the placeholders.

from google.cloud import aiplatform

# Replace with your values
# PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
# LOCATION = "us-central1"
# DISPLAY_NAME_MODEL = "my-partner-model"
# PUBLISHER_NAME = "partner-name"
# PUBLISHER_MODEL_NAME = "partner-model-name"
# DISPLAY_NAME_ENDPOINT = "my-partner-endpoint"
# DISPLAY_NAME_DEPLOYED_MODEL = "my-deployed-partner-model"
# MACHINE_TYPE = "g2-standard-4"
# ACCELERATOR_TYPE = "NVIDIA_L4"
# ACCELERATOR_COUNT = 1
# REQUEST_PAYLOAD = {"instances": [...]}

aiplatform.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location=LOCATION)

# Upload a model
model = aiplatform.Model.upload(
    display_name=DISPLAY_NAME_MODEL,
    model_garden_source_model_name = f"publishers/{PUBLISHER_NAME}/models/{PUBLISHER_MODEL_NAME}",
)

# Create endpoint
my_endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint.create(display_name=DISPLAY_NAME_ENDPOINT)

# Deploy model
model.deploy(
    endpoint=my_endpoint,
    deployed_model_display_name=DISPLAY_NAME_DEPLOYED_MODEL,
    traffic_split={"0": 100},
    machine_type=MACHINE_TYPE,
    accelerator_type=ACCELERATOR_TYPE,
    accelerator_count=ACCELERATOR_COUNT,
    min_replica_count=1,
    max_replica_count=1,
)

# Unary call for predictions
PAYLOAD = REQUEST_PAYLOAD
request = json.dumps(PAYLOAD)
response = my_endpoint.raw_predict(
    body = request,
    headers = {'Content-Type':'application/json'}
)
print(response)

# Streaming call for predictions
PAYLOAD = REQUEST_PAYLOAD
request = json.dumps(PAYLOAD)
for stream_response in my_endpoint.stream_raw_predict(
    body = request,
    headers = {'Content-Type':'application/json'}
):
    print(stream_response)

Before you begin, specify a quota project to run the following commands. For more information, see Set the quota project.

Deploy an open model

1. List deployable models

Run the gcloud ai model-garden models list command to find the model ID to deploy.

gcloud ai model-garden models list

The output shows model IDs and whether they support deployment. To view supported Hugging Face models, add the --can-deploy-hugging-face-models flag.

MODEL_ID                                                                SUPPORTS_DEPLOYMENT
google/gemma2@gemma-2-27b                                               Yes
google/gemma2@gemma-2-27b-it                                            Yes
...

2. View deployment specifications

Run the gcloud ai model-garden models list-deployment-config command to view supported machine types, accelerators, and container URIs.

gcloud ai model-garden models list-deployment-config \
    --model=MODEL_ID

Replace MODEL_ID with the ID from the previous step (e.g., google/gemma@gemma-2b).

3. Deploy a model to an endpoint

Run the gcloud ai model-garden models deploy command. Model Garden uses default settings unless you specify them.

gcloud ai model-garden models deploy \
    --model=MODEL_ID \
    [--machine-type=MACHINE_TYPE] \
    [--accelerator-type=ACCELERATOR_TYPE] \
    [--endpoint-display-name=ENDPOINT_NAME] \
    [--hugging-face-access-token=HF_ACCESS_TOKEN] \
    [--reservation-affinity reservation-affinity-type=any-reservation] \
    [--reservation-affinity reservation-affinity-type=specific-reservation,key="compute.googleapis.com/reservation-name",values=RESERVATION_RESOURCE_NAME] \
    [--asynchronous]

Replace the placeholders: * MODEL_ID: The model ID to deploy. For Hugging Face models, use the URL format (e.g., stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0). * MACHINE_TYPE: The machine type for deployment (e.g., g2-standard-4). * ACCELERATOR_TYPE: The accelerator type (e.g., NVIDIA_L4). * ENDPOINT_NAME: A name for the Vertex AI endpoint. * HF_ACCESS_TOKEN: An access token for gated Hugging Face models. * RESERVATION_RESOURCE_NAME: The name of a specific Compute Engine reservation.

4. View deployment details

Run the gcloud ai endpoints list --list-model-garden-endpoints-only command to see details about your deployment.

gcloud ai endpoints list --list-model-garden-endpoints-only \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

Replace LOCATION_ID with the region where you deployed the model.

You can list all deployable models and then deploy a model with default or custom configurations.

Deploy an open model

1. List models that you can deploy

Make a GET request to list available models. Before using the request data, replace PROJECT_ID and QUERY_PARAMETERS. * To list Model Garden models, use listAllVersions=True&filter=is_deployable(true). * To list Hugging Face models, use alt=json&is_hf_wildcard(true)+AND+labels.VERIFIED_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIG%3DVERIFIED_DEPLOYMENT_SUCCEED&listAllVersions=True.

HTTP method and URL:

GET https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/publishers/*/models?QUERY_PARAMETERS

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curlPowerShell 
curl -X GET \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "x-goog-user-project: PROJECT_ID" \
     "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/publishers/*/models?QUERY_PARAMETERS"

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred"; "x-goog-user-project" = "PROJECT_ID" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method GET `
    -Headers $headers `
    -Uri "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/publishers/*/models?QUERY_PARAMETERS" | Select-Object -Expand Content

2. Deploy a model

You can deploy a model from Model Garden, a Hugging Face model, or deploy with custom configurations.

Deploy a model with its default configuration

Before using the request data, replace LOCATION, PROJECT_ID, and MODEL_ID. The MODEL_ID format is publishers/PUBLISHER_NAME/models/MODEL_NAME@MODEL_VERSION.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION:deploy

Request JSON body:

{
  "publisher_model_name": "MODEL_ID",
  "model_config": {
    "accept_eula": "true"
  }
}

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curlPowerShell

Save the request body in a file named request.json, then execute the command:

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION:deploy"

Save the request body in a file named request.json, then execute the command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION:deploy" | Select-Object -Expand Content
Deploy a Hugging Face model

Before using the request data, replace LOCATION, PROJECT_ID, MODEL_ID (format: PUBLISHER_NAME/MODEL_NAME), and ACCESS_TOKEN (if the model is gated).

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION:deploy

Request JSON body:

{
  "hugging_face_model_id": "MODEL_ID",
  "hugging_face_access_token": "ACCESS_TOKEN",
  "model_config": {
    "accept_eula": "true"
  }
}

To send your request, use the curl or PowerShell commands from the previous section with this request body.

Deploy a model with customizations

Before using the request data, replace the placeholders in the JSON body.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION:deploy

Request JSON body:

{
  "publisher_model_name": "MODEL_ID",
  "deploy_config": {
    "dedicated_resources": {
      "machine_spec": {
        "machine_type": "MACHINE_TYPE",
        "accelerator_type": "ACCELERATOR_TYPE",
        "accelerator_count": ACCELERATOR_COUNT,
        "reservation_affinity": {
          "reservation_affinity_type": "ANY_RESERVATION"
        }
      },
      "spot": "false"
    },
    "fast_tryout_enabled": false
  },
  "model_config": {
    "accept_eula": "true",
    "container_spec": {
      "image_uri": "IMAGE_URI",
      "args": [CONTAINER_ARGS ],
      "ports": [
        {
          "container_port": CONTAINER_PORT
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

To send your request, use the curl or PowerShell commands from the previous sections with this request body.

Deploy a partner model

Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Note: The values for the machine type, accelerator type, and accelerator count, must all match one of the partner's recommended configurations.

In the sample curl commands, replace the placeholders.

1. Upload a model to your Model Registry

curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapi.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/models:upload \
-d '{
  "model": {
    "displayName": "DISPLAY_NAME_MODEL",
    "baseModelSource": {
      "modelGardenSource": {
        "publicModelName": f"publishers/PUBLISHER_NAME/models/PUBLISHER_MODEL_NAME",
      }
    }
  }
}'

2. Create an endpoint

curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapi.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints \
-d '{
  "displayName": "DISPLAY_NAME_ENDPOINT"
}'

3. Deploy the uploaded model to the endpoint

curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapi.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints/ENDPOINT_ID:deployModel \
-d '{
  "deployedModel": {
    "model": f"projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/models/MODEL_ID",
    "displayName": "DISPLAY_NAME_DEPLOYED_MODEL",
    "dedicatedResources": {
     "machineSpec": {
        "machineType": "MACHINE_TYPE",
        "acceleratorType": "ACCELERATOR_TYPE",
        "acceleratorCount":"ACCELERATOR_COUNT",
     },
     "minReplicaCount": 1,
     "maxReplicaCount": 1
    },
  },
  "trafficSplit": {
    "0": 100
  }
}'

4. Make prediction requests

After the model is deployed, you can make a unary or streaming call for predictions.

  • Sample unary call:

    curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapi.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints/ENDPOINT_ID:rawPredict \
-d 'REQUEST_PAYLOAD'

  • Sample streaming call:

    curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapi.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints/ENDPOINT_ID:streamRawPredict \
-d 'REQUEST_PAYLOAD'

docs.title: Manage and clean up resources
docs.text: To avoid incurring unnecessary charges to your Google Cloud account, it's important to clean up the resources you created. This involves undeploying the model from its endpoint, then deleting the endpoint and the model from the Model Registry.

docs.title: View or manage an endpoint
docs.text:
To view and manage your endpoint, go to the Vertex AI Online prediction page.

Go to Online prediction

docs.title: Clean up resources
docs.text:
To stop a deployed model from using resources, you must perform the following steps in order: 1. Undeploy the model from its endpoint. 2. Delete the endpoint. 3. Delete the model from the Model Registry.

ConsoleVertex AI SDK for Pythongcloud Undeploy a model

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Endpoints tab on the Online prediction page.

    Go to Endpoints

  2. In the Region drop-down list, choose the region where your endpoint is located.

  3. Click the endpoint name to open the details page.
  4. On the row for the model, click more_vert Actions, and then select Undeploy model from endpoint.
  5. In the Undeploy model from endpoint dialog, click Undeploy.
Delete an endpoint

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Endpoints tab on the Online prediction page.

    Go to Endpoints

  2. In the Region drop-down list, choose the region your endpoint is located.

  3. At the end of the endpoint's row, click more_vert Actions, and then select Delete endpoint.
  4. In the confirmation prompt, click Confirm.
Delete a model

  1. Go to the Model Registry page from the Vertex AI section in the Google Cloud console.

    Go to the Model Registry page

  2. In the Region drop-down list, choose the region where you deployed your model.

  3. On the row for your model, click more_vert Actions and then select Delete model.
  4. In the confirmation prompt, click Delete.

Replace the placeholders in the code snippets with your PROJECT_ID, LOCATION, ENDPOINT_ID, and MODEL_ID.

Undeploy a model 
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location=LOCATION)

# To find out which endpoints are available, un-comment the line below:
# endpoints = aiplatform.Endpoint.list()

endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint(ENDPOINT_ID)
endpoint.undeploy_all()
Delete an endpoint 
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location=LOCATION)

# To find out which endpoints are available, un-comment the line below:
# endpoints = aiplatform.Endpoint.list()

endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint(ENDPOINT_ID)
endpoint.delete()
Delete a model 
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location=LOCATION)

# To find out which models are available in Model Registry, un-comment the line below:
# models = aiplatform.Model.list()

model = aiplatform.Model(MODEL_ID)
model.delete()

Replace the placeholders in the commands with your PROJECT_ID, LOCATION_ID, ENDPOINT_ID, MODEL_ID, and DEPLOYED_MODEL_ID.

Undeploy a model

  1. Find the endpoint ID associated with your deployment.

    gcloud ai endpoints list \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

  2. Find the model ID.

    gcloud ai models list \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

  3. Get the deployed model ID using the model ID from the previous step.

    gcloud ai models describe MODEL_ID \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

    In the output, find the deployedModelId.

  4. Undeploy the model from the endpoint.

    gcloud ai endpoints undeploy-model ENDPOINT_ID \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID \
    --deployed-model-id=DEPLOYED_MODEL_ID
Delete an endpoint

  1. Get the endpoint ID to delete.

    gcloud ai endpoints list \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

  2. Delete the endpoint.

    gcloud ai endpoints delete ENDPOINT_ID \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

    When prompted, type y to confirm.

Delete a model

  1. Find the model ID to delete.

    gcloud ai models list \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

  2. Delete the model.

    gcloud ai models delete MODEL_ID \
    --project=PROJECT_ID \
    --region=LOCATION_ID

docs.title: Generative AI on Vertex AI inference API errors
docs.text: This guide lists common errors you might encounter when using the Generative AI on Vertex AI inference API. The errors align with the Google Cloud API error model, with specific causes and solutions tailored for generative AI models. For more information on the API itself, see the Model API reference for Generative AI.

docs.title: API errors
docs.text:
The following sections describe common API error codes, their causes, and potential solutions.

400 Bad Request (INVALID_ARGUMENT / FAILED_PRECONDITION)

Cause: The request fails API validation, or you tried to access a model that requires allowlisting or is disallowed by your organization's policy.

Example: The request exceeds the model's input token limit.

Solution: Refer to the Model API reference for Generative AI for details on request parameters, token count, and other parameters.

403 Permission Denied (PERMISSION_DENIED)

Cause: The client does not have sufficient permission to call the API.

Example: A service account does not have permission to access the Cloud Storage bucket that hosts image or video resources.

Solution:

  • Verify that all necessary APIs are enabled and that the service account has the correct permission to access the selected Vertex AI service.
  • Ensure the Vertex AI per-product, per-project service account (P4SA) is granted the necessary permission to access resources referenced in the input.
404 Not Found (NOT_FOUND)

Cause: No valid object is found at the designated URL.

Example: The image file is not found in the specified storage URL.

Solution: Check and fix the file location.

429 Resource Exhausted (RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED)

Cause: Depending on the error message, this could be caused by one of the following:

  • API quota has been exceeded.
  • The server is overloaded due to shared capacity.
  • You've reached the daily limit for requests using logprobs.

Example: The Gemini API request rate exceeds the per-minute limit.

Solution:

  • Check your Vertex AI Generative AI quota limits. If needed, request a higher quota.
  • Retry after a few seconds. If the error persists for a prolonged period (hours), contact Vertex AI support.
499 Cancelled (CANCELLED)

Cause: The request was cancelled by the client.

Solution: This error is initiated by the client; no server-side solution is applicable.

500 Internal Server Error (UNKNOWN / INTERNAL)

Cause: A server error occurred due to overload or a dependency failure.

Example: The request is throttled because the service is temporarily overloaded.

Solution: Retry after a few seconds. If the error persists for a prolonged period (hours), contact Vertex AI support.

503 Service Unavailable (UNAVAILABLE)

Cause: The service is temporarily unavailable.

Example: The server is not responding to incoming requests.

Solution: The unavailable status might be temporary. Retry your request after a short delay. If the error persists, contact Vertex AI support.

504 Deadline Exceeded (DEADLINE_EXCEEDED)

Cause: The client set a deadline shorter than the server's default timeout (10 minutes), and the request did not finish within the client-provided deadline.

Solution: Consider increasing the deadline in your client configuration.

docs.title: Handle errors
docs.text:
To minimize errors, consider the following best practices:

  • Avoid traffic spikes: Sudden, large increases in request volume can trigger quota limits or cause server overloading. Distribute your API calls more evenly over time.
  • Implement retry logic carefully: When retrying a failed request, use an exponential backoff strategy. We recommend a minimum delay of one second for the first retry and retrying no more than twice.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues not listed here, refer to the general Vertex AI Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Get batch predictions for Gemini
docs.text:
Batch predictions let you send a large number of multimodal prompts in a single batch request.

For more information about the batch workflow and how to format your input data, see Get batch predictions for Gemini.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
• Gemini 1.5 Pro
  • Gemini 1.5 Flash
  • Gemini 1.0 Pro

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Batch Prediction: A process for sending a large number of inference requests to a model in a single asynchronous job, which is ideal for offline processing of non-real-time data.
  • Cloud Storage: A scalable and durable object storage service for unstructured data, often used to store input files (like JSONL) and receive model outputs.
  • BigQuery: A serverless, highly scalable data warehouse that enables super-fast SQL queries using the processing power of Google's infrastructure, used here as both an input source and output destination.
  • JSONL: A text format for storing structured data where each line is a valid JSON object, commonly used for streaming data and batch inputs.
  • REST API: A standardized architectural style for creating web services that allows different systems to communicate over HTTP, used here for making direct calls to the Vertex AI service.

docs.title: Batch prediction workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the high-level workflow for getting batch predictions.

flowchart TD
    A[Prepare your inputs] --> B[Create a batch prediction job]
    B --> C[Check job status]
    C --> D[Retrieve batch output]

    click A "#prepare-your-inputs"
    click B "#create-a-batch-prediction-job"
    click C "#check-job-status"
    click D "#retrieve-batch-output"

docs.title: Prepare your inputs
docs.text:
Before you can create a batch prediction job, you need to prepare your input data. Inputs can be stored in either Cloud Storage as a JSONL file or in a BigQuery table.

For detailed instructions on how to format your data for different multimodal prompts, see Prepare your batch request inputs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: The following tables describe the parameters for a batch prediction job request.

docs.title: Request body
docs.text: Parameter Description displayName A name you choose for your job. model The model to use for batch prediction. inputConfig The configuration for your input data source. Gemini batch prediction supports Cloud Storage and BigQuery. outputConfig The configuration for your output location. Cloud Storage and BigQuery are supported.

docs.title: inputConfig
docs.text: Parameter Description instancesFormat The prompt input format. Use jsonl for Cloud Storage or bigquery for BigQuery. gcsSource.uris The input source URI. This is a Cloud Storage location of the JSONL file in the format gs://bucketname/path/to/file.jsonl. bigquerySource.inputUri The input source URI. This is a BigQuery table URI in the format bq://project_id.dataset.table. The region of the input BigQuery dataset must be the same as the Vertex AI batch prediction job.

docs.title: outputConfig
docs.text: Parameter Description predictionsFormat The output format of the prediction. Use jsonl for Cloud Storage or bigquery for BigQuery. gcsDestination.outputUriPrefix The Cloud Storage bucket and directory location, in the format gs://mybucket/path/to/output. bigqueryDestination.outputUri The BigQuery URI of the target output table, in the format bq://project_id.dataset.table. If the table doesn't already exist, it is created for you. The region of the output BigQuery dataset must be the same as the Vertex AI batch prediction job.

docs.title: Create a batch prediction job
docs.text:
You can create a batch prediction job using the REST API or client libraries for various programming languages. Depending on the number of input items you submitted, a batch generation task can take some time to complete.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

To create a batch prediction job, use the projects.locations.batchPredictionJobs.create method.

Cloud Storage inputBigQuery input

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: A region that supports Gemini models.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • MODEL_PATH: The publisher model name (e.g., publishers/google/models/gemini-1.5-flash-001) or the tuned endpoint name (e.g., projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/models/MODEL_ID).
  • INPUT_URI: The Cloud Storage location of your JSONL batch prediction input (e.g., gs://bucketname/path/to/file.jsonl).
  • OUTPUT_FORMAT: To output to a BigQuery table, specify bigquery. To output to a Cloud Storage bucket, specify jsonl.
  • DESTINATION: For BigQuery, specify bigqueryDestination. For Cloud Storage, specify gcsDestination.
  • OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME: For BigQuery, specify outputUri. For Cloud Storage, specify outputUriPrefix.
  • OUTPUT_URI: For BigQuery, specify the table location (e.g., bq://myproject.mydataset.output_result). For Cloud Storage, specify the bucket and directory location (e.g., gs://mybucket/path/to/output).

Request JSON body:

{
  "displayName": "my-cloud-storage-batch-prediction-job",
  "model": "MODEL_PATH",
  "inputConfig": {
    "instancesFormat": "jsonl",
    "gcsSource": {
      "uris" : ["INPUT_URI"]
    }
  },
  "outputConfig": {
    "predictionsFormat": "OUTPUT_FORMAT",
    "DESTINATION": {
      "OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME": "OUTPUT_URI"
    }
  }
}

// Import the aiplatform library
const aiplatformLib = require('@google-cloud/aiplatform');
const aiplatform = aiplatformLib.protos.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1;

/**

// URI of the input file in Google Cloud Storage.

// Or try:
// "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/batch/gemini_multimodal_batch_predict.jsonl"
// for a batch prediction that uses audio, video, and an image.
const inputUri =
  'gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/batch/batch_requests_for_multimodal_input.jsonl';
const location = 'us-central1';
const parent = `projects/${projectId}/locations/${location}`;
const modelName = `${parent}/publishers/google/models/gemini-1.0-pro-001`;

// Specify the location of the api endpoint.
const clientOptions = {
  apiEndpoint: `${location}-aiplatform.googleapis.com`,
};

// Instantiate the client.
const jobServiceClient = new aiplatformLib.JobServiceClient(clientOptions);

// Create a Gemini batch prediction job using Google Cloud Storage input and output buckets.
async function create_batch_prediction_gemini_gcs() {
  const gcsSource = new aiplatform.GcsSource({
    uris: [inputUri],
  });

  const inputConfig = new aiplatform.BatchPredictionJob.InputConfig({
    gcsSource: gcsSource,
    instancesFormat: 'jsonl',
  });

  const gcsDestination = new aiplatform.GcsDestination({
    outputUriPrefix: outputUri,
  });

  const outputConfig = new aiplatform.BatchPredictionJob.OutputConfig({
    gcsDestination: gcsDestination,
    predictionsFormat: 'jsonl',
  });

  const batchPredictionJob = new aiplatform.BatchPredictionJob({
    displayName: 'Batch predict with Gemini - GCS',
    model: modelName,
    inputConfig: inputConfig,
    outputConfig: outputConfig,
  });

  const request = {
    parent: parent,
    batchPredictionJob,
  };

  // Create batch prediction job request
  const [response] = await jobServiceClient.createBatchPredictionJob(request);
  console.log('Response name: ', response.name);
  // Example response:
  // Response name: projects/<project>/locations/us-central1/batchPredictionJobs/<job-id>
}

import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.BatchPredictionJob;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.GcsDestination;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.GcsSource;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.JobServiceClient;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.JobServiceSettings;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.LocationName;
import java.io.IOException;

public class CreateBatchPredictionGeminiJobSample {

  public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
    // TODO(developer): Update these variables before running the sample.
    String project = "PROJECT_ID";
    String gcsDestinationOutputUriPrefix = "gs://MY_BUCKET/";

    createBatchPredictionGeminiJobSample(project, gcsDestinationOutputUriPrefix);
  }

  // Create a batch prediction job using a JSONL input file and output URI, both in Cloud
  // Storage.
  public static BatchPredictionJob createBatchPredictionGeminiJobSample(
      String project, String gcsDestinationOutputUriPrefix) throws IOException {
    String location = "us-central1";
    JobServiceSettings settings =
        JobServiceSettings.newBuilder()
            .setEndpoint(String.format("%s-aiplatform.googleapis.com:443", location))
            .build();

    // Initialize client that will be used to send requests. This client only needs to be created
    // once, and can be reused for multiple requests.
    try (JobServiceClient client = JobServiceClient.create(settings)) {
      GcsSource gcsSource =
          GcsSource.newBuilder()
              .addUris(
                  "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/batch/"
                      + "batch_requests_for_multimodal_input.jsonl")
              // Or try
              // "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/batch/gemini_multimodal_batch_predict.jsonl"
              // for a batch prediction that uses audio, video, and an image.
              .build();
      BatchPredictionJob.InputConfig inputConfig =
          BatchPredictionJob.InputConfig.newBuilder()
              .setInstancesFormat("jsonl")
              .setGcsSource(gcsSource)
              .build();
      GcsDestination gcsDestination =
          GcsDestination.newBuilder().setOutputUriPrefix(gcsDestinationOutputUriPrefix).build();
      BatchPredictionJob.OutputConfig outputConfig =
          BatchPredictionJob.OutputConfig.newBuilder()
              .setPredictionsFormat("jsonl")
              .setGcsDestination(gcsDestination)
              .build();
      String modelName =
          String.format(
              "projects/%s/locations/%s/publishers/google/models/%s",
              project, location, "gemini-1.0-pro-001");

      BatchPredictionJob batchPredictionJob =
          BatchPredictionJob.newBuilder()
              .setDisplayName("my-display-name")
              .setModel(modelName) // Add model parameters per request in the input jsonl file.
              .setInputConfig(inputConfig)
              .setOutputConfig(outputConfig)
              .build();

      LocationName parent = LocationName.of(project, location);
      BatchPredictionJob response = client.createBatchPredictionJob(parent, batchPredictionJob);
      System.out.format("\tName: %s\n", response.getName());
      // Example response:
      //   Name: projects/<project>/locations/us-central1/batchPredictionJobs/<job-id>
      return response;
    }
  }
}

              "projects/%s/locations/%s/publishers/google/models/%s",
              project, location, "gemini-1.0-pro-001");

      BatchPredictionJob batchPredictionJob =
          BatchPredictionJob.newBuilder()
              .setDisplayName("my-display-name")
              .setModel(modelName) // Add model parameters per request in the input BigQuery table.
              .setInputConfig(inputConfig)
              .setOutputConfig(outputConfig)
              .build();

      LocationName parent = LocationName.of(project, location);
      BatchPredictionJob response = client.createBatchPredictionJob(parent, batchPredictionJob);
      System.out.format("\tName: %s\n", response.getName());
      // Example response:
      //   Name: projects/<project>/locations/us-central1/batchPredictionJobs/<job-id>
      return response;
    }
  }
}
