RESTPythonNode.js

Before you begin

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_NUMBER_OR_ID: The numeric or alphanumeric ID of your Google Cloud project.
  • LOCATION: The location to process the request. ??? "View a partial list of available regions" * us-central1 * us-west4 * northamerica-northeast1 * us-east4 * us-west1 * asia-northeast3 * asia-southeast1 * asia-northeast1
  • MODEL_ID: The ID of the model, such as gemini-1.0-pro-002.
  • SOURCE_LANGUAGE_CODE: The language of the input text.
  • TARGET_LANGUAGE_CODE: The target language to translate the input text to.
  • SOURCE_TEXT: The text to translate.
View parameter definitions
  • TEMPERATURE: The temperature is used for sampling during response generation, which occurs when topP and topK are applied. Temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection. Lower temperatures are good for prompts that require a less open-ended or creative response, while higher temperatures can lead to more diverse or creative results. A temperature of 0 means that the highest probability tokens are always selected. In this case, responses for a given prompt are mostly deterministic, but a small amount of variation is still possible. If the model returns a response that's too generic, too short, or the model gives a fallback response, try increasing the temperature.
  • TOP_P: Top-P changes how the model selects tokens for output. Tokens are selected from the most probable to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. For example, if tokens A, B, and C have a probability of 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 and the top-P value is 0.5, then the model will select either A or B as the next token by using temperature and excludes C as a candidate. Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.
  • TOP_K: Top-K changes how the model selects tokens for output. A top-K of 1 means the next selected token is the most probable among all tokens in the model's vocabulary (also called greedy decoding), while a top-K of 3 means that the next token is selected from among the three most probable tokens by using temperature. For each token selection step, the top-K tokens with the highest probabilities are sampled. Then tokens are further filtered based on top-P with the final token selected using temperature sampling. Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.
  • MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS: Maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately four characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words. Specify a lower value for shorter responses and a higher value for potentially longer responses.
  • SAFETY_CATEGORY: The safety category to configure a threshold for. ??? "View safety categories" * HARM_CATEGORY_SEXUALLY_EXPLICIT * HARM_CATEGORY_HATE_SPEECH * HARM_CATEGORY_HARASSMENT * HARM_CATEGORY_DANGEROUS_CONTENT
  • THRESHOLD: The threshold for blocking responses that could belong to the specified safety category based on probability. ??? "View blocking thresholds" * BLOCK_NONE * BLOCK_ONLY_HIGH * BLOCK_MEDIUM_AND_ABOVE (default) * BLOCK_LOW_AND_ABOVE BLOCK_LOW_AND_ABOVE blocks the most while BLOCK_ONLY_HIGH blocks the least.

import os

# Import the Google Cloud Translation library.
from google.cloud import [translate](https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/translate/latest/google.cloud.translate_v2.client.Client.html)_v3

PROJECT_ID = os.environ.get("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT")


def translate_text(
    text: str = "YOUR_TEXT_TO_TRANSLATE",
    source_language_code: str = "en-US",
    target_language_code: str = "fr",
) -> translate_v3.TranslationServiceClient:
    """Translate Text from a Source language to a Target language.
    Args:
        text: The content to translate.
        source_language_code: The code of the source language.
        target_language_code: The code of the target language.
            For example: "fr" for French, "es" for Spanish, etc.
            Find available languages and codes here:
            https://cloud.google.com/translate/docs/languages#neural_machine_translation_model
    """

    # Initialize Translation client.
    client = translate_v3.TranslationServiceClient()
    parent = f"projects/{PROJECT_ID}/locations/global"

    # MIME type of the content to translate.
    # Supported MIME types:
    # https://cloud.google.com/translate/docs/supported-formats
    mime_type = "text/plain"

    # Translate text from the source to the target language.
    response = [client](https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/translate/latest/google.cloud.translate_v2.client.html).[translate_text](https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/translate/latest/google.cloud.translate_v3.services.translation_service.TranslationServiceClient.html#google_cloud_translate_v3_services_translation_service_TranslationServiceClient_translate_text)(
        contents=[text],
        parent=parent,
        mime_type=mime_type,
        source_language_code=source_language_code,
        target_language_code=target_language_code,
    )

    # Display the translation for the text.
    # For example, for "Hello! How are you doing today?":
    # Translated text: Bonjour comment vas-tu aujourd'hui?
    for translation in response.translations:
        print(f"Translated text: {translation.translated_text}")

    return response

  const [response] = await translationClient.translateText(request);

  for (const translation of response.translations) {
    console.log(`Translation: ${translation.translatedText}`);
  }
}

translateText();

docs.title: Customize translations with the Translation LLM
docs.text:
You can customize responses from the Translation LLM by providing your own example translations. This feature, also known as adaptive translation, is only available for the Translation LLM.

You can request customized translations through the Vertex AI Studio or the API. The console supports custom translations by uploading a file with examples (TMX or TSV), while the API supports providing up to five example sentence pairs inline with the request.

Data requirements

If you provide example translations in a file for the Google Cloud console, the examples must be written as segment pairs in a TMX or TSV file. Each pair includes a source language segment and its translated counterpart. For more information, see Prepare example translations in the Cloud Translation documentation.

To get the most accurate results, include specific examples from a wide variety of scenarios. You must include at least five sentence pairs but no more than 10,000 pairs. Also, a segment pair can be at most a total of 512 characters.

ConsoleAPI Customize translations using Vertex AI Studio

  1. In the Vertex AI section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Translate text page in Vertex AI Studio.

    Go to Vertex AI Studio

  2. In the Run settings pane, configure your translation settings.

    • In the Model field, select Translation LLM.
    • To change the temperature, expand Advanced.

  3. Click Add examples.

    • Select a local file or a file from Cloud Storage. Vertex AI Studio determines the source and target languages from your file.
    • Select the number of examples for the model to use before generating a response. The number of examples you select counts toward the input character limit per request of 3,000.

  4. In the input field, enter the text to translate.

  5. Click Submit. Vertex AI automatically selects your specified number of reference sentences that are most similar to your input. The translation model identifies patterns from your examples and then applies those patterns when generating a response. The output limit per request is 3,000 characters. Any text beyond this limit is dropped.

  6. To get the code or curl command that demonstrate how to request translations, click code Get code.

To request custom translations via the API, include up to five reference sentence pairs in your translation request. The translation model uses all of them to identify patterns from your examples and then applies those patterns when generating a response.

RESTPythonNode.js

Before you begin

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_NUMBER_OR_ID: The numeric or alphanumeric ID of your Google Cloud project.
  • LOCATION: The location where you want to run this operation. For example, us-central1.
  • REFERENCE_SOURCE: A sentence in the source language that is part of a reference sentence pair.
  • REFERENCE_TARGET: A sentence in the target language that is part of a reference sentence pair.
  • SOURCE_LANGUAGE: The language code of the input text.
  • TARGET_LANGUAGE: The target language to translate the input text to.
  • SOURCE_TEXT: Text in the source language to translate.
  • MIME_TYPE (Optional): The format of the source text, such as text/html or text/plain. By default, the MIME type is set to text/plain.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/translate-llm:predict

Request JSON body:

{
  "instances": [
    {
      "reference_sentence_config": {
        "reference_sentence_pair_lists": [
          {
            "reference_sentence_pairs": [
              {
                "source_sentence": "REFERENCE_SOURCE_1_1",
                "target_sentence": "REFERENCE_TARGET_1_1"
              },
              {
                "source_sentence": "REFERENCE_SOURCE_1_2",
                "target_sentence": "REFERENCE_SOURCE_1_2"
              }
            ]
          }
        ],
        "source_language_code": "SOURCE_LANGUAGE_CODE",
        "target_language_code": "TARGET_LANGUAGE_CODE"
      },
      "content": [
        "SOURCE_TEXT"
      ],
      "mimeType": "MIME_TYPE"
    }
  ]
}

To send your request, expand one of these options:

cURLPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \  
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \  
     -H "x-goog-user-project: PROJECT_NUMBER_OR_ID" \  
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \  
     -d @request.json \  
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/translate-llm:predict"

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token  
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred"; "x-goog-user-project" = "PROJECT_NUMBER_OR_ID" }  

Invoke-WebRequest `  
    -Method POST `  
    -Headers $headers `  
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `  
    -InFile request.json `  
    -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/translate-llm:predict" | Select-Object -Expand Content

You should receive a JSON response similar to the following:

{
  "predictions": [
    {
      "languageCode": "TARGET_LANGUAGE",
      "translations": [
        {
          "translatedText": "TRANSLATED_TEXT"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Before trying this sample, follow the Python setup instructions in the Vertex AI quickstart using client libraries. For more information, see the Vertex AI Python API reference documentation.

To authenticate to Vertex AI, set up Application Default Credentials. For more information, see Set up authentication for a local development environment.

from google.cloud import aiplatform
from google.protobuf.json_format import MessageToDict

def translate():
  # Create a client
  client_options = {"api_endpoint": "LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com"}
  client = aiplatform.gapic.PredictionServiceClient(client_options=client_options)

  # Initialize the request
  endpoint_id = f"projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/translate-llm"
  instances=[{
      "reference_sentence_config": {
        "reference_sentence_pair_lists": [{
          "reference_sentence_pairs": [{
            "source_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_SOURCE_1',
            "target_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_TARGET_1'
          },
          {
            "source_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_SOURCE_2',
            "target_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_TARGET_2'
          }]
        }],
        "source_language_code": 'SOURCE_LANGUAGE_CODE',
        "target_language_code": 'TARGET_LANGUAGE_CODE'
      },
      "content": ["SOURCE_TEXT"]
  }]
  # Make the request
  response = client.[predict](https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/aiplatform/latest/google.cloud.aiplatform_v1.services.prediction_service.PredictionServiceClient.html)(
      endpoint=endpoint_id, instances=instances,
  )
  # Handle the response
  print(response)

  # The predictions are a google.protobuf.Value representation of the model's predictions.
  predictions = MessageToDict(response._pb)['predictions']
  for prediction in predictions:
      print(prediction['translations'])

Before trying this sample, follow the Node.js setup instructions in the Vertex AI quickstart using client libraries. For more information, see the Vertex AI Node.js API reference documentation.

To authenticate to Vertex AI, set up Application Default Credentials. For more information, see Set up authentication for a local development environment.

async function translate() {
  const request = {
    instances: [{
        "reference_sentence_config": {
          "reference_sentence_pair_lists": [{
            "reference_sentence_pairs": [{
              "source_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_SOURCE_1',
              "target_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_TARGET_1'
            },
            "reference_sentence_pairs": {
              "source_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_SOURCE_2',
              "target_sentence": 'SAMPLE_REFERENCE_TARGET_2'
            }]
          }],
          "source_language_code": 'SOURCE_LANGUAGE_CODE',
          "target_language_code": 'TARGET_LANGUAGE_CODE'
        },
        "contents": ["SOURCE_TEXT"]
    }]
  };
  const {google} = require('googleapis');
  const aiplatform = google.cloud('aiplatform');
  const endpoint = aiplatform.predictionEndpoint('projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/translate-llm');

  const [response] = await endpoint.predict(request)
  console.log('Translating')
  console.log(response)
}

You can also use the Cloud Translation API to create a dataset and import your example sentence pairs. When you use the Cloud Translation API to request translations, you can include your dataset to customize responses. The dataset persists and can be reused with multiple translation requests. For more information, see Request adaptive translations in the Cloud Translation documentation.

docs.text:
This section shows you how to generate a video from an image and a text prompt.

The following workflow diagram provides a high-level overview of the steps:

flowchart TD
    A[Set up your environment] --> B{Choose generation method};
    B -- Console --> C[Generate video in the Console];
    B -- REST API --> D[Generate video with the REST API];
    B -- Python SDK --> E[Generate video with the Python SDK];

    click A "#before-you-begin"
    click B "#generate-videos-from-an-image"
    click C "#generate-video-in-the-console"
    click D "#generate-video-with-the-rest-api"
    click E "#generate-video-with-the-python-sdk"
| Sample input | Sample output | | :--- | :--- | | 1. Input image¹ ![Input PNG file of a crocheted elephant](../images/ITV_elephant_base2.png) 2. Text prompt: `the elephant moves around naturally` | ![Output video of a crocheted elephant](../images/ITV_elephant_output.gif) | ¹ Image generated using Imagen on Vertex AI from the prompt: A Crochet elephant in intricate patterns walking on the savanna.

You can generate videos using the Google Cloud console for a graphical interface, or programmatically using the REST API or the Python SDK.

Method Best for Google Cloud console Quickly experimenting with prompts and model settings without writing any code. REST API Integrating video generation into your applications using standard web requests. Python SDK A streamlined, high-level programmatic experience for Python developers. ConsoleREST APIPython SDK

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Studio > Media Studio page.

Media Studio

  1. Click Video.
  2. Optional: In the Settings pane, configure the following settings:
    • Model: Choose a model from the available options.
    • Aspect ratio: Choose either 16:9 or 9:16. Note: The 9:16 aspect ratio isn't supported by veo-3.0-generate-preview.
    • Number of results: Adjust the slider or enter a value between 1 and 4.
    • Video length: Select a length between 5 seconds and 8 seconds.
    • Output directory: Click Browse to create or select a Cloud Storage bucket to store output files.
  3. Optional: In the Safety section, select one of the following Person generation settings:
    • Allow (Adults only): Default value. Generate adult people or faces only. Don't generate youth or children people or faces.
    • Don't allow: Don't generate people or faces.
  4. Optional: In the Advanced options section, enter a Seed value for randomizing video generation.
  5. In the Write your prompt box, click upload Upload.
  6. Choose a local image to upload and click Select.
  7. In the Write your prompt box, enter your text prompt that describes the videos to generate.
  8. Click send Generate.

The following samples show how to send a video generation request. This request begins a long-running operation. For more information, see the Veo API reference.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Step 1: Send a video generation request

Use the following command to send a video generation request. This request begins a long-running operation and returns an operation name.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: The model ID to use. Available values:
    • veo-2.0-generate-001 (GA)
    • veo-3.0-generate-preview (Preview)
  • TEXT_PROMPT: The text prompt used to guide video generation.
  • INPUT_IMAGE: Base64-encoded bytes string representing the input image. To ensure quality, the input image should be 720p or higher (1280 x 720 pixels) and have a 16:9 or 9:16 aspect ratio. Images of other aspect ratios or sizes may be resized or centrally cropped during the upload process.
  • MIME_TYPE: The MIME type of the input image. Supported MIME types: image/jpeg or image/png.
  • OUTPUT_STORAGE_URI: Optional: The Cloud Storage bucket to store the output videos. If not provided, video bytes are returned in the response. For example: gs://video-bucket/output/.
  • RESPONSE_COUNT: The number of video files you want to generate. Accepted integer values: 1-4.
  • DURATION: The length of video files that you want to generate. Accepted integer values are 5-8.
  • Additional optional parameters: Use the following optional variables in the "parameters": {} object.
    • ASPECT_RATIO: (string) Defines the aspect ratio of the generated videos. Values: 16:9 (default, landscape) or 9:16 (portrait).
    • NEGATIVE_PROMPT: (string) A text string that describes what you want to discourage the model from generating.
    • PERSON_SAFETY_SETTING: (string) The safety setting that controls whether people or face generation is allowed. Values: allow_adult (default) or disallow.
    • SEED_NUMBER: (uint32) A number to make generated videos deterministic. Specifying a seed number guides the model to produce the same videos. Values: 0 - 4294967295.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:predictLongRunning

Request JSON body:

{
  "instances": [
    {
      "prompt": "TEXT_PROMPT",
      "image": {
        "bytesBase64Encoded": "INPUT_IMAGE",
        "mimeType": "MIME_TYPE"
      }
    }
  ],
  "parameters": {
    "storageUri": "OUTPUT_STORAGE_URI",
    "sampleCount": RESPONSE_COUNT
  }
}

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curl

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:predictLongRunning"

PowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:predictLongRunning" | Select-Object -Expand Content

This request returns a full operation name with a unique operation ID. Use this operation name in the next step to check the status of the video generation request.

{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID/operations/a1b07c8e-7b5a-4aba-bb34-3e1ccb8afcc8"
}
Step 2: Check the operation status

After you start a video generation job, it might take some time to complete. You can use the operation name returned from the previous step to check the status of the job.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacement:

  • OPERATION_NAME: The full operation name returned from the video generation request. For example: projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID/operations/a1b07c8e-7b5a-4aba-bb34-3e1ccb8afcc8.

HTTP method and URL:

GET https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/OPERATION_NAME

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curl

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Execute the following command:

curl -X GET \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/OPERATION_NAME"

PowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method GET `
    -Headers $headers `
    -Uri "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/OPERATION_NAME" | Select-Object -Expand Content

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Install the SDK

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Run the Python code

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI:

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

import time
from google import genai
from google.genai.types import GenerateVideosConfig, Image

client = genai.Client()

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below line
# output_gcs_uri = "gs://your-bucket/your-prefix"

operation = client.models.generate_videos(
    model="veo-3.0-generate-preview",
    image=Image(
        gcs_uri="gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/image/flowers.png",
        mime_type="image/png",
    ),
    config=GenerateVideosConfig(
        aspect_ratio="16:9",
        output_gcs_uri=output_gcs_uri,
    ),
)

while not operation.done:
    time.sleep(15)
    operation = client.operations.get(operation)
    print(operation)

if operation.response:
    print(operation.result.generated_videos[0].video.uri)

# Example response:
# gs://your-bucket/your-prefix

View the PowerShell command 
$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:predictLongRunning" | Select-Object -Expand Content

This request returns a full operation name with a unique ID.

{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID/operations/a1b07c8e-7b5a-4aba-bb34-3e1ccb8afcc8"
}

3. Check the operation status

Use the operation name from the previous step to check the status of the video generation. Before using the request data, replace the following:

  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: The model ID you used.
  • OPERATION_ID: The unique operation ID returned in the previous step.

HTTP method and URL: POST https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:fetchPredictOperation

Request JSON body:

{
  "operationName": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID/operations/OPERATION_ID"
}

To send your request, save the request body in a file named request.json and choose one of the following options:

View the cURL command 
curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:fetchPredictOperation"
View the PowerShell command 
$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:fetchPredictOperation" | Select-Object -Expand Content

When the operation is complete, the response will contain "done": true and the Cloud Storage URI of the generated video.

Response:

{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID/operations/OPERATION_ID",
  "done": true,
  "response": {
    "@type": "type.googleapis.com/cloud.ai.large_models.vision.GenerateVideoResponse",
    "videos": [
      {
        "gcsUri":"gs://BUCKET_NAME/TIMESTAMPED_FOLDER/sample_0.mp4",
        "mimeType": "video/mp4"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Use the Gen AI SDK for Python to integrate video generation into your Python applications.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

1. Install the SDK

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

2. Configure your environment

Set the following environment variables to authenticate the SDK to Vertex AI.

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

3. Generate a video

The following code sends a request to generate a video and polls the operation until it is complete.

import time
from google import genai
from google.genai.types import GenerateVideosConfig

client = genai.Client()

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below line
# output_gcs_uri = "gs://your-bucket/your-prefix"

operation = client.models.generate_videos(
    model="veo-3.0-generate-preview",
    prompt="a cat reading a book",
    config=GenerateVideosConfig(
        aspect_ratio="16:9",
        output_gcs_uri=output_gcs_uri,
    ),
)

while not operation.done:
    time.sleep(15)
    operation = client.operations.get(operation)
    print(operation)

if operation.response:
    print(operation.result.generated_videos[0].video.uri)

# Example response:
# gs://your-bucket/your-prefix

docs.title: Responsible AI and usage guidelines for Veo
docs.text:
Veo on Vertex AI is designed with Google's AI principles in mind. It is important for developers to understand how to test and deploy Google's models safely and responsibly. To aid developers, Veo on Vertex AI has built-in safety features to help you block potentially harmful outputs within your use cases. For more information, see the Safety filters section.

We encourage you to use fairness, interpretability, privacy, and security best practices when developing AI applications. For more information, see The People + AI Guidebook.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Veo: A high-quality, text-to-video generative AI model from Google that creates video content from text, image, and video prompts.
  • Safety filters: Built-in mechanisms that assess prompts and generated content against a list of harmful categories to prevent policy violations.

docs.title: Safety filters
docs.text:
Veo on Vertex AI offers several ways to input prompts to generate videos, including text, video, and images. Prompts provided to Veo are assessed against a list of safety filters, which include harmful categories such as violence, sexual, derogatory, and toxic. These safety filters aim to filter out input and output that violates the Google Cloud Platform Acceptable Use Policy, Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy, or Our AI Principles.

If the model responds to a request with an error message, such as The prompt couldn't be submitted or it might violate our policies, then the input is triggering a safety filter. If fewer videos than requested are returned, then some generated output is being blocked for not meeting safety requirements.

docs.title: Safety filter code categories
docs.text:
When a safety filter is triggered, your output might contain a safety code similar to the following example: "Veo could not generate videos because the input image violates Vertex AI's usage guidelines. If you think this was an error, send feedback. Support codes: 15236754"

The code listed in the output corresponds to a specific harmful category. The following table maps the error codes to their respective safety categories.

Error code Safety category Description 5806121417301594 Child Detects child content where it isn't allowed due to the API request settings or allowlisting. 2931047215236754 Celebrity Detects a photorealistic representation of a celebrity in the request. 62263041 Dangerous content Detects content that is potentially dangerous in nature. 5773494022137204 Hate Detects hate-related topics or content. 748032812957879042876398 Other Detects other miscellaneous safety issues with the request. 92201652 Personal information Detects Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in the text, such as credit card numbers or home addresses. 893710324911466272817394 Prohibited content Detects prohibited content in the request. 907891796342908943188360 Sexual Detects content that is sexual in nature. 78610348 Toxic Detects toxic topics or content in the text. 6149386356562880 Violence Detects violence-related content from the image or text. 32635315 Vulgar Detects vulgar topics or content from the text.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with safety filters or receive unexpected error codes, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide for Vertex AI.

docs.title: Turn the prompt rewriter off
docs.text:
Veo offers an LLM-based prompt enhancement tool, also known as a prompt rewriter. The prompt rewriter can modify your prompts to add details like video description, camera motions, transcription, and sound effects. More detailed prompts generally result in higher-quality videos.

If you disable prompt enhancement, the quality of the videos and how well the output matches your original prompt may be impacted. This feature is enabled by default for the following model versions:

  • veo-2.0-generate-001
  • veo-3.0-generate-preview

Preview

veo-3.0-generate-preview is in Preview.

Important: You can't disable the prompt rewriter when you use the veo-3.0-generate-preview model.

A rewritten prompt is delivered by the API response only if the original prompt is fewer than 30 words long.

For more information about writing effective text prompts for video generation, see the Veo prompt guide.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Veo: A generative AI model from Google that creates high-definition video from text, image, and video prompts.
  • LLM (Large Language Model): A type of artificial intelligence model trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human-like language.
  • Cloud Storage bucket: A container for storing your data, such as videos and other files, in Google Cloud.
  • REST API: A standardized way for applications to communicate with each other over the internet, allowing you to send requests and receive responses programmatically.
  • Long-running operation: An asynchronous task, like video generation, that may take a significant amount of time to complete, allowing you to check its status without waiting for it to finish.
Set up your environment

  1. Sign in and set up your project

    Sign in to your Google Cloud account. If you're new to Google Cloud, create an account to evaluate how our products perform in real-world scenarios. New customers also get $300 in free credits to run, test, and deploy workloads.

    In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.

    Note: If you don't plan to keep the resources that you create in this procedure, create a project instead of selecting an existing project. After you finish these steps, you can delete the project, removing all resources associated with the project.

    Go to project selector

  2. Enable the API

    Enable the Vertex AI API.

    Enable the API

  3. Set up authentication

    Set up authentication for your environment. Select the tab for how you plan to use the samples on this page.

    ConsoleREST

    When you use the Google Cloud console to access Google Cloud services and APIs, you don't need to set up authentication.

    To use the REST API samples on this page in a local development environment, you use the credentials you provide to the gcloud CLI.

    After installing the Google Cloud CLI, initialize it by running the following command:

    gcloud init

    If you're using an external identity provider (IdP), you must first sign in to the gcloud CLI with your federated identity.

    For more information, see Authenticate for using REST in the Google Cloud authentication documentation.

docs.title: Turn off prompt rewriter
docs.text:
To turn prompt enhancement off, use either the Google Cloud console or the REST API.

ConsoleREST

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Studio > Media Studio page.

    Go to Media Studio

  2. Click Veo.

  3. In Settings, click the Enable prompt enhancement toggle to turn it off.

  4. In the Write your prompt box, enter your prompt and then click Generate.

To turn off the prompt rewriter using the API, send a video generation request with the enhancePrompt parameter set to False. For more information about the Veo API, see the Veo on Vertex AI API reference.

  1. Use the following command to send a video generation request. This request begins a long-running operation and stores output to a Cloud Storage bucket you specify.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: The model ID to use. Available values:
    • veo-2.0-generate-001
    • veo-3.0-generate-preview (Preview)
  • TEXT_PROMPT: The text prompt used to guide video generation.
  • OUTPUT_STORAGE_URI: Optional: The Cloud Storage bucket to store the output videos. If not provided, video bytes are returned in the response. For example: gs://video-bucket/output/.
  • RESPONSE_COUNT: The number of video files you want to generate. Accepted integer values: 1-4.
  • DURATION: The length of video files that you want to generate. Accepted integer values are 5-8.
  • ENHANCED_PROMPT: Whether to use enhanced prompts. Use one of the following:
    • True: (default) Use Gemini to enhance your prompts.
    • False: Don't use Gemini to enhance your prompts.

Additional optional parameters

Use the following optional variables depending on your use case. Add some or all of the following parameters in the "parameters": {} object.

"parameters": {
  "aspectRatio": "ASPECT_RATIO",
  "negativePrompt": "NEGATIVE_PROMPT",
  "personGeneration": "PERSON_SAFETY_SETTING",
  "sampleCount": RESPONSE_COUNT,
  "seed": SEED_NUMBER
}
  • ASPECT_RATIO: string. Optional. Defines the aspect ratio of the generated videos. Values: 16:9 (default, landscape) or 9:16 (portrait).
  • NEGATIVE_PROMPT: string. Optional. A text string that describes what you want to discourage the model from generating.
  • PERSON_SAFETY_SETTING: string. Optional. The safety setting that controls whether people or face generation is allowed. Values:
    • allow_adult (default value): Allow generation of adults only.
    • disallow: Disallows inclusion of people or faces in images.
  • RESPONSE_COUNT: int. Optional. The number of output images requested. Values: 1-4.
  • SEED_NUMBER: uint32. Optional. A number to make generated videos deterministic. Specifying a seed number with your request without changing other parameters guides the model to produce the same videos. Values: 0 - 4294967295.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:predictLongRunning

Request JSON body:

{
  "instances": [
    {
      "prompt": "TEXT_PROMPT"
    }
  ],
  "parameters": {
    "storageUri": "OUTPUT_STORAGE_URI",
    "sampleCount": "RESPONSE_COUNT",
    "durationSeconds": "DURATION",
    "enhancePrompt": ENHANCED_PROMPT
  }
}

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curlPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:predictLongRunning"

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:predictLongRunning" | Select-Object -Expand Content

This request returns a full operation name with a unique operation ID. Use this full operation name to poll the status of the video generation request.

{
  "name": "**projects/ PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID/operations/a1b07c8e-7b5a-4aba-bb34-3e1ccb8afcc8**"
}

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Prompt: A text description of what you want a generative AI model to create.
  • Image-to-video: A capability that generates a video based on a starting reference image and a text prompt.
  • Negative prompt: A parameter that specifies what elements to exclude from the generated video.
  • Aspect ratio: The proportional relationship between the width and height of the video.

docs.title: Safety filters
docs.text:
Veo applies safety filters across Vertex AI to help ensure that generated videos and uploaded photos don't contain offensive content. Prompts that violate responsible AI guidelines are blocked.

If you suspect abuse of Veo or any generated output that contains inappropriate material or inaccurate information, use the Report suspected abuse on Google Cloud form.

docs.title: Basics of a good prompt
docs.text:
Good prompts are descriptive and clear. To get your generated video closer to what you want, start with your core idea and then refine it by adding keywords and modifiers.

A comprehensive prompt should include the following elements:

  1. Subject: The main object, person, animal, or scenery in your video.
  2. Context: The background or setting where the subject is placed.
  3. Action: What the subject is doing (for example, walking, running, or turning their head).
  4. Style: The artistic look of the video. This can be general (e.g., photorealistic) or specific (e.g., film noir, 3D cartoon style).
  5. Camera motion: How the camera moves (e.g., aerial view, top-down shot, low-angle shot).
  6. Composition: How the shot is framed (e.g., wide shot, close-up, extreme close-up).
  7. Ambiance: How color and light contribute to the scene's mood (e.g., blue tones, night, warm tones).

docs.title: Prompt examples
docs.text:
The following examples demonstrate how providing different levels of detail in your prompt allows you to get closer to your desired output.

Refining a prompt step-by-stepCreating a stylized character

These videos demonstrate how you can revise your prompt with more specific details to get a more focused and richer result.

Initial prompt

Prompt: The camera dollies to show a close up of a desperate man in a green trench coat that's making a call on a rotary-style wall phone with a green neon light and a movie scene.

Generated output: The first generated video based on the initial prompt.

More detailed prompt

Prompt: A close-up cinematic shot follows a desperate man in a weathered green trench coat as he dials a rotary phone mounted on a gritty brick wall, bathed in the eerie glow of a green neon sign. The camera dollies in, revealing the tension in his jaw and the desperation etched on his face as he struggles to make the call. The shallow depth of field focuses on his furrowed brow and the black rotary phone, blurring the background into a sea of neon colors and indistinct shadows, creating a sense of urgency and isolation.

Generated output: A more detailed prompt results in a video that is more focused with a richer environment.

Highly detailed prompt

Prompt: A video with smooth motion that dollies in on a desperate man in a green trench coat, using a vintage rotary phone against a wall bathed in an eerie green neon glow. The camera starts from a medium distance, slowly moving closer to the man's face, revealing his frantic expression and the sweat on his brow as he urgently dials the phone. The focus is on the man's hands, his fingers fumbling with the dial as he desperately tries to connect. The green neon light casts long shadows on the wall, adding to the tense atmosphere. The scene is framed to emphasize the isolation and desperation of the man, highlighting the stark contrast between the vibrant glow of the neon and the man's grim determination.

Generated output: Adding more detail gave the subject a realistic expression and created an intense and vibrant scene.

These prompts demonstrate how adding more detail can generate an output that is closer to what you want for a stylized character.

Simple prompt

Prompt: A cute creature with snow leopard-like fur is walking in winter forest, 3D cartoon style render.

Generated output:

Detailed prompt

Prompt: Create a short 3D animated scene in a joyful cartoon style. A cute creature with snow leopard-like fur, large expressive eyes, and a friendly, rounded form happily prances through a whimsical winter forest. The scene should feature rounded, snow-covered trees, gentle falling snowflakes, and warm sunlight filtering through the branches. The creature's bouncy movements and wide smile should convey pure delight. Aim for an upbeat, heartwarming tone with bright, cheerful colors and playful animation. Consider adding subtle, whimsical sound effects to enhance the joyful winter atmosphere.

Generated output:

docs.title: Add details to your prompt
docs.text:
These examples show how to refine your prompts by specifying different elements to control the generated video.

SubjectContextActionStyleCamera MotionCompositionAmbiance

The subject description can include a single subject, multiple subjects, and their actions.

Prompt: An architectural rendering of a white concrete apartment building with flowing organic shapes, seamlessly blending with lush greenery and futuristic elements.

Generated output:

The background or context in which the subject is placed is very important. Try placing your subject in a variety of backgrounds, such as on a busy street or in outer space.

Prompt: A satellite floating through outer space with the moon and some stars in the background.

Generated output:

Specify what the subject is doing, such as walking, running, or turning their head.

Prompt: A wide shot of a woman walking along the beach, looking content and relaxed and looking towards the horizon at sunset.

Generated output:

Add keywords to improve generation quality and steer it closer to your intended style, such as shallow depth of field, movie still, minimalistic, surreal, vintage, futuristic, or double-exposure.

Prompt: Film noir style, man and woman walk on the street, mystery, cinematic, black and white.

Generated output:

Specify the camera's movement, such as POV shot, aerial view, tracking drone view, or tracking shot.

Prompt: A POV shot from a vintage car driving in the rain, Canada at night, cinematic.

Generated output:

Define how the shot is framed, such as wide shot, close-up, or low angle.

Extreme close-up

Prompt: Extreme close-up of an eye with city reflected in it.

Generated output:

Wide shot

Prompt: Create a video of a wide shot of surfer walking on a beach with a surfboard, beautiful sunset, cinematic.

Generated output:

Adding colors helps make the video look unique and convey intended emotions. Color palettes play a vital role, influencing the mood and emotional impact. For example, a warm, golden palette can infuse a romantic and atmospheric feel. Examples of color palettes include pastel blue and pink tones, dim ambient lighting, and cold muted tones.

Warm tones

Prompt: A close-up of a girl holding adorable golden retriever puppy in the park, sunlight.

Generated output:

Cool tones

Prompt: Cinematic close-up shot of a sad woman riding a bus in the rain, cool blue tones, sad mood.

Generated output:

docs.title: Use reference images to generate videos
docs.text:
You can bring images to life by using Veo's image-to-video capability. Use your existing assets or generate a new image with a model like Imagen.

When using image-to-video, we recommend the following:

  • Ensure that actions and speech descriptions align with each subject present in the input image.
  • When multiple subjects are present, clearly specify which character is performing an action or speaking. Use distinguishing descriptive details, for example:
    • The man in the red hat.
    • The woman in the blue dress.
View an image-to-video example

Reference image and prompt: Bunny with a chocolate candy bar.

Action prompt: Bunny runs away.

Generated output:

docs.title: Use negative prompts
docs.text:
Negative prompts are a powerful tool to specify what elements to exclude from the video. Instead of using instructive language like "no" or "don't," describe what you want to discourage the model from generating.

  • ❌ Don't: "No walls" or "don't show walls".
  • ✅ Do: "wall, frame".
View a negative prompt example

Initial prompt: Generate a short, stylized animation of a large, solitary oak tree with leaves blowing vigorously in a strong wind. The tree should have a slightly exaggerated, whimsical form, with dynamic, flowing branches. The leaves should display a variety of autumn colors, swirling and dancing in the wind. The animation should feature a gentle, atmospheric soundtrack and use a warm, inviting color palette.

Generated output (without negative prompt):

Negative prompt added: urban background, man-made structures, dark, stormy, or threatening atmosphere.

Generated output (with negative prompt):

docs.title: Add audio
docs.text:

docs.title: General tips for writing prompts
docs.text:
• Use descriptive language: Use adjectives and adverbs to paint a clear picture for Veo.
  • Provide context: If necessary, include background information to help the model understand what you want.
  • Reference specific artistic styles: If you have a particular aesthetic in mind, reference specific artistic styles or art movements.
  • Utilize prompt engineering tools: Consider exploring prompt engineering tools or resources to help you refine your prompts and achieve optimal results. For more information, see Introduction to prompting.
  • Enhance facial details: To improve facial details in your personal and group images, specify facial details as a focus by using words like portrait in the prompt.

To use the generative AI features on Vertex AI, principals such as users, groups, and service accounts must be granted the appropriate Identity and Access Management (IAM) role. You can use predefined roles for common use cases or create custom roles to grant a user-defined set of permissions.

This page describes the predefined roles and specific permissions applicable to generative AI features.

docs.title: Predefined roles
docs.text:
The simplest way to grant access to generative AI features is to assign a predefined role. The following table compares the most common predefined roles for Vertex AI.

Role Description Common Use Case Vertex AI Administrator (roles/aiplatform.admin) Provides full access to all Vertex AI resources, including generative AI features. For principals who need to manage all aspects of Vertex AI, including creating, deleting, and managing resources and permissions. Vertex AI User (roles/aiplatform.user) Provides permissions to use Vertex AI resources, but not to create or delete them. This includes making predictions with generative AI models. docs.title: Bounding box detection
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

With bounding box detection, you can identify and localize objects within images and video. By accurately identifying and delineating objects with bounding boxes, you can unlock a wide range of applications, such as object tracking, image search, and real-world scene analysis.

Key Benefits:

  • Simple: Integrate object detection capabilities into your applications with ease, regardless of your computer vision expertise.
  • Customizable: Produce bounding boxes based on custom instructions (for example, "I want to see bounding boxes of all the green objects in this image"), without having to train a custom model.

Technical Details:

  • Input: Your prompt and associated images or video frames.
  • Output: Bounding boxes in the [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max] format. The top-left corner is the origin. The x and y axes go horizontally and vertically, respectively. Coordinate values are normalized to 0-1000 for every image.
  • Visualization: AI Studio users will see bounding boxes plotted within the UI. Vertex AI users should visualize their bounding boxes through custom visualization code.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text:
Follow the steps to detect bounding boxes

Before you begin

  1. Install the Python SDK for generative AI.

    pip install --upgrade google-genai

    To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

  2. Set environment variables to use the SDK with Vertex AI.

    # Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Step 1: Import libraries and define helpers

Import the necessary libraries and define a helper class and function to handle and visualize the bounding box data.

import requests

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import GenerateContentConfig, HttpOptions, Part, SafetySetting

from PIL import Image, ImageColor, ImageDraw

from pydantic import BaseModel

# Helper class to represent a bounding box
class BoundingBox(BaseModel):
    """
    Represents a bounding box with its 2D coordinates and associated label.

    Attributes:
        box_2d (list[int]): A list of integers representing the 2D coordinates of the bounding box,
                            typically in the format [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max].
        label (str): A string representing the label or class associated with the object within the bounding box.
    """

    box_2d: list[int]
    label: str

# Helper function to plot bounding boxes on an image
def plot_bounding_boxes(image_uri: str, bounding_boxes: list[BoundingBox]) -> None:
    """
    Plots bounding boxes on an image with markers for each a name, using PIL, normalized coordinates, and different colors.

    Args:
        img_path: The path to the image file.
        bounding_boxes: A list of bounding boxes containing the name of the object
        and their positions in normalized [y1 x1 y2 x2] format.
    """
    with Image.open(requests.get(image_uri, stream=True, timeout=10).raw) as im:
        width, height = im.size
        draw = ImageDraw.Draw(im)

        colors = list(ImageColor.colormap.keys())

        for i, bbox in enumerate(bounding_boxes):
            y1, x1, y2, x2 = bbox.box_2d
            abs_y1 = int(y1 / 1000 * height)
            abs_x1 = int(x1 / 1000 * width)
            abs_y2 = int(y2 / 1000 * height)
            abs_x2 = int(x2 / 1000 * width)

            color = colors[i % len(colors)]

            draw.rectangle(
                ((abs_x1, abs_y1), (abs_x2, abs_y2)), outline=color, width=4
            )
            if bbox.label:
                draw.text((abs_x1 + 8, abs_y1 + 6), bbox.label, fill=color)

        im.show()

Step 2: Initialize the client and configure the model

Initialize the client and configure the model parameters, including system instructions, safety settings, and the response schema. The response_schema ensures the output is structured according to the BoundingBox class.

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))

config = GenerateContentConfig(
    system_instruction="""
    Return bounding boxes as an array with labels.
    Never return masks. Limit to 25 objects.
    If an object is present multiple times, give each object a unique label
    according to its distinct characteristics (colors, size, position, etc..).
    """,
    temperature=0.5,
    safety_settings=[
        SafetySetting(
            category="HARM_CATEGORY_DANGEROUS_CONTENT",
            threshold="BLOCK_ONLY_HIGH",
        ),
    ],
    response_mime_type="application/json",
    response_schema=list[BoundingBox],  # Add BoundingBox class to the response schema
)

Step 3: Send the request and visualize the results

Prepare the request with an image and a text prompt. Send the request to the model, then print the structured response and use the helper function to plot the bounding boxes on the image.

image_uri = "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/socks.jpg"

response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents=[
        Part.from_uri(
            file_uri=image_uri,
            mime_type="image/jpeg",
        ),
        "Output the positions of the socks with a face. Label according to position in the image.",
    ],
    config=config,
)
print(response.text)
plot_bounding_boxes(image_uri, response.parsed)

Example response:

[
    {"box_2d": [36, 246, 380, 492], "label": "top left sock with face"},
    {"box_2d": [260, 663, 640, 917], "label": "top right sock with face"},
]

docs.title: Control access to Model Garden models
docs.text:
Vertex AI Model Garden's organization policy lets you centrally control which foundation models your users can access and what actions they can take. By default, any principal with permissions to use Vertex AI can use Model Garden to discover, customize, and deploy a wide variety of Google and third-party models.

Setting a Model Garden policy is useful when you need to enforce that only an approved set of models can be used in your environments. You can define a policy at the organization, folder, or project level to ensure users can only access the models you've approved.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Understand policy evaluation: Policies are evaluated hierarchically. When multiple policies apply to a resource, any explicit deny value overrides any allow value. For more information on how policies are merged and evaluated, see Understanding hierarchy evaluation in the Resource Manager documentation.
  • Required permissions: To manage organization policies, you need the Organization Policy Administrator (roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin) IAM role.
  • Policy limitations:
    • The Model Garden organization policy applies only to models available in Model Garden. It does not apply to models registered in the Vertex AI Model Registry.
    • A single policy cannot exceed 500 total allowed and denied values.
    • Custom policies require you to specify each model individually. You cannot use wildcards or group models by publisher (for example, you can't deny all third-party models with a single rule).

docs.title: How to control access
docs.text: You can control access to Model Garden models by setting an organization policy. This policy can allow all models, deny all models, or define a custom list of allowed or denied models and actions.

docs.title: Choose a policy type
docs.text:
First, decide which type of policy enforcement best suits your governance needs.

Policy Type Description Use Case Allow all models This is the default behavior. All models and actions in Model Garden are accessible to users. Suitable for open development environments where no access restrictions are needed. Deny all models Blocks access to all models and actions in Model Garden. Useful for completely locking down Model Garden access while you define a more granular policy. Custom policy Allows you to specify a list of models and actions to either explicitly allow or deny. - Custom Allow: All models are denied except those on your list. - Custom Deny: All models are allowed except those on your list. Ideal for enforcing a curated list of approved models or blocking specific models that don't meet your compliance or cost requirements.

docs.title: Set a Model Garden access policy
docs.text:
The following workflow outlines the process for configuring a custom policy.

flowchart LR
    A[Choose a policy type] --> B[Identify the model and action];
    B --> C{Set the policy};
    C --> D[Using the Google Cloud console];
    C --> E[Using the gcloud CLI];

    click A "#choose-a-policy-type"
    click B "#step-1-identify-the-model-and-action"
    click C "#step-2-set-the-organization-policy"
    click D "#step-2-set-the-organization-policy"
    click E "#step-2-set-the-organization-policy"
Steps to set a Model Garden access policy

Step 1: Identify the model and action

To specify a model in a custom policy, you need its model ID and the action you want to control. The format is:

publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL_NAME:ACTION

  • PUBLISHER: The publisher of the model (e.g., google, meta).
  • MODEL_NAME: The name of the model (e.g., gemini-1.5-flash-001).
  • ACTION: The specific action to allow or deny.

For example, to control prediction access for the Gemini 1.5 Flash model, you would use publishers/google/models/gemini-1.5-flash-001:predict.

You can find the fully qualified model ID (publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL_NAME) on the model card for each model in Model Garden. For a list of available models, see Explore AI models in Model Garden.

Available Actions

You can control the following actions for each model: * predict: Controls access to online and batch predictions for models with a managed API. * deploy: Controls one-click deployment for models that are deployed on Google Cloud. * tune: Controls access to model tuning features.

Step 2: Set the organization policy

You can set the policy using either the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI. The policy constraint for Model Garden is vertexai.allowedModels.

Google Cloud consolegcloud CLI
  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Organization policies page.
  2. Select the project, folder, or organization for which you want to set the policy.
  3. In the filter bar, search for the policy allowedModels.
  4. Click the Vertex AI Allowed Models policy to open the Policy details page.
  5. Click Edit to configure the policy.
  6. On the Edit policy page, select Customize.
  7. Choose a Policy enforcement option:
    • To allow a specific list, select Allow. Add policy values for each model and action you want to permit.
    • To deny a specific list, select Deny. Add policy values for each model and action you want to block.
  8. Click Save to apply the policy.

For more detailed instructions, see Setting a policy in the Google Cloud console.

  1. Create a YAML file that defines your policy. See the examples in the Policy examples section.
  2. Run the gcloud org-policies set command to apply the policy file to your organization, folder, or project.

To set the policy on an organization: 

gcloud org-policies set POLICY_FILE --organization=ORGANIZATION_ID

To set the policy on a folder: 

gcloud org-policies set POLICY_FILE --folder=FOLDER_ID

To set the policy on a project: 

gcloud org-policies set POLICY_FILE --project=PROJECT_ID
Replace POLICY_FILE with the path to your YAML policy file.

For more detailed instructions, see Setting a policy with the gcloud CLI.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with gcloud CLI commands or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Policy examples
docs.text:
The following examples show the YAML format used to set a policy with the gcloud CLI. Replace ORGANIZATION_ID with your Google Cloud organization ID. For more information, see Getting your organization ID.

Deny a set of models (allow all others)Allow a set of models (deny all others)

This policy denies specific actions on a list of models. All other models and actions are implicitly allowed.

name: organizations/ORGANIZATION_ID/policies/vertexai.allowedModels
spec:
  rules:
  - values:
      deniedValues:
      - publishers/meta/models/llama3:deploy
      - publishers/google/models/gemini-1.5-flash-001:tune
      - publishers/hf-google/models/gemma-2b:deploy

This policy allows specific actions on a list of models. All other models and actions are implicitly denied.

name: organizations/ORGANIZATION_ID/policies/vertexai.allowedModels
spec:
  rules:
  - values:
      allowedValues:
      - publishers/meta/models/llama3:deploy
      - publishers/google/models/gemini-1.5-flash-001:tune
      - publishers/hf-google/models/gemma-2b:deploy

docs.title: Generative AI and data governance
docs.text: Google was the first in the industry to publish an AI/ML Privacy Commitment, which outlines our belief that customers should have the highest level of security and control over their data that is stored in the cloud. That commitment extends to Google Cloud's generative AI products. Google ensures that its teams are following these commitments through robust data governance practices, which include reviews of the data that Google Cloud uses in the development of its products. More details about how Google processes data can also be found in Google's Cloud Data Processing Addendum (CDPA).

docs.title: Training restriction
docs.text: As outlined in Section 17 "Training Restriction" in the Service Terms section of Service Specific Terms, Google won't use your data to train or fine-tune any AI/ML models without your prior permission or instruction. This applies to all managed models on Vertex AI, including GA and pre-GA models.

docs.title: Customer data retention and achieving zero data retention
docs.text:
By default, customer data is retained for limited periods in specific scenarios. To achieve zero data retention, you must take specific actions for each case. The following table summarizes the data retention scenarios for Google models on Vertex AI.

Scenario Data Retention Purpose & Duration How to Achieve Zero Data Retention Data caching for Google models Caches inputs to reduce latency for subsequent prompts. Data is stored for up to 24 hours. Disable data caching at the project level. See Manage data caching. Prompt logging for abuse monitoring Logs prompts to detect potential abuse and policy violations. Applies only to customers governed by the Google Cloud Platform Terms of Service without an Invoiced Cloud Billing account. Request an exception for abuse monitoring. See Abuse monitoring. Grounding with Google Search Stores prompts, contextual information, and generated output for 30 days to improve grounded results and for debugging. There is no way to disable this data storage if you use Grounding with Google Search. Session resumption for Gemini Live API If enabled by the user per API call, stores cached data (text, video, audio) for up to 24 hours to allow reconnection to a previous session. Do not enable the session resumption feature in the API request. See Live API.

docs.title: Manage data caching
docs.text:
You can manage data caching for your Google Cloud project by checking the current status and then enabling or disabling it as needed. The change applies to all Google Cloud regions for your project.

flowchart LR
    A[Get current cache setting] --> B{Decide action};
    B -- Need to disable --> C[Disable caching];
    B -- Need to enable --> D[Enable caching];

click A "#get-current-cache-setting"
click C "#disable-caching"
click D "#enable-caching"

For more information about the permissions required, see Vertex AI access control with IAM.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Get current cache settingDisable cachingEnable caching

Run the following command to determine if caching is enabled or disabled for a project. To run this command, a user must be granted one of the following roles: roles/aiplatform.viewer, roles/aiplatform.user, or roles/aiplatform.admin.

PROJECT_ID=PROJECT_ID
# Setup project_id
$ gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID

# GetCacheConfig
$ curl -X GET -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig

# Response if caching is enabled (caching is enabled by default).
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig"
}

# Response if caching is disabled.
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig"
  "disableCache": true
}

Run the following curl command to disable caching for a Google Cloud project. To run this command, a user must be granted the Vertex AI Administrator role, roles/aiplatform.admin.

PROJECT_ID=PROJECT_ID
# Setup project_id
$ gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID

# Opt-out of caching.
$ curl -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig -d '{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig",
  "disableCache": true
}'

# Response.
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig/operations/${OPERATION_ID}",
  "done": true,
  "response": {
    "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.Empty"
  }
}

If you previously disabled caching and want to re-enable it, run the following curl command. To run this command, a user must be granted the Vertex AI Administrator role, roles/aiplatform.admin.

PROJECT_ID=PROJECT_ID
LOCATION_ID="us-central1"
# Setup project_id
$ gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID

# Opt in to caching.
$ curl -X PATCH     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig -d '{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig",
  "disableCache": false
}'

# Response.
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig/operations/${OPERATION_NUMBER}",
  "done": true,
  "response": {
    "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.Empty"
  }
}

docs.title: Dynamic shared quota (DSQ)
docs.text: Dynamic shared quota (DSQ) serves your pay-as-you-go (PayGo) requests with greater flexibility to adapt to your workload needs without you having to manage quotas and quota increase requests (QIR). With DSQ, there are no predefined quota limits on your usage. Instead, DSQ provides access to a large, shared pool of resources, dynamically allocated based on real-time availability and demand across all customers of that model. When more customers are active, each customer gets a lower amount of throughput. Similarly, if there are fewer active customers, each customer might get higher throughput.

docs.title: When to use Dynamic Shared Quota
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers two main ways to manage throughput for generative AI models: Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) and Provisioned Throughput. DSQ is ideal for applications with variable traffic, while Provisioned Throughput is designed for applications requiring stable performance and high availability.

Use this comparison to decide which option is best for your workload.

Feature Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) Provisioned Throughput Cost Model Pay-as-you-go (PayGo). You only pay for what you use. Billed per hour for a reserved number of processing units. Performance Throughput is dynamic and depends on shared resource availability and overall demand. Stable, predictable, and guaranteed throughput. Use Case Development, testing, and applications with intermittent or unpredictable traffic patterns. Production-grade applications requiring high availability and consistent performance. Availability Access to a large, shared pool of resources. Subject to resource contention during peak demand, which can result in 429 errors. Reserved capacity ensures high availability and protects against "noisy neighbor" issues.

To learn more about Provisioned Throughput, see the Provisioned Throughput overview.

docs.title: How DSQ works
docs.text:
Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) adapts to your traffic patterns and needs and minimizes usage friction. Your project's access to resources under DSQ is not capped by a predefined limit. Instead, it's determined by the overall capacity of the shared pool and the current collective demand from all customers. This model is designed to offer significant flexibility, allowing your workloads to burst and consume more resources when available. Conversely, it also allows all customers of the shared pool to have a chance to access resources when available without requiring per-customer quota configuration.

To ensure a fair and stable experience for all users in the shared resource environment, DSQ intelligently manages how requests are handled, especially during periods of very high demand from isolated sources. Rather than a fixed cap, DSQ employs a dynamic prioritization approach. This means that while the system is designed to accommodate bursts, unusually large and rapid spikes in traffic from a single source might be handled with a different priority than more consistent, steady traffic. This sophisticated management ensures that broad user activity and regular workloads are protected from transient, extreme spikes, promoting overall system stability and equitable access.

Gemini requests with multi-modal inputs are subject to the corresponding system rate limits that include image, audio, video, and document.

docs.title: Understanding Resource Exhaustion 429 errors under DSQ
docs.text:
Encountering a 'resource exhausted' (429) error can be frustrating. With DSQ, this error does not mean you have hit a specific quota limit on your project. Instead, these errors indicate that the shared pool of resources for a specific model in a specific region is experiencing extremely high demand from many users simultaneously. Think of it like trying to get on a very popular train during peak rush hour. There isn't a 'ticket limit' specifically for you, but the train itself might be momentarily full. It's a temporary state of contention for resources, not a fixed limit imposed on your project.

DSQ constantly works to manage and distribute the available capacity fairly and efficiently. When you receive a 429 error, it means instantaneous demand has outstripped the available supply in that shared pool. Unlike a hard quota where you'd be blocked even if resources were idle, DSQ aims to give you access whenever resources are free. The exhaustion error is a reflection of the entire system's current load, not a ceiling on your account.

We recommend implementing retry mechanisms, as availability in this dynamic environment can change quickly. For more tactics on handling Resource Exhaustion errors, see Error code 429.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide for Vertex AI.

docs.title: Enable Data Access audit logs
docs.text:
To monitor who is accessing your Vertex AI resources and how they are being used, you can enable Data Access audit logs. These logs help you track API calls that read configuration or metadata, as well as calls that read or write user-provided data. Enabling these logs is essential for security auditing, tracking usage patterns, and troubleshooting issues.

Data Access audit logs for Vertex AI are categorized into three types:

Log Type Description Admin Read Records operations that read metadata or configuration information. For example, getting the details of a model endpoint. Data Read Records operations that read user-provided data. For example, making a prediction request to an endpoint. Data Write Records operations that write user-provided data. For example, uploading a dataset.

These logs are sent to Cloud Logging, where you can view, query, and set up alerts. For more detailed information about audit logging in Vertex AI, see Vertex AI audit logging information.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Prerequisites

  • To enable or disable Data Access audit logs, you need a role with the logging.configWriter permission, such as the Logging Config Writer (roles/logging.configWriter) IAM role.

  • To view the data_access log stream after it's enabled, you need a role with the logging.privateLogViewer permission, such as the Private Logs Viewer (roles/logging.privateLogViewer) IAM role.

  • Note that enabling Data Access audit logs might affect your Cloud Logging costs. For more information, see Logging pricing.

docs.title: Enable Data Access audit logs workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Go to Audit Logs] --> B[Select Vertex AI service] --> C[Enable log types] --> D[Save configuration]

    click A "#navigate-to-audit-logs"
    click B "#select-vertex-ai"

docs.title: Steps to enable Data Access audit logs
docs.text:
The following steps guide you through enabling Data Access audit logs for Vertex AI in the Google Cloud console.

Step-by-step guide

1. Navigate to the Audit Logs page

In the Google Cloud console, go to the IAM & Admin > Audit Logs page.

Go to Audit Logs

2. Select the Vertex AI service

In the filter bar at the top of the services list, enter Vertex AI. Click on the Vertex AI API result to open its audit logging configuration.

3. Enable the desired log types

In the Log Types tab, select the checkboxes for the Data Access audit log types you want to enable: - Admin Read: To log access to metadata and configuration. - Data Read: To log access to user data. - Data Write: To log modifications to user data.

4. Save the configuration

Click Save. The selected log types are now enabled for your project.

docs.title: View audit logs
docs.text:
After you enable Data Access audit logs, they are sent to Cloud Logging. You can view them using the Logs Explorer.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Logging > Logs Explorer page.

    Go to Logs Explorer

  2. In the Query pane, build a query to filter for the logs you want to see. For example, to view all Data Access logs for Vertex AI, you can use the following query:

    resource.type="audited_resource"
resource.labels.service="aiplatform.googleapis.com"
logName:"data_access"

  3. Click Run query to see the results.
