docs.title: Deploy multiple models to the same endpoint
docs.text: You can deploy more than one model to an endpoint. When you deploy a second model to an endpoint that already has a model deployed, you can choose to deploy the second model with a zero traffic split. After the second model is successfully deployed, you can change the traffic split as needed.

docs.title: Split traffic between models
docs.text:
After you deploy two or more models to the same endpoint, you can split the traffic between them. By splitting traffic, you can assign a percentage of traffic to each model.

For more information, see Update a model's traffic split.

For SDK and curl commands, use the model name claude-3-sonnet@20240229. For pricing details, see the Partner models pricing page.

Use cases

Claude 3 Sonnet is engineered to be dependable for scaled AI deployments across a variety of use cases. It is optimized for the following:

  • Data processing, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and search retrieval.
  • Sales tasks, such as product recommendations, forecasting, and targeted marketing.
  • Time-saving tasks, such as code generation, quality control, and optical character recognition (OCR) in images.
  • Vision tasks, such as processing images to return text output. Also, analysis of charts, graphs, technical diagrams, reports, and other visual content.

docs.title: Get text embeddings
docs.text:
This document describes how to create a text embedding using the Vertex AI Text embeddings API.

Text embeddings are dense vector representations of text. For example, the gemini-embedding-001 model generates 3072-dimensional vectors. Dense vector embedding models use deep-learning methods similar to those used by large language models. Unlike sparse vectors, which tend to map words to numbers directly, dense vectors are designed to represent the meaning of a piece of text. The benefit of using dense vector embeddings in generative AI is that instead of searching for direct word or syntax matches, you can search for passages that align with the meaning of your query, even if the passages don't use the same words.

The vectors are normalized, so you can use cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance to get the same similarity rankings.

  • To learn more about embeddings, see the Embeddings for generative AI overview.
  • For information about which languages each embeddings model supports, see Supported text languages.

To see an example of getting text embeddings, run the "Getting Started with Text Embeddings + Vertex AI Vector Search" Jupyter notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab Open in Colab Enterprise Open in Vertex AI Workbench View on GitHub

Before you begin

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
You can get text embeddings by using the following models. For superior embedding quality, gemini-embedding-001 is our large model designed to provide the highest performance.

Model name Description Output Dimensions Max sequence length Supported text languages gemini-embedding-001 State-of-the-art performance across English, multilingual and code tasks. It unifies the previously specialized models like text-embedding-005 and text-multilingual-embedding-002 and achieves better performance in their respective domains. Read our Tech Report for more detail. up to 3072 2048 tokens Supported text languages text-embedding-005 Specialized in English and code tasks. up to 768 2048 tokens English text-multilingual-embedding-002 Specialized in multilingual tasks. up to 768 2048 tokens Supported text languages

Note: Only use the models as listed in the supported models table. Don't specify a model without the @version suffix or @latest. These model names are not considered valid.

docs.title: Get text embeddings for a snippet of text
docs.text: You can get text embeddings for a snippet of text by using the Vertex AI API or the Vertex AI SDK for Python.

docs.title: API limits
docs.text:
For each request, you're limited to 250 input texts for non-Gemini models, and a single input text for Gemini Embedding models. The API has a maximum input token limit of 20,000. Inputs exceeding this limit result in a 400 error. Each individual input text is further limited to 2048 tokens; any excess is silently truncated. You can also disable silent truncation by setting autoTruncate to false.

For more information, see Text embedding limits.

docs.title: Choose an embedding dimension
docs.text:
All models produce a full-length embedding vector by default. For gemini-embedding-001, this vector has 3072 dimensions, and other models produce 768-dimensional vectors. However, by using the output_dimensionality parameter, you can control the size of the output embedding vector. Selecting a smaller output dimensionality can save storage space and increase computational efficiency for downstream applications, while sacrificing little in terms of quality.

The following examples use the gemini-embedding-001 model.

Troubleshooting

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Set environment variables

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI.

docs.title: Choose an embeddings task type
docs.text: Vertex AI embeddings models can generate optimized embeddings for various task types, such as document retrieval, question and answering, and fact verification. Task types are labels that optimize the embeddings that the model generates based on your intended use case. This document describes how to choose the optimal task type for your embeddings.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
Task types are supported by the following models:

  • text-embedding-005
  • text-multilingual-embedding-002
  • gemini-embedding-001

docs.title: Benefits of task types
docs.text:
Task types can improve the quality of embeddings generated by an embeddings model.

Figure 1. Questions and their answers aren't semantically similar, which means that embeddings won't automatically show their relation.

For example, when building Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, a common design is to use text embeddings and Vector Search to perform a similarity search. In some cases, this can lead to degraded search quality because questions and their answers are not always semantically similar. A question like "Why is the sky blue?" and its answer "The scattering of sunlight causes the blue color" have distinctly different meanings as statements. Without task types, a RAG system won't automatically recognize their relation, as demonstrated in Figure 1. A RAG developer would need to train their model to learn this relationship, which requires advanced data science skills, or use methods like LLM-based query expansion or HyDE, which can introduce high latency and costs.

Figure 2. Task types optimize embeddings for specific tasks. In this case, questions and answers are brought closer together in the embeddings space.

Task types enable you to generate optimized embeddings for specific tasks, saving the time and cost of developing your own task-specific embeddings. As shown in Figure 2, the generated embedding for a query "Why is the sky blue?" and its answer "The scattering of sunlight causes the blue color" would exist in a shared embedding space that represents their relationship. In this RAG example, the optimized embeddings lead to improved similarity searches.

In addition to the query and answer use case, task types also provide optimized embeddings for tasks such as classification, clustering, and fact verification.

docs.title: Task type categories and recommendations
docs.text:
Embedding use cases typically fall into one of two categories: asymmetric or symmetric.

  • Asymmetric: The use case involves a short query and a longer document. This is common in information retrieval tasks like search, question answering, and RAG.
  • Symmetric: The use case involves inputs of similar length or importance, such as comparing two sentences for similarity or classifying a single piece of text.

The following table provides a comprehensive comparison to help you select the best task type for your use case.

Use Case Category Task Type Description Information Retrieval (Asymmetric) RETRIEVAL_QUERY Use for the query text in a search or retrieval task. This is the default query task type. RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT Use for the documents in your corpus that will be searched. QUESTION_ANSWERING Use for queries that are formatted as questions. Use RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT for the corpus. FACT_VERIFICATION Use for queries that are statements to be verified against documents in the corpus. Use RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT for the corpus. CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY Use for natural language queries to retrieve code blocks. Use RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT to embed the code blocks. Semantic Similarity (Symmetric) SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY Use to assess the similarity between two texts of comparable length. Not intended for retrieval. Classification (Symmetric) CLASSIFICATION Use to generate embeddings optimized for classifying texts against a set of labels. Clustering (Symmetric) CLUSTERING Use to generate embeddings optimized for grouping texts based on similarity.

Key takeaway

If your embeddings use case doesn't align with a documented use case, use the RETRIEVAL_QUERY task type by default for your queries and RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT for your corpus.

docs.title: Information retrieval (Asymmetric)
docs.text:
If you want to use embeddings for document search, RAG, or other information retrieval use cases, you need to generate embeddings for both your query and your document corpus using different task types.

  1. Use the RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT task type to create optimized embeddings for your documents (your corpus).
  2. Use one of the following task types to create optimized embeddings for your queries, depending on the nature of the queries:
    • RETRIEVAL_QUERY: Use as the default task type for search queries, such as "best restaurants in Vancouver" or "What is the best cookie recipe?".
    • QUESTION_ANSWERING: Use when queries are formatted as proper questions, such as "Why is the sky blue?".
    • FACT_VERIFICATION: Use when you want to retrieve a document from your corpus that proves or disproves a statement, such as "apples grow underground".
    • CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY: Use to retrieve a relevant code block based on a natural language query, such as "sort an array". Embeddings of the code blocks are computed using RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT.

Key takeaway

To get embeddings for information retrieval, use RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT to embed your documents and an appropriate query task type (like RETRIEVAL_QUERY) to embed your queries.

Code retrieval examples

The text-embedding-005 and gemini-embedding-001 models support the CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY task type, which can be used to retrieve relevant code blocks using plain text queries. To use this feature, embed code blocks using the RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT task type and embed text queries using CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY.

To explore all task types, see the model reference.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

RESTPython

The following example uses the text-embedding-005 model.

PROJECT_ID=PROJECT_ID

curl \
-X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/text-embedding-005:predict -d \
$'{
  "instances": [
    {
      "task_type": "CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY",
      "content": "Function to add two numbers"
    }
  ],
}'

To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Vertex AI SDK for Python API reference documentation.

The following example uses the gemini-embedding-001 model.

from vertexai.language_models import TextEmbeddingInput, TextEmbeddingModel

MODEL_NAME = "gemini-embedding-001"
DIMENSIONALITY = 3072


def embed_text(
    texts: list[str] = ["Retrieve a function that adds two numbers"],
    task: str = "CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY",
    model_name: str = "gemini-embedding-001",
    dimensionality: int | None = 3072,
) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Embeds texts with a pre-trained, foundational model."""
    model = TextEmbeddingModel.from_pretrained(model_name)
    kwargs = dict(output_dimensionality=dimensionality) if dimensionality else {}

    embeddings = []
    # gemini-embedding-001 takes one input at a time
    for text in texts:
        text_input = TextEmbeddingInput(text, task)
        embedding = model.get_embeddings([text_input], **kwargs)
        print(embedding)
        # Example response:
        # [[0.006135190837085247, -0.01462465338408947, 0.004978656303137541, ...]]
        embeddings.append(embedding[0].values)

    return embeddings


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Embeds code block with a pre-trained, foundational model.
    # Using this function to calculate the embedding for corpus.
    texts = ["Retrieve a function that adds two numbers"]
    task = "CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY"
    code_block_embeddings = embed_text(
        texts=texts, task=task, model_name=MODEL_NAME, dimensionality=DIMENSIONALITY
    )

    # Embeds code retrieval with a pre-trained, foundational model.
    # Using this function to calculate the embedding for query.
    texts = [
        "def func(a, b): return a + b",
        "def func(a, b): return a - b",
        "def func(a, b): return (a ** 2 + b ** 2) ** 0.5",
    ]
    task = "RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT"
    code_query_embeddings = embed_text(
        texts=texts, task=task, model_name=MODEL_NAME, dimensionality=DIMENSIONALITY
    )

docs.title: Semantic similarity (Symmetric)
docs.text:
If you want to use embeddings to assess text similarity, use the SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY task type. This task type generates embeddings that are optimized for generating similarity scores between texts of similar length.

For example, you could generate embeddings to compare the similarity of the following texts: * "The cat is sleeping" * "The feline is napping"

When the embeddings are used to create a similarity score, the score is high because both texts have nearly the same meaning.

Key takeaway

To get embeddings that are optimized to assess text similarity, use the SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY task type. This task type is not intended for retrieval use cases.

docs.title: Classification (Symmetric)
docs.text:
If you want to use embeddings to classify texts according to preset labels, use the CLASSIFICATION task type. This task type generates embeddings in an embeddings space that is optimized for classification.

For example, if you generate embeddings for the social media post "I don't like traveling on airplanes," a classification model using these embeddings would likely classify the sentiment as negative.

Key takeaway

To get embeddings that are optimized to classify text using predefined labels, use the CLASSIFICATION task type.

docs.title: Clustering (Symmetric)
docs.text:
If you want to use embeddings to cluster texts based on their similarities, use the CLUSTERING task type. This task type generates embeddings that are optimized for being grouped based on their similarities.

For example, you can generate embeddings for news articles to show users articles that are topically related to the ones they have previously read. After the embeddings are generated and clustered, you can suggest additional sports-related articles to users who read a lot about sports.

Additional use cases for clustering include:

  • Customer segmentation: Group customers with similar embeddings generated from their profiles or activities for targeted marketing.
  • Product segmentation: Cluster product embeddings based on their title and description to help businesses analyze their product segments.
  • Market research: Cluster consumer survey responses or social media data embeddings to reveal hidden patterns and trends in consumer opinions.

Key takeaway

To get embeddings that are optimized for clustering based on similarities, use the CLUSTERING task type.

Preview

The following limitations apply when using these models:

  • Don't use these preview models on mission critical or production systems.
  • These models are available in us-central1 only.
  • Batch predictions are not supported.
  • Customization is not supported.

docs.title: Ground responses using RAG
docs.text:
Grounding is a technique that helps produce model responses that are more trustworthy and factual by connecting them to verifiable sources of information. A common and recommended best practice to implement grounding is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). RAG works by first retrieving relevant data from your specified sources (like documents or websites) and then using that data to inform the generative AI model's response.

For example, without RAG, asking a model "What are our company's latest support policies?" might yield a generic or outdated answer. With RAG, the system first searches your internal policy documents for the most current information and then uses that retrieved text to generate a precise and accurate answer.

Vertex AI provides multiple ways to build a RAG solution, from fully managed services to individual components for custom pipelines.

docs.title: Choose a RAG implementation method
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers flexible options for implementing RAG. You can use the fully managed RAG Engine for a streamlined, end-to-end experience, or build a custom RAG pipeline using individual Vertex AI components for greater control.

The following table compares these two approaches to help you decide which is best for your use case.

Method Description Best for Pros Cons Vertex AI RAG Engine A fully managed, end-to-end service that handles the entire RAG lifecycle, from document ingestion and indexing to retrieval and response generation. Users who want a quick and easy way to implement RAG without managing underlying infrastructure. Ideal for rapid prototyping and common use cases. - Simplified setup and management.- Optimized for performance.- Integrated directly into Vertex AI Studio. - Less control over individual components (e.g., chunking strategy, embedding models). Custom RAG with Vertex AI components A mix-and-match approach where you build your own RAG pipeline using individual, powerful Vertex AI services. Users who need fine-grained control over the RAG process, want to integrate existing systems, or have complex, specialized requirements. - Maximum flexibility and customization.- Ability to swap components (e.g., use a different vector database).- Full control over data processing and retrieval logic. - More complex to design, build, and maintain.- Requires deeper technical expertise.

docs.title: Components for a custom RAG pipeline
docs.text:
If you choose to build a custom solution, you can use the following Vertex AI services as building blocks:

  • Document layout parser: Combines Document AI and Gemini to parse and understand complex document layouts. For more information, see Use the layout parser.
  • Vertex AI Vector Search: A high-performance vector database for storing and searching embeddings.
  • Grounding generation API: An API to implement grounding and connect to a retrieval provider.
  • Check grounding API: An API that compares the model's generated response against the retrieved facts to verify that all statements are grounded.

docs.title: Use Google Search suggestions
docs.text:
When you use grounding with Google Search, you must display any Search suggestions included in the model's response in your production applications. This page outlines the requirements for displaying these suggestions.

For more information on grounding with Google Search, see Grounding with Google Search.

docs.title: Example API response
docs.text:
When you ground a prompt with Google Search, the response metadata contains the search queries that you must display as Search suggestions. The response includes:

  • "content": The LLM-generated response.
  • "webSearchQueries": The list of queries to be used for Search suggestions.

For example, in the following snippet, the model responds to a prompt about a tropical plant and includes a relevant search query in the groundingMetadata.

"predictions": [
  {
    "content": "Monstera is a type of vine that thrives in bright indirect light…",
    "groundingMetadata": {
      "webSearchQueries": ["What's a monstera?"],
    }
  }
]

You must take the queries from the webSearchQueries field and display them as Search suggestions according to the following requirements.

docs.title: Display and behavior requirements
docs.text: The following are the requirements for displaying Search suggestions.

docs.title: General requirements
docs.text:
Do

  • Display the Search suggestion exactly as provided, without any changes.
  • Ensure that interacting with a Search suggestion takes the user directly to the Google Search results page (SRP).

Don't

  • Insert any intermediate screens or additional steps between the user's interaction and the display of the SRP.
  • Display any other search results or suggestions next to the Search suggestion or its associated grounded LLM response.

docs.title: Display and branding
docs.text:
• Display the Search suggestion exactly as provided, without modifying colors, fonts, or appearance. The suggestion must render as specified in the following light and dark mode examples.

    Search suggestion chips in light and dark mode.

  • Whenever a grounded response is shown, its corresponding Search suggestion must remain visible.

  • The field that contains the suggestion chips must be the same width as the grounded response from the LLM.
  • For branding, you must strictly follow Google's guidelines at the Brand Resource Center.

docs.title: Interaction behavior
docs.text:
When a user taps a suggestion chip, they must be taken directly to a Search results page (SRP) for the search term displayed in the chip. The SRP can open either within your application's browser or in a separate browser application. Do not minimize, remove, or obstruct the SRP's display in any way.

The following animation illustrates the required tap-to-SRP interaction.

Example of the tap-to-SRP interaction.

docs.title: Implement Search suggestions
docs.text:
When you use the API to ground a response to Search, the model response provides compliant HTML and CSS styling in the renderedContent field. You can implement this field directly to display the Search suggestions in your application. The provided HTML and CSS automatically adapt to the user's device settings, displaying in either light or dark mode based on the prefers-color-scheme media feature.

For an example of the API response containing renderedContent, see the response section in Grounding with Google Search.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with the API response or implementation, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Grounding with Elasticsearch
docs.text:
This page explains how you can use your Elasticsearch instance to ground model responses on your private data.

Grounding involves using datasets to provide context and facts to ground Large Language Model (LLM) responses. By grounding with Elasticsearch, you can use your existing Elasticsearch indexes to enhance the quality and reliability of Gemini's output. This helps reduce hallucinations and ensures responses are relevant to your data. This lets you build powerful Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) applications such as:

  • Generative search summaries
  • Question-and-answer chatbots with enterprise data
  • Agents grounded in your data

You can ground a model on up to 10 data sources at one time. You can also combine grounding with Elasticsearch with Grounding with Google Search to connect the model with world knowledge or up-to-date information from the internet.

docs.title: Set up a search template in Elasticsearch
docs.text:
This section explains how to configure a search template in your Elasticsearch instance to ground on your data.

Best practices for search templates

For the best grounding responses, use these principles when creating a search template:

  • Include only relevant and useful data. For example, in a product catalog, specifying an image URL might not help the LLM answer prompts about product properties unless the prompt specifically asks for a URL. Similarly, avoid outputting embedding vectors.
  • Provide a higher number of results. Grounding removes Elasticsearch results with low relevance to your prompts. You should provide a higher number of Elasticsearch results to capture all relevant context.
  • Structure results data. Results data can be in one field or spread across multiple fields.
View a sample kNN search template

You can use your own search templates. However, we recommend that you use the generic kNN search template with Elasticsearch grounding. This semantic search with Vertex AI is a generic kNN search.

For additional search templates, see the GitHub repository.

PUT _scripts/google-template-knn-multioutput
{
  "script": {
    "lang": "mustache",
    "source": {
      "_source": {
        "excludes": [ "title_embedding", "description_embedding", "images"]
      },
        "size": "num_hits",
          "knn" : [
          {
            "field": "description_embedding",
            "k": 5,
            "num_candidates": 10,
            "query_vector_builder": {
              "text_embedding": {
                "model_id": "googlevertexai_embeddings_004",
                "model_text": "query"
              }
            },
            "boost": 0.4
          },
          {
            "field": "title_embedding",
            "k": 5,
            "num_candidates": 10,
            "query_vector_builder": {
              "text_embedding": {
                "model_id": "googlevertexai_embeddings_004",
                "model_text": "query"
            }
          },
          "boost": 0.6
          }
          ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Generate grounded responses with Elasticsearch
docs.text:
You can generate grounded responses using the Google Cloud console or the REST API.

ConsoleREST

To ground with Elasticsearch in the Google Cloud console, follow these steps.

Go to Create prompt

Steps to generate a grounded response in the Google Cloud console
  1. In the Settings panel, to ground your data, click the Grounding: Your data toggle.
  2. In the Customize Grounding pane, select Elasticsearch.
  3. Enter the endpoint in the Elasticsearch endpoint field.
  4. Enter the API Key in the Elasticsearch API Key field.
  5. Enter the index in the Elasticsearch index field.
  6. Enter the search template in the Elasticsearch search template field.
  7. Adjust the number of hits by sliding the Number of hits slider.
  8. Click Save.
  9. Enter your prompt.
  10. Click Submit.

This section explains how you use the Vertex AI API to ground your LLM responses.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Before you begin

Before you can ground LLM responses with Elasticsearch, you must complete the following:

  1. Activate the Vertex AI API: Ensure that the Vertex AI API is enabled for your Google Cloud project.
  2. Install and sign in to the Google Cloud CLI: Install and initialize the gcloud CLI.
  3. Elasticsearch setup: Use an existing Elasticsearch cluster and index that you want to use for grounding. Obtain the following information from your Elasticsearch setup:
    • Endpoint: The URL of your Elasticsearch cluster.
    • Index Name: The name of the index you want to search (for example, my-data-index).
    • API Key: An API key that allows access to your Elasticsearch cluster. The API key must start with the prefix ApiKey.
  4. Create an Elasticsearch search template: Use an Elasticsearch data source that uses a reference template that returns result data for grounding.
Prepare and send the API request

To send a text prompt and ground it with Elasticsearch, send a POST request to the Vertex AI API.

1. Prepare the request body

At a minimum, you must provide the request body. Save the following JSON to a file named request.json. Make sure to replace the placeholder variables.

  • QUERY: The text prompt to ground.
  • ELASTIC_SEARCH_ENDPOINT: The absolute endpoint path for the Elasticsearch resource to use.
  • ELASTIC_SEARCH_API_KEY: The API key for the Elasticsearch data endpoint.
  • INDEX_NAME: The name of the Elasticsearch index used for grounding.
  • SEARCH_TEMPLATE_NAME: The Elasticsearch search template used for grounding.
  • NUM_HITS: The number of results returned from the Elasticsearch data source and used for grounding.
{
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "QUERY"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "tools": [{
    "retrieval": {
      "externalApi": {
        "api_spec": "ELASTIC_SEARCH",
        "endpoint": "ELASTIC_SEARCH_ENDPOINT",
        "apiAuth": {
          "apiKeyConfig": {
            "apiKeyString": "ApiKey ELASTIC_SEARCH_API_KEY"
          }
        },
        "elasticSearchParams": {
          "index": "INDEX_NAME",
          "searchTemplate": "SEARCH_TEMPLATE_NAME",
          "numHits": "NUM_HITS",
        }
      }
    }
  }]
}

For more information on other API fields such as system instructions and multi-turn chats, see Generative AI beginner's guide.

2. Send the API request

Execute the following curl command. Make sure to replace the placeholder variables:

  • LOCATION: The region to process the request. For more information, see Generative AI on Vertex AI locations.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: The ID of the multimodal model.
curl -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
    -d @request.json \
"https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:generateContent"

docs.title: Understand your response
docs.text:
If your model prompt successfully grounds to Elasticsearch data stores, the model's responses include metadata with citations and source content. If low source relevance or incomplete information occurs within the model's response, then metadata might not be provided, and the prompt response won't be grounded.

You should receive a JSON response similar to the following:

{
  "candidates": [
    {
      "content": {
        "role": "model",
        "parts": [
          {
            "text": "Based on the information ..."
          }
        ]
      },
      "finishReason": "STOP",
      "safetyRatings": [ "..." ],
      "groundingMetadata": {
        "groundingChunks": [
          {
            "retrievedContext": {
              "text": "ipsum lorem ..."
            }
          },
          {...},
          {...},
        ],
        "groundingSupports": [
          {
            "segment": {
              "startIndex": 25,
              "endIndex": 147,
              "text": "ipsum lorem ..."
            },
            "groundingChunkIndices": [1,2],
            "confidenceScores": [0.6626542, 0.82018316],
          },
        ],
      },
    }
  ],
}

The following is a breakdown of the output data:

  • role: Indicates the sender of the grounded answer. Because the response always contains grounded text, the role is always model.
  • text: The grounded answer generated by the LLM.
  • groundingMetadata: Information about the grounding source, which contains the following elements:
    • groundingChunks: A list of results from your Elasticsearch index that support the answer.
    • groundingSupports: Information about a specific claim within the answer that can be used to show citations:
      • segment: The part of the model's answer that is substantiated by a grounding chunk.
      • groundingChunkIndices: The index of the grounding chunks in the groundingChunks list that corresponds to this claim.
      • confidenceScores: A number from 0 to 1 that indicates how grounded the claim is in the provided set of grounding chunks. Not available for Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and later models.

docs.title: Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI
docs.text:
Preview

Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI is covered by the Pre-GA Offerings Terms of the Google Cloud Terms of Service. Pre-GA features may have limited support, and changes to pre-GA features may not be compatible with other pre-GA versions. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI is available for testing by customers in the United States.

Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI combines the power of Gemini with Google Maps, which has access to information on over 250 million places. This integration, available through Vertex AI, is designed to help you create a new generation of generative applications.

This page explains how you can use Google Maps to ground your LLM responses.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI is a service that lets you use Google Maps data with LLMs to provide more accurate and context-aware responses to your prompts. Grounding with Google Maps is integrated with Vertex AI to support your use of geographical data with your Gemini model.

Grounding with Google Maps helps you to discover new places, plan for events, and get recommendations for a variety of locations. You can do the following:

  • Ask a conversational assistant about the area and any nearby places. Your assistant has access to travel time information and can let you know how far a place is from your location. For example, Are there any parks nearby?
  • See personalized descriptions of the place that matches your criteria. For example, Can you tell me more about the parks and any family-friendly restaurants that are within a walkable distance?

Grounding with Google Maps lets you create generative AI applications from an LLM-powered chat using geospatial context to generate a personalized location-based summary to help you make better decisions.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
This section lists the models that support grounding with Google Maps.

  • Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (Preview)
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash with Live API native audio (Preview)
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash with Live API (Preview)
  • Gemini 2.5 Pro
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash

For more information about the Gemini models, see Gemini models.

docs.title: Access to Grounding with Google Maps
docs.text:
The following workflow outlines the steps to gain access and enable Grounding with Google Maps for your project.

flowchart LR
    A[Request Access] --> B[Enable Maps Grounding API]
    B --> C[Enable Maps JavaScript API]
    C --> D[Configure in Vertex AI Studio]

    click A "#request-access"
    click B "#enable-maps-grounding-api"
    click C "#enable-maps-javascript-api"
    click D "#configure-in-vertex-ai-studio"
Steps to access Grounding with Google Maps

1. Request access

To request access to use Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI for specific projects, complete and submit the Opt-in or Opt-out to use Google Maps form. This form requires your email address, company name, project ID, and your acceptance of the terms.

If you don't have a project, see Creating and managing projects.

2. Enable the Maps Grounding API

In the Google Cloud console, go to the Maps Grounding API page.

Go to Maps Grounding API

Click Enable. Select a project, and the Maps Grounding API page displays.

3. Enable the Maps JavaScript API

In the Google Cloud console, go to the Maps JavaScript API page.

Go to Maps JavaScript API

Click Enable. Select a project, and the APIs & Services page displays.

4. Configure and verify in Vertex AI Studio

To verify that Google Maps is enabled, go to Vertex AI Studio.

Go to Vertex AI Studio

  • Select the project for which you enabled the APIs.
  • In the Tools section of the model's pane, click the Grounding: Google toggle to turn on the feature.
  • Select Google Maps Preview.
  • Enter the API Key.
    • If you don't have an API Key, see Creating API keys.
    • To limit the use of the APIs, see Restricting API keys.
  • Select the Location for a location-based response.
  • Click Apply.

docs.title: Place properties
docs.text: This section lists place properties that are used to describe locations and are used by Grounding with Google Maps to generate responses. These properties determine the types of questions that Grounding with Google Maps can answer.

docs.title: Sample place properties
docs.text:
This list provides an alphabetized sampling of properties about places that your model might use to generate responses.

  • Address
  • Cash only
  • Credit card
  • Curbside pickup
  • Debit card

docs.title: Examples of using place properties
docs.text:
The following examples use place properties in questions about different types of places. Grounding with Google Maps uses the properties to understand your intent and then provides relevant answers based on the data associated with places in Google Maps.

  • Plan a family dinner: You might ask, Is "The Italian Place" good for children, and do they offer takeout? What is their rating? Answers to these questions help you determine if a restaurant is suitable for a family and if it offers a convenient service.

  • Check accessibility for a friend: You might ask, I need a restaurant that has a wheelchair accessible entrance. A response to this prompt might help you determine if the location meets specific accessibility needs.

  • Find a location for a late-night snack: You might ask, Is "Burger Joint" open now? Do they serve dinner? What are their opening hours for Friday? Answers to these questions help you find an open establishment serving a specific meal during a particular time.

  • Meet a client for coffee: You might ask, Does "Cafe Central" have Wifi? Do they serve coffee? What is their price level, and do they accept credit cards? Answers to these questions help you assess the suitability of a cafe for a business meeting based on amenities, offerings, and payment options.

docs.title: Use Grounding with Google Maps to ground your model
docs.text:
You can use the Google Maps API to ground your model's responses. These code samples demonstrate how to use the Maps API to ground your model's responses using Grounding with Google Maps.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Gen AI SDK for PythonREST

Install the SDK

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Set environment variables

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI:

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

Run the code

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import (
    ApiKeyConfig,
    AuthConfig,
    GenerateContentConfig,
    GoogleMaps,
    HttpOptions,
    Tool,
)

# TODO(developer): Update below line with your Google Maps API key
GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY = "YOUR_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY"

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))

response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents="Recommend a good restaurant in San Francisco.",
    config=GenerateContentConfig(
        tools=[
            # Use Google Maps Tool
            Tool(
                google_maps=GoogleMaps(
                    auth_config=AuthConfig(
                        api_key_config=ApiKeyConfig(
                            api_key_string=GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY,
                        )
                    )
                )
            )
        ],
    ),
)

print(response.text)
# Example response:
# 'San Francisco boasts a vibrant culinary scene...'

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: The region to process the request.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: The model ID of the multimodal model.
  • TEXT: The text instructions to include in the prompt.
  • API_KEY: Your API key.
  • LATITUDE: The latitude of the location.
  • LONGITUDE: The longitude of the location.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:generateContent

Request JSON body:

{
  "contents": [{
    "role": "user",
    "parts": [{
      "text": "TEXT"
    }]
  }],
  "tools": [{
    "googleMaps": {
      "authConfig": {
        "apiKeyConfig": {
          "apiKeyString": "API_KEY"
        }
      }
    }
  }],
  "toolConfig": {
    "retrievalConfig": {
      "latLng": {
        "latitude": LATITUDE,
        "longitude": LONGITUDE
      }
    }
  },
  "model": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID"
}

To send your request, expand one of these options:

curl (Linux, macOS, or Cloud Shell)PowerShell (Windows)

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \  
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \  
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \  
     -d @request.json \  
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:generateContent"

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token  
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }  

Invoke-WebRequest `  
    -Method POST `  
    -Headers $headers `  
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `  
    -InFile request.json `  
    -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:generateContent" | Select-Object -Expand Content

docs.title: Render the Google Maps contextual widget
docs.text:
Rendering the Google Maps contextual widget is required as part of using Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI. In any response that is grounded with Google Maps, there is a corresponding googleMapsWidgetContextToken that is used to render the contextual widget in close proximity to the generated response.

  "googleMapsWidgetContextToken": "widgetcontent/AcBXPQdpWQWbap9H-OH8sEKmOXxmEKAYvff0tvthhneMQC3VrqWCjpnPBl4-Id98FGiA_S_t8aeAeJj0T6JkWFX56Bil8oBSR0W8JH3C_RSYLbTjxKdpxc9yNn6JcZTtolIRZon9xi6WpNGuSyjcIxWu2S0hwpasNOpUlWrG1RxVCB4WD1fsz_pwR236mG36lMxevXTQ_JnfdYNuQwQ4Lc3vn...<snip>...
  Ts5VJE_b3IC5eE_6wez0nh61r7foTUZpP7BXMwxR-7Wyfcj6x1v6mIWsFGr1o0p_HSAMNqWPg-aFVnkPLhAkOR6MaNZOfezTva-gxHlu7z_haFvYxcUE1qfNVQ",

Your page that displays the widget must use the alpha version of the Google Maps JS API. For more information, see Load the Maps JavaScript API.

You must use the API key that was enabled for Grounding with Google Maps in Vertex AI to load the Google Maps JS API.

Example: Create a widget using HTML

This code sample demonstrates how to create a widget using HTML.

  <body>
    <gmp-place-contextual id="widget"></gmp-place-contextual>
  </body>
Example: Update the context token with JavaScript

In your Javascript, use the following method to update the context token:

function updateWidget(contextToken) {
  let widget = document.querySelector('#widget');
  widget.contextToken = contextToken;
}
Example: Create a widget dynamically with JavaScript

You can also create a widget dynamically with the following code:

async function createWidget(contextToken) {
  await google.maps.importLibrary('places');
  let widgetContainer = document.querySelector('#wc');  // a div that contains the widget
  const placeContextualElement = new
      google.maps.places.PlaceContextualElement({ contextToken });
  widgetContainer.appendChild(placeContextualElement);
}
Example: Configure widget layout with HTML

This HTML code sample demonstrates how to use configuration options to toggle between two different layouts (compact or vertical).

    <gmp-place-contextual id="widget">
      <gmp-place-contextual-list-config layout="compact">
      </gmp-place-contextual-list-config>
    </gmp-place-contextual>
Example: Disable the map with HTML

This HTML code sample demonstrates how to disable the map.

    <gmp-place-contextual id="widget">
      <gmp-place-contextual-list-config map-hidden>
      </gmp-place-contextual-list-config>
    </gmp-place-contextual>
Example: Configure widget layout and map visibility with JavaScript

This JavaScript code sample demonstrates how to specify a compact layout and how to hide the map.

  const widgetConfig = new google.maps.places.PlaceContextualListConfigElement({
    layout: 'compact',
    mapHidden: true
  });
  widget.appendChild(widgetConfig);

docs.title: Grounding with Google Search
docs.text:
This page explains how to ground a model's responses using Google Search, which uses publicly available web data. Grounding helps ensure responses are based on the latest and most accurate information available on the internet.

If you want to connect your model with world knowledge, a wide range of topics, or up-to-date information, use grounding with Google Search.

Important: If you receive Google Search suggestions with a response, that response is a "Grounded Result" subject to the Grounding with Google Search terms in the Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. To use Google Search suggestions, see Use Google Search suggestions.

Note for web publishers: Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI does not use web pages for grounding that have disallowed Google-Extended. Web publishers can manage inclusion in Google-Extended with a robots.txt file.

To learn more about model grounding in Vertex AI, see the Grounding overview.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
Using Google Search as a tool enables complex prompts and workflows that require planning, reasoning, and up-to-date information. Key benefits include:

  • Grounding responses to the latest and most accurate information.
  • Retrieving and analyzing artifacts from the web.
  • Finding relevant images, videos, or other media to assist in multimodal reasoning.
  • Performing coding, technical troubleshooting, and other specialized tasks.
  • Finding region-specific information or assisting in content translation.
  • Finding relevant websites for browsing.

docs.text:
You can ground a model with publicly available web data using the Vertex AI Studio, the Generative AI SDKs, or the REST API.

Example

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"

    genai "google.golang.org/genai"
)

// generateWithGoogleSearch shows how to generate text using Google Search.
func generateWithGoogleSearch(w io.Writer) error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    client, err := genai.NewClient(ctx, &genai.ClientConfig{
        HTTPOptions: genai.HTTPOptions{APIVersion: "v1"},
    })
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to create genai client: %w", err)
    }

    modelName := "gemini-2.0-flash-001"
    contents := []*genai.Content{
        {Parts: []*genai.Part{
            {Text: "When is the next total solar eclipse in the United States?"},
        }},
    }
    config := &genai.GenerateContentConfig{
        Tools: []*genai.Tool{
            {GoogleSearch: &genai.GoogleSearch{}},
        },
    }

    resp, err := client.Models.GenerateContent(ctx, modelName, contents, config)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to generate content: %w", err)
    }

    respText, err := resp.Text()
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to convert model response to text: %w", err)
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(w, respText)

    // Example response:
    // The next total solar eclipse in the United States will occur on March 30, 2033, but it will only ...

    return nil
}

docs.title: Use of alternative search engine options

docs.title: Grounding with Vertex AI Search
docs.text:
This page explains how you can ground model responses by using your data from Vertex AI Search. Grounding connects a model to your enterprise data to provide responses that are more accurate, specific, and relevant. This process is also known as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

Grounding with your data supports a maximum of 10 Vertex AI Search data sources and can be combined with Grounding with Google Search.

Grounding on proprietary or unstructured documents (PDF, HTML, TXT, etc.) stored in Cloud Storage. Data Source URLs of websites to include or exclude. Files in a Cloud Storage bucket.   2. In the Website Content box, click Select. The Specify the websites for your data store pane is displayed.

  1. Open the Create Data Store page in the Google Cloud console.

docs.title: Step 3: Understand your response
docs.text:
The API response includes the LLM-generated text, called a candidate. If your model prompt successfully grounds to your data source, the response includes grounding metadata that identifies the parts of the response derived from your data. However, this metadata might not be provided if source relevance is low or information is incomplete.

The following is a breakdown of the output data:

  • Role: Indicates the sender of the grounded answer. Because the response always contains grounded text, the role is always model.
  • Text: The grounded answer generated by the LLM.
  • Grounding metadata: Information about the grounding source, which contains the following elements:
    • Grounding chunks: A list of results from your data store that support the answer.
    • Grounding supports: Information about a specific claim within the answer that can be used to show citations:
      • Segment: The part of the model's answer that is substantiated by a grounding chunk.
      • Grounding chunk index: The index of the grounding chunks in the groundingChunks list that corresponds to this claim.
      • Confidence scores: A number from 0 to 1 that indicates how grounded the claim is in the provided set of grounding chunks. Not available for Gemini 2.5 and later.

docs.title: Grounding with your search API
docs.text:
You can connect Gemini to your external data sources by grounding with your search API. This lets you use any search service as a grounding source for Gemini, which helps to ensure that responses are based on the latest and most relevant information from your systems. This is particularly useful for enterprise-specific data that isn't publicly available.

This page explains how to configure and use grounding using any search API with Gemini.

docs.title: Choose your approach
docs.text:
Before you begin, decide whether you will use an existing, compatible API endpoint or set up a new one.

Approach Description Best for... Use a compatible endpoint Configure Gemini to call your existing search API directly. You already have a search API that meets the required schema and can be secured with an API key. Set up a new search API endpoint Create a new, secure API endpoint using Cloud Functions and API Gateway to wrap your data source. You need to build a new API to interface with your data source (e.g., a database or internal search engine) and make it compatible with Gemini.

docs.title: How grounding with your search API works
docs.text:
When you ground with your search API, Gemini can query an external API endpoint that you provide. This allows Gemini to use your custom search functionality as a tool to enhance its responses. It enables more dynamic and context-aware interactions, as the model can seek out information from your specified data sources when needed.

During a generation request, Gemini can make a call to the external API endpoint with a search query. Your API should then return relevant data snippets. Gemini uses these snippets as a source of truth to generate a more accurate and grounded response.

You can combine grounding using your search API with other grounding sources like Google Search. A generation request supports up to 10 grounding sources and multi-tool queries where Gemini can take advantage of different information sources to generate the best possible answer.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
The following models support grounding with your API:

  • Gemini 1.5 Pro
  • Gemini 1.5 Flash
  • Gemini 1.0 Pro

For more information, see Gemini models.

docs.title: Search API requirements
docs.text: To use your existing search infrastructure with Gemini, your API endpoint must meet the following requirements.

docs.title: API schema
docs.text:
• HTTP method: POST
  • Request Body (from Gemini to your API): 
    {
  "query": "the user's search query string"
}
  • Response body (from your API to Gemini): A JSON array of objects. Each object represents a search result and must contain snippet and uri fields. 
    [
  {
    "snippet": "A text snippet containing the answer or relevant information.",
    "uri": "A URI/URL linking to the source of the information, or a relevant identifier."
  },
  {
    "snippet": "Another piece of information.",
    "uri": "https://example.com/another-source"
  }
]
    If no results are found, your API endpoint should return an empty array [].

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Grounding with your search API supports the use of an API key to secure your API endpoint. Gemini sends this API key as a query parameter named key.

docs.title: Considerations for your search API
docs.text:
Review the following considerations to help you choose your search API:

  • Snippet quality: The snippet text returned by your API is crucial. It should be concise yet informative enough for Gemini to use as a factual basis for its response.
  • Latency: Your search API should respond quickly. High latency in your API increases the overall response time from Gemini.
  • Error handling: Implement robust error handling in your Cloud Function or search API. If your API frequently errors or times out, it negatively impacts Gemini's ability to generate grounded responses.
Use a compatible endpointSet up a new search API endpoint

If you already have an API endpoint that meets the schema and authentication requirements, you can directly configure it in your Gemini API calls.

If you don't have a compatible API endpoint, this guide walks you through setting one up using Cloud Functions and API Gateway.

flowchart LR
    A[Step 1: Create Cloud Function] --> B[Step 2: Secure with API Gateway]
    B --> C[Step 3: Create and Restrict API Key]

click A "#step-1-create-the-cloud-function"
click B "#step-2-secure-with-api-gateway"
click C "#step-3-create-and-restrict-an-api-key"
Before you begin
  1. Ensure that the Vertex AI API is enabled in your Google Cloud project.
  2. Make sure you have the Google Cloud CLI installed and initialized.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Step 1: Create the Cloud Function

A Cloud Function can act as an intermediary that receives queries from Gemini, issues appropriate queries to your existing search infrastructure (such as a database, internal search engine, or vector search), and then formats the results in the schema Gemini understands. For more information, see the Cloud Functions documentation.

This example uses a hardcoded product list for demonstration. You'll need to replace the data retrieval logic with calls to your actual search system.

1. Create the function files

  • main.py 

    import functions_framework
import json
from flask import jsonify

@functions_framework.http
def custom_search_wrapper_minimal(request):
    """
    HTTP Cloud Function to provide a minimal, fixed response for Gemini grounding.
    """
    if request.method != 'POST':
        return 'Only POST requests are accepted', 405

    request_json = request.get_json(silent=True)

    if not request_json or 'query' not in request_json:
        return jsonify({"error": "Invalid request. JSON body with 'query' field is required."}), 400

    user_query = request_json['query']
    print(f"Received query: '{user_query}'. Responding with fixed data.")

    # --- FIXED RESPONSE ---
    # This is a hardcoded response. In a real scenario, you would
    # use the 'user_query' to fetch relevant data.
    fixed_results = [
        {
            "snippet": "This is a fixed snippet from your custom Search API. The original query was: " + user_query,
            "uri": "https://example.com/docs/fixed-test-data"
        },
        {
            "snippet": "Another piece of fixed information to demonstrate the list format.",
            "uri": "https://example.com/another-fixed-source"
        }
    ]
    # --- END OF FIXED RESPONSE ---

    return jsonify(fixed_results)

  • requirements.txt 

    functions-framework>=3.0.0
Flask>=2.0.0

2. Deploy the function

Navigate to the directory containing main.py and requirements.txt and run the following command. Replace YOUR_REGION with your chosen Google Cloud region (e.g., us-central1).

gcloud functions deploy custom_search_wrapper \
  --runtime python311 \
  --trigger-http \
  --entry-point custom_search_wrapper_minimal \
  --region YOUR_REGION \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --gen2
* --allow-unauthenticated is specified because API Gateway will handle authentication.

Important: After deployment, note the trigger URL, which has a format of https://....run.app. You will use this URL in the next step.

Step 2: Secure with API Gateway

API Gateway provides a secure, managed entry point to your Cloud Function and lets you enforce API key authentication. For more information, see the API Gateway documentation.

1. Create an OpenAPI specification

Create a file named openapi-spec.yaml. This file defines how API Gateway exposes your Cloud Function. Replace YOUR_CLOUD_FUNCTION_TRIGGER_URL with the trigger URL you noted in the previous step.

swagger: '2.0'
info:
  title: Custom Search API for Gemini Grounding
  description: Wraps an internal search function, secured by API Key for Gemini.
  version: 1.0.0
schemes:
  - https
produces:
  - application/json
consumes:
  - application/json
paths:
  /v0/search:
    post:
      summary: Custom search endpoint for Gemini
      operationId: customSearchForGemini
      x-google-backend:
        address: YOUR_CLOUD_FUNCTION_TRIGGER_URL # Replace with your Cloud Function trigger URL
      parameters:
        - name: body
          in: body
          required: true
          schema:
            type: object
            properties:
              query:
                type: string
      security:
        - api_key_query: []
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Search results
          schema:
            type: array
            items:
              type: object
              properties:
                snippet:
                  type: string
                uri:
                  type: string
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
        '401':
          description: Unauthorized (Missing or invalid API key)
        '500':
          description: Internal server error
securityDefinitions:
  api_key_query:
    type: apiKey
    name: key # Gemini will send its API key using this query parameter name
    in: query

2. Deploy API Gateway

Execute the following gcloud CLI commands, replacing YOUR_PROJECT_ID and YOUR_REGION.

# 1. Create an API
gcloud api-gateway apis create custom-search-gemini-api --project=YOUR_PROJECT_ID

# 2. Create an API Config from your OpenAPI spec
gcloud api-gateway api-configs create v1 \
  --api=custom-search-gemini-api \
  --openapi-spec=openapi-spec.yaml \
  --project=YOUR_PROJECT_ID \
  --display-name="Version 1"

# 3. Create a Gateway
gcloud api-gateway gateways create custom-search-gateway \
  --api=custom-search-gemini-api \
  --api-config=v1 \
  --location=YOUR_REGION \
  --project=YOUR_PROJECT_ID

After deployment, the hostname (gateway URL) has the format https://custom-search-gateway-UNIQUE_ID.nw.gateway.dev. You can use this to construct the full endpoint URL for Gemini (e.g., https://custom-search-gateway-UNIQUE_ID.nw.gateway.dev/v0/search).

Step 3: Create and restrict an API key

You must create an API key that Gemini will use to access your API Gateway endpoint. For more information, see Managing API keys.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the APIs & Services > Credentials page. Go to Credentials
  2. Click Create credentials and select API key.
  3. Click Show key and copy the generated API key. Store the key in a secure location. This is the key you will provide to Gemini.
  4. Click Edit API key or click the key name to open the key's settings.
  5. In the API restrictions section, do the following:
    1. Select the Restrict key option.
    2. In the dropdown menu, select your API Gateway managed service. It should be named after your API, such as Custom Search API for Gemini Grounding API.
    3. If the key isn't included or if you intend to manage the gateway with the API using this key, ensure that the API Gateway API (apigateway.googleapis.com) is also selected. For grounding, the key needs access to your specific API service hosted by API Gateway. Note: It is a best practice to use a separate key or service account for management tasks.
  6. Click Save.

Your API Gateway endpoint is now secured. When you use the endpoint, you must pass the API key as a query parameter. For example: https://custom-search-gateway-UNIQUE_ID.nw.gateway.dev/v0/search?key=YOUR_GENERATED_API_KEY

docs.title: Configure the externalApi tool
docs.text:
When making a request to the Gemini API, include the tools parameter with a retrieval tool configured for the externalApi. Key fields include the following:

  • api_spec:"SIMPLE_SEARCH": This tells Gemini to use the predefined input and output schema.
  • endpoint: The full URL to your API Gateway endpoint, such as https://YOUR_GATEWAY_HOSTNAME/v0/search.
  • apiAuth.apiKeyConfig.apiKeyString: The API key that Gemini uses to authenticate with your API. Gemini appends this key as ?key=<YOUR_API_KEY> to the endpoint URL.

docs.title: Send the request
docs.text:
Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: The region to process the request, such as us-central1.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: The model ID of a compatible Gemini model, such as gemini-1.0-pro-002.
  • USER_PROMPT: The text instructions to include in the prompt.
  • EXTERNAL_API_ENDPOINT: The full URL to your secured API Gateway endpoint that Gemini calls, such as https://YOUR_GATEWAY_HOSTNAME/v0/search. This endpoint must adhere to the specified API schema.
  • EXTERNAL_API_KEY: The API key you generated and configured for your API Gateway. Gemini uses this key to authenticate with your endpoint.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:generateContent

Request JSON body:

{
  "contents": [{
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [{
          "text": "USER_PROMPT"
      }]
  }],
  "tools": [{
      "retrieval": {
        "externalApi": {
          "api_spec": "SIMPLE_SEARCH",
          "endpoint": "EXTERNAL_API_ENDPOINT",
          "apiAuth": {
            "apiKeyConfig": {
              "apiKeyString": "EXTERNAL_API_KEY"
            }
          }
        }
      }
  }]
}

To send your request, choose one of the following options:

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

cURLPowerShell

curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d @request.json \
"https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:generateContent"

docs.title: Grounding overview
docs.text:
In generative AI, grounding is the process of connecting a model's responses to verifiable sources of information. For example, if you ask a model about your company's latest product features, grounding ensures the model bases its answer on your internal product documentation rather than on public, and possibly outdated, information.

By providing models with access to specific data sources, grounding tethers their output to your data, which reduces the chances of the model inventing content (a behavior known as hallucination). This is particularly important in situations where accuracy and reliability are critical.

docs.title: Benefits of grounding
docs.text:
Grounding provides the following benefits:

  • Reduces model hallucinations, which are instances where the model generates content that isn't factual.
  • Anchors model responses to your specific data sources.
  • Enhances auditability by providing citations to the original sources.

docs.title: Grounding options in Vertex AI
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers several ways to ground model output. Use the following table to help you decide which option is best for your use case.

Grounding option Best for... Data source Grounding with Google Search Connecting your model to the vast, publicly available information on the internet. Google Search index Grounding with Google Maps Providing location-based, context-aware responses using Google Maps data. Google Maps Platform APIs Grounding Gemini with Elasticsearch Using your own private data stored in Elasticsearch to generate grounded responses (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). Your Elasticsearch indexes Web Grounding for Enterprise Grounding responses using a curated index of specific websites you define. A custom web index

docs.title: Web Grounding for Enterprise
docs.text: This page describes how to use the Web Grounding for Enterprise API to generate responses that are grounded on the web. The indexed content is a subset of what's available on Google Search and is suitable for customers in highly-regulated industries, such as finance, healthcare, and the public sector.

docs.title: When to use Web Grounding for Enterprise
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers two methods for grounding models on web content. Web Grounding for Enterprise is designed for organizations that require stringent compliance controls. If you don't require these controls, Grounding with Google Search offers access to a broader web index.

The following table provides a comparison between the two web grounding methods:

Feature Web Grounding for Enterprise Grounding with Google Search Compliance Designed for highly-regulated industries. Supports ML processing in US or EU multi-regions, no logging of customer data, and VPC Service Controls. General purpose; does not offer the same compliance controls. Data Handling No customer data is persisted. CMEK and Access Transparency are not applicable. Standard data handling policies apply. Web Index Uses a curated subset of the Google Search index suitable for enterprise use cases. Uses the comprehensive, full Google Search index. Ideal Use Case Generating grounded responses where data residency, no-logging, and other compliance features are critical. Applications that benefit from the broadest possible web knowledge and do not have strict compliance constraints.

docs.title: Use the API
docs.text:
To generate grounded responses with Web Grounding for Enterprise, you must provide the enterpriseWebSearch tool in your request to a Gemini model.

In your request, set the following fields:

  • Contents.parts.text: The text query you want to send to the API.
  • tools.enterpriseWebSearch: The tool that enables Web Grounding for Enterprise for Gemini.

The following examples show how to send a grounded request.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Python SDKREST

Install the SDK

To get started, install the Python SDK. 

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Send a grounded request

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI, then run the following Python code.

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import (
    EnterpriseWebSearch,
    GenerateContentConfig,
    HttpOptions,
    Tool,
)

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))

response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents="When is the next total solar eclipse in the United States?",
    config=GenerateContentConfig(
        tools=[
            # Use Enterprise Web Search Tool
            Tool(enterprise_web_search=EnterpriseWebSearch())
        ],
    ),
)

print(response.text)
# Example response:
# 'The next total solar eclipse in the United States will occur on ...'

Replace the following variables with your project's values:

  • PROJECT_NUMBER: Your project number.
  • LOCATION: Your region (for example, us-central1).
  • TEXT: Your prompt.
  curl -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "x-server-timeout: 60" \
    https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/gemini-2.0-flash:generateContent -d '{
      "contents": [{
        "role": "user",
        "parts": [{
          "text": "TEXT"
        }]
      }],
      "tools": [{
        "enterpriseWebSearch": {}
      }]
    }'

docs.title: Base64 encode and decode files
docs.text: To include image or other binary data in a JSON REST request, you must encode that data as a Base64 string. This document shows you how to Base64 encode and decode files for use in Google Cloud API requests.

docs.title: Base64 encode files
docs.text:
When making a REST request, you must use JSON as the request body. JSON is a text format that doesn't support binary data directly, so you need to convert binary data into text using Base64 encoding.

Most development environments provide a native base64 utility to encode a binary file into ASCII text data. You can also use client libraries to handle encoding within your application workflow.

Method Best for Command line Quick, one-off tasks or simple shell scripting without a full application context. Client libraries Integrating encoding directly into your application's code for automated and repeatable workflows.

docs.title: Encode using the command line
docs.text:
To encode a file from the command line, use the utility that corresponds to your operating system.

LinuxmacOSWindowsPowerShell

Encode the file using the base64 command-line tool. Use the -w 0 flag to prevent line-wrapping.

base64 INPUT_FILE -w 0 > OUTPUT_FILE

Encode the file using the base64 command-line tool.

base64 -i INPUT_FILE -o OUTPUT_FILE

Encode the file using the Base64.exe tool.

Base64.exe -e INPUT_FILE > OUTPUT_FILE

Encode the file using the Convert.ToBase64String method.

[Convert]::ToBase64String([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes("./INPUT_FILE")) > OUTPUT_FILE

After encoding your file, you can inline the Base64-encoded data in your JSON request payload.

{
  "instances": [
    {
      "prompt": "TEXT_PROMPT",
      "image": {
        "bytes_base64_encoded": "B64_BASE_IMAGE"
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Encode using client libraries
docs.text:
Embedding binary data into requests manually is not practical for most applications. Instead, you can embed Base64-encoded files within your client code. All supported programming languages have built-in functions for Base64 encoding.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

PythonNode.jsJavaGo 
# Import the base64 encoding library.
import base64

# Pass the image data to an encoding function.
def encode_image(image):
    with open(image, "rb") as image_file:
        encoded_string = base64.b64encode(image_file.read())
    return encoded_string

// Read the file into memory.
var fs = require('fs');
var imageFile = fs.readFileSync('/path/to/file');

// Convert the image data to a Buffer and base64 encode it.
var encoded = Buffer.from(imageFile).toString('base64');

// Import the Base64 encoding library.
import org.apache.commons.codec.binary.Base64;

// Encode the image.
String encodedString = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(imageFile.getBytes());

import (
    "bufio"
    "encoding/base64"
    "io"
    "os"
)

// Open image file.
f, _ := os.Open("image.jpg")

// Read entire image into byte slice.
reader := bufio.NewReader(f)
content, _ := io.ReadAll(reader)

// Encode image as base64.
base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(content)

docs.title: Base64 decode files
docs.text:
API responses return generated or edited images as Base64-encoded strings. You can use the following client library samples to decode this data and save it locally as an image file.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

PythonNode.jsJavaGo 
# Import the base64 encoding library.
import base64

# Pass the base64 encoded image data to a decoding function and save image file.
def decode_image(b64_encoded_string):
   with open("b64DecodedImage.png", "wb") as fh:
     fh.write(base64.decodebytes(b64_encoded_string))

var fs = require('fs');

// Create buffer object, specifying base64 as encoding
var buf = Buffer.from(base64str,'base64');

// Write buffer content to a file
fs.writeFile("b64DecodedImage.png", buf, function(error){
  if(error){
    throw error;
  }else{
    console.log('File created from base64 string');
    return true;
  }
});

// Import libraries
import org.apache.commons.codec.binary.Base64;
import org.apache.commons.io.FileUtils;

// Create new file
File file = new File("./b64DecodedImage.png");
// Convert base64 encoded string to byte array
byte[] bytes = Base64.decodeBase64("base64");
// Write out file
FileUtils.writeByteArrayToFile(file, bytes);

// Import packages
import (
   "encoding/base64"
   "io"
   "os"
)

// Add encoded file string
var b64 = `TWFuIGlz...Vhc3VyZS4=`

// Decode base64-encoded string
dec, err := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(b64)
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

// Create output file
f, err := os.Create("b64DecodedImage.png")
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}
defer f.Close()

if _, err := f.Write(dec); err != nil {
    panic(err)
}
if err := f.Sync(); err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

docs.title: Controlled Customization
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is in Preview.

To request access to use this Imagen feature, fill out the Imagen on Vertex AI access request form.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Controlled customization lets you influence the structure of a generated image by providing a guide image alongside your text prompt. This technique gives you fine-grained control over the output, ensuring the generated image adheres to the composition and shapes of the guide image while adopting the style described in your prompt.

Key parameters include: * Guide image type: The type of image used to control the generation. This can be a standard color image or a structural map like a Canny edge detection image. * Imagen Control scale: A value that determines how strongly the generated image should adhere to the guide image. A higher value means stricter adherence.

docs.title: Choosing a guide image type
docs.text:
You can guide the image generation process using different types of images. The primary methods involve using a standard RGB image or a pre-processed Canny edge map. The following table helps you decide which to use.

Guide Image Type Description Use Case Standard RGB The model automatically extracts structural cues (like edges and depth) from a standard color image to guide the generation. Best for when you want to quickly restyle an existing image without manual pre-processing. The model infers the structure for you. Canny Edge You provide a black-and-white image showing only the detected edges of a source image. Best for when you need precise control over the output's structure. By providing the edge map directly, you explicitly define the composition.

docs.text:
