docs.title: Model monitoring metrics
docs.text:
Generative AI on Vertex AI provides a prebuilt model observability dashboard to view the behavior, health, and performance of fully-managed models. Fully-managed models, also known as Model as a Service (MaaS), are provided by Google and include Google's Gemini models and partner models with managed endpoints. Metrics from self-hosted models aren't included in the dashboard.

Generative AI on Vertex AI automatically collects and reports activity from MaaS models to help you quickly troubleshoot latency issues and monitor capacity.

Model observability dashboard example.

docs.title: Available monitoring metrics
docs.text:
The model observability dashboard displays a subset of metrics that are collected by Cloud Monitoring, such as model request per second (QPS), token throughput, and first token latencies. View the dashboard to see all the available metrics.

For descriptions of each metric, see the aiplatform section on the Google Cloud metrics page.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
As an application developer, you can view how your users are interacting with the models that you've exposed. For example, you can view how model usage (model requests per second) and the compute intensity of user prompts (model invocation latencies) are trending over time. Consequently, because these metrics are related to model usage, you can also estimate costs for running each model.

When an issue arises, you can quickly troubleshoot from the dashboard. You can check if models are responding reliably and in a timely manner by viewing API error rates, first token latencies, and token throughput.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Vertex AI captures dashboard metrics only for API calls to a model's endpoint. Google Cloud console usage, such as metrics from Vertex AI Studio, aren't added to the dashboard.

docs.title: View the dashboard
docs.text:
The following workflow shows how to navigate to the model observability dashboard.

flowchart LR
    A[Navigate to the Vertex AI Dashboard] --> B[Open the Model Observability dashboard] --> C[Filter metrics];

click A "#navigate-to-the-vertex-ai-dashboard"
click B "#open-the-model-observability-dashboard"
click C "#filter-metrics"
Steps to view the dashboard

1. Go to the Vertex AI Dashboard

In the Vertex AI section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Dashboard page.

Go to Vertex AI

2. Open the Model Observability dashboard

In the Model observability section, click Show all metrics to view the model observability dashboard in the Google Cloud Observability console.

Note

The observability section is available only if you or another user has made API calls to a MaaS model in your project.

3. Filter metrics

To view metrics for a specific model or in a particular location, set one or more filters at the top of the dashboard page.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Model versions and lifecycle
docs.text: This document defines key terms related to the lifecycle stages and important dates for Gemini and embedding models that are available on Vertex AI. It also provides recommended upgrades for the models and points you to available migration paths.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text:
• Stable model: A publicly released version of the model that is available and supported for production use starting on the release date. A stable model version is typically released with a retirement date, which indicates the last day that the model is available. After this date, the model is no longer accessible or supported by Google.

    • Latest stable model: The latest version within the model family recommended for new and active projects. It should be the target for migrations from earlier versions. See Latest stable models.
    • Legacy stable model: A model version that has been superseded by the latest stable model. Although legacy stable models are still supported, you should strongly consider migrating to the latest model to receive the latest features and improvements. Access to legacy stable models might be restricted for new projects. See Legacy stable models.

  • Retired model: The model version is past its retirement date and has been permanently deactivated. Retired models are no longer accessible or supported by Google. API requests referencing a retired model ID typically return a 404 error. See Retired models.

  • Recommended upgrade: The latest stable model that we recommend switching to. Latest stable models tend to offer better performance and more capabilities as compared to legacy stable models. See the recommended upgrades in the Legacy stable models and Retired models sections.

docs.title: Generative AI beginner's guide
docs.text:
This beginner's guide introduces you to the core technologies of generative AI and explains how they fit together to power chatbots and applications. Generative AI (also known as genAI or gen AI) is a field of machine learning (ML) that develops and uses ML models for generating new content.

Generative AI models are often called large language models (LLMs) because of their large size and ability to understand and generate natural language. However, depending on the data that the models are trained on, these models can understand and generate content from multiple modalities, including text, images, videos, and audio. Models that work with multiple modalities of data are called multimodal models.

Google provides the Gemini family of generative AI models designed for multimodal use cases, capable of processing information from multiple modalities, including images, videos, and text.

docs.title: Content generation
docs.text:
For generative AI models to generate content that's useful in real-world applications, they need to have the following capabilities:

  • Learn how to perform new tasks: Generative AI models are designed to perform general tasks. If you want a model to perform tasks that are unique to your use case, you need to be able to customize the model. On Vertex AI, you can customize your model through model tuning.

  • Access external information: Generative AI models are trained on vast amounts of data. However, for these models to be useful, they need to be able to access information outside of their training data. For example, if you want to create a customer service chatbot powered by a generative AI model, the model needs access to information about your products and services. In Vertex AI, you use grounding and function calling to help the model access external information.

  • Block harmful content: Generative AI models might generate unexpected output, including text that's offensive or insensitive. To maintain safety and prevent misuse, the models need safety filters to block prompts and responses that are determined to be potentially harmful. Vertex AI has built-in safety features that promote the responsible use of our generative AI services.

docs.title: Generative AI workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows how these different capabilities work together to generate content. Each step in the diagram is explained in the section below.

flowchart LR
    A[Prompt] --> B[Foundation models] --> C[Model customization] --> D[Access external information] --> E[Citation check] --> F[Responsible AI and safety] --> G[Response]

    click A "#prompt"
    click B "#foundation-models"
    click C "#model-customization"
    click D "#access-external-information"
    click E "#citation-check"
    click F "#responsible-ai-and-safety"
    click G "#response"
An overview of the generative AI workflow

Prompt

The generative AI workflow typically starts with a prompt. A prompt is a natural language request sent to a generative AI model to elicit a response. Depending on the model, a prompt can contain text, images, videos, audio, documents, or a combination of modalities (multimodal).

For example, a simple text prompt could be: "Write a short poem about the moon."

Creating a prompt to get the desired response from the model is a practice called prompt design. While prompt design is a process of trial and error, there are principles and strategies you can use to guide the model toward the desired output. Vertex AI Studio offers a prompt management tool to help you manage your prompts.

Foundation models

Prompts are sent to a generative AI foundation model for response generation. Vertex AI provides access to a variety of models through a managed API. You can explore Google models, as well as open models and models from Google partners, in Model Garden.

Model Family Primary Use Case Modalities Gemini API Advanced reasoning, multi-turn chat, code generation Text, images, video, audio (multimodal) Imagen API High-quality image generation, editing, and captioning Images, text MedLM (Deprecated) Medical question answering and summarization Text

Model customization

You can customize the default behavior of Google's foundation models so that they consistently generate desired results without requiring complex prompts. This customization process is called model tuning. Model tuning can help reduce the cost and latency of your requests by allowing you to simplify your prompts. Vertex AI also offers model evaluation tools to help you assess the performance of your tuned model. After your tuned model is production-ready, you can deploy it to an endpoint and monitor its performance, similar to standard MLOps workflows.

Access external information

Vertex AI offers multiple ways to give the model access to external APIs and real-time information.

Method Description Best for... Grounding Connects model responses to a specified source of truth (your data or web search) to reduce hallucinations and anchor responses in factual data. Ensuring responses are based on specific, verifiable information and providing citations. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Connects models to external knowledge sources like document repositories or databases to retrieve relevant information before generating a response. Building chatbots or Q&A systems that need to answer questions based on a large, private knowledge base. Function calling Lets the model interact with external APIs to get real-time information (e.g., weather, stock prices) or perform actions (e.g., book a flight, send an email). Integrating the model with other tools and services to perform real-world tasks.

Citation check

After the response is generated, Vertex AI checks whether citations need to be included. If a significant amount of text in the response comes from a particular source, that source is added to the citation metadata in the response.

Responsible AI and safety

The final check that the prompt and response go through is the safety filters. Vertex AI evaluates both the prompt and the response against safety categories. If the score for one or more categories exceeds the configured threshold, the response is blocked, and Vertex AI returns a fallback response.

Response

If the prompt and response pass the safety filter checks, the response is returned. Typically, the response is returned all at once. However, with Vertex AI, you can also receive responses progressively as they are generated by enabling streaming.

docs.title: Best practices with large language models (LLMs)
docs.text: This document outlines best practices for working with large language models (LLMs) on Vertex AI. It covers guidance for multimodal prompts and strategies for reducing response latency.

docs.title: Multimodal prompts
docs.text:
For information on best practices for multimodal prompts, see the following pages based on the modality that you're working with:

  • Image understanding
  • Video understanding
  • Audio understanding
  • Document understanding

docs.title: Reduce latency
docs.text: When you build interactive applications, response time, also known as latency, plays a crucial role in the user experience. This section explores the concept of latency in the context of Vertex AI LLM APIs and provides actionable strategies to minimize it and improve the response time of your AI-powered applications.

docs.title: Understand latency metrics for LLMs
docs.text:
Latency refers to the time it takes for a model to process your input prompt and generate a corresponding output response.

When examining latency with a model, consider the following:

  • Time to first token (TTFT) is the time that it takes for the model to produce the first token of the response after receiving the prompt. TTFT is particularly relevant for applications utilizing streaming, where providing immediate feedback is crucial.

  • Time to last token (TTLT) measures the overall time taken by the model to process the prompt and generate the response.

docs.title: Choose the right model for your use case
docs.text: Vertex AI provides a diverse range of models with varying capabilities and performance characteristics. Carefully evaluate your requirements regarding speed and output quality to choose the model that best aligns with your use case. For a list of available models, see Explore all models.

docs.title: Optimize prompt and output length
docs.text:
The number of tokens in both your input prompt and expected output directly impacts processing time. Minimize your token count to reduce latency.

  • Craft clear and concise prompts that effectively convey your intent without unnecessary details or redundancy. Shorter prompts reduce your time to first token.

  • Use system instructions to control the length of the response. Instruct the model to provide concise answers or limit the output to a specific number of sentences or paragraphs. This strategy can reduce your time to last token.

  • Adjust the temperature. Experiment with the temperature parameter to control the randomness of the output. Lower temperature values can lead to shorter, more focused responses, while higher values can result in more diverse, but potentially longer, outputs.

  • Restrict output by setting a limit. Use the max_output_tokens parameter to set a maximum limit on the length of the generated response length, preventing overly long output. However, be cautious as this might cut off responses mid-sentence.

docs.title: Stream responses
docs.text:
With streaming, the model starts sending its response before it generates the complete output. This enables real-time processing of the output, and you can immediately update your user interface and perform other concurrent tasks.

Streaming enhances perceived responsiveness and creates a more interactive user experience.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Responsible AI
docs.text:
Large language models (LLMs) can translate language, summarize text, generate creative writing, generate code, power chatbots and virtual assistants, and complement search engines and recommendation systems. At the same time, as an early-stage technology, their evolving capabilities and uses create potential for misapplication, misuse, and unintended or unforeseen consequences. LLMs can generate output that you don't expect, including text that's offensive, insensitive, or factually incorrect.

Given these risks and complexities, Vertex AI generative AI features are designed with Google's AI Principles in mind. However, it is important for developers to understand and test their models to deploy them safely and responsibly. To aid developers, Vertex AI Studio has built-in content filtering, and our generative AI APIs have safety attribute scoring to help you test Google's safety filters and define confidence thresholds that are right for your use case and business. For more information, see the following section on safety filters and attributes.

When you integrate our generative AI APIs into your unique use case and context, you might need to consider additional responsible AI factors and limitations. We encourage customers to follow recommended practices for fairness, interpretability, privacy, and security.

docs.title: Safety filters and attributes
docs.text: The safety filters and attributes available depend on the model you use. To learn how to use the safety features available for the Gemini API, see Safety settings for Gemini.

docs.title: Model limitations
docs.text: You might encounter the following limitations when using generative AI models.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text: Edge cases are unusual, rare, or exceptional situations that are not well-represented in the training data. These cases can lead to limitations in model performance, such as overconfidence, misinterpretation of context, or inappropriate outputs.

docs.title: Model hallucinations, grounding, and factuality
docs.text: Generative AI models can lack factuality about real-world knowledge, physical properties, or accurate understanding. This limitation can lead to model hallucinations, which are instances where the model generates outputs that sound plausible but are factually incorrect, irrelevant, inappropriate, or nonsensical. To reduce this chance, you can ground models in your specific data. To learn more, see Grounding overview.

docs.title: Data quality and tuning
docs.text: The quality, accuracy, and bias of the prompt or data input into a model can have a significant impact on its performance. If users enter inaccurate data or poorly constructed prompts, the model can produce suboptimal or false outputs.

docs.title: Bias amplification
docs.text: Generative AI models can inadvertently amplify existing biases present in their training data, leading to outputs that can reinforce societal prejudices and the unequal treatment of certain groups.

docs.title: Language quality
docs.text: While models demonstrate impressive multilingual capabilities on many benchmarks, the majority of these benchmarks (including all fairness evaluations) are in English. Performance can be less effective for non-English languages or for English dialects with less representation in the training data. For more information, see the Google Research blog.

docs.title: Fairness benchmarks and subgroups
docs.text: Google Research's fairness analyses of our generative AI models don't provide an exhaustive account of all potential risks. For example, we focus on biases along gender, race, ethnicity, and religion axes, but perform the analysis only on English language data and model outputs. For more information, see the Google Research blog.

docs.title: Limited domain expertise
docs.text: Generative AI models can lack the depth of knowledge required to provide accurate and detailed responses on highly specialized or technical topics, leading to superficial or incorrect information. For specialized, complex use cases, models should be tuned on domain-specific data. Meaningful human supervision is required in contexts with the potential to materially impact individual rights.

docs.title: Length and structure of inputs and outputs
docs.text: Generative AI models have a maximum input and output token limit. If the input or output exceeds this limit, the model might perform poorly, and safety classifiers are not applied. While our models are designed to handle a wide range of text formats, their performance can be affected if the input data has an unusual or complex structure.

docs.title: Recommended practices
docs.text:
To use this technology safely and responsibly, it is important to consider risks specific to your use case, users, and business context in addition to the built-in technical safeguards.

We recommend taking the following steps:

  1. Assess your application's security risks.
  2. Perform safety testing appropriate to your use case.
  3. Configure safety filters if required.
  4. Solicit user feedback and monitor content.

docs.title: Report abuse
docs.text: You can report suspected abuse of the Service or any generated output that contains inappropriate material or inaccurate information by using the following form: Report suspected abuse on Google Cloud.

docs.title: Additional resources
docs.text:
• Learn about abuse monitoring.
  • Learn more about Google's recommendations for Responsible AI practices.
  • Read our blog, A shared agenda for responsible AI progress.

docs.title: Experiment with parameter values
docs.text:
Each call that you send to a generative model includes parameter values that control how the model generates a response. The model can generate different results for different parameter values. Experimenting with these values is key to finding the optimal settings for your specific task.

The parameters available can differ between models. The most common parameters are temperature, top-P, max output tokens, and seed.

docs.title: Parameter overview
docs.text:
This table provides a high-level overview of the most common generative model parameters.

Parameter Description Effect Max output tokens The maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. Specify a lower value for shorter responses and a higher value for longer responses. Temperature Controls the degree of randomness in token selection. Lower temperatures are ideal for prompts requiring a more deterministic and less open-ended response. Higher temperatures can lead to more diverse or creative results. Top-P Changes how the model selects tokens for output. Tokens are selected from most to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses. Seed An integer that, when fixed, helps produce more deterministic responses. When you use the same seed value, the model attempts to return the same response. However, deterministic output is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Max output tokens
docs.text:
The maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately four characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words.

Specify a lower value for shorter responses and a higher value for potentially longer responses.

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text:
The temperature is used for sampling during response generation, which occurs when topP and topK are applied. Temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection. Lower temperatures are good for prompts that require a less open-ended or creative response, while higher temperatures can lead to more diverse or creative results. A temperature of 0 is deterministic, meaning the highest probability tokens are always selected.

If the model returns a response that's too generic, too short, or gives a fallback response, try increasing the temperature.

Gemini models support a temperature value between 0.0 and 2.0. The default temperature is 1.0.

docs.title: Top-P
docs.text:
Top-P changes how the model selects tokens for output. Tokens are selected from the most probable to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. For example, if tokens A, B, and C have a probability of 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 and the top-P value is 0.5, then the model selects either A or B as the next token by using temperature and excludes C as a candidate.

Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.

docs.title: Seed
docs.text:
Preview

This is a preview feature.

When the seed is fixed to a specific value, the model makes a best effort to provide the same response for repeated requests. Deterministic output isn't guaranteed. Also, changing the model or other parameter settings, such as the temperature, can cause variations in the response even when you use the same seed value. By default, a random seed value is used.

docs.title: Break down complex tasks into simpler prompts
docs.text:
For complex tasks that require multiple instructions or steps, you can improve the model's responses by breaking your prompts into subtasks. Smaller prompts can help you improve controllability, debugging, and accuracy.

There are two primary methods for breaking down complex prompts:

  • Chain prompts: Split a task into sequential subtasks.
  • Aggregate responses: Split a task into parallel subtasks and combine the results.

docs.title: When to use each method
docs.text:
Before you start, use the following table to decide which method is best suited for your task.

Method Best for... Data Flow Chain prompts Tasks with sequential dependencies, where the output of one step is the required input for the next. Sequential: Task 1 -> Task 2 -> Task 3 Aggregate responses Tasks that can be performed independently and in parallel, with their results combined in a final step. Parallel: Task 1a + Task 1b -> Final Task

docs.title: Chain prompts
docs.text: For complex tasks that involve multiple sequential steps, make each step a prompt and chain the prompts together in a sequence. In this sequential chain of prompts, the output of one prompt in the sequence becomes the input of the next prompt. The output of the last prompt in the sequence is the final output.

docs.title: Example: Analyze customer feedback
docs.text:
Suppose you run a telecommunications business and want to use a model to analyze customer feedback. The workflow involves identifying common issues, classifying them into categories, and then generating solutions for each category.

flowchart LR
    A[Customer Feedback] --> B(Task 1: Identify customer issues)
    B --> C(Task 2: Classify issues into categories)
    C --> D(Task 3: Generate solutions)
    D --> E[Final Output]

click B "#task-1-identify-customer-issues"
click C "#task-2-classify-issues-into-categories"
click D "#task-3-generate-solutions"
Steps to analyze customer feedback

Task 1: Identify customer issues

The first task is to extract meaningful data from raw customer feedback. A prompt that achieves this task might be similar to the following, where CUSTOMER_FEEDBACK is a file that contains the customer feedback:

Prompt: 

Extract the main issues and sentiments from the customer feedback on our telecom services.
Focus on comments related to service disruptions, billing issues, and customer support interactions.
Please format the output into a list with each issue/sentiment in a sentence, separated by semicolon.

Input: CUSTOMER_FEEDBACK
The expected model response is a list of extracted issues and sentiments from the customer feedback.

Task 2: Classify issues into categories

Next, use the output from the previous task to classify the data into categories. This helps you understand the types of issues customers face. A prompt that achieves this task might look similar to the following, where TASK_1_RESPONSE is the response from the previous task:

Prompt: 

Classify the extracted issues into categories such as service reliability, pricing concerns, customer support quality, and others.
Please organize the output into JSON format with each issue as the key, and category as the value.

Input: TASK_1_RESPONSE
The expected model response is a set of categorized issues in JSON format.

Task 3: Generate solutions

Finally, prompt the model to generate actionable recommendations based on the categorized issues to improve customer satisfaction. This prompt uses the response from the previous task, where TASK_2_RESPONSE is the response from the previous task:

Prompt: 

Generate detailed recommendations for each category of issues identified from the feedback.
Suggest specific actions to address service reliability, improving customer support, and adjusting pricing models, if necessary.
Please organize the output into a JSON format with each category as the key, and recommendation as the value.

Input: TASK_2_RESPONSE
The expected model response contains recommendations for each category, aimed at improving customer experience and service quality.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Aggregate responses
docs.text: In cases where you have complex tasks that don't need to be performed in a specific order, you can run parallel prompts and aggregate the model's responses in a final step.

docs.title: Example: Create a record store stocklist
docs.text:
Suppose you own a record store and want to use a model to help you decide which records to stock. You can analyze music streaming trends and your store's sales data in parallel and then combine the insights to create a stocklist.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Parallel Tasks"
        A[Store Sales Data] --> B(Task 1a: Analyze sales data)
        C[Streaming Data] --> D(Task 1b: Analyze streaming data)
    end
    B --> E(Task 2: Aggregate data)
    D --> E
    E --> F[Final Stocklist]

click B "#task-1a-analyze-sales-data"
click D "#task-1b-analyze-streaming-data"
click E "#task-2-aggregate-data"
Steps to create a stocklist

Task 1a: Analyze sales data

First, analyze your store's sales data. A prompt that achieves this task might be similar to the following, where STORE_SALES_DATA is a file that contains the sales data:

Prompt: 

Analyze the sales data to identify the number of sales of each record.
Please organize the output into a JSON format with each record as the key, and sales as the value.

Input: STORE_SALES_DATA
The expected output is a JSON object containing the number of sales for each record.

Task 1b: Analyze streaming data

In parallel, analyze the streaming data. A prompt that achieves this task might be similar to the following, where STREAMING_DATA is a file that contains the streaming data:

Prompt: 

Analyze the streaming data to provide a the number of streams for each album.
Please organize the output into a JSON format with each album as the key, and streams as the value.

Input: STREAMING_DATA
The expected output is a JSON object containing the number of streams for each album.

Task 2: Aggregate data

Now, aggregate the data from both parallel tasks to help plan your purchasing decisions. To aggregate the data, include the output from both tasks as the input. A prompt that achieves this might look similar to the following, where TASK_1A_RESPONSE and TASK_1B_RESPONSE are the responses from the previous tasks:

Prompt: 

Recommend a stocklist of about 20 records based on the most sold and most streamed records.
Roughly three quarters of the stock list should be based on record sales, and the rest on streaming.

Input: TASK_1A_RESPONSE and TASK_1B_RESPONSE
The expected output is a suggested stocklist of about 20 records, prioritizing records with a proven sales history while also considering streaming popularity.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Give clear and specific instructions
docs.text: Giving a model instructions on what to do is an effective and efficient way to customize its behavior. Be clear, concise, and direct in your instructions, providing the necessary context and outlining the desired output. Instructions can be as simple as a list of step-by-step directions or as complex as mapping out a user's experience and mindset.

docs.title: How to write effective instructions
docs.text:
Effective instructions apply the following principles:

  • Tell the model what to do.
  • Be clear and specific.
  • Specify any constraints or formatting requirements for the output.

docs.title: Compare generic and specific instructions
docs.text:
Suppose you own a cheeseburger restaurant and want to use a model to learn which menu items are the most popular. You want the model to format transcripts of customer orders in JSON so that you can quickly identify menu items.

The following examples demonstrate how the model's response changes when you provide generic instructions versus specific instructions that follow the principles of effective instruction writing.

Generic instructionsSpecific instructions

With generic instructions, the model produces a response with more JSON fields than you need to identify the menu items customers are ordering.

Prompt:

**Extract the transcript in JSON.**
Transcript:
Speaker 1 (Customer): Hi, can I get a cheeseburger and large fries, please?
Speaker 2 (Restaurant employee): Coming right up! Anything else you'd like to add to your order?
Speaker 1: Hmmm, maybe a small orange juice. And could I get the fries with ketchup on the side?
Speaker 2: No problem, one cheeseburger, one large fries with ketchup on the side, and a small
orange juice. That'll be $5.87. Drive through to the next window please.

Response:

{
  "speakers": [
    {
      "speaker": "Customer",
      "utterances": [
        "Hi, can I get a cheeseburger and large fries, please?"
      ]
    },
    {
      "speaker": "Restaurant Employee",
      "utterances": [
        "Coming right up! Anything else you'd like to add to your order?"
      ]
    },
    {
      "speaker": "Customer",
      "utterances": [
        "Hmm, maybe a small orange juice. And could I get the fries with ketchup on the
        side?"
      ]
    },
    {
      "speaker": "Restaurant Employee",
      "utterances": [
        "No problem, one cheeseburger, one large fries with ketchup on the side, and a
        small orange juice. That'll be $5.87. Drive through to the next window please."
      ]
    }
  ]
}
(gemini-pro)

By making the output constraints more specific, you can guide the model to deliver a more helpful response for your use case.

Prompt:

**Extract the items from this transcript in JSON and separate drinks from food.**
Transcript:
Speaker 1 (Customer): Hi, can I get a cheeseburger and large fries, please?
Speaker 2 (Restaurant employee): Coming right up! Anything else you'd like to add to your order?
Speaker 1: Hmmm, maybe a small orange juice. And could I get the fries with ketchup on the side?
Speaker 2: No problem, one cheeseburger, one large fries with ketchup on the side, and a small
orange juice. That'll be $5.87. Drive through to the next window please.

Response:

{
  "drinks": [
    "orange juice"
  ],
  "food": [
    "cheeseburger",
    "large fries"
  ]
}
(gemini-pro)

By applying the principles of effective instruction, the prompt was improved to generate a response that contained exactly the data required for this use case.

docs.title: Add contextual information
docs.text:
In your prompt, you can include instructions and information that the model needs to solve a problem instead of assuming that the model has all of the required information. This contextual information helps the model understand the constraints and details of what you're asking it to do.

Effective contextual information includes the following:

  • Background information (context) for the model to refer to when generating responses.
  • Rules or pre-programmed responses to steer the model's behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The following examples ask the model to give troubleshooting guidance for a router. The first prompt provides no context, while the second includes a troubleshooting guide for the model to use.

Without contextual informationWith contextual information

When a prompt lacks specific context, the model relies on its general training data, which can result in generic or inaccurate responses.

Prompt:

What should I do to fix my disconnected wifi? The light on my Google Wifi router is yellow and
blinking slowly.

Response:

1. **Check the Cables:**
- Make sure that all cables are securely connected to your Google Wifi router and modem.
- Try replacing the cables with new ones to ensure they are not faulty.


2. **Reboot the Router:**
- Unplug your Google Wifi router and modem from the power outlet.
- Wait for at least 30 seconds.
- Plug the modem and router back in and wait for them to start up.


3. **Factory Reset the Router:**
- Resetting the router will restore it to its default settings.
- Find the small reset button on the back of the router.
- Press and hold the reset button with a paper clip or similar object for 10 seconds.
- Release the button and wait for the router to restart.


4. **Check Your Internet Connection:**
- Use a wired connection to connect a device directly to your modem.
- If the internet works, the issue may be with your router.
- If the internet still doesn't work, contact your Internet Service Provider (ISP).


5. **Update Router's Firmware:**
- Check if there is a firmware update available for your Google Wifi router.
- Download and install the latest firmware update from the Google Wifi app.


6. **Interference and Obstacles:**
- Make sure the router is not near electronic devices that can cause interference, like microwaves or cordless phones.
- Remove any obstacles between the router and your devices, such as furniture or thick walls.


7. **Change Wi-Fi Channel:**
- In the Google Wifi app, go to Settings > Network & General > Advanced Networking.
- Try changing the Wi-Fi channel to a less congested one.


8. **Contact Google Support:**
- If you've tried the above steps and the issue persists, contact Google support for further assistance.

(gemini-pro)

This response provides generic troubleshooting information that isn't specific to the router or the status of its LED indicator lights.

To customize the response for the specific router, you can add the router's troubleshooting guide to the prompt as context for the model to refer to.

Prompt:

Answer the question using the text below. Respond with only the text provided.
Question: What should I do to fix my disconnected wifi? The light on my Google Wifi router is yellow and blinking slowly.

Text:
Color: Slowly pulsing yellow
What it means: There is a network error.
What to do:
Check that the Ethernet cable is connected to both your router and your modem and both devices are turned on. You might need to unplug and plug in each device again.

Color: Fast blinking yellow
What it means: You are holding down the reset button and are factory resetting this device.
What to do:
If you keep holding down the reset button, after about 12 seconds, the light will turn solid yellow. Once it is solid yellow, let go of the factory reset button.

Color: Solid yellow
What it means: Router is factory resetting.
What to do:
This can take up to 10 minutes. When it's done, the device will reset itself and start pulsing white, letting you know it's ready for setup.

Color: Solid red
What it means: Something is wrong.
What to do:
Critical failure. Factory reset the router. If the light stays red, contact Wifi customer support.

Response:

Check that the Ethernet cable is connected to both your router and your modem and both devices are turned on. You might need to unplug and plug in each device again.

(gemini-pro)

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Instruct the model to explain its reasoning
docs.text:
When you instruct a large language model (LLM) to explain its reasoning, you prompt it to provide the steps it took to arrive at an answer. This technique, often called chain-of-thought prompting, can improve the accuracy and quality of the model's response, especially for complex queries. It also provides transparency into the model's process.

A prompt is the query or instruction you provide to the model. For more information, see Introduction to prompts.

docs.title: Why ask the model to explain its reasoning?
docs.text:
Asking a model to detail its reasoning process offers several benefits:

  • Improved Accuracy: Forcing the model to follow a logical path can help it avoid simple errors and produce more accurate results, particularly for challenging queries.
  • Better Transparency: Understanding the model's "thought process" helps you trust its outputs and identify any logical flaws.
  • Easier Debugging: If a response is incorrect, the reasoning steps make it easier to pinpoint where the model went wrong, allowing you to refine your prompt.

docs.title: Methods for eliciting reasoning
docs.text:
You can elicit reasoning from a model using several techniques, ranging from simple instructions to more complex, structured prompting. The best method depends on your specific use case and the complexity of your task.

Method Description Best for Explain reasoning A direct instruction in the prompt, such as "Explain your reasoning." Simple to moderately complex queries where you need to understand the model's logic. Think step-by-step A more detailed instruction that asks the model to break down the problem and show its work. Complex problems that require multi-step reasoning, such as math word problems or logical puzzles. Structured output Combining a reasoning instruction with a request for a specific output format, like JSON or XML. Integrating model output into applications where you need to parse the answer and the reasoning steps separately.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The following examples demonstrate how different prompting techniques affect the model's response for the same query.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Baseline (No reasoning instruction)Explain reasoningThink step-by-step with structured output

Without a specific instruction to explain its reasoning, the model provides a direct but less detailed answer.

Prompt:

**What is the most likely interpretation of this sentence?**
The sentence: "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

Response:

The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it lacked color and needed cooking.
(gemini-pro)

By adding a simple instruction to explain its reasoning, the model provides a more nuanced answer and breaks down its logic.

Prompt:

**What is the most likely interpretation of this sentence? Explain your reasoning**
The sentence: "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

Response:

  Interpreting "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

  The most likely interpretation is that the chef seasoned the chicken to add flavor and color, then put it in the oven to cook it.

  Here's the reasoning:

  - Seasoning is typically used to enhance the flavor of food. Chefs often use spices, herbs, and other ingredients to make their dishes more appealing.
  - "Pale" suggests the chicken lacked visual appeal before being seasoned. This could imply it was unseasoned or simply lacking color from spices.
  - Putting the chicken in the oven is a common cooking method. The sentence implies the chef's intention is to cook the chicken, not just season it.

  Therefore, the chef's actions are likely aimed at both improving the taste and appearance of the chicken through seasoning and then cooking it in the oven.
(gemini-pro)

Asking the model to think step-by-step and format the output as JSON provides a thorough, machine-readable response that separates the final answer from the reasoning process.

Prompt:

**What is the most likely interpretation of this sentence? Think step by step and print out
the thinking process.

Please output in JSON format with final answer in 'answer', and thinking steps in 'think' fields.**
The sentence: "The chef seasoned the chicken and put it in the oven because it looked pale."

Response:

{
  "answer": "The chef seasoned the chicken to enhance its flavor and put it in the oven to cook it because it appeared to be undercooked.",
  "think": [
    {
      "step": 1,
      "thought": "The chef seasoned the chicken. This suggests that the chef is preparing the chicken for cooking."
    },
    {
      "step": 2,
      "thought": "The chef put the chicken in the oven. This indicates that the chef is cooking the chicken."
    },
    {
      "step": 3,
      "thought": "The sentence states that the chicken looked pale. Pale chicken is often undercooked."
    },
    {
      "step": 4,
      "thought": "Combining these observations, it is most likely that the chef seasoned the chicken to enhance its flavor and put it in the oven to cook it because it appeared to be undercooked."
    }
  ]
}
(gemini-pro)

docs.title: Include few-shot examples in prompts
docs.text:
You can improve model responses by including examples in your prompt that demonstrate the desired output format and style. The model identifies patterns from your examples and applies them to its own response. Prompts that contain examples are called few-shot prompts, while prompts with no examples are called zero-shot prompts.

Few-shot prompts are highly effective for guiding the model's output, including its formatting, phrasing, and scope. For best results, use specific and varied examples and always accompany them with clear instructions. Without explicit instructions, the model might infer unintended patterns from the examples, leading to inaccurate responses.

docs.title: When to use few-shot prompts
docs.text:
Use the following table to decide whether a zero-shot or few-shot prompt is better suited for your use case.

Prompting Method Best for... Key Characteristic Zero-shot Simple tasks where the model already has sufficient knowledge to generate a correct response. Provides a direct instruction without any preceding examples. Few-shot Complex tasks that require a specific output format, style, or pattern that the model needs to learn. Includes one or more examples of the desired input and output to guide the model's response.

docs.title: Examples of zero-shot and few-shot prompts
docs.text:
The following examples demonstrate how to extract technical specifications from text. The zero-shot prompt relies on the model's existing capabilities, while the few-shot prompt provides an example to enforce a specific JSON key format.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Zero-shot promptFew-shot prompt

A zero-shot prompt provides an instruction without any examples. The following prompt asks the model to extract technical specifications from text and output them in JSON format.

Prompt:

Extract the technical specifications from the text below in JSON format.

Google Pixel 7, 5G network, 8GB RAM, Tensor G2 processor, 128GB of storage, Lemongrass

Response:

{
  "Network": "5G",
  "RAM": "8GB",
  "Processor": "Tensor G2",
  "Storage": "128GB",
  "Color": "Lemongrass"
}
Example response from the Gemini Pro model.

A few-shot prompt includes one or more examples to guide the model. If your use case requires a specific format, such as lowercase JSON keys, you can provide an example that demonstrates this format.

Prompt:

Extract the technical specifications from the text below in a JSON format.

<EXAMPLE>
  INPUT: Google Nest Wifi, network speed up to 1200Mpbs, 2.4GHz and 5GHz frequencies, WP3 protocol

  OUTPUT:
  {
    "product":"Google Nest Wifi",
    "speed":"1200Mpbs",
    "frequencies": ["2.4GHz", "5GHz"],
    "protocol":"WP3"
  }
</EXAMPLE>

  Google Pixel 7, 5G network, 8GB RAM, Tensor G2 processor, 128GB of storage, Lemongrass

Response:

{
  "product": "Google Pixel 7",
  "network": "5G",
  "ram": "8GB",
  "processor": "Tensor G2",
  "storage": "128GB",
  "color": "Lemongrass"
}
Example response from the Gemini Pro model.

docs.title: Best practices for few-shot prompting
docs.text:
To create effective few-shot prompts, follow these best practices:

  • Use clear markup for examples. Use distinct and consistent markup, such as XML-like tags (<EXAMPLE>), to separate examples from the main prompt instruction. This helps the model distinguish between the instructions and the examples it should learn from. To learn more, see Structure prompts.
  • Experiment with the number of examples. While models like Gemini can often learn from just a few examples, the optimal number can vary. Experiment to find what works best for your use case. Too few examples might be ineffective, while too many can cause the model to overfit and mimic the examples too closely instead of generalizing the underlying pattern.
  • Ensure consistent formatting. Apply the same formatting and structure across all of your examples to help the model identify the pattern accurately.

docs.title: Introduction to prompting
docs.text:
A prompt is a natural language request submitted to a language model to receive a response. Prompts can contain questions, instructions, contextual information, and examples to help guide the model. After the model receives a prompt, it can generate various outputs, such as text, code, images, and more, depending on the model's capabilities.

For example, a simple prompt to a text model could be:

What are the three primary colors?

This page introduces the basic concepts and components of prompt design.

docs.title: What is prompt design and prompt engineering?
docs.text:
Prompt design is the process of creating prompts that elicit the desired response from a language model. Writing well-structured prompts is essential for ensuring accurate, high-quality responses. The iterative process of refining prompts and assessing the model's responses is often called prompt engineering.

While Gemini models often perform well with straightforward requests, effective prompt engineering becomes crucial for more complex tasks that require nuanced or specific outputs.

docs.title: Components of a prompt
docs.text:
A prompt can include any information you believe is relevant to the task. Generally, prompt content falls into an optional combination of the following components. The only required component is the Task.

Component Description When to Use Task (Required) The specific instruction or question you want the model to address. Always. This is the core of your request. System instructions (Optional) High-level directives that define the model's persona, style, tone, or rules for the entire conversation. When you need to set a consistent personality or enforce specific constraints (e.g., "You are a helpful assistant that only speaks in rhyme"). Few-shot examples (Optional) A set of example request-and-response pairs that demonstrate the desired output format or behavior. When you need to guide the model on specific output styles, formats, or complex tasks where showing is more effective than telling. Contextual information (Optional) Additional information for the model to use or reference when generating a response. When the model needs external information (like a document, table, or passage) to answer the question accurately.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
A task is the part of the prompt that specifies what you want the model to do. It can be a direct question or an instruction.

Example question task:

Prompt: 

What are the colors in the rainbow?

Response: 

A rainbow has seven colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. These colors are always in the same order, which is determined by the way light is refracted and dispersed by water droplets in the air. This order is sometimes remembered by the acronym ROYGBIV. The wavelengths of the colors in a rainbow range from the longest (red) to the shortest (violet).

Example instruction task:

Prompt: 

Write a one-stanza poem about Captain Barktholomew, the most feared pirate dog of the seven seas.

Response: 

Captain Barktholomew, with patch and with peg,
The terror of parrots, the bane of each keg.
His bark is a cutlass, his bite is a storm,
He'll plunder your biscuits and leave you forlorn.

docs.title: System instructions
docs.text:
System instructions are passed to the model before the user's prompt to guide its behavior throughout a conversation. You can add system instructions in the dedicated systemInstruction parameter.

In the following example, system instructions dictate the model's persona, style, and conversational constraints.

System: 

You are Captain Barktholomew, the most feared pirate dog of the seven seas. You are from the 1700s and have no knowledge of anything after that time. You only talk about topics related to being a pirate. End every message with "woof!"

Prompt: 

Hello! Who might you be?

Response: 

Avast there! You can call me Captain Barktholomew, the scourge of the seven seas!

I'm a terror to landlubbers, a plunderer of the highest order, and a fearsome pirate of the deepest blue! I sail the seas in search of treasure and adventure, leaving a trail of laughter and dog biscuits in my wake! Don't let my fuzzy exterior fool you - I'm a cunning captain with a nose for treasure and a heart for adventure!

Now, if you'll excuse me, I must away! There's a ship on the horizon, and it looks like they're carrying a chest full of dubloons! Yo ho ho, and a bottle of rum! Woof!

To learn more, see Use system instructions.

docs.title: Few-shot examples
docs.text:
Few-shot examples demonstrate the desired output format and style. They are particularly effective for customizing the model's behavior for specific tasks.

Prompt: 

Classify the following as red wine or white wine:

<examples>
  Name: Chardonnay
  Type: White wine
  Name: Cabernet
  Type: Red wine
  Name: Moscato
  Type: White wine
</examples>

Name: Riesling
Type:

Response: 

White wine

docs.title: Contextual information
docs.text:
Contextual information, or context, is data you provide for the model to reference when generating a response. This information can be in various formats, such as text or tables.

Prompt: 

| Marble color | Number of marbles |
| ------------ | ----------------- |
| Red          | 12                |
| Blue         | 28                |
| Yellow       | 15                |
| Green        | 17                |

How many green marbles are there?

Response: 

There are 17 green marbles.

docs.title: Safety and fallback responses
docs.text:
A model might not fulfill a user's request if the prompt could lead to a response that violates Google's safety policies. In such cases, the model may provide a generic or "fallback" response instead.

The model is likely to refuse to respond to prompts related to:

  • Hate Speech: Content that is negative or harmful towards individuals based on their identity or protected attributes.
  • Harassment: Malicious, intimidating, or abusive content targeting an individual.
  • Sexually Explicit Content: Prompts containing references to sexual acts or other lewd material.
  • Dangerous Content: Prompts that promote or facilitate access to harmful goods, services, or activities.

docs.title: Overview of prompting strategies
docs.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast amounts of text data to learn the patterns and relationships between units of language. When you provide text (a "prompt"), a language model can predict what is likely to come next, acting as a sophisticated autocompletion tool.

While there is no single correct way to design a prompt, applying certain strategies can significantly influence the model's response quality and relevance. Effective prompt design, also known as prompt engineering, is an iterative process of refining prompts to optimize model performance through rigorous testing and evaluation.

docs.title: Prompt engineering workflow
docs.text:
Prompt engineering is an iterative, test-driven process. To enhance model performance, it's important to clearly define the objectives for each prompt and systematically test them to identify areas for improvement.

The following diagram illustrates the typical prompt engineering workflow:

The prompt engineering workflow.

docs.title: How to create an effective prompt
docs.text:
The effectiveness of a prompt depends on two key aspects: its content and its structure.

  • Content: To complete a task, the model needs all relevant information. This can include instructions, examples, and contextual details. For more information, see the Components of a prompt section.

  • Structure: Even with all the necessary information, the way it's organized helps the model parse the prompt correctly. The ordering of information, use of labels, and delimiters can all affect the quality of the response. For an example, see the Sample prompt template.

docs.title: Components of a prompt
docs.text: A prompt is composed of various components. While some are essential for any task, others are optional and can be used to refine the model's output.

docs.title: Essential components
docs.text:
These components form the core of most prompts.

Component Description Example Objective A clear and specific statement of what you want the model to achieve. Also called "mission" or "goal." Your objective is to help students with math problems without directly giving them the answer. Instructions Step-by-step directions on how to perform the task. Also called "task," "steps," or "directions." 1. Understand the problem.2. Identify where the student is stuck.3. Provide a hint for the next step of the problem.

docs.title: Optional components
docs.text:
These components can be added to further guide and constrain the model's response.

Component Description Example System instructions Technical directives that control the model's behavior across tasks. Available in Gemini 1.5 Flash and later models. You are a coding expert specializing in front-end interfaces. When I describe a website component, return the HTML and CSS for it. Do not explain the code. Offer UI design suggestions. Persona The role or character the model should adopt. Also called "role." You are a math tutor helping students with their homework. Constraints Rules on what the model must or must not do. Also called "guardrails" or "boundaries." Don't give the student the answer directly. Instead, give hints toward the next step. If the student is completely lost, provide the detailed steps to solve the problem. Tone The desired style of the response. This can also be influenced by the persona. Also called "style" or "voice." Respond in a casual and technical manner. Context Background information the model needs to perform the task. Also called "input data." A copy of the student's math lesson plans. Few-shot examples Examples of the desired input and output. Also called "exemplars." See the example below. Reasoning steps An instruction for the model to explain its reasoning, which can improve response quality. Also called "thinking steps." Explain your reasoning step-by-step. Response format The desired output format, such as JSON, Markdown, or a bulleted list. Also called "structure" or "layout." Format your response in Markdown. Recap A concise summary of the prompt's key points, especially constraints and format, placed at the end. Remember: Don't give away the answer and provide hints instead. Always format your response in Markdown. Safeguards Rules that ground the model's responses to its core mission. Also called "safety rules." N/A View an example of few-shot prompting

Few-shot examples provide the model with demonstrations of the desired input/output format.

input: I'm trying to calculate how many golf balls can fit into a box that has a one cubic meter volume. I've converted one cubic meter into cubic centimeters and divided it by the volume of a golf ball in cubic centimeters, but the system says my answer is wrong.

output: Golf balls are spheres and cannot be packed into a space with perfect efficiency. Your calculation likely assumes they can be packed without any wasted space, but you need to account for the gaps between the spheres.

Depending on the specific task, you might choose to include or exclude some of the optional components. Experimenting with the ordering of these components can also affect the response.

docs.title: Sample prompt template
docs.text:
The following template shows how you can structure the components of a prompt:

<OBJECTIVE_AND_PERSONA>
You are a [insert a persona, such as a "math teacher" or "automotive expert"]. Your task is to...
</OBJECTIVE_AND_PERSONA>

<INSTRUCTIONS>
To complete the task, you need to follow these steps:
1.
2.
...
</INSTRUCTIONS>

------------- Optional Components ------------

<CONSTRAINTS>
Dos and don'ts for the following aspects:
1. Dos
2. Don'ts
</CONSTRAINTS>

<CONTEXT>
[Provide any relevant context here]
</CONTEXT>

<OUTPUT_FORMAT>
The output format must be:
1.
2.
...
</OUTPUT_FORMAT>

<FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES>
Here are some examples:
1. Example #1
    Input:
    Thoughts:
    Output:
...
</FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES>

<RECAP>
[Re-emphasize the key aspects of the prompt, especially the constraints and output format.]
</RECAP>

docs.title: Best practices for prompt design
docs.text:
The following are best practices for prompt design:

  • Give clear and specific instructions
  • Include few-shot examples
  • Assign a role
  • Add contextual information
  • Use system instructions
  • Structure prompts
  • Instruct the model to explain its reasoning
  • Break down complex tasks
  • Experiment with parameter values
  • Prompt iteration strategies

docs.title: Prompt iteration strategies
docs.text:
Prompt design often requires several iterations to achieve the desired response consistently. A successful prompt design strategy applies the Prompt design best practices through incremental refinements. You can introduce these best practices iteratively while testing to ensure the model's performance meets your use case needs.

The order of content within a prompt can also affect the response. For example, try reordering instructions, context, and input data to see how the output changes. For multimodal prompts, you might place the files before the text instructions.

As you receive responses from the model, analyze what you like and dislike, then modify your prompts to guide the model toward responses that better align with your goals.

flowchart LR
    A[Design initial prompt] --> B[Test with model]
    B --> C[Analyze response]
    C --> D{Response meets requirements?}
    D -- No --> E[Refine prompt]
    E --> B
    D -- Yes --> F[Finalize prompt]

click A "#example-iterating-on-an-ad-copy-prompt"
click B "#example-iterating-on-an-ad-copy-prompt"
click C "#example-iterating-on-an-ad-copy-prompt"
click D "#example-iterating-on-an-ad-copy-prompt"
click E "#example-iterating-on-an-ad-copy-prompt"
click F "#example-iterating-on-an-ad-copy-prompt"

docs.title: Example: Iterating on an ad copy prompt
docs.text:
In this example, the goal is to generate ad copy for a product. You start by defining the following prompt content:

  • Objective: Create ad copy.
  • Context:
    • Categories: scarcity, exclusivity.
    • Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."
  • Constraints: Each response should be two sentences or less.

Experimenting with how you provide this content to the model helps you refine the response to fit your needs.

Iteration 1: Initial attemptIteration 2: Reformatting the promptIteration 3: Refining constraintsIteration 4: Finalizing the prompt structure

Prompt:

Create ad copy.

Categories: scarcity, exclusivity

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Constraints: Each response should be two sentences or less.

Response:

Scarcity

*  Time is running out to experience the future of entertainment! Get your Chromecast before they're gone.
*  Limited quantities available! Don't miss your chance to own the streaming device everyone's talking about.

Exclusivity

*  Unlock a world of entertainment with Chromecast. Experience the freedom of streaming like never before.
*  Upgrade your home entertainment with the exclusive Chromecast device. Join the elite group of cord-cutters who stream smarter.
(gemini-pro)

You can try reformatting the prompt to see how the response changes when the prompt objective, constraints, and some of the context are combined into a single sentence.

Prompt:

Create scarcity and exclusivity-focused ad copy that is less than two sentences.

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Response:

Options for Scarcity & Exclusivity-Driven Chromecast Ads:

Option 1 (Scarcity): "Limited quantities available! Get your Chromecast today before they're gone and unlock a world of on-demand entertainment."

Option 2 (Exclusivity): "Experience entertainment like never before. Chromecast: the ultimate upgrade for your TV, available for a limited time."
(gemini-pro)

This time, the model's response contained only one copy option for each category. If you realize that you need at least two options for each category and that you don't want to limit the length of the response, you can modify the constraints and try your prompt again.

Prompt:

Create two ad-copies about scarcity and two ad-copies about exclusivity.

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Response:

Scarcity Ad Copies:
Ad 1:

Headline: Don't miss out! Chromecast is flying off the shelves!

Body: Experience the magic of Chromecast before it's too late! Limited quantities are available, so grab yours now and start enjoying your favorite entertainment on the big screen. 

Ad 2:

Headline: Last chance! Chromecast is almost sold out.

Body: Time is running out to get your hands on Chromecast. Upgrade your TV experience today and enjoy seamless streaming from all your devices. Don't wait, supplies are limited!


Exclusivity Ad Copies:

Ad 1:

Headline: Unlock a world of entertainment with the exclusive Chromecast.

Body: Join the elite group of Chromecast users and experience the future of television. Enjoy effortless streaming, endless entertainment options, and unparalleled convenience. Chromecast: It's not just TV, it's an experience.

Ad 2:

Headline: Elevate your home entertainment with the Chromecast advantage.

Body: Go beyond ordinary TV with Chromecast. Seamlessly stream content from all your devices and enjoy a personalized entertainment experience like no other. Discover the exclusivity of Chromecast today.
(gemini-pro)

In the third iteration, the model's response contained both headline and body fields for the ad copy. For this example, let's say that this response aligns with your ad copy requirements. Now that you've adjusted the prompt to get a response that aligns with your ad copy requirements, you can update and test the prompt to ensure the model produces similarly formatted responses in the future.

Prompt:

Create two ad-copies about scarcity and two ad-copies about exclusivity.

Include a headline and body for each ad copy.

Product description: "Chromecast is a device that allows users to wirelessly cast their content from other devices, so they can watch their favorite movies, TV shows, photos, websites, and more on their TV. Chromecast can display content from Android smartphones and tablets, iPhones & iPads, Windows and Mac laptops, and the Chromebook Pixel."

Response:

Scarcity Ads:

Ad 1:

Headline: Last Chance! Chromecast is Selling Out Fast
Body: Get the Chromecast experience before it's gone! Limited quantities remain. Upgrade your TV time today!

Ad 2:

Headline: Don't Miss Out! Chromecast Stock is Running Low
Body: Time is running out to grab your Chromecast. Enjoy seamless streaming on the big screen. Order now while supplies last!

Exclusivity Ads:

Ad 1:

Headline: Unlock the Ultimate Viewing Experience with Chromecast
Body: Join the elite group of Chromecast users and enjoy unparalleled streaming convenience. Elevate your entertainment today!

Ad 2:

Headline: Experience the Future of Entertainment: Get Your Chromecast
Body: Be among the first to enjoy the cutting-edge technology of Chromecast. Stream anything, anytime, effortlessly.  Upgrade your home entertainment now!
(gemini-pro)

This time, the model's response is very similar to the previous iteration, even with the additional constraints, which means that you successfully iterated upon your prompt.

As demonstrated by the example, prompt iteration is an integral part of the prompt design process that can be used to help you guide the model to produce the best results for your use case.

docs.title: Optimize prompts
docs.text:
Preview

This product or feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

This document describes how to use the Vertex AI prompt optimizer to automatically improve the performance of a set of prompts by refining the system instructions.

The Vertex AI prompt optimizer helps you improve your prompts quickly and at scale, without manually rewriting system instructions or individual prompts. This is especially useful when you want to adapt system instructions and prompts written for one model to a different model.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text: The prompt optimizer supports all Gemini models.

docs.title: How the prompt optimizer works
docs.text:
The Vertex AI prompt optimizer takes your existing system instructions, a set of sample prompts, and a target model, and then generates an optimized version of the system instructions.

The optimizer runs a custom training job that iteratively rewrites your system instructions and evaluates them against your sample prompts using specified metrics. At the end of the job, it outputs the version of the system instructions that achieved the best evaluation score for the target model.

docs.title: Key parameters
docs.text:
The prompt optimizer uses the following parameters to guide the optimization process:

  • Optimization mode: Specifies whether the optimizer refines the system instructions, selects sample prompts to use as few-shot examples, or both.
  • Evaluation metrics: The metrics used to score the model's responses and determine the best-performing system instructions. You can use standard metrics or define your own.
  • Target model: The Google model for which the system instructions are being optimized.

docs.title: Prompt optimization example
docs.text:
To optimize system instructions for answering questions about cooking, you would provide the following inputs to the prompt optimizer.

Initial system instructions

You are a professional chef. Your goal is teaching how to cook healthy cooking recipes to your apprentice.

Given a question from your apprentice and some context, provide the correct answer to the question.
Use the context to return a single and correct answer with some explanation.

Prompt template

Question: {input_question}
Facts: {input_context}

Sample prompts

input_question input_context What are some techniques for cooking red meat and pork that maximize flavor and tenderness while minimizing the formation of unhealthy compounds? Red meat and pork should be cooked to an internal temperature of 145 degrees fahrenheit (63 degrees celsius) to ensure safety. Marinating meat in acidic ingredients like lemon juice or vinegar can help tenderize it by breaking down tough muscle fibers. High-heat cooking methods like grilling and pan-searing can create delicious browning and caramelization, but it's important to avoid charring, which can produce harmful compounds. What are some creative ways to add flavor and nutrition to protein shakes without using added sugars or artificial ingredients? Adding leafy greens like spinach or kale is a great way to boost the nutritional value of your shake without drastically altering the flavor. Using unsweetened almond milk or coconut water instead of regular milk can add a subtle sweetness and a boost of healthy fats or electrolytes, respectively. Did you know that over-blending your shake can actually heat it up? To keep things cool and refreshing, blend for shorter bursts and give your blender a break if needed.

Optimized system instructions

After running the job, the optimizer produces a refined version of the system instructions.

As a highly skilled chef with a passion for healthy cooking, you love sharing your knowledge with
aspiring chefs. Today, a culinary intern approaches you with a question about healthy cooking. Given
the intern's question and some facts, provide a clear, concise, and informative answer that will help
the intern excel in their culinary journey.

docs.title: Evaluation metrics
docs.text:
You can use standard evaluation metrics, custom metrics, or a combination of both. However, you can only use one custom metric per optimization job.

  • Custom metrics: Useful when standard metrics don't fit your specific application. To learn how to create them, see Create custom metrics.
  • Standard metrics: Pre-defined metrics for common tasks.

The following table describes the available standard evaluation metrics.

Metric type Use case Metric Description Model-based Summarization summarization_quality Describes the model's ability to answer questions given a body of text to reference. Question answering question_answering_correctness* Describes the model's ability to correctly answer a question. question_answering_quality Describes the model's ability to answer questions given a body of text to reference. Coherence coherence Describes the model's ability to provide a coherent response and measures how well the generated text flows logically and makes sense. Safety safety Describes the model's level of safety, that is, whether the response contains any unsafe text. Fluency fluency Describes the model's language mastery. Groundedness groundedness Describes the model's ability to provide or reference information included only in the input text. Computation-based Tool use and function calling tool_call_valid* Describes the model's ability to predict a valid tool call. tool_name_match* Describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct tool name. Only the first tool call is inspected. tool_parameter_key_match* Describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct parameter names. tool_parameter_kv_match* Describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct parameter names and key values. General text generation bleu* Holds the result of an algorithm for evaluating the quality of the prediction, which has been translated from one natural language to another natural language. The quality of the prediction is considered to be the correspondence between a prediction parameter and its reference parameter. exact_match* Computes whether a prediction parameter matches a reference parameter exactly. rouge_1* Used to compare the provided prediction parameter against a reference parameter. rouge_2* rouge_l* rouge_l_sum*
  • If you want to optimize your prompts using question_answering_correctness or computation-based evaluations, you must provide a ground truth for comparison. You can do this in one of two ways:
    • Add a {target} variable to your prompt template that represents the ground truth response.
    • Set the source_model parameter in your configuration. The optimizer runs your sample prompts on the source_model to generate ground truth responses automatically. This is useful if you have a model that already produces your desired results.

docs.text:
This section walks you through the process of optimizing a prompt.

flowchart LR
