docs.title: View and interpret evaluation results
docs.text:
This page describes how to view and interpret your model evaluation results after running an online evaluation service task.

The process for viewing and interpreting evaluation results involves running the evaluation task, accessing the results object, visualizing the summary metrics, and understanding the detailed results for different metric types.

flowchart LR
    A[Run Evaluation Task] --> B[Access EvalResult Object]
    B --> C[Visualize Summary Metrics]
    B --> D[Interpret Detailed Metrics]
    D --> E[Review Examples]

    click A "#run-evaluation-task"
    click B "#access-evaluation-results"
    click C "#visualize-evaluation-results"
    D --- C
    click D "#understand-metric-results"
    click E "#review-examples"

docs.title: Access evaluation results
docs.text:
After you define and run your evaluation task, the service returns an EvalResult object that contains the results of your evaluation run.

The following code shows how to run an evaluation task:

from vertexai.evaluation import EvalTask

eval_result = EvalTask(
    dataset=DATASET,
    metrics=[METRIC_1, METRIC_2, METRIC_3],
    experiment=EXPERIMENT_NAME,
).evaluate(
    model=MODEL,
    experiment_run=EXPERIMENT_RUN_NAME,
)

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

The EvalResult class represents the result of an evaluation run and has the following key attributes:

  • summary_metrics: A dictionary of aggregated evaluation metrics for the entire evaluation run.
  • metrics_table: A pandas.DataFrame containing detailed, row-by-row results, including dataset inputs, model responses, explanations, and metric scores.
  • metadata: The experiment name and experiment run name associated with the evaluation run.

With the use of helper functions, the evaluation results can be displayed in a Colab notebook.

Summary metrics and row-based metrics tables. View the EvalResult class definition

The EvalResult class is defined as follows:

@dataclasses.dataclass
class EvalResult:
    """Evaluation result.

    Attributes:
      summary_metrics: A dictionary of aggregated evaluation metrics for an evaluation run.
      metrics_table: A pandas.DataFrame table containing evaluation dataset inputs,
        responses, explanations, and metric results per row.
      metadata: the experiment name and experiment run name for the evaluation run.
    """

    summary_metrics: Dict[str, float]
    metrics_table: Optional["pd.DataFrame"] = None
    metadata: Optional[Dict[str, str]] = None

docs.title: Visualize evaluation results
docs.text:
You can plot summary metrics in a radar or bar chart for visualization and comparison between results from different evaluation runs. This visualization can be helpful for evaluating different models and different prompt templates.

In the following example, we visualize four metrics (coherence, fluency, instruction following, and overall text quality) for responses generated using four different prompt templates. From the radar and bar plots, we can infer that prompt template #2 consistently outperforms the other templates across all four metrics. This is particularly evident in its significantly higher scores for instruction following and text quality. Based on this analysis, prompt template #2 appears to be the most effective choice among the four options.

Radar chart comparing prompt template performance. Bar chart comparing mean metric scores for prompt templates.

docs.title: Understand metric results
docs.text:
The evaluation service supports three types of metrics. The following table provides a high-level comparison.

Metric Type Description Primary Use Case PointwiseMetric Evaluates the quality of a single model's response based on a predefined rubric (e.g., a 1-5 Likert scale). Assessing the absolute quality of a model's output for a given task, such as text quality or safety. PairwiseMetric Compares the responses from two models (a candidate and a baseline) and determines which one is better. A/B testing models or prompts to determine relative performance improvement. Computation-based metrics Calculates scores by comparing a model's response to a reference (ground truth) answer using computational methods. Evaluating tasks with objective correct answers, such as ROUGE for summarization or BLEU for translation.

The following tabs show the components of instance-level and aggregate results included in metrics_table and summary_metrics for each metric type.

PointwiseMetricPairwiseMetricComputation-based metrics

Instance-level results

Column Description response The response generated for the prompt by the model. score The rating given to the response as per the criteria and rating rubric. The score can be binary (0 and 1), Likert scale (1 to 5, or -2 to 2), or float (0.0 to 1.0). explanation The judge model's reason for the score. We use chain-of-thought reasoning to guide the judge model to explain its rationale behind each verdict. Forcing the judge model to reason is shown to improve evaluation accuracy. Note: Results for translation metrics only include score.

Aggregate results

Column Description mean score Average score for all instances. standard deviation Standard deviation for all the scores.

Instance-level results

Column Description response The response generated for the prompt by the candidate model. baseline_model_response The response generated for the prompt by the baseline model. pairwise_choice The model with the better response. Possible values are CANDIDATE, BASELINE, or TIE. explanation The judge model's reason for the choice.

Aggregate results

Column Description candidate_model_win_rate Ratio of times the judge model decided the candidate model had the better response to total responses. Ranges between 0 and 1. baseline_model_win_rate Ratio of times the judge model decided the baseline model had the better response to total responses. Ranges between 0 and 1.

Instance-level results

Column Description response The model's response being evaluated. reference The reference response. score The score is calculated for each pair of responses and references.

Aggregate results

Column Description mean score Average score for all instances. standard deviation Standard deviation for all the scores.

docs.title: Review examples
docs.text:
The examples in this section demonstrate how to read and understand the evaluation results for different metric types.

Example 1: Pointwise evaluation for text quality

In this example, a pointwise evaluation is performed for TEXT_QUALITY. The score is 4 (on a scale of 1 to 5), which indicates the response is good. The explanation clarifies why the judge model assigned a score of 4, noting that while the summary is effective and grounded, the language could be less verbose.

Dataset

  • prompt: "Summarize the following text in a way that a five-year-old can understand: Social Media Platform Faces Backlash Over Content Moderation Policies\nA prominent social media platform finds itself embroiled in controversy as users and content creators express discontent over its content moderation policies. Allegations of biased censorship, inconsistent enforcement, and suppression of certain viewpoints have sparked outrage among users who claim that the platform is stifling free speech. On the other hand, the platform asserts that its policies are designed to maintain a safe and inclusive online environment. This controversy raises broader questions about the role of social media in shaping public discourse and the responsibilities of platforms in curating online content."
  • response: "People are upset with a website because they think it's not being fair with what people can post. Some people say the website is stopping them from saying what they want. But the website says it's trying to keep everyone safe. This makes people wonder if websites should control what people can say online."

Result

  • score: 4
  • explanation: The summary in the response follows the instruction to summarize the context in a way that a five-year old can understand. It is grounded in the context and provides important details in its summarization. However, the language used in the response is a bit verbose.
Example 2: Pairwise comparison for question answering quality

This example shows a pairwise comparison for PAIRWISE_QUESTION_ANSWERING_QUALITY. The pairwise_choice result shows the judge model preferred the CANDIDATE response because it was more helpful and directly answered the question from the prompt, whereas the BASELINE response was correct but less complete.

Dataset

  • prompt: "Can you answer where France is based on the following paragraph? France is a country located in Western Europe. It's bordered by Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Monaco, Spain, and Andorra. France's coastline stretches along the English Channel, the North Sea, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Mediterranean Sea. Known for its rich history, iconic landmarks like the Eiffel Tower, and delicious cuisine, France is a major cultural and economic power in Europe and throughout the world."
  • response: "France is a country located in Western Europe."
  • baseline_model_response: "France is a country."

Result

  • pairwise_choice: CANDIDATE
  • explanation: The BASELINE response is grounded but does not fully answer the question. The CANDIDATE response, however, is correct and provides helpful details on the location of France.

docs.title: Document tuning
docs.text: This page provides an overview of supervised fine-tuning for Gemini models using your own document data. It covers use cases, limitations, and the required dataset format.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Fine-tuning lets you customize powerful language models for your specific needs. Here are some key use cases where fine-tuning with your own set of PDFs can significantly enhance a model's performance:

  • Internal knowledge base: Convert your internal documents into an AI-powered knowledge base that provides instant answers and insights. For example, a sales representative could instantly access product specifications and pricing details from past training materials.
  • Research assistant: Create a research assistant capable of analyzing a collection of research papers, articles, and books. A researcher studying climate change could quickly analyze scientific papers to identify trends in sea level rise or assess the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies.
  • Legal or regulatory compliance: Fine-tuning on legal documents can help automate contract review, flagging potential inconsistencies or areas of risk. This allows legal professionals to focus on higher-level tasks while ensuring compliance.
  • Automated report generation: Automate the analysis of complex financial reports, extracting key performance indicators and generating summaries for stakeholders. This can save time and reduce the risk of errors compared to manual analysis.
  • Content summarization and analysis: Summarize lengthy PDF documents, extract key insights, and analyze trends. For example, a market research team could analyze a collection of customer surveys to identify key themes and sentiment.
  • Document comparison and version control: Compare different versions of a document to identify changes and track revisions. This can be particularly useful in collaborative environments where multiple authors contribute to a document.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The following limitations apply to document tuning for both Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite and Gemini 2.0 Flash models:

  • Maximum PDF pages per example: 300
  • Maximum PDF files per example: 4
  • Maximum PDF file size: 20 MB

To learn more about document understanding requirements, see Document understanding.

docs.title: Dataset format
docs.text:
The fileUri for your dataset can be the URI for a file in a Cloud Storage bucket, or it can be a publicly available HTTP or HTTPS URL.

To see the generic format example, see Dataset example for Gemini.

The following is an example of a document dataset.

{
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "fileData": {
            "mimeType": "application/pdf",
            "fileUri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/pdf/2403.05530.pdf"
            }
        },
        {
          "text": "You are a very professional document summarization specialist. Please summarize the given document."
        }
      ]
    }, 
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "The report introduces Gemini 2.0 Flash, a multimodal AI model developed by Google DeepMind. The report positions Gemini 2.0 Flash as a significant advancement in multimodal AI, pushing the boundaries of long-context understanding and opening new avenues for future research and applications."
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Image tuning
docs.text: This page provides prerequisites and detailed instructions for fine-tuning Gemini on image data using supervised learning.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Fine-tuning lets you adapt base Gemini models for specialized tasks. Here are some image use cases:

  • Product catalog enhancement: Extract key attributes from images (e.g., brand, color, size) to automatically build and enrich your product catalog.
  • Image moderation: Fine-tune a model to detect and flag inappropriate or harmful content in images, ensuring a safer online experience.
  • Visual inspection: Train a model to identify specific objects or defects within images, automating quality control or inspection processes.
  • Image classification: Improve the accuracy of image classification for specific domains, such as medical imaging or satellite imagery analysis.
  • Image-based recommendations: Analyze images to provide personalized recommendations, such as suggesting similar products or complementary items.
  • Table content extraction: Extract data from tables within images and convert it into structured formats like spreadsheets or databases.

docs.title: Image requirements
docs.text:
• Maximum images per example: 30
  • Maximum image file size: 20MB

To learn more about image sample requirements, see the Image understanding page.

docs.title: Dataset format
docs.text:
Your dataset must be in JSON Lines (JSONL) format, where each line contains a single training example. The fileUri for your image can be a URI for a file in a Cloud Storage bucket or a publicly available HTTP or HTTPS URL.

To see the generic format example, see Dataset example for Gemini.

The following is an example of a JSONL entry for an image dataset.

{
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "fileData": {
            "mimeType": "image/jpeg",
            "fileUri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini-2_0/image/longcap100/100.jpeg"
            }
        }, 
        {
          "text": "Describe this image in detail that captures the essence of it."
        }
      ]
    }, 
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "A man stands on a road, wearing a blue denim jacket, tan pants, and white sneakers. He has his hands in his pockets and is wearing a white t-shirt under his jacket. The man's pants are cuffed, and his shoes are white. The road is dark grey, and the leaves are green. The man is standing in the shade, and the light is shining on the ground."
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Text tuning
docs.text:
This page provides prerequisites and detailed instructions for preparing your data to fine-tune Gemini models using supervised learning. Fine-tuning helps you customize a model for specific tasks by training it on your own dataset.

For examples of how to use a tuned model for classification, sentiment analysis, and extraction, see Model tuning for Gemini text models.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Fine-tuning lets you adapt base Gemini models for specialized tasks. Here are some common text use cases:

  • Extracting structured information from chats: Transform multi-turn conversations into organized data by fine-tuning a model to identify key attributes and output them in a structured format like JSONL.
  • Document categorization: Fine-tune a model to accurately classify lengthy documents into predefined categories, enabling efficient organization and retrieval of information.
  • Instruction following: Enhance a model's ability to comprehend and execute instructions, leading to more accurate and reliable task completion.
  • Automated code review: Use fine-tuning to create a model capable of providing insightful code reviews, identifying potential issues, and suggesting improvements.
  • Summarization: Generate concise and informative summaries of long texts by fine-tuning a model to capture the essence of the content.
  • Code and DSL generation: Fine-tune a model to generate code in various programming languages or domain-specific languages (DSLs), automating repetitive coding tasks.
  • Improved RAG performance: Enhance the helpfulness and accuracy of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by fine-tuning the underlying language model.

docs.title: Prepare your dataset
docs.text:
To tune a model, you need to provide a dataset in JSON Lines (JSONL) format where each line contains a single training example. The fileUri for your dataset can be the URI for a file in a Cloud Storage bucket, or it can be a publicly available HTTP or HTTPS URL.

For general information on the dataset format, see Dataset example for Gemini.

View a dataset format example

The following is an example of a text dataset in JSONL format.

{
  "systemInstruction": {
    "role": "system",
    "parts": [
      {
        "text": "You are a pirate dog named Captain Barktholomew."
      }
    ]
  },
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "Hi"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "Argh! What brings ye to my ship?"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "What's your name?"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "I be Captain Barktholomew, the most feared pirate dog of the seven seas."
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.text:
You can use the following sample datasets to learn how to tune a Gemini model. To use these datasets, specify the URIs in the applicable parameters when creating a text model supervised fine-tuning job.

To use the sample tuning dataset, specify its location as follows:

"training_dataset_uri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini-2_0/text/sft_train_data.jsonl",

To use the sample validation dataset, specify its location as follows:

docs.title: Tune a Gemini model with video data
docs.text:
This document describes how to tune the Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision model to better follow instructions for tasks involving video inputs. By tuning the model, you can customize it to adhere to specific instructions for your use cases.

This document focuses on tuning Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision for video understanding tasks. To learn about tuning this model for image-related tasks, see Tune a Gemini model with image data.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the workflow for tuning a Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision model.

flowchart LR
    A[Before you begin] --> B[Choose a tuning method];
    B --> C[Prepare your data];
    C --> D[Create a model tuning job];
    D --> E[View and use the tuned model];

    click A "#before-you-begin"

    click E "#view-and-use-the-tuned-model"

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Before you begin

Complete the following steps before you start the tuning process:

  1. Set up your project and development environment to work with Vertex AI.

  2. If you are the project owner, grant the Vertex AI Service Agent role to the service account in your project.

  3. Install the required SDKs:

    pip install --upgrade google-cloud-aiplatform

  4. Authenticate to Google Cloud:

    gcloud auth application-default login

docs.title: Choose a tuning method
docs.text:
You can tune Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision using supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The following table provides a comparison of these two methods.

Tuning Method Description Use Case Data Requirements Supervised fine-tuning Adapts the model to a specific task by training it on a labeled dataset of examples. Best for teaching the model a new skill or format, such as generating responses in a specific style or performing a classification task. A JSONL file containing video URIs, questions, and corresponding answers. RLHF tuning Aligns the model's behavior with human preferences by training it on a dataset of ranked responses. Best for improving the model's safety, helpfulness, and overall quality by teaching it what kind of responses humans prefer. A JSONL file containing video URIs, questions, and ranked candidate responses (one chosen, one rejected).

docs.title: Prepare your data
docs.text:
To tune the model, you must provide a dataset in a JSON Lines (JSONL) file stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. Each line in the file represents a single training example.

The data format depends on the tuning method you choose:

Supervised fine-tuningRLHF tuning

Each JSON object in the dataset must contain the following fields: * context: A string containing the question or prompt. * response: A string containing the ideal answer. * video_file: A Cloud Storage URI pointing to the video file (e.g., gs://my-bucket/video.mp4).

Example:

{"context": "What is the person in the video doing?", "response": "The person is playing the guitar.", "video_file": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/video/guitar.mp4"}
{"context": "Describe the activity in the video.", "response": "A person is surfing on a large wave.", "video_file": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/video/surfing.mp4"}

Each JSON object in the dataset must contain the following fields: * context: A string containing the question or prompt. * candidate_0: The less preferred (rejected) response. * candidate_1: The more preferred (chosen) response. * video_file: A Cloud Storage URI pointing to the video file (e.g., gs://my-bucket/video.mp4).

Example:

{"context": "What is the person in the video doing?", "candidate_0": "The person is playing a violin.", "candidate_1": "The person is playing the guitar.", "video_file": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/video/guitar.mp4"}
{"context": "Describe the activity in the video.", "candidate_0": "A person is swimming in the ocean.", "candidate_1": "A person is surfing on a large wave.", "video_file": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/video/surfing.mp4"}

After creating your dataset file, upload it to a Cloud Storage bucket.

docs.title: Create a model tuning job
docs.text:
You can create a model tuning job using the Vertex AI SDK for Python or the REST API.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Python SDKREST API

Use the following code to create a model tuning job. This example demonstrates a supervised fine-tuning job. For an RLHF job, change the tune method to rlhf_tune_model.

import vertexai
from vertexai.generative_models import GenerativeModel

# TODO: Fill in your project details
project_id = "your-project-id"
location = "us-central1"
vertexai.init(project=project_id, location=location)

# Load the base model
model = GenerativeModel("gemini-1.0-pro-vision-001")

# Start the tuning job
tuning_job = model.tune_model(
    training_data="gs://your-bucket/your-data.jsonl",
    tuning_job_location="europe-west4",
    tuned_model_location=location,
)

# The tuning job takes time to complete. You can check the status using the job ID.
print(tuning_job.gca_resource.name)

To create a model tuning job, send a POST request to the tuningJobs endpoint. This example demonstrates a supervised fine-tuning job. For an RLHF job, replace supervisedTuningSpec with rlhfTuningSpec.

Request:

curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/your-project-id/locations/us-central1/tuningJobs \
-d '{
  "baseModel": "publishers/google/models/gemini-1.0-pro-vision-001",
  "supervisedTuningSpec": {
    "trainingDatasetUri": "gs://your-bucket/your-data.jsonl"
  },
  "tunedModelDisplayName": "my-tuned-gemini-model"
}'

docs.title: View and use the tuned model
docs.text:
After the tuning job is complete, your tuned model is deployed to a Vertex AI endpoint. You can find your tuned model in the Vertex AI Model Registry.

To use the tuned model, specify its endpoint ID in your request.

import vertexai
from vertexai.generative_models import GenerativeModel, Part

# TODO: Fill in your project and endpoint details
project_id = "your-project-id"
location = "us-central1"
endpoint_id = "your-endpoint-id" # e.g., "1234567890123456789"

vertexai.init(project=project_id, location=location)

# Load the tuned model
tuned_model = GenerativeModel(
    model_name=f"projects/{project_id}/locations/{location}/endpoints/{endpoint_id}"
)

# Prepare the video content
video_file_uri = "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/video/skating.mp4"
video_content = Part.from_uri(video_file_uri, mime_type="video/mp4")

# Generate content
prompt = "What is the person in the video doing?"
response = tuned_model.generate_content([video_content, prompt])

print(response.text)

docs.title: Custom metadata labels
docs.text: You can add custom metadata to generateContent and streamGenerateContent API calls by using labels. This page explains what labels are and shows you how to use them to organize your API calls and analyze your spending.

docs.title: What are labels?
docs.text:
A label is a key-value pair that you can assign to generateContent and streamGenerateContent API calls. They help you organize these calls and manage your costs at scale with the granularity you need. You can attach a label (e.g., "team": "research") to each API call and then filter the calls based on their labels.

Label information is forwarded to the billing system, which lets you break down your billed charges by label. With built-in billing reports, you can filter and group costs by labels. You can also use labels to query billing data exports.

docs.title: Requirements for labels
docs.text:
The labels applied to an API call must meet the following requirements:

  • Each API call can have up to 64 labels.
  • Each label must be a key-value pair.
  • Keys have a minimum length of 1 character and a maximum length of 63 characters, and cannot be empty. Values can be empty and have a maximum length of 63 characters.
  • Keys and values can contain only lowercase letters, numeric characters, underscores, and dashes. All characters must use UTF-8 encoding, and international characters are allowed. Keys must start with a lowercase letter or international character.
  • The key portion of a label must be unique within a single API call. However, you can use the same key with multiple calls.

These limits apply to the key and value for each label and to the individual API calls that have labels. There is no limit on how many labels you can apply across all API calls within a project.

docs.title: Common uses of labels
docs.text:
Here are some common use cases for labels:

  • Team or cost center labels: Add labels based on team or cost center to distinguish API calls owned by different teams (for example, team:research and team:analytics). You can use this type of label for cost accounting or budgeting.
  • Component labels: For example, component:redis, component:frontend, component:ingest, and component:dashboard.
  • Environment or stage labels: For example, environment:production and environment:test.
  • Ownership labels: Used to identify the teams that are responsible for operations, for example: team:shopping-cart.

Note

Don't include sensitive information in labels, including personally identifiable information, such as an individual's name or title. Labels are not designed to handle sensitive information.

We don't recommend creating large numbers of unique labels, such as for timestamps or individual values for every API call. This approach makes it difficult to effectively filter and report on API calls because the values change frequently and clutter the catalog.

docs.title: Add a label to an API call
docs.text:
You can add labels to a generateContent or streamGenerateContent API call using the REST API or the Python SDK.

REST

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • GENERATE_RESPONSE_METHOD: The method for generating the model response.
Method Description Use Case generateContent The full response is returned only after it has been completely generated. Best for offline tasks or when the entire response is needed before processing. streamGenerateContent The response is streamed back in chunks as it's being generated. Ideal for interactive applications or chatbots to reduce perceived latency for users. 
*   **`LOCATION`**: The region to process the request.

??? "Click to expand a partial list of available regions"

    *   `us-central1`
    *   `us-west4`
    *   `northamerica-northeast1`
    *   `us-east4`
    *   `us-west1`
    *   `asia-northeast3`
    *   `asia-southeast1`
    *   `asia-northeast1`

*   **`PROJECT_ID`**: Your project ID.
*   **`MODEL_ID`**: The ID of the model you want to use (e.g., `gemini-1.0-pro`).
*   **`ROLE`**: The role in a conversation associated with the content. Specifying a role is required even in single-turn use cases. Acceptable values include:
    *   `USER`: Specifies content that's sent by you.
    *   `MODEL`: Specifies the model's response.
*   **`PROMPT_TEXT`**: The text instructions to include in the prompt.
*   **`LABEL_KEY`**: The label metadata that you want to associate with this API call.
*   **`LABEL_VALUE`**: The value of the label.

To send your request, choose one of these options:

=== "curl"

    !!! note
        The following command assumes that you have logged in to the `gcloud` CLI with your user account by running `gcloud init` or `gcloud auth login`, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the `gcloud` CLI. You can check the currently active account by running `gcloud auth list`.

    Save the request body in a file named `request.json`.

    ```bash
    cat > request.json << 'EOF'
    {
      "contents": {
        "role": "ROLE",
        "parts": { "text": "PROMPT_TEXT" }
      },
      "labels": {
        "LABEL_KEY": "LABEL_VALUE"
      },
    }
    EOF
    ```

    Execute the following command to send your REST request:

    ```bash
    curl -X POST \
         -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
         -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
         -d @request.json \
         "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:GENERATE_RESPONSE_METHOD"
    ```

=== "PowerShell"

    !!! note
        The following command assumes that you have logged in to the `gcloud` CLI with your user account by running `gcloud init` or `gcloud auth login`. You can check the currently active account by running `gcloud auth list`.

    Save the request body in a file named `request.json`.

    ```powershell
    @'
    {
      "contents": {
        "role": "ROLE",
        "parts": { "text": "PROMPT_TEXT" }
      },
      "labels": {
        "LABEL_KEY": "LABEL_VALUE"
      },
    }
    '@  | Out-File -FilePath request.json -Encoding utf8
    ```

    Execute the following command to send your REST request:

    ```powershell
    $cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
    $headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

    Invoke-WebRequest `
        -Method POST `
        -Headers $headers `
        -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
        -InFile request.json `
        -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:GENERATE_RESPONSE_METHOD" | Select-Object -Expand Content
    ```

!!! tip "Troubleshooting"
    If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the [Troubleshooting Guide](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/general/troubleshooting?component=any).

??? "View an example JSON response"

    You should receive a JSON response similar to the following.

docs.title: Summarize an audio file
docs.text:
This section shows you how to use an audio file of a podcast and ask the model to summarize it.

ConsoleGen AI SDK for PythonGen AI SDK for GoREST

The following workflow shows how to use the Google Cloud console to summarize an audio file.

flowchart LR
    A[Go to Vertex AI Studio] --> B[Create a new prompt]
    B --> C{Configure model and parameters}
    C --> D[Insert audio file]
    D --> E[Enter text prompt]
    E --> F[Submit request]

click A "#go-to-vertex-ai-studio"
click B "#create-a-new-prompt"
click C "#configure-model-and-parameters"
click D "#insert-audio-file"
click E "#enter-text-prompt"
click F "#submit-request"
Steps to summarize audio in the console

1. Go to Vertex AI Studio

In the Vertex AI section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Studio page.

Go to Vertex AI Studio

2. Create a new prompt

Click Create prompt.

3. Configure model and parameters (Optional)

  • Model: Select a model that supports audio.
  • Region: Select the region you want to use.
Configure advanced parameters
  • Temperature: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for temperature. The temperature is used for sampling during response generation, which occurs when topP and topK are applied. Temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection. Lower temperatures are good for prompts that require a less open-ended or creative response, while higher temperatures can lead to more diverse or creative results. A temperature of 0 is deterministic, meaning the highest probability response is always selected.
  • Output token limit: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for the max output limit. This is the maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately four characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words.
  • Top-K: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for top-K. Top-K changes how the model selects tokens for output. A top-K of 1 means the selected token is the most probable among all tokens in the model's vocabulary (greedy decoding). A top-K of 3 means that the next token is selected from among the three most probable tokens by using temperature.
  • Top-P: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for top-P. Tokens are selected from most to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. For example, if tokens A, B, and C have a probability of 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 and the top-P value is 0.5, then the model will select either A or B as the next token by using temperature.
  • Add stop sequence: Enter a stop sequence. A stop sequence is a series of characters that stops response generation if the model encounters it. The sequence is not included in the response. You can add up to five stop sequences.
  • Max responses: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for the number of responses to generate.
  • Streaming responses: Enable to print responses as they're generated.
  • Safety filter threshold: Select the threshold of how likely you are to see responses that could be harmful.
  • Enable Grounding: Grounding isn't supported for multimodal prompts.

4. Insert audio file

Click Insert Media, and select a source for your file. If you don't have an audio file, you can use the following publicly available file: gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/audio/pixel.mp3. To listen to this audio, open the sample MP3 file.

Choose a file source

Upload

Select the file that you want to upload and click Open.

By URL

Enter the URL of the file that you want to use and click Insert.

Cloud Storage

Select the bucket and then the file from the bucket that you want to import and click Select.

Google Drive

  1. Choose an account and give consent to Vertex AI Studio to access your account the first time you select this option. You can upload multiple files that have a total size of up to 10 MB. A single file can't exceed 7 MB.
  2. Click the file that you want to add.
  3. Click Select.

The file thumbnail displays in the Prompt pane.

5. Enter text prompt

Enter your text prompt in the Prompt pane. For example:

Provide a concise summary of the main points in the audio file.

6. Submit request

Click Submit. You can also save your prompt or view the equivalent code.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Install the SDK

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Run the code

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI:

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import HttpOptions, Part

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))
prompt = """
Provide a concise summary of the main points in the audio file.
"""
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents=[
        prompt,
        Part.from_uri(
            file_uri="gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/audio/pixel.mp3",
            mime_type="audio/mpeg",
        ),
    ],
)
print(response.text)
# Example response:
# Here's a summary of the main points from the audio file:

# The Made by Google podcast discusses the Pixel feature drops with product managers Aisha Sheriff and De Carlos Love.  The key idea is that devices should improve over time, with a connected experience across phones, watches, earbuds, and tablets.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Install the SDK

Learn how to install or update the Gen AI SDK for Go. To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Run the code

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI:

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"

    genai "google.golang.org/genai"
)

// generateWithAudio shows how to generate text using an audio input.
func generateWithAudio(w io.Writer) error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    client, err := genai.NewClient(ctx, &genai.ClientConfig{
        HTTPOptions: genai.HTTPOptions{APIVersion: "v1"},
    })
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to create genai client: %w", err)
    }

    modelName := "gemini-2.0-flash-001"
    contents := []*genai.Content{
        {Parts: []*genai.Part{
            {Text: `Provide the summary of the audio file.
Summarize the main points of the audio concisely.
Create a chapter breakdown with timestamps for key sections or topics discussed.`},
            {FileData: &genai.FileData{
                FileURI:  "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/audio/pixel.mp3",
                MIMEType: "audio/mpeg",
            }},
        }},
    }

    resp, err := client.Models.GenerateContent(ctx, modelName, contents, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to generate content: %w", err)
    }

    respText, err := resp.Text()
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to convert model response to text: %w", err)
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(w, respText)

    // Example response:
    // Here is a summary and chapter breakdown of the audio file:
    //
    // **Summary:**
    //

docs.text:
This section shows you how to use an audio file of an interview and ask the model to transcribe it with timestamps. To enable timestamp understanding for audio-only files, you must enable the audioTimestamp parameter in GenerationConfig.

ConsoleGen AI SDK for PythonGen AI SDK for GoREST

The following workflow shows how to use the Google Cloud console to transcribe an audio file.

flowchart LR
    A[Go to Vertex AI Studio] --> B[Create a new prompt]
    B --> C{Configure model and parameters}
    C --> D[Insert audio file]
    D --> E[Enter text prompt]
    E --> F[Submit request]

click A "#go-to-vertex-ai-studio-transcribe"
click B "#create-a-new-prompt-transcribe"
click C "#configure-model-and-parameters-transcribe"
click D "#insert-audio-file-transcribe"
click E "#enter-text-prompt-transcribe"
click F "#submit-request-transcribe"
Steps to transcribe audio in the console

1. Go to Vertex AI Studio

In the Vertex AI section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Studio page.

Go to Vertex AI Studio

2. Create a new prompt

Click Create prompt.

3. Configure model and parameters (Optional)

  • Model: Select a model that supports audio.
  • Region: Select the region you want to use.
Configure advanced parameters
  • Temperature: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for temperature. The temperature is used for sampling during response generation, which occurs when topP and topK are applied. Temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection. Lower temperatures are good for prompts that require a less open-ended or creative response, while higher temperatures can lead to more diverse or creative results. A temperature of 0 is deterministic, meaning the highest probability response is always selected.
  • Output token limit: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for the max output limit. This is the maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately four characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words.
  • Top-K: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for top-K. Top-K changes how the model selects tokens for output. A top-K of 1 means the selected token is the most probable among all tokens in the model's vocabulary (greedy decoding). A top-K of 3 means that the next token is selected from among the three most probable tokens by using temperature.
  • Top-P: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for top-P. Tokens are selected from most to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. For example, if tokens A, B, and C have a probability of 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 and the top-P value is 0.5, then the model will select either A or B as the next token by using temperature.
  • Add stop sequence: Enter a stop sequence. A stop sequence is a series of characters that stops response generation if the model encounters it. The sequence is not included in the response. You can add up to five stop sequences.
  • Max responses: Use the slider or textbox to enter a value for the number of responses to generate.
  • Streaming responses: Enable to print responses as they're generated.
  • Safety filter threshold: Select the threshold of how likely you are to see responses that could be harmful.
  • Enable Grounding: Grounding isn't supported for multimodal prompts.

4. Insert audio file

Click Insert Media, and select a source for your file. If you don't have an audio file, you can use the following publicly available file: gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/audio/pixel.mp3. To listen to this audio, open the sample MP3 file.

Choose a file source

Upload

Select the file that you want to upload and click Open.

By URL

Enter the URL of the file that you want to use and click Insert.

Cloud Storage

Select the bucket and then the file from the bucket that you want to import and click Select.

Google Drive

  1. Choose an account and give consent to Vertex AI Studio to access your account the first time you select this option. You can upload multiple files that have a total size of up to 10 MB. A single file can't exceed 7 MB.
  2. Click the file that you want to add.
  3. Click Select.

The file thumbnail displays in the Prompt pane.

5. Enter text prompt

Enter your text prompt in the Prompt pane. For example:

Transcribe the interview, in the format of timecode, speaker, caption. Use speaker A, speaker B, etc. to identify speakers.

6. Submit request

Click Submit. You can also save your prompt or view the equivalent code.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Install the SDK

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Run the code

Set environment variables and run the following code. Note the use of config=GenerateContentConfig(audio_timestamp=True), which is required to enable timestamp understanding.

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import GenerateContentConfig, HttpOptions, Part

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))
prompt = """
Transcribe the interview, in the format of timecode, speaker, caption.
Use speaker A, speaker B, etc. to identify speakers.
"""
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents=[
        prompt,
        Part.from_uri(
            file_uri="gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/audio/pixel.mp3",
            mime_type="audio/mpeg",
        ),
    ],
    # Required to enable timestamp understanding for audio-only files
    config=GenerateContentConfig(audio_timestamp=True),
)
print(response.text)
# Example response:
# [00:00:00] **Speaker A:** your devices are getting better over time. And so ...
# [00:00:14] **Speaker B:** Welcome to the Made by Google podcast where we meet ...
# [00:00:20] **Speaker B:** Here's your host, Rasheed Finch.
# [00:00:23] **Speaker C:** Today we're talking to Aisha Sharif and DeCarlos Love. ...
# ...

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Install the SDK

Learn how to install or update the Gen AI SDK for Go. To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Run the code

Set environment variables and run the following code. To enable timestamps, you would need to add the equivalent of audio_timestamp: true to the generation configuration, similar to the Python and REST examples.

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"

    genai "google.golang.org/genai"
)

// generateAudioTranscript shows how to generate an audio transcript.
func generateAudioTranscript(w io.Writer) error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    client, err := genai.NewClient(ctx, &genai.ClientConfig{
        HTTPOptions: genai.HTTPOptions{APIVersion: "v1"},
    })
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to create genai client: %w", err)
    }

    modelName := "gemini-2.0-flash-001"
    contents := []*genai.Content{
        {Parts: []*genai.Part{
            {Text: `Transcribe the interview, in the format of timecode, speaker, caption.
Use speaker A, speaker B, etc. to identify speakers.`},
            {FileData: &genai.FileData{
                FileURI:  "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/audio/pixel.mp3",
                MIMEType: "audio/mpeg",
            }},
        }},
    }

    resp, err := client.Models.GenerateContent(ctx, modelName, contents, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to generate content: %w", err)
    }

    respText, err := resp.Text()
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to convert model response to text: %w", err)
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(w, respText)

    // Example response:
    // 00:00:00, A: your devices are getting better over time.
    // 00:01:13, A: And so we think about it across the entire portfolio from phones to watch, ...
    // ...

    return nil
}

docs.title: Set optional model parameters

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
While Gemini multimodal models are powerful in many multimodal use cases, it's important to understand their limitations:

  • Non-speech sound recognition: The models that support audio might make mistakes recognizing sound that's not speech.
  • Audio-only timestamps: To accurately generate timestamps for audio-only files, you must configure the audio_timestamp parameter in generation_config.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Start building with Gemini multimodal models - new customers get $300 in free Google Cloud credits to explore what they can do with Gemini.
  • Learn how to send chat prompt requests.
  • Learn about responsible AI best practices and Vertex AI's safety filters.

docs.title: Batch prediction
docs.text:
Batch prediction is a valuable technique for applying machine learning models to large datasets efficiently. Instead of processing individual data points, you can submit a batch of data to Gemini for prediction, saving time and computational resources. Unlike online prediction, where you are limited to one input prompt at a time, you can send a large number of multimodal prompts in a single batch request. Your responses then asynchronously populate in your specified BigQuery or Cloud Storage output location.

Batch requests for Gemini models are discounted 50% from standard requests. To learn more, see the Pricing page.

Important: Batch predictions prioritize off-peak capacity and might take longer to process during busy periods. Turnaround time is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Example notebook
docs.text:
To see a hands-on example of using batch predictions, you can run the "Intro to Batch Predictions with the Gemini API" Jupyter notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab Open in Colab Enterprise Open in Vertex AI Workbench View on GitHub

docs.title: Batch prediction use case
docs.text:
Consider an online bookstore with thousands of books in its database. Instead of generating descriptions individually for each book, which would be time-consuming, this store can use Gemini batch prediction to process all book information at once. This approach dramatically improves efficiency by reducing the overall processing time and minimizing the computational resources required.

Batch prediction can also improve consistency with automation. By processing all descriptions simultaneously, the model maintains a uniform tone and style across book descriptions, reinforcing brand identity. This bookstore can also integrate batch prediction into their workflow to automatically generate descriptions for new book entries, eliminating manual effort and ensuring their website remains up-to-date with minimal human intervention.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: Before you start a batch prediction job, familiarize yourself with the supported models and system limitations.

docs.title: Gemini models that support batch predictions
docs.text:
The following base and tuned Gemini models support batch predictions:

  • Gemini 2.5 Pro
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Execution Time: After submission, batch jobs are validated and queued. Once a job starts running, it has a 24-hour execution limit. If it doesn't complete within that time, all completed requests are exported, and you are only charged for those that completed.
  • Total Time: The maximum time that a batch job can spend in the queue and running is 72 hours.
  • Request Size: We recommend that your input source (table or file) include a minimum of 25,000 requests per job. There's no maximum number of requests per job.
  • Quotas: For quotas and limits on batch prediction jobs, see Generative AI on Vertex AI quotas and system limits.

docs.title: Batch prediction workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the typical workflow for getting batch predictions.

flowchart LR
    A[Understand fundamentals] --> B[Choose data source]
    B --> C[Get batch predictions]
    C --> D[Explore next steps]

    click A "#before-you-begin"
    click B "#choose-your-input-and-output-source"
    click C "#get-batch-predictions"
    click D "#whats-next"

docs.title: Choose your input and output source
docs.text:
Batch requests for Gemini models accept input from Cloud Storage or BigQuery. You can independently choose to output predictions to either a Cloud Storage bucket (as a JSONL file) or a BigQuery table. Use the following table to help decide which source is right for you.

Source Input Format Output Format Best for... Cloud Storage JSON Lines (JSONL) file in a bucket. JSON Lines (JSONL) file in a bucket. Unstructured or semi-structured data, such as prompts stored in files. Ideal for workflows that already use Cloud Storage for data pipelines. BigQuery A request column in a BigQuery table containing valid JSON. A response column in a BigQuery table. Structured data already stored in BigQuery. Ideal for analyzing model outputs alongside your original data using SQL.

docs.title: Get batch predictions
docs.text:
After choosing your data source, follow the steps in the corresponding tab to prepare your data, request a batch job, and retrieve the results.

From Cloud StorageFrom BigQuery Step 1: Prepare your Cloud Storage input

Input file requirements

  • File Format: Your input file must be in JSON Lines (JSONL) format.
  • Location: The Cloud Storage bucket must be in the us-central1 region.

  • Permissions: The service account running the job must have read permissions for the input bucket. To grant the storage.objectUser role, use the following command:

    gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
    --member="serviceAccount:SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/storage.objectUser"
    Replace PROJECT_ID and SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID with your project and service account details.

Caution Soft delete might be enabled on your Cloud Storage buckets, which can retain content in a deleted state and lead to significant storage costs. We highly recommend you Disable soft delete to prevent unexpected charges.

View an example JSONL input

Each line in the file is a separate JSON object representing a single request.

{"request":{"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "What is the relation between the following video and image samples?"}, {"fileData": {"fileUri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/video/animals.mp4", "mimeType": "video/mp4"}}, {"fileData": {"fileUri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/image/cricket.jpeg", "mimeType": "image/jpeg"}}]}]}}
{"request":{"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Describe what is happening in this video."}, {"fileData": {"fileUri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/generative-ai/video/another_video.mov", "mimeType": "video/mov"}}]}]}}
Step 2: Request the batch prediction job

You can request a batch prediction job using the REST API or the Python SDK.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

REST APIPython SDK

To create a batch prediction job, send a POST request to the projects.locations.batchPredictionJobs.create method.

Before you begin, replace the following placeholders in the request body: * LOCATION: A region that supports Gemini models (e.g., us-central1). * PROJECT_ID: Your project ID. * MODEL_PATH: The model name (e.g., publishers/google/models/gemini-2.0-flash-001) or a tuned model endpoint. * INPUT_URI: The Cloud Storage URI of your input file (e.g., gs://bucket-name/path/to/file.jsonl). * OUTPUT_FORMAT: The desired output format (jsonl for Cloud Storage or bigquery for BigQuery). * DESTINATION: gcsDestination for Cloud Storage or bigqueryDestination for BigQuery. * OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME: outputUriPrefix for Cloud Storage or outputUri for BigQuery. * OUTPUT_URI: The output location (e.g., gs://bucket-name/path/to/output/ for Cloud Storage or bq://project.dataset.table for BigQuery).

Request Body: 

{
  "displayName": "my-cloud-storage-batch-prediction-job",
  "model": "MODEL_PATH",
  "inputConfig": {
    "instancesFormat": "jsonl",
    "gcsSource": {
      "uris" : ["INPUT_URI"]
    }
  },
  "outputConfig": {
    "predictionsFormat": "OUTPUT_FORMAT",
    "DESTINATION": {
      "OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME": "OUTPUT_URI"
    }
  }
}

Choose one of the following options to send your request.

==== "curl" Save the request body to a file named request.json and execute the following command:

```bash
curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs"
```

==== "PowerShell" Save the request body to a file named request.json and execute the following command:

```powershell
$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs" | Select-Object -Expand Content
```

A successful request returns a JSON response with a unique BATCH_JOB_ID. You can poll the job status using this ID.

First, install the SDK and set your environment variables.

pip install --upgrade google-genai

# Replace with your project and location
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=your-gcp-project-id
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

Then, use the following Python script to create the job.

import time
from google import genai
from google.genai.types import CreateBatchJobConfig, JobState, HttpOptions

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))
# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below line
# output_uri = "gs://your-bucket/your-prefix"

# See the documentation: https://googleapis.github.io/python-genai/genai.html#genai.batches.Batches.create
job = client.batches.create(
    # To use a tuned model, set the model param to your tuned model using the following format:
    # model="projects/{PROJECT_ID}/locations/{LOCATION}/models/{MODEL_ID}
    model="gemini-2.0-flash-001",
    # Source link: https://storage.cloud.google.com/cloud-samples-data/batch/prompt_for_batch_gemini_predict.jsonl
    src="gs://cloud-samples-data/batch/prompt_for_batch_gemini_predict.jsonl",
    config=CreateBatchJobConfig(dest=output_uri),
)
print(f"Job name: {job.name}")
print(f"Job state: {job.state}")

# Poll for job completion
completed_states = {
    JobState.JOB_STATE_SUCCEEDED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_FAILED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_CANCELLED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_PAUSED,
}

while job.state not in completed_states:
    time.sleep(30)
    job = client.batches.get(name=job.name)
    print(f"Job state: {job.state}")
Step 3: Retrieve the output from Cloud Storage

When the job completes, the output is stored as a JSONL file in the Cloud Storage bucket you specified. For successful rows, the model response is in the response field. For failed rows, error details are in the status field.

During long-running jobs, completed predictions are continuously exported to the output destination, beginning after approximately 90 minutes.

Step 1: Prepare your BigQuery input

Input table requirements

  • Required Column: Your input table must have a request column containing valid JSON that matches the structure of a GenerateContentRequest.
  • Location: The BigQuery dataset must be in the same region as the batch prediction job. Multi-region datasets are not supported.

  • Permissions: The service account must have the BigQuery User (roles/bigquery.user) role. To grant it, use the following command:

    gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
    --member="serviceAccount:SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/bigquery.user"
    Replace PROJECT_ID and SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID with your project and service account details.

  • Other Columns: Other columns in your table are ignored for content generation but are included in the output table. The column names response and status are reserved for the output.

View an example JSON input for the request column

The following JSON shows the required structure for the content in the request column.

{

    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "Give me a recipe for banana bread."
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "system_instruction": {
    "parts": [
      {
        "text": "You are a chef."
      }
    ]
  }
}
Step 2: Request the batch prediction job

You can request a batch prediction job using the REST API or the Python SDK.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

REST APIPython SDK

To create a batch prediction job, send a POST request to the projects.locations.batchPredictionJobs.create method.

Before you begin, replace the following placeholders in the request body: * LOCATION: A region that supports Gemini models (e.g., us-central1). * PROJECT_ID: Your project ID. * MODEL_PATH: The model name (e.g., publishers/google/models/gemini-2.0-flash-001) or a tuned model endpoint. * INPUT_URI: The BigQuery URI of your input table (e.g., bq://project.dataset.table). * OUTPUT_FORMAT: The desired output format (bigquery for BigQuery or jsonl for Cloud Storage). * DESTINATION: bigqueryDestination for BigQuery or gcsDestination for Cloud Storage. * OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME: outputUri for BigQuery or outputUriPrefix for Cloud Storage. * OUTPUT_URI: The output location (e.g., bq://project.dataset.output_table for BigQuery or gs://bucket-name/path/to/output/ for Cloud Storage).

Request Body:

  "model": "MODEL_PATH",

    "instancesFormat": "bigquery",
    "bigquerySource":{
      "inputUri" : "INPUT_URI"
    }
  },
  "outputConfig": {
    "predictionsFormat": "OUTPUT_FORMAT",
    "DESTINATION": {
      "OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME": "OUTPUT_URI"
    }
  }
}

```powershell

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `

    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs" | Select-Object -Expand Content
```

A successful request returns a JSON response with a unique BATCH_JOB_ID. You can poll the job status using this ID.

When the job completes, the output is stored in the BigQuery table you specified. The output table includes all columns from your input table, plus two new columns: * response: Contains the model's JSON response for successful rows. * status: Contains error details for any rows that failed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Gemini API code execution feature enables the model to generate and run Python code and learn iteratively from the results until it arrives at a final output. You can use this capability to build applications that benefit from code-based reasoning and that produce text output. For example, you could use code execution in an application that solves equations or processes text.

The Gemini API provides code execution as a tool, similar to function calling. After you add code execution as a tool, the model decides when to use it.

The code execution environment includes the following pre-installed libraries. You can't install your own libraries.

  • Altair
  • Chess
  • Cv2
  • Matplotlib
  • Mpmath
  • NumPy
  • Pandas
  • Pdfminer
  • Reportlab
  • Seaborn
  • Sklearn
  • Statsmodels
  • Striprtf
  • SymPy
  • Tabulate

docs.text:

docs.title: Code execution versus function calling
docs.text:
Code execution and function calling are both tools that connect Gemini to external systems. The following table outlines the key differences to help you decide which to use.

Feature Code Execution Function Calling Core Purpose Lets the model write and run Python code in a sandboxed environment managed by the API backend. Lets you define functions in your application code that the model can ask to run. Environment Fixed, isolated, and secure environment with a pre-set list of Python libraries. Your own environment. You run the functions requested by the model and have full control over the execution. Use Case Best for tasks that can be solved with standard Python libraries, like data analysis or mathematical calculations. Best when you need to interact with external APIs, databases, or proprietary codebases. Operational Flow Resolves in a single API request. You enable the tool, and the model returns the final result. Requires two API requests: one for the model to request a function call, and a second to return the function output to the model.

In general, prefer code execution if it can handle your use case, as it is simpler to implement. Use function calling when you need to execute your own local functions or connect to external services.

docs.title: Get started with code execution
docs.text:
This section assumes that you've completed the setup and configuration steps shown in the Gemini API quickstart.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

To enable code execution, declare it as a tool when you initialize your model.

Python SDKGo SDKREST

Install the SDK

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the Python SDK reference documentation.

Configure your environment

Set the following environment variables to use the SDK with Vertex AI:

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

Run the code

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import (
    HttpOptions,
    Tool,
    ToolCodeExecution,
    GenerateContentConfig,
)

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))
model_id = "gemini-2.5-flash"

code_execution_tool = Tool(code_execution=ToolCodeExecution())
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model=model_id,
    contents="Calculate 20th fibonacci number. Then find the nearest palindrome to it.",
    config=GenerateContentConfig(
        tools=[code_execution_tool],
        temperature=0,
    ),
)
print("# Code:")
print(response.executable_code)
print("# Outcome:")
print(response.code_execution_result)

# Example response:
# # Code:
# def fibonacci(n):
#     if n <= 0:
#         return 0
#     elif n == 1:
#         return 1
#     else:
#         a, b = 0, 1
#         for _ in range(2, n + 1):
#             a, b = b, a + b
#         return b
#
# fib_20 = fibonacci(20)
# print(f'{fib_20=}')
#
# # Outcome:
# fib_20=6765

Install the SDK

Learn how to install or update the Gen AI SDK for Go. To learn more, see the Go SDK reference documentation.

Configure your environment

Set the following environment variables to use the SDK with Vertex AI:

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

Run the code

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"

    genai "google.golang.org/genai"
)

// generateWithCodeExec shows how to generate text using the code execution tool.
func generateWithCodeExec(w io.Writer) error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    client, err := genai.NewClient(ctx, &genai.ClientConfig{
        HTTPOptions: genai.HTTPOptions{APIVersion: "v1"},
    })
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to create genai client: %w", err)
    }

    prompt := "Calculate 20th fibonacci number. Then find the nearest palindrome to it."
    contents := []*genai.Content{
        {Parts: []*genai.Part{
            {Text: prompt},
        }},
    }
    config := &genai.GenerateContentConfig{
        Tools: []*genai.Tool{
            {CodeExecution: &genai.ToolCodeExecution{}},
        },
        Temperature: genai.Ptr(0.0),
    }
    modelName := "gemini-2.0-flash-001"

    resp, err := client.Models.GenerateContent(ctx, modelName, contents, config)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to generate content: %w", err)
    }

    for _, p := range resp.Candidates[0].Content.Parts {
        if p.Text != "" {
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "Gemini: %s", p.Text)
        }
        if p.ExecutableCode != nil {
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "Language: %s\n%s\n", p.ExecutableCode.Language, p.ExecutableCode.Code)
        }
        if p.CodeExecutionResult != nil {
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "Outcome: %s\n%s\n", p.CodeExecutionResult.Outcome, p.CodeExecutionResult.Output)
        }
    }

    // Example response:
    // Gemini: Okay, I can do that. First, I'll calculate the 20th Fibonacci number. Then, I need ...
    //
    // Language: PYTHON
    //
    // def fibonacci(n):
    //    ...
    //
    // fib_20 = fibonacci(20)
    // print(f'{fib_20=}')
    //
    // Outcome: OUTCOME_OK
    // fib_20=6765
    //
    // Now that I have the 20th Fibonacci number (6765), I need to find the nearest palindrome. ...
    // ...

    return nil
}

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • GENERATE_RESPONSE_METHOD: The response generation method. Choose one:
    • streamGenerateContent: The response is streamed as it's generated.
    • generateContent: The response is returned after it's fully generated.
  • LOCATION: The region to process the request. ??? "Click to expand a partial list of available regions" * us-central1 * us-west4 * northamerica-northeast1 * us-east4 * us-west1 * asia-northeast3 * asia-southeast1 * asia-northeast1
  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: The ID of the model you want to use (e.g., gemini-2.5-flash).
  • ROLE: The role in the conversation. Required even for single-turn requests. Use USER.
  • TEXT: The text instructions to include in the prompt.

To send your request, choose one of the following options:

curlPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have authenticated to the gcloud CLI by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login.

  1. Save the request body in a file named request.json: 

    cat > request.json << 'EOF'
{
  "tools": [{'codeExecution': {}}],
  "contents": {
    "role": "ROLE",
    "parts": { "text": "TEXT" }
  },
}
EOF

  2. Execute the following command to send your REST request: 

    curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/MODEL_ID:GENERATE_RESPONSE_METHOD"

Note: The following command assumes that you have authenticated to the gcloud CLI by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login.

{

    "role": "ROLE",

  },

'@  | Out-File -FilePath request.json -Encoding utf8

  2. Execute the following command to send your REST request:

$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
