docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Expand to see the prerequisites

Before you begin, complete the following prerequisites:

  • A Google Cloud project with billing enabled.
  • The Vertex AI and Compute Engine APIs enabled.
  • Sufficient quota for the machine type and accelerator that you intend to use, such as NVIDIA L4 GPUs. To check your quotas, see Quotas and system limits in the Google Cloud console.
  • A Hugging Face account and a User Access Token with read access.
  • If you are using shared reservations, grant IAM permissions between projects. These permissions are covered in the notebook.

docs.title: Deploy the Llama-3.1 model
docs.text:
The following steps guide you through deploying the model using the Colab Enterprise notebook.

Open the Colab Enterprise notebook

docs.title: Step 1: Set up your environment
docs.text:
Expand to see environment setup details

1. Configure your Google Cloud project

In the first section of the Colab notebook, set the PROJECT_ID, SHARED_PROJECT_ID (if applicable), BUCKET_URI, and REGION variables.

If you intend to use a reservation that was created in a different project, ensure that SHARED_PROJECT_ID is correctly set. The notebook grants the compute.viewer role to the service account of both projects, which allows the Vertex AI endpoint in your primary project to use the reservation capacity in the shared project.

2. Set up Hugging Face authentication

To download the Llama-3.1 model, you must provide your Hugging Face User Access Token in the HF_TOKEN variable within the Colab notebook. If you don't provide one, you will receive a Cannot access gated repository for URL error.

Figure 1. Hugging Face Access Token Settings page.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose a deployment method
docs.text:
Deploy with Spot VMsDeploy with a reservation

To deploy the Llama model to a Spot VM, navigate to the Spot VM Vertex AI Endpoint Deployment section in the Colab notebook and set is_spot=True. This instructs Vertex AI to use a preemptible VM instance, which can provide significant cost savings.

View the Python code for Spot VM deployment 
base_model_name = "Meta-Llama-3.1-8B"
hf_model_id = "meta-llama/" + base_model_name

if "8b" in base_model_name.lower():
    accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_L4"
    machine_type = "g2-standard-12"
    accelerator_count = 1
    max_loras = 5
else:
    raise ValueError(
        f"Recommended GPU setting not found for: {accelerator_type} and {base_model_name}."
    )

common_util.check_quota(
    project_id=PROJECT_ID,
    region=REGION,
    accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
    accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
    is_for_training=False,
)

gpu_memory_utilization = 0.95
max_model_len = 8192

models["vllm_gpu_spotvm"], endpoints["vllm_gpu_spotvm"] = deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name=common_util.get_job_name_with_datetime(prefix="llama3_1-serve-spotvm"),
    model_id=hf_model_id,
    base_model_id=hf_model_id,
    service_account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT,
    machine_type=machine_type,
    accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
    accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
    gpu_memory_utilization=gpu_memory_utilization,
    max_model_len=max_model_len,
    max_loras=max_loras,
    enforce_eager=True,
    enable_lora=True,
    use_dedicated_endpoint=False,
    model_type="llama3.1",
    is_spot=True,
)

Deploying with a reservation guarantees that the required GPU and machine resources are available for your endpoint. You can use two types of reservation affinity:

  • ANY_RESERVATION: The endpoint can use any available reservation in the project that matches the hardware requirements. This is useful for flexibility.
  • SPECIFIC_RESERVATION: The endpoint must use a specific, named reservation. This provides strict control over resource allocation.
Step 2a: Create and share a reservation

Before deploying, you must create a reservation. This tutorial focuses on shared reservations, which can be used by multiple projects within the same organization.

1. Configure the reservation

In the Set Up Reservations for Vertex AI Predictions section of the notebook, set the variables for your reservation, including RES_ZONE, RESERVATION_NAME, RES_MACHINE_TYPE, RES_ACCELERATOR_TYPE, and RES_ACCELERATOR_COUNT.

RES_ZONE = "a"
RES_ZONE = f"{REGION}-{RES_ZONE}"

RESERVATION_NAME = "shared-reservation-1"
RESERVATION_NAME = f"{PROJECT_ID}-{RESERVATION_NAME}"
RES_MACHINE_TYPE = "g2-standard-12"
RES_ACCELERATOR_TYPE = "nvidia-l4"
RES_ACCELERATOR_COUNT = 1
rev_names.append(RESERVATION_NAME)

create_reservation(
    res_project_id=PROJECT_ID,
    res_zone=RES_ZONE,
    res_name=RESERVATION_NAME,
    res_machine_type=RES_MACHINE_TYPE,
    res_accelerator_type=RES_ACCELERATOR_TYPE,
    res_accelerator_count=RES_ACCELERATOR_COUNT,
    shared_project_id=SHARED_PROJECT_ID,
)

2. Share the reservation

In the Google Cloud console, navigate to your reservation and enable sharing with other Google Cloud services. For more information, see How shared reservations work.

Figure 2. Share reservation with other Google services.

Step 2b: Deploy with ANY_RESERVATION

To deploy the endpoint using any available matching reservation, go to the Deploy Llama-3.1 Endpoint with ANY_RESERVATION section of the notebook and set reservation_affinity_type="ANY_RESERVATION".

hf_model_id = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B"

models["vllm_gpu_any_reserve"], endpoints["vllm_gpu_any_reserve"] = deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name=common_util.get_job_name_with_datetime(
        prefix=f"llama3_1-serve-any-{RESERVATION_NAME}"
    ),
    model_id=hf_model_id,
    base_model_id=hf_model_id,
    service_account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT,
    machine_type=MACHINE_TYPE,
    accelerator_type=ACCELERATOR_TYPE,
    accelerator_count=ACCELERATOR_COUNT,
    model_type="llama3.1",
    reservation_affinity_type="ANY_RESERVATION",
)
Step 2c: Deploy with SPECIFIC_RESERVATION

To deploy the endpoint using a specific reservation, go to the Deploy Llama-3.1 Endpoint with SPECIFIC_RESERVATION section of the notebook. Set reservation_affinity_type="SPECIFIC_RESERVATION" and provide the reservation_name, reservation_project, and reservation_zone.

hf_model_id = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B"

MACHINE_TYPE = "g2-standard-12"
ACCELERATOR_TYPE = "NVIDIA_L4"
ACCELERATOR_COUNT = 1

(
    models["vllm_gpu_specific_reserve"],
    endpoints["vllm_gpu_specific_reserve"],
) = deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name=common_util.get_job_name_with_datetime(
        prefix=f"llama3_1-serve-specific-{RESERVATION_NAME}"
    ),
    model_id=hf_model_id,
    base_model_id=hf_model_id,
    service_account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT,
    machine_type=MACHINE_TYPE,
    accelerator_type=ACCELERATOR_TYPE,
    accelerator_count=ACCELERATOR_COUNT,
    model_type="llama3.1",
    reservation_name=RESERVATION_NAME,
    reservation_affinity_type="SPECIFIC_RESERVATION",
    reservation_project=PROJECT_ID,
    reservation_zone=RES_ZONE,
)

docs.title: Step 3: Test and verify the endpoint
docs.text:
After your endpoint is deployed, send it a few test prompts to ensure it is working correctly. If you used a reservation, you can verify that it is being consumed by Vertex AI online prediction in the Google Cloud console.

Figure 3. Check that the reservation is consumed by Vertex AI online prediction.

docs.title: Step 4: Clean up
docs.text:
Clean up resources

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the models, endpoints, and reservations created during this tutorial. The Colab notebook provides code in the Clean Up section to automate this process.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
View troubleshooting guidance
  • Hugging Face Token Errors: Double-check that your Hugging Face token has read permissions and is correctly set in the notebook.
  • Quota Errors: Verify that you have sufficient GPU quota in the region you are deploying to. Request a quota increase if needed.
  • Reservation Conflicts: Ensure that the machine type and accelerator configuration of your endpoint deployment match the settings of your reservation. Also, ensure that the reservation is enabled to be shared with other Google Cloud services.

docs.title: vLLM serving for text-only and multimodal language models on Cloud GPUs
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through deploying and serving Llama 3.1 (text-only) and Llama 3.2 (multimodal) models using vLLM in Vertex AI. It shows you how to efficiently handle model inference on GPUs and customize models for diverse applications.

By the end of this guide, you will understand how to:

  • Download prebuilt Llama models from Hugging Face with a vLLM container.
  • Use vLLM to deploy these models on GPU instances within Vertex AI Model Garden.
  • Serve models efficiently to handle inference requests at scale.
  • Run inference on text-only requests and text-with-image requests.
  • Clean up your resources.
  • Debug common deployment issues.

docs.title: vLLM key features
docs.text:
vLLM is a high-throughput and memory-efficient serving engine for Large Language Models (LLMs).

Feature Description PagedAttention An optimized attention mechanism that efficiently manages memory during inference. It supports high-throughput text generation by dynamically allocating memory, enabling scalability for multiple concurrent requests. Continuous batching Consolidates multiple input requests into a single batch for parallel processing, maximizing GPU utilization and throughput. Token streaming Enables real-time, token-by-token output during text generation. Ideal for applications that require low latency, such as chatbots or interactive AI systems. Model compatibility Supports a wide range of pre-trained models from popular frameworks like Hugging Face Transformers, making it easy to integrate and experiment with different LLMs. Multi-GPU & multi-host Distributes the workload across multiple GPUs and machines, significantly increasing throughput and scalability. Efficient deployment Offers seamless integration with APIs, such as the OpenAI chat completions API, making deployment straightforward for production use cases. Seamless integration with Hugging Face models vLLM is compatible with the Hugging Face model format and supports loading from the Hub, simplifying the deployment of Llama models alongside others like Gemma, Phi, and Qwen. Community-driven open-source project vLLM is open-source and encourages community contributions, promoting continuous improvement in LLM serving efficiency.

For a technical overview of the vLLM system, see the vLLM paper.

docs.title: Google Cloud customizations for vLLM
docs.text:
The vLLM implementation in Vertex AI Model Garden is a customized version optimized for performance, reliability, and integration within Google Cloud.

  • Performance optimizations:

    • Parallel downloading from Cloud Storage: Significantly accelerates model loading by enabling parallel data retrieval from Cloud Storage.
    • Host memory prefix caching: Extends vLLM's GPU memory prefix caching to include host memory.
    • Speculative decoding: Includes pre-tuned configurations for high-performing model setups.

  • Feature enhancements:

    • Dynamic LoRA with enhanced caching: Extends dynamic LoRA capabilities with local disk caching, robust error handling, and support for loading LoRA weights directly from Cloud Storage.
    • Llama 3.1/3.2 function calling parsing: Implements specialized, robust parsing for Llama 3.1/3.2 function calling.

  • Vertex AI ecosystem integration:

    • Vertex AI prediction format support: Ensures seamless compatibility with Vertex AI prediction input and output formats.
    • Vertex AI environment variable awareness: Leverages Vertex AI environment variables (AIP_*) for streamlined configuration and resource management.
    • Enhanced error handling: Implements comprehensive error handling, I/O validation, and server termination mechanisms to ensure stability.
    • Nginx server integration: Integrates an Nginx server to facilitate the deployment of multiple replicas, enhancing scalability and high availability.

docs.title: Additional benefits of vLLM
docs.text:
• Benchmark performance: vLLM offers competitive throughput and latency compared to other serving systems like Hugging Face Text Generation Inference and NVIDIA's FasterTransformer.
  • Ease of use: The library provides a straightforward API for deploying Llama 3.1 and 3.2 models with minimal setup.
  • Advanced features: vLLM supports streaming outputs and efficiently handles variable-length prompts, enhancing interactivity in applications.

docs.text:

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Set up your project and access Llama models

This section outlines the necessary steps for setting up your Google Cloud project, ensuring you have the required resources, and getting access to the Llama models on Hugging Face.

1. Configure your Google Cloud project

  • Enable Billing: Make sure that billing is enabled for your project. For more information, see Enable, disable, or change billing for a project.

  • Check GPU availability and quotas: To run predictions using high-performance GPUs (NVIDIA A100 or H100), check your quotas for these GPUs in your selected region.

    Machine Type Accelerator Type Recommended Regions a2-ultragpu-1g 1 NVIDIA_A100_80GB us-central1, us-east4, europe-west4, asia-southeast1 a3-highgpu-8g 8 NVIDIA_H100_80GB us-central1, us-west1, europe-west4, asia-southeast1

  • Initialize your environment: Run the following code to install necessary libraries and configure your Google Cloud environment variables, APIs, Cloud Storage bucket, and service account permissions.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

BUCKET_URI = "gs://"

REGION = ""

! pip3 install --upgrade --quiet 'google-cloud-aiplatform>=1.64.0'
! git clone https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/vertex-ai-samples.git

import datetime
import importlib
import os
import uuid
from typing import Tuple

import requests
from google.cloud import aiplatform

common_util = importlib.import_module(
    "vertex-ai-samples.community-content.vertex_model_garden.model_oss.notebook_util.common_util"
)

models, endpoints = {}, {}

PROJECT_ID = os.environ["GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT"]

if not REGION:
    REGION = os.environ["GOOGLE_CLOUD_REGION"]

print("Enabling Vertex AI API and Compute Engine API.")
! gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com compute.googleapis.com

now = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d%H%M%S")
BUCKET_NAME = "/".join(BUCKET_URI.split("/")[:3])

if BUCKET_URI is None or BUCKET_URI.strip() == "" or BUCKET_URI == "gs://":
    BUCKET_URI = f"gs://{PROJECT_ID}-tmp-{now}-{str(uuid.uuid4())[:4]}"
    BUCKET_NAME = "/".join(BUCKET_URI.split("/")[:3])
    ! gsutil mb -l {REGION} {BUCKET_URI}
else:
    assert BUCKET_URI.startswith("gs://"), "BUCKET_URI must start with `gs://`."
    shell_output = ! gsutil ls -Lb {BUCKET_NAME} | grep "Location constraint:" | sed "s/Location constraint://"
    bucket_region = shell_output[0].strip().lower()
    if bucket_region != REGION:
        raise ValueError(
            "Bucket region %s is different from notebook region %s"
            % (bucket_region, REGION)
        )
print(f"Using this Bucket: {BUCKET_URI}")

STAGING_BUCKET = os.path.join(BUCKET_URI, "temporal")
MODEL_BUCKET = os.path.join(BUCKET_URI, "llama3_1")

print("Initializing Vertex AI API.")
aiplatform.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location=REGION, staging_bucket=STAGING_BUCKET)

shell_output = ! gcloud projects describe $PROJECT_ID
project_number = shell_output[-1].split(":")[1].strip().replace("'", "")
SERVICE_ACCOUNT = "your service account email"
print("Using this default Service Account:", SERVICE_ACCOUNT)

! gsutil iam ch serviceAccount:{SERVICE_ACCOUNT}:roles/storage.admin $BUCKET_NAME

! gcloud config set project $PROJECT_ID
! gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding --no-user-output-enabled {PROJECT_ID} --member=serviceAccount:{SERVICE_ACCOUNT} --role="roles/storage.admin"
! gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding --no-user-output-enabled {PROJECT_ID} --member=serviceAccount:{SERVICE_ACCOUNT} --role="roles/aiplatform.user"

2. Get access to Llama models on Hugging Face

Meta's Llama 3.1 and 3.2 models are gated and require you to request access and agree to their terms of use.

Figure 1. Meta Llama 3 Community License Agreement.

You also need a Hugging Face user access token to download the models.

  1. Request model access: Visit the Hugging Face page for the model you want to use (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and submit the form to request access.
  2. Generate a read access token:
    • Navigate to your Hugging Face account settings.
    • Create a new token with the Read role and copy it securely.

Figure 2. Hugging Face Access Token Settings link.

Figure 3. Manage Hugging Face Access Token page.

When you set your token as an environment variable during deployment, it remains private to your project. For more information, see Hugging Face Access Tokens Best Practices.

docs.title: Deploy and predict with your model
docs.text: This tutorial supports two main deployment paths: text-only models (Llama 3.1) for language tasks and multimodal models (Llama 3.2) for tasks involving both text and images.

docs.title: Choose your deployment path
docs.text:
Use the following table to decide which model type best suits your needs.

Feature Text-only Models (Llama 3.1) Multimodal Models (Llama 3.2) Primary Use Case Dialogue, summarization, code generation, text classification. Image captioning, visual question answering, describing content in images. Input Format Text only. Text and images. Supported Models Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.1-405B (and Instruct variants). Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision, Llama-3.2-90B-Vision (and Instruct variants). Key Feature Optimized for high-quality, multilingual text generation. Capable of reasoning about both visual and textual information. Dynamic LoRA Supported. Not supported.

Once you have chosen a path, select the corresponding tab below for a step-by-step tutorial.

Text-only models (Llama 3.1)Multimodal models (Llama 3.2)

docs.title: Deploy and predict with text-only models
docs.text:
This tutorial guides you through deploying a Llama 3.1 text-only model with vLLM and making predictions.

Steps to deploy and run predictions

1. Choose a model to deploy

Select the Llama 3.1 model variant you want to deploy.

base_model_name = "Meta-Llama-3.1-8B"  # @param ["Meta-Llama-3.1-8B", "Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", "Meta-Llama-3.1-70B", "Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct", "Meta-Llama-3.1-405B-FP8", "Meta-Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct-FP8"]
hf_model_id = "meta-Llama/" + base_model_name

2. Configure deployment hardware

The following code sets the appropriate GPU and machine type based on the model size and checks for sufficient quota in your project and region.

if "8b" in base_model_name.lower():
    accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_L4"
    machine_type = "g2-standard-12"
    accelerator_count = 1
elif "70b" in base_model_name.lower():
    accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_L4"
    machine_type = "g2-standard-96"
    accelerator_count = 8
elif "405b" in base_model_name.lower():
    accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_H100_80GB"
    machine_type = "a3-highgpu-8g"
    accelerator_count = 8
else:
    raise ValueError(f"Recommended GPU setting not found for: {accelerator_type} and {base_model_name}.")

common_util.check_quota(
    project_id=PROJECT_ID,
    region=REGION,
    accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
    accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
    is_for_training=False,
)

3. Define the deployment function

This function uploads the model to Vertex AI, configures deployment settings, and deploys it to an endpoint using a prebuilt vLLM Docker image.

def deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name: str,
    model_id: str,
    service_account: str,
    base_model_id: str = None,
    machine_type: str = "g2-standard-8",
    accelerator_type: str = "NVIDIA_L4",
    accelerator_count: int = 1,
    gpu_memory_utilization: float = 0.9,
    max_model_len: int = 4096,
    dtype: str = "auto",
    enable_trust_remote_code: bool = False,
    enforce_eager: bool = False,
    enable_lora: bool = False,
    max_loras: int = 1,
    max_cpu_loras: int = 8,
    use_dedicated_endpoint: bool = False,
    max_num_seqs: int = 256,
) -> Tuple[aiplatform.Model, aiplatform.Endpoint]:
    """Deploys trained models with vLLM into Vertex AI."""
    endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint.create(
        display_name=f"{model_name}-endpoint",
        dedicated_endpoint_enabled=use_dedicated_endpoint,
    )

    if "8b" in base_model_name.lower():
        accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_L4"
        machine_type = "g2-standard-12"
        accelerator_count = 1
    elif "70b" in base_model_name.lower():
        accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_L4"
        machine_type = "g2-standard-96"
        accelerator_count = 8
    elif "405b" in base_model_name.lower():
        accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_H100_80GB"
        machine_type = "a3-highgpu-8g"
        accelerator_count = 8
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Recommended GPU setting not found for: {accelerator_type} and {base_model_name}.")

    common_util.check_quota(
        project_id=PROJECT_ID,
        region=REGION,
        accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
        accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
        is_for_training=False,
    )

    vllm_args = [
        "python", "-m", "vllm.entrypoints.api_server", 
        "--host=0.0.0.0", 
        "--port=8080",
        f"--model={model_id}", 
        f"--tensor-parallel-size={accelerator_count}",
        "--swap-space=16",
        f"--gpu-memory-utilization={gpu_memory_utilization}",
        f"--max-model-len={max_model_len}", f"--dtype={dtype}",
        f"--max-loras={max_loras}", f"--max-cpu-loras={max_cpu_loras}",
        f"--max-num-seqs={max_num_seqs}", "--disable-log-stats"
    ]

    if enable_trust_remote_code:
        vllm_args.append("--trust-remote-code")
    if enforce_eager:
        vllm_args.append("--enforce-eager")
    if enable_lora:
        vllm_args.append("--enable-lora")
    if model_type:
        vllm_args.append(f"--model-type={model_type}")

    env_vars = {
        "MODEL_ID": model_id,
        "DEPLOY_SOURCE": "notebook",
        "HF_TOKEN": HF_TOKEN
    }

    model = aiplatform.Model.upload(
        display_name=model_name,
        serving_container_image_uri=VLLM_DOCKER_URI,
        serving_container_args=vllm_args,
        serving_container_ports=[8080],
        serving_container_predict_route="/generate",
        serving_container_health_route="/ping",
        serving_container_environment_variables=env_vars,
        serving_container_shared_memory_size_mb=(16 * 1024),
        serving_container_deployment_timeout=7200,
    )
    print(f"Deploying {model_name} on {machine_type} with {accelerator_count} {accelerator_type} GPU(s).")

    model.deploy(
        endpoint=endpoint,
        machine_type=machine_type,
        accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
        accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
        deploy_request_timeout=1800,
        service_account=service_account,
    )
    print("endpoint_name:", endpoint.name)

    return model, endpoint

4. Execute the deployment

Run the deployment function with your Hugging Face token and selected configuration. Deployment can take up to an hour depending on the model size.

HF_TOKEN = "" # Paste your Hugging Face token here

VLLM_DOCKER_URI = "us-docker.pkg.dev/vertex-ai/vertex-vision-model-garden-dockers/pytorch-vllm-serve:20241001_0916_RC00"

model_name = common_util.get_job_name_with_datetime(prefix=f"{base_model_name}-serve-vllm")
gpu_memory_utilization = 0.9
max_model_len = 4096
max_loras = 1

models["vllm_gpu"], endpoints["vllm_gpu"] = deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name=common_util.get_job_name_with_datetime(prefix=f"{base_model_name}-serve"),
    model_id=hf_model_id,
    service_account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT,
    machine_type=machine_type,
    accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
    accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
    gpu_memory_utilization=gpu_memory_utilization,
    max_model_len=max_model_len,
    max_loras=max_loras,
    enforce_eager=True,
    enable_lora=True,
    use_dedicated_endpoint=use_dedicated_endpoint,
)

You can monitor the deployment progress in the Vertex AI console.

Figure 4. Llama 3.1 Deployment Endpoint in Vertex Dashboard.

5. Make predictions

Once the model is deployed, send text prompts to the endpoint.

  • Define your prompt and parameters:
    • prompt: The input text.
    • max_tokens: The maximum number of tokens in the generated output.
    • temperature: Controls the randomness of the output (e.g., 1.0 for more creative, 0.2 for more deterministic).
    • top_p, top_k: Control nucleus and top-k sampling.
    • lora_id (optional): Path to LoRA weights in Cloud Storage or on Hugging Face. Requires --enable-lora to be set during deployment.
prompt = "What is a car?"
max_tokens = 50
temperature = 1.0
top_p = 1.0
top_k = 1
raw_response = False
lora_id = ""
  • Send the prediction request:
response = endpoints["vllm_gpu"].predict(
    instances=instances, use_dedicated_endpoint=use_dedicated_endpoint
)

for prediction in response.predictions:
    print(prediction)
  • Example output:
Human: What is a car?
Assistant: A car, or a motor car, is a road-connected human-transportation system
used to move people or goods from one place to another.

docs.title: Deploy and predict with multimodal models
docs.text:
This tutorial guides you through deploying a Llama 3.2 multimodal model with vLLM and making predictions using either the default prediction route or the OpenAI Chat Completions API format.

Steps to deploy and run predictions

1. Choose a model to deploy

Select the Llama 3.2 model variant you want to deploy. This tutorial supports both base and Instruct-tuned vision models.

base_model_name = "Llama-3.2-11B-Vision"  # @param ["Llama-3.2-1B", "Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct", "Llama-3.2-3B", "Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct", "Llama-3.2-11B-Vision", "Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct", "Llama-3.2-90B-Vision", "Llama-3.2-90B-Vision-Instruct"]
hf_model_id = "meta-Llama/" + base_model_name

2. Configure deployment hardware

The following code selects the appropriate GPU and machine type based on the model size and checks for sufficient quota.

if "3.2-1B" in base_model_name or "3.2-3B" in base_model_name:
    accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_L4"
    machine_type = "g2-standard-8"
    accelerator_count = 1
elif "3.2-11B" in base_model_name:
    accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_TESLA_A100"
    machine_type = "a2-highgpu-1g"
    accelerator_count = 1
elif "3.2-90B" in base_model_name:
    accelerator_type = "NVIDIA_H100_80GB"
    machine_type = "a3-highgpu-8g"
    accelerator_count = 8
else:
    raise ValueError(f"Recommended GPU setting not found for: {base_model_name}.")

common_util.check_quota(
    project_id=PROJECT_ID,
    region=REGION,
    accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
    accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
    is_for_training=False,
)

3. Define the deployment function

This function handles the deployment of the Llama 3.2 model on Vertex AI, configuring the environment, memory utilization, and vLLM settings.

def deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name: str,
    model_id: str,
    service_account: str,
    base_model_id: str = None,
    machine_type: str = "g2-standard-8",
    accelerator_type: str = "NVIDIA_L4",
    accelerator_count: int = 1,
    gpu_memory_utilization: float = 0.9,
    max_model_len: int = 4096,
    dtype: str = "auto",
    enable_trust_remote_code: bool = False,
    enforce_eager: bool = False,
    enable_lora: bool = False,
    max_loras: int = 1,
    max_cpu_loras: int = 8,
    use_dedicated_endpoint: bool = False,
    max_num_seqs: int = 12,
    model_type: str = None,
) -> Tuple[aiplatform.Model, aiplatform.Endpoint]:
    """Deploys trained models with vLLM into Vertex AI."""
    endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint.create(
        display_name=f"{model_name}-endpoint",
        dedicated_endpoint_enabled=use_dedicated_endpoint,
    )

    if not base_model_id:
        base_model_id = model_id

    vllm_args = [
        "python",
        "-m",
        "vllm.entrypoints.api_server",
        "--host=0.0.0.0",
        "--port=8080",
        f"--model={model_id}",
        f"--tensor-parallel-size={accelerator_count}",
        "--swap-space=16",
        f"--gpu-memory-utilization={gpu_memory_utilization}",
        f"--max-model-len={max_model_len}",
        f"--dtype={dtype}",
        f"--max-loras={max_loras}",
        f"--max-cpu-loras={max_cpu_loras}",
        f"--max-num-seqs={max_num_seqs}",
        "--disable-log-stats",
    ]

    if enable_trust_remote_code:
        vllm_args.append("--trust-remote-code")
    if enforce_eager:
        vllm_args.append("--enforce-eager")
    if enable_lora:
        vllm_args.append("--enable-lora")
    if model_type:
        vllm_args.append(f"--model-type={model_type}")

    env_vars = {
        "MODEL_ID": base_model_id,
        "DEPLOY_SOURCE": "notebook",
    }

    # HF_TOKEN is not a compulsory field and may not be defined.
    try:
        if HF_TOKEN:
            env_vars["HF_TOKEN"] = HF_TOKEN
    except NameError:
        pass

    model = aiplatform.Model.upload(
        display_name=model_name,
        serving_container_image_uri=VLLM_DOCKER_URI,
        serving_container_args=vllm_args,
        serving_container_ports=[8080],
        serving_container_predict_route="/generate",
        serving_container_health_route="/ping",
        serving_container_environment_variables=env_vars,
        serving_container_shared_memory_size_mb=(16 * 1024),
        serving_container_deployment_timeout=7200,
    )
    print(f"Deploying {model_name} on {machine_type} with {accelerator_count} {accelerator_type} GPU(s).")

    model.deploy(
        endpoint=endpoint,
        machine_type=machine_type,
        accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
        accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
        deploy_request_timeout=1800,
        service_account=service_account,
    )
    print("endpoint_name:", endpoint.name)

    return model, endpoint

4. Execute the deployment

Run the deployment function. Deployment can take up to an hour.

model_name = common_util.get_job_name_with_datetime(prefix=f"{base_model_name}-serve-vllm")
models["vllm_gpu"], endpoints["vllm_gpu"] = deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name=model_name
    model_id=hf_model_id,
    base_model_id=hf_model_id,
    service_account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT,
    machine_type=machine_type,
    accelerator_type=accelerator_type,
    accelerator_count=accelerator_count,
    gpu_memory_utilization=gpu_memory_utilization,
    max_model_len=max_model_len,
    enforce_eager=True,
    use_dedicated_endpoint=use_dedicated_endpoint,
    max_num_seqs=max_num_seqs,
)

Figure 5. Llama 3.2 Deployment Endpoint in Vertex Dashboard.

5. Make predictions

You can interact with the deployed multimodal model in two ways.

Method 1: Use the default prediction route

This method is suitable for base vision models.

  • Define your prompt and parameters: Provide an image URL and a text prompt.

    Figure 6. Sample image input for prompting Llama 3.2. 

    image_url = "https://images.pexels.com/photos/1254140/pexels-photo-1254140.jpeg"
raw_prompt = "This is a picture of"
prompt = f"<|begin_of_text|><|image|>{raw_prompt}"

max_tokens = 64
temperature = 0.5
top_p = 0.95

  • Prepare and send the prediction request:

    instances = [
    {
        "prompt": prompt,
        "multi_modal_data": {"image": image_url},
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        "temperature": temperature,
        "top_p": top_p,
    },
]

response = endpoints["vllm_gpu"].predict(instances=instances)

for raw_prediction in response.predictions:
    prediction = raw_prediction.split("Output:")
    print(prediction[1])

Method 2: Use the OpenAI Chat Completions API

This method is ideal for Instruct-tuned vision models and provides a familiar, chat-like interface.

  • Deploy an Instruct model: First, deploy an Instruct-tuned model like Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct.

    base_model_name = "Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct"
hf_model_id = f"meta-llama/{base_model_name}"
model_name = common_util.get_job_name_with_datetime(prefix=f"{base_model_name}-serve-vllm")
model, endpoint = deploy_model_vllm(
    model_name=model_name,
    model_id=hf_model_id,
    base_model_id=hf_model_id,
    service_account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT,
    machine_type="a2-highgpu-1g",
    accelerator_type="NVIDIA_TESLA_A100",
    accelerator_count=1,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.9,
    max_model_len=4096,
    enforce_eager=True,
    max_num_seqs=12,
)

  • Install libraries and authenticate:

    !pip install -qU openai google-auth requests

import google.auth
import openai

creds, project = google.auth.default()
auth_req = google.auth.transport.requests.Request()
creds.refresh(auth_req)

ENDPOINT_RESOURCE_NAME = f"projects/{PROJECT_ID}/locations/{REGION}/endpoints/{endpoint.name}"
BASE_URL = f"https://{REGION}-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/{ENDPOINT_RESOURCE_NAME}"

  • Define inputs and send the request:

    user_image = "https://images.freeimages.com/images/large-previews/ab3/puppy-2-1404644.jpg"
user_message = "Describe this image?"
max_tokens = 50
temperature = 1.0

client = openai.OpenAI(base_url=BASE_URL, api_key=creds.token)

model_response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": user_image}},
                {"type": "text", "text": user_message},
            ],
        }
    ],
    temperature=temperature,
    max_tokens=max_tokens,
)

print(model_response)

docs.title: Cleanup
Debugging common issues
docs.text:
This section provides guidance on resolving common issues encountered during vLLM model deployment and inference.

How to check logs for errors

To identify the root cause of a deployment failure, check the logs in the Google Cloud console.

  1. Go to the Vertex AI Endpoints page.
  2. Click the name of your endpoint.
  3. On the endpoint details page, find your model deployment. A failed deployment will have an error status.
  4. Click View logs to open Cloud Logging, which will be filtered to show logs for your deployment.
  5. Analyze the logs for error messages related to resource constraints (like CUDA OOM), authentication, or configuration.

Figure 7. Failed Llama 3.2 deployment status.

Issue 1: CUDA Out of Memory (OOM) during deployment

Problem: A torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory error occurs when the model's memory requirements exceed the available GPU memory. This often happens with multimodal models if max_num_seqs is set too high.

Figure 8. CUDA Out of Memory error in logs.

Explanation: The max_num_seqs parameter defines the maximum number of concurrent requests the model can handle. Multimodal models consume significantly more memory per sequence than text-only models because they must process image data. For example, a max_num_seqs value of 256 might work for an 8B text model on an L4 GPU but will cause an OOM error for an 11B vision model on the same hardware.

Solution: Reduce the max_num_seqs value. For the Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, a value of 12 is a reasonable starting point. You can also resolve this by using a machine type with more or larger GPUs.

Issue 2: Hugging Face token needed

Problem: The deployment fails with an error message like Cannot access gated repository.

Figure 9. Hugging Face token error in logs.

Explanation: This error occurs because Llama models are gated, and your deployment is missing a valid Hugging Face token or the token does not have the correct permissions.

Solution: 1. Ensure you have requested and been granted access to the model on Hugging Face. 2. Generate a new Read access token from your Hugging Face account settings. 3. Provide this token in the HF_TOKEN environment variable when deploying your model.

Issue 3: Chat template needed

Problem: The deployment fails with a ValueError indicating that a chat template is missing.

Figure 10. Chat template error in logs.

Explanation: Recent versions of the transformers library require an explicit chat template if the tokenizer does not define one.

Solution: Provide a chat template during deployment using the --chat-template argument in the vllm_args. You can find sample templates in the vLLM examples repository.

Issue 4: Model max sequence length too large

Problem: The deployment fails with a ValueError stating The model's max seq len (4096) is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache (2256).

Figure 11. Max sequence length error in logs.

Explanation: The combination of model size and other parameters (gpu_memory_utilization, max_num_seqs) does not leave enough GPU memory to allocate the Key-Value (KV) cache for the specified max_model_len.

Solution: * Option 1 (Recommended): Decrease the max_model_len to a value smaller than the available KV cache size indicated in the error message (e.g., 2048). * Option 2: Increase the available GPU memory by using a machine type with more or larger GPUs. If using multiple GPUs, ensure tensor-parallel-size is set correctly. * Option 3: Slightly increase gpu_memory_utilization (e.g., to 0.95), but this may risk OOM errors during inference.

docs.title: Vertex AI partner models for MaaS
docs.text:
Vertex AI supports a curated list of models developed by Google partners. Partner models can be used with Vertex AI as a model as a service (MaaS) and are offered as a managed API. When you use a partner model, you send your requests to Vertex AI endpoints. Partner models are serverless, so there's no need to provision or manage infrastructure.

You can discover and deploy partner models using Model Garden. For more information, see Explore AI models in Model Garden. While information about each available partner model can be found on its model card in Model Garden, only third-party models that perform as a MaaS with Vertex AI are documented in this guide.

Anthropic's Claude and Mistral models are examples of third-party managed models that are available to use on Vertex AI.

docs.title: Vertex AI partner model pricing with capacity assurance
docs.text: Google offers provisioned throughput for some partner models, which reserves throughput capacity for your models for a fixed fee. You decide on the throughput capacity and in which regions to reserve that capacity. Because provisioned throughput requests are prioritized over the standard pay-as-you-go requests, provisioned throughput provides increased availability. When the system is overloaded, your requests can still be completed as long as the throughput remains under your reserved capacity. For more information or to subscribe to the service, contact sales.

docs.title: Regional and global endpoints
docs.text:
You can send requests to partner models using either regional or global endpoints. Regional endpoints serve requests from a specific Google Cloud region, while the global endpoint can serve requests from any supported region.

Preview

The global endpoint is in Preview.

The following table provides a comparison of regional and global endpoints:

Feature Regional Endpoint Global Endpoint Request Routing Serves requests from the specified region. Serves requests from any supported region. Best for Data residency requirements, lower latency for specific regions. Higher availability and error reduction. Provisioned Throughput Supported Not supported Prompt Caching Supported Not supported Availability Standard Higher, as requests can be rerouted. Latency Potentially lower if the client is near the region. Potentially higher due to cross-region routing. Pricing No difference. No difference.

docs.title: Specify an endpoint
docs.text:
You can specify an endpoint when you send a request to a model.

Global endpointRegional endpoint

To use the global endpoint, set the region to global.

For example, the request URL for a curl command uses the following format: https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/publishers/PUBLISHER_NAME/models/MODEL_NAME

For the Vertex AI SDK, set the region to global to use the global endpoint.

To use a regional endpoint, set the region to one of the supported locations for that model.

For example, the request URL for a curl command uses the following format: https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/publishers/PUBLISHER_NAME/models/MODEL_NAME

For the Vertex AI SDK, a regional endpoint is used by default.

docs.title: Supported models for the global endpoint
docs.text:
The global endpoint is available for the following models:

  • Claude Sonnet 4
  • Claude 3.7 Sonnet
  • Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2

Note

When using the global endpoint, Provisioned Throughput and prompt caching aren't supported. Use regional endpoints for these features.

docs.title: Grant user access to partner models
docs.text:
To enable partner models and make prompt requests, a Google Cloud administrator must set the required permissions and verify that the organization policy allows the use of required APIs.

flowchart LR
    A[Grant required IAM roles] --> B[Verify organization policy]

click A "#grant-iam-roles"
click B "#verify-org-policy"
Steps to grant user access

Grant required IAM roles

To use partner models, you need the following IAM roles: * Consumer Procurement Entitlement Manager (roles/consumerprocurement.entitlementManager): Allows users to enable partner models in Model Garden. * Vertex AI User (roles/aiplatform.user): Includes the aiplatform.endpoints.predict permission, which is required to make prompt requests. For more information, see Vertex AI User and Access control.

You can grant these roles using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

Google Cloud consolegcloud

  1. Go to the IAM page in the Google Cloud console.

    Go to IAM

  2. In the Principal column, find the user for whom you want to enable access and click edit Edit principal in that row.

  3. In the Edit access pane, click add Add another role.

  4. In the Select a role field, select Consumer Procurement Entitlement Manager.

  5. In the Edit access pane, click add Add another role.

  6. In the Select a role field, select Vertex AI User.

  7. Click Save.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, activate Cloud Shell.

    Activate Cloud Shell

  2. Grant the Consumer Procurement Entitlement Manager role required to enable partner models in Model Garden. 

    gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
--member=PRINCIPAL --role=roles/consumerprocurement.entitlementManager

  3. Grant the Vertex AI User role, which includes the permission required to make prompt requests. 

    gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
--member=PRINCIPAL --role=roles/aiplatform.user
    Replace PRINCIPAL with the identifier for the principal, which takes the form user:email, group:email, serviceAccount:email, or domain:domain. For example, user:cloudysanfrancisco@gmail.com.

    The output is a list of policy bindings that includes the following: 

    - members:
  - user:PRINCIPAL
  role: roles/consumerprocurement.entitlementManager
- members:
  - user:PRINCIPAL
  role: roles/aiplatform.user

For more information, see Grant a single role and gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Verify organization policy

To enable partner models, your organization policy must allow the Cloud Commerce Consumer Procurement API (cloudcommerceconsumerprocurement.googleapis.com).

If your organization sets an organization policy to restrict service usage, an organization administrator must verify that cloudcommerceconsumerprocurement.googleapis.com is allowed.

Additionally, if you have an organization policy that restricts model usage in Model Garden, the policy must allow access to partner models. For more information, see Control model access.

docs.title: Data privacy and compliance
docs.text:
The certifications for Generative AI on Vertex AI continue to apply when partner models are used as a managed API through Vertex AI. If you need details about the models themselves, you can find more information in the respective model card or contact the model publisher.

Your data is stored at rest within the selected region or multi-region for partner models on Vertex AI, but the regionalization of data processing might vary. For a detailed list of partner models' data processing commitments, see Data residency for partner models.

Customer prompts and model responses are not shared with third parties when using the Vertex AI API, including with partner models. Google only processes Customer Data as instructed by the Customer, which is further described in our Cloud Data Processing Addendum.

docs.title: Batch predictions with Anthropic Claude models
docs.text: Batch predictions let you send a large number of non-latency-sensitive prompts to an Anthropic Claude model in a single request. This is more efficient for large-scale tasks compared to online predictions, where you send one prompt per request.

docs.title: Supported Anthropic Claude models
docs.text:
Vertex AI supports batch predictions for the following Anthropic Claude models:

  • Claude 3 Opus
  • Claude 3 Sonnet
  • Claude 3 Haiku

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text: By default, you can make up to 4 concurrent batch requests in a single project.

docs.title: Batch prediction workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the typical workflow for getting batch predictions.

flowchart LR
    A[Prepare input] --> B[Request a batch prediction]
    B --> C[Get job status]
    C --> D[Retrieve output]

click A "#prepare-input"
click B "#request-a-batch-prediction"
click C "#get-the-status-of-a-batch-prediction-job"
click D "#retrieve-batch-prediction-output"
Batch prediction tutorial

Prepare input

Before you begin, prepare your input dataset. You can use either a BigQuery table or a JSON Lines (JSONL) file stored in Cloud Storage. The input for both sources must follow the Anthropic Claude API Schema in JSON format.

Here is an example of a single input instance:

{
  "custom_id": "request-1",
  "request":  {
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
    "anthropic_version": "vertex-2023-10-16",
    "max_tokens": 50
  }
}

Choose the input source that best fits your needs.

Input Source Best for Schema Requirements BigQuery Large, structured datasets already stored in BigQuery. Requires a table with specific columns: custom_id and request. Cloud Storage Flexible, file-based workflows using JSONL format. Requires one valid JSON object per line in the file.

BigQuery schema

Your BigQuery input table must contain the following columns:

  • custom_id: A unique identifier for each request to match inputs with outputs.
  • request: The request body, which contains your prompt and must follow the Anthropic Claude API Schema.

Your input table can have other columns, but they will be ignored by the batch job. Do not use the column names response(JSON) or status, as they are reserved for the batch prediction output.

Cloud Storage format

For Cloud Storage, your input must be a JSONL file where each line is a complete JSON object representing a single prediction request. The file must be located in a Cloud Storage bucket.

Request a batch prediction

After preparing your input data, you can request a batch prediction job. You can choose to output the results to either a BigQuery table or a JSONL file in a Cloud Storage bucket, regardless of your input source.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

BigQueryCloud Storage

Specify your BigQuery input table, model, and output location. The batch prediction job and your table must be in the same Google Cloud region.

Vertex AI SDK for PythonREST

To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Vertex AI SDK for Python API reference.

import time

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import CreateBatchJobConfig, JobState, HttpOptions

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below line
# output_uri = f"bq://your-project.your_dataset.your_table"

job = client.batches.create(
    # Check Anthropic Claude region availability in https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/partner-models/use-claude#regions
    # More about Anthropic model: https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/publishers/anthropic/model-garden/claude-3-5-haiku
    model="publishers/anthropic/models/claude-3-5-haiku",
    # The source dataset needs to be created specifically in us-east5
    src="bq://python-docs-samples-tests.anthropic_bq_sample.test_data",
    config=CreateBatchJobConfig(dest=output_uri),
)
print(f"Job name: {job.name}")
print(f"Job state: {job.state}")
# Example response:
# Job name: projects/%PROJECT_ID%/locations/us-central1/batchPredictionJobs/9876453210000000000
# Job state: JOB_STATE_PENDING

# See the documentation: https://googleapis.github.io/python-genai/genai.html#genai.types.BatchJob
completed_states = {
    JobState.JOB_STATE_SUCCEEDED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_FAILED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_CANCELLED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_PAUSED,
}

while job.state not in completed_states:
    time.sleep(30)
    job = client.batches.get(name=job.name)
    print(f"Job state: {job.state}")
# Example response:
# Job state: JOB_STATE_PENDING
# Job state: JOB_STATE_RUNNING
# Job state: JOB_STATE_RUNNING
# ...
# Job state: JOB_STATE_SUCCEEDED
Before you begin

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: A region that supports the selected Anthropic Claude model (see Claude Regions).
  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • MODEL: The name of the model.
  • INPUT_URI: The BigQuery table where your batch prediction input is located, such as bq://myproject.mydataset.input_table.
  • OUTPUT_FORMAT: To output to a BigQuery table, specify bigquery. To output to a Cloud Storage bucket, specify jsonl.
  • DESTINATION: For BigQuery, specify bigqueryDestination. For Cloud Storage, specify gcsDestination.
  • OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME: For BigQuery, specify outputUri. For Cloud Storage, specify outputUriPrefix.
  • OUTPUT_URI: For BigQuery, specify the table location, such as bq://myproject.mydataset.output_result. For Cloud Storage, specify the bucket and folder location, such as gs://mybucket/path/to/outputfile.

HTTP method and URL

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs

Request JSON body

'{
  "displayName": "JOB_NAME",
  "model": "publishers/anthropic/models/MODEL",
  "inputConfig": {
    "instancesFormat":"bigquery",
    "bigquerySource":{
      "inputUri" : "INPUT_URI"
    }
  },
  "outputConfig": {
    "predictionsFormat":"OUTPUT_FORMAT",
    "DESTINATION":{
      "OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME": "OUTPUT_URI"
    }
  }
}'

Send the request

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curlPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs"

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs" | Select-Object -Expand Content

You should receive a JSON response similar to the following:

{
"name":
  "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs/BATCH_JOB_ID",
  "displayName": "JOB_NAME",
  "model": "publishers/anthropic/models/MODEL",
  "inputConfig": {
    "instancesFormat":"bigquery",
    "bigquerySource":{
      "inputUri" : "INPUT_URI"
    }
  },
  "outputConfig": {
    "predictionsFormat":"OUTPUT_FORMAT",
    "DESTINATION":{
      "OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME": "OUTPUT_URI"
    }
  },
  "state": "JOB_STATE_PENDING",
  "createTime": "2024-10-16T19:33:59.153782Z",
  "updateTime": "2024-10-16T19:33:59.153782Z",
  "modelVersionId": "1"
}

Specify your JSONL file's Cloud Storage location, model, and output location.

Vertex AI SDK for PythonREST

To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Vertex AI SDK for Python API reference.

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import CreateBatchJobConfig, JobState, HttpOptions

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))
# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below line
# output_uri = "gs://your-bucket/your-prefix"

# See the documentation: https://googleapis.github.io/python-genai/genai.html#genai.batches.Batches.create
job = client.batches.create(
    # More about Anthropic model: https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/publishers/anthropic/model-garden/claude-3-5-haiku
    model="publishers/anthropic/models/claude-3-5-haiku",
    # Source link: https://storage.cloud.google.com/cloud-samples-data/batch/anthropic-test-data-gcs.jsonl
    src="gs://cloud-samples-data/anthropic-test-data-gcs.jsonl",
    config=CreateBatchJobConfig(dest=output_uri),
)
print(f"Job name: {job.name}")
print(f"Job state: {job.state}")
# Example response:
# Job name: projects/%PROJECT_ID%/locations/us-central1/batchPredictionJobs/9876453210000000000
# Job state: JOB_STATE_PENDING

# See the documentation: https://googleapis.github.io/python-genai/genai.html#genai.types.BatchJob
completed_states = {
    JobState.JOB_STATE_SUCCEEDED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_FAILED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_CANCELLED,
    JobState.JOB_STATE_PAUSED,
}

while job.state not in completed_states:
    time.sleep(30)
    job = client.batches.get(name=job.name)
    print(f"Job state: {job.state}")
# Example response:
# Job state: JOB_STATE_PENDING
# Job state: JOB_STATE_RUNNING
# Job state: JOB_STATE_RUNNING
# ...
# Job state: JOB_STATE_SUCCEEDED
Before you begin

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: A region that supports the selected Anthropic Claude model (see Claude Regions).
  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • MODEL: The name of the model.
  • INPUT_URIS: A comma-separated list of the Cloud Storage locations of your JSONL batch prediction input, such as gs://bucketname/path/to/jsonl.
  • OUTPUT_FORMAT: To output to a BigQuery table, specify bigquery. To output to a Cloud Storage bucket, specify jsonl.
  • DESTINATION: For BigQuery, specify bigqueryDestination. For Cloud Storage, specify gcsDestination.
  • OUTPUT_URI_FIELD_NAME: For BigQuery, specify outputUri. For Cloud Storage, specify outputUriPrefix.
  • OUTPUT_URI: For BigQuery, specify the table location, such as bq://myproject.mydataset.output_result. For Cloud Storage, specify the bucket and folder location, such as gs://mybucket/path/to/outputfile.

HTTP method and URL

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs

Request JSON body

'{
  "displayName": "JOB_NAME",
  "model": "publishers/anthropic/models/MODEL",
  "inputConfig": {
    "instancesFormat":"jsonl",
    "gcsSource":{
      "uris" : "INPUT_URIS"
    }
  },

    "DESTINATION":{

    }

}'

Send the request

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curl -X POST \

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token

  "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/batchPredictionJobs/BATCH_JOB_ID",

Get the status of a batch prediction job

After submitting your job, you can check its status to see if it has completed.

Vertex AI SDK for PythonREST

The Python code example in the request step includes a while loop that polls the job status until it completes. You can also get the status of a job at any time using its name.

# The job object is returned by the client.batches.create() call
# or can be retrieved with client.batches.get(name=job_name)

Before you begin

Retrieve batch prediction output

When a batch prediction job completes, the output is saved to the destination you specified.

  • For BigQuery output: The results are in the response(JSON) column of your destination BigQuery table.
  • For Cloud Storage output: The results are saved as one or more JSONL files in your specified Cloud Storage location.

You can access the full batch prediction results after all rows have been processed or after 24 hours, whichever comes first.

docs.title: Count tokens for Claude models
docs.text:
The count-tokens endpoint lets you determine the number of tokens in a message before sending it to a Claude model. This helps you make informed decisions about your prompts and manage usage.

There is no cost for using the count-tokens endpoint.

docs.title: Supported Claude models
docs.text:
The following models support the count-tokens endpoint:

  • Claude Opus 4
  • Claude Sonnet 4
  • Claude 3.7 Sonnet
  • Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2
  • Claude 3.5 Haiku
  • Claude 3.5 Sonnet
  • Claude 3 Opus
  • Claude 3 Haiku

docs.title: Supported regions
docs.text:
The following regions support the count-tokens endpoint:

  • us-east5
  • europe-west1
  • asia-southeast1
  • us-central1
  • europe-west4

docs.title: Count tokens using the REST API
docs.text:
To count tokens, send a rawPredict request to the count-tokens endpoint. The body of the request must contain the model ID of the model you want to count tokens against.

Before you begin

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: A region that supports Anthropic Claude models. To use the global endpoint, see Specify the global endpoint.
  • MODEL: The model to count tokens against.
  • ROLE: The role associated with a message. You can specify a user or an assistant. The first message must use the user role. Claude models operate with alternating user and assistant turns. If the final message uses the assistant role, then the response content continues immediately from the content in that message. You can use this to constrain part of the model's response.
  • CONTENT: The content, such as text, of the user or assistant message.

HTTP method and URL

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/anthropic/models/count-tokens:rawPredict

Request JSON body

{
  "model": "MODEL",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content":"how many tokens are in this request?"
    }
  ],
}

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curlPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \  
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \  
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \  
     -d @request.json \  
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/anthropic/models/count-tokens:rawPredict"

docs.title: Prompt caching
docs.text:
The Anthropic Claude models offer prompt caching to reduce latency and costs when reusing the same content in multiple requests. When you send a query, you can cache all or specific parts of your input so that subsequent queries can use the cached results from the previous request. This avoids additional compute and network costs. Caches are unique to your Google Cloud project and cannot be used by other projects.

For details about how to structure your prompts, see the Anthropic Prompt caching documentation.

docs.title: Supported Anthropic Claude models
docs.text:
Vertex AI supports prompt caching for the following Anthropic Claude models:

  • Claude 3.5 Haiku
  • Claude 3.5 Sonnet
  • Claude 3 Haiku
  • Claude 3 Sonnet
  • Claude 3 Opus

docs.title: Use prompt caching
docs.text:
You can enable prompt caching by using the Anthropic Claude SDK or by making direct calls to the Vertex AI REST API. Before you begin, choose the method that best fits your application's needs.

Method Pros Cons Best for Anthropic Claude SDK - Simpler, more intuitive Python interface.- Handles API authentication and request formatting automatically. - Adds a dependency to your project (anthropic library). Python developers who want a quick and easy way to integrate Claude models. Vertex AI REST API - Language-agnostic; can be used from any client that can make HTTP requests.- No additional SDK dependencies required. - More complex; requires manual construction of JSON request bodies and handling of authentication tokens. Non-Python environments or applications where minimizing dependencies is critical.

Caching automatically occurs when subsequent requests contain the identical text, images, and cache_control parameter as the first request. All requests must also include the cache_control parameter in the same blocks. The cache has a five-minute lifetime and is refreshed each time the cached content is accessed.

Anthropic SDKVertex AI REST API

The following Python example demonstrates how to use prompt caching with the Anthropic SDK. The first request populates the cache, and the second request uses the cached content, resulting in lower latency and cost.

import anthropic
import os

# Set up the Anthropic client
# Ensure your GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable is set
# and you have run `gcloud auth application-default login`
project_id = os.environ.get("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT")
location = "us-east5" # Or any other supported region
client = anthropic.AnthropicVertex(project_id=project_id, region=location)

# A long document to be cached
long_document = "This is a very long document that we want to cache..." * 100

# --- First request: Populate the cache ---
print("Sending first request to populate the cache...")
response1 = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-3-sonnet@20240229",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": long_document,
                },
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "What is the main topic of this document?",
                },
            ],
        }
    ],
    # Use cache_control to enable caching for the long document
    tool_choice={"type": "tool_use"},
    cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},
)
print("First response received. Usage:", response1.usage)

# --- Second request: Use the cache ---
print("\nSending second request to use the cache...")
response2 = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-3-sonnet@20240229",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": long_document, # Identical content to be read from cache
                },
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "Now, summarize this document in one sentence.", # New question
                },
            ],
        }
    ],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool_use"},
    cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},
)
print("Second response received. Usage:", response2.usage)
print("\nNotice the 'cache_creation_input_tokens' in the first response and 'cache_read_input_tokens' in the second.")

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

The following example demonstrates how to use prompt caching with the Vertex AI REST API using curl. The first request populates the cache, and the second request uses the cached content.

1. Create the request body files

Save the following JSON to a file named request1.json. This request will populate the cache.

{
  "anthropic_version": "vertex-2023-10-16",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        {
          "type": "text",
          "text": "This is a very long document that we want to cache..."
        },
        {
          "type": "text",
          "text": "What is the main topic of this document?"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "cache_control": {
    "type": "ephemeral"
  },
  "max_tokens": 256
}

Save the following JSON to a file named request2.json. This request will read from the cache. Note that the first part of the content is identical to request1.json.

{
  "anthropic_version": "vertex-2023-10-16",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        {
          "type": "text",
          "text": "This is a very long document that we want to cache..."
        },
        {
          "type": "text",
          "text": "Now, summarize this document in one sentence."
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "cache_control": {
    "type": "ephemeral"
  },
  "max_tokens": 256
}

2. Send the requests

Run the following curl commands in your terminal. Replace PROJECT_ID with your Google Cloud project ID and LOCATION with a supported region like us-east5.

# First request to populate the cache
echo "--- Sending first request to populate cache ---"
curl -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/anthropic/models/claude-3-sonnet@20240229:streamRawPredict" -d @request1.json

echo -e "\n\n--- Sending second request to use cache ---"
# Second request to use the cache
curl -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/anthropic/models/claude-3-sonnet@20240229:streamRawPredict" -d @request2.json

docs.text:
Prompt caching can affect billing costs. Note that:

  • Cache read tokens are 90% cheaper than base input tokens.
  • Regular input and output tokens are priced at standard rates.

For more information, see the Pricing page.

docs.title: Data processing and privacy
docs.text:
Anthropic explicit prompt caching is a feature of Anthropic Claude models. The Vertex AI offering of these Anthropic models behaves as described in the Anthropic documentation.

Prompt caching is an optional feature. Claude computes the hashes (fingerprints) of requests for caching keys. These hashes are only computed for requests that have caching enabled.

Although prompt caching is a feature implemented by the Claude models, from a data handling perspective, Google considers these hashes to be a type of "User Metadata." They are treated as customer "Service Data" under the Google Cloud Privacy Notice and not as "Customer Data" under the Cloud Data Processing Addendum (Customers). In particular, additional protections for "Customer Data" don't apply to these hashes. Google does not use these hashes for any other purpose.

If you want to completely disable this prompt caching feature and make it unavailable in particular Google Cloud projects, you can request this by contacting customer support and providing the relevant project numbers. After explicit caching is disabled for a project, requests from the project with prompt caching enabled are rejected.

To use Anthropic Claude models with Vertex AI, you must first set up your project.

1. Set up your Google Cloud project

  • Sign in to your Google Cloud account. If you're new to Google Cloud, create an account to evaluate how our products perform in real-world scenarios. New customers also get $300 in free credits to run, test, and deploy workloads.

2. Enable the Vertex AI API

Anthropic recommends that you enable 30-day logging of your prompt and completion activity to record any model misuse. To enable logging, see Log requests and responses.

docs.title: Send prediction requests
docs.text:
After you complete the setup, you can send requests to the Claude models. You can use the Anthropic SDK for a higher-level programmatic interface or cURL for direct REST API calls.

Method Best for Pros Cons Anthropic SDK Application development and integration. - Simplified API calls.- Handles authentication and request formatting automatically.- Available for Python and TypeScript. - Requires installing and managing a client library.- Adds a dependency to your project. cURL Quick testing, scripting, and environments where installing an SDK is not feasible. - No installation required (pre-installed on most systems).- Direct control over the HTTP request. - Requires manual construction of JSON payloads.- Authentication token management is manual.- Can be more verbose and error-prone.

Select a tab for instructions on how to use each method.

Anthropic SDKcURL

You can make API requests to the Claude models using the Anthropic Claude SDK. For more information, see the following resources: * Claude messages API reference * Anthropic Python API library * Anthropic Vertex AI TypeScript API Library

To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Vertex AI SDK for Python API reference documentation.

docs.title: Build the request
docs.text:
HTTP method and URL:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/anthropic/models/MODEL:streamRawPredict
View parameter descriptions

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: A region that supports Anthropic Claude models. To use the global endpoint, see Specify the global endpoint.
  • MODEL: The model name you want to use.
  • ROLE: The role associated with a message. You can specify a user or an assistant. The first message must use the user role. Claude models operate with alternating user and assistant turns. If the final message uses the assistant role, then the response content continues immediately from the content in that message. You can use this to constrain part of the model's response.
  • STREAM: A boolean that specifies whether the response is streamed or not. Stream your response to reduce the end-use latency perception. Set to true to stream the response and false to return the response all at once.
  • CONTENT: The content, such as text, of the user or assistant message.
  • MAX_TOKENS: Maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately 3.5 characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words. Specify a lower value for shorter responses and a higher value for potentially longer responses.
  • TOP_P (Optional): Top-P changes how the model selects tokens for output. Tokens are selected from the most probable to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. For example, if tokens A, B, and C have a probability of 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 and the top-P value is 0.5, then the model will select either A or B as the next token by using temperature and excludes C as a candidate. Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.
  • TOP_K (Optional): Top-K changes how the model selects tokens for output. A top-K of 1 means the next selected token is the most probable among all tokens in the model's vocabulary (also called greedy decoding), while a top-K of 3 means that the next token is selected from among the three most probable tokens by using temperature. For each token selection step, the top-K tokens with the highest probabilities are sampled. Then tokens are further filtered based on top-P with the final token selected using temperature sampling. Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.
  • TYPE: For Claude 3.7 Sonnet and later Claude models, to enable extended thinking mode, specify enable.
  • BUDGET_TOKENS: If you enable extended thinking, you must specify the number of tokens that the model can use for its internal reasoning as part of the output. Larger budgets can enable more thorough analysis for complex problems and improve response quality. You must specify a value greater than or equal to 1024 but less than MAX_TOKENS.

Request JSON body:

{
  "anthropic_version": "vertex-2023-10-16",
  "messages": [
   {
    "role": "ROLE",
    "content": "CONTENT"
   }],
  "max_tokens": MAX_TOKENS,
  "stream": STREAM,
  "thinking": {
    "type": "TYPE",
    "budget_tokens": BUDGET_TOKENS
  }
}

docs.text:
The Anthropic Claude models support tools and function calling to enhance a model's capabilities. For more information, see the Tool use overview in the Anthropic documentation.

The following samples demonstrate how to use tools to search for nearby restaurants in San Francisco that are open.

Vertex AI SDK for PythonREST

The following sample uses regional endpoints. To use the global endpoint, see Specify the global endpoint.

docs.title: Use Vertex AI Studio
docs.text:
For some of the Anthropic Claude models, you can use Vertex AI Studio to quickly prototype and test generative AI models in the Google Cloud console. As an example, you can use Vertex AI Studio to compare Claude model responses with other supported models such as Google Gemini.

For more information, see Quickstart: Send text prompts to Gemini using Vertex AI Studio.

docs.title: Anthropic Claude quotas and region availability
docs.text:
Claude models have regional quotas and, for models that support a global endpoint, a global quota. The quota is specified in queries per minute (QPM) and tokens per minute (TPM). TPM includes both input and output tokens.

To maintain overall service performance and acceptable use, the maximum quotas might vary by account and, in some cases, access might be restricted. View your project's quotas on the Quotas & Systems Limits page in the Google Cloud console. You must also have the following quotas available:

  • online_prediction_requests_per_base_model and global_online_prediction_requests_per_base_model defines your QPM quota.
  • For TPM, there are three quota values that apply to particular models:
    • For models that count input and output tokens together, online_prediction_tokens_per_minute_per_base_model and global_online_prediction_tokens_per_minute_per_base_model defines the model TPM quota.
    • For models that count input and output tokens separately, online_prediction_input_tokens_per_minute_per_base_model and global_online_prediction_input_tokens_per_minute_per_base_model defines the input TPM quota and online_prediction_output_tokens_per_minute_per_base_model and global_online_prediction_output_tokens_per_minute_per_base_model defines the output TPM quota.

To see which models count input and output tokens separately, see Quotas by model and region.

docs.title: Input tokens
docs.text:
The following list defines the input tokens that can count towards your input TPM quota. The input tokens that each model counts can vary. To see which input tokens a model counts, see Quotas by model and region.

  • Input tokens includes all input tokens, including cache read and cache write tokens.
  • Uncached input tokens includes only the input tokens that weren't read from a cache (cache read tokens).
  • Cache write tokens includes tokens that were used to create or update a cache.
