Preview

Some of the RAG features are Preview offerings, subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" of the Google Cloud Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features may have limited support, and changes to Pre-GA products and features may not be compatible with other Pre-GA versions. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions. Further, by using the Gemini API on Vertex AI, you agree to the Generative AI Preview terms and conditions (Preview Terms).

The VPC-SC security control is supported by RAG Engine. Data residency, CMEK, and AXT security controls aren't supported.

This page shows you how to connect your RAG Engine corpus to your Weaviate database. You can use your Weaviate database instance, which is an open-source database, with RAG Engine to index and conduct a vector-based similarity search.

With RAG Engine, you can continue to use your fully-managed vector database instance, which you are responsible for provisioning. RAG Engine uses the vector database for storage, index management, and search.

To see a complete example, you can run the "RAG Engine with Weaviate" Jupyter notebook in one of the following environments:

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Expand to see all prerequisite steps

Provision the Weaviate database

Before using the Weaviate database with RAG Engine, you must configure and deploy your Weaviate database instance, prepare the HTTPS endpoint, and create your Weaviate collection.

1. Configure and deploy your Weaviate database instance

Follow the Weaviate official quickstart guide. You can set up your Weaviate instance anywhere, as long as the Weaviate endpoint is accessible to your project. You are responsible for managing your Weaviate database instance lifecycle.

2. Prepare the HTTPS endpoint

During Weaviate provisioning, ensure that you create an HTTPS endpoint. While HTTP connections are supported, an HTTPS connection is recommended for traffic between RAG Engine and your Weaviate database.

3. Create your Weaviate collection

The RAG Engine corpus and the Weaviate collection have a one-to-one mapping. You must create a collection in your Weaviate database before associating it with a RAG Engine corpus. When creating the collection, you must use the following schema:

Property name Data type fileId text corpusId text chunkId text chunkDataType text chunkData text fileOriginalUri text

The following is an example REST call to create a collection:

# TODO(developer): Update the variables.
# The HTTPS/HTTP Weaviate endpoint you created during provisioning.
HTTP_ENDPOINT_NAME="https://your.weaviate.endpoint.com"

# Your Weaviate API Key.
WEAVIATE_API_KEY="example-api-key"

# Select your Weaviate collection name, which roughly corresponds to a Vertex AI Knowledge Engine Corpus.
# For example, "MyCollectionName"
# Note that the first letter needs to be capitalized.
# Otherwise, Weavaite will capitalize it for you.
WEAVIATE_COLLECTION_NAME="MyCollectionName"

# Create a collection in Weaviate which includes the required schema fields shown below.
echo '{
  "class": "'${WEAVIATE_COLLECTION_NAME}'",
  "properties": [
    { "name": "fileId", "dataType": [ "string" ] },
    { "name": "corpusId", "dataType": [ "string" ] },
    { "name": "chunkId", "dataType": [ "string" ] },
    { "name": "chunkDataType", "dataType": [ "string" ] },
    { "name": "chunkData", "dataType": [ "string" ] },
    { "name": "fileOriginalUri", "dataType": [ "string" ] }
  ]
}' | curl \
    -X POST \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer "${WEAVIATE_API_KEY} \
    -d @- \
    ${HTTP_ENDPOINT_NAME}/v1/schema

4. Provision Weaviate with an API key for authentication

RAG Engine connects to your Weaviate database using an API key. You must create a Weaviate API key, store it securely in Secret Manager, and grant the RAG Engine service account access to it.

  • Create the Weaviate API key: Follow the Weaviate official guide to authentication to configure API key-based authentication in your Weaviate database instance.

  • Store your API key in Secret Manager: To protect your API key, store it in Secret Manager.

ConsoleRESTPython
  1. Go to the Secret Manager page. Go to Secret Manager
  2. Click + Create Secret.
  3. Enter a Name for your secret (e.g., MyWeaviateApiKeySecret).
  4. In the Secret value field, enter your Weaviate API key.
  5. Click Create secret.
# TODO(developer): Update the variables.
# Select a resource name for your Secret, which contains your API Key.
SECRET_NAME="MyWeaviateApiKeySecret"

# Your Weaviate API Key.
WEAVIATE_API_KEY="example-api-key"

# Create a secret in SecretManager.
curl "https://secretmanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/secrets?secretId=${SECRET_NAME}" \
    --request "POST" \
    --header "authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    --header "content-type: application/json" \
    --data "{\"replication\": {\"automatic\": {}}}"

# Encode your WEAVIATE_API_KEY using base 64.
SECRET_DATA=$(echo ${WEAVIATE_API_KEY} | base64)

# Create a new version of your secret which uses SECRET_DATA as payload
curl "https://secretmanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/secrets/${SECRET_NAME}:addVersion" \
    --request "POST" \
    --header "authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    --header "content-type: application/json" \
    --data "{\"payload\": {\"data\": \"${SECRET_DATA}\"}}"

# Import the Secret Manager client library.
from google.cloud import secretmanager
import google_crc32c  # type: ignore
from typing import Optional


def create_secret(
    project_id: str, secret_id: str
) -> secretmanager.Secret:
    """
    Create a new secret with the given name.
    """
    client = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient()
    parent = f"projects/{project_id}"
    response = client.create_secret(
        request={
            "parent": parent,
            "secret_id": secret_id,
            "secret": {"replication": {"automatic": {}}},
        }
    )
    print(f"Created secret: {response.name}")
    return response

def add_secret_version(
    project_id: str, secret_id: str, payload: str
) -> secretmanager.SecretVersion:
    """
    Add a new secret version to the given secret with the provided payload.
    """
    client = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient()
    parent = client.secret_path(project_id, secret_id)
    payload_bytes = payload.encode("UTF-8")
    crc32c = google_crc32c.Checksum()
    crc32c.update(payload_bytes)
    response = client.add_secret_version(
        request={
            "parent": parent,
            "payload": {
                "data": payload_bytes,
                "data_crc32c": int(crc32c.hexdigest(), 16),
            },
        }
    )
    print(f"Added secret version: {response.name}")
    return response

# TODO(developer): Update the variables before running.
# project_id = "your-project-id"
# secret_id = "MyWeaviateApiKeySecret"
# payload = "your-weaviate-api-key"
# create_secret(project_id, secret_id)
# add_secret_version(project_id, secret_id, payload)
  • Grant permissions to the RAG Engine service account: When you create your first RAG resource, a dedicated service account is created in your project. You must grant this service account permission to access the secret containing your API key.
    1. Find your RAG Engine service account on the IAM page. It follows the format service-{project_number}@gcp-sa-vertex-rag.iam.gserviceaccount.com.
    2. Grant this service account the Secret Manager Secret Accessor (roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor) role on the secret you created.

Set up your Google Cloud environment

Expand to see environment setup instructions

Before you can use the Vertex AI SDK, you need to set up your project and development environment.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project. Go to project selector
  2. Enable the Vertex AI API. Enable the API
  3. To run commands in a local shell, install and initialize the Google Cloud CLI.
  4. Create local authentication credentials for your user account: 
    gcloud auth application-default login
  5. Install the client library for your preferred language.
PythonNode.jsJavaGoC#REST

Install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python.

pip3 install --upgrade "google-cloud-aiplatform>=1.38"

Install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Node.js.

npm install @google-cloud/vertexai

Add google-cloud-vertexai as a dependency.

Maven with BOM

Add the following to your pom.xml: 

<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.google.cloud</groupId>
      <artifactId>libraries-bom</artifactId>
      <version>26.32.0</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.google.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>google-cloud-vertexai</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Gradle with BOM

Add the following to your build.gradle: 

implementation platform('com.google.cloud:libraries-bom:26.32.0')
implementation 'com.google.cloud:google-cloud-vertexai'

Install the desired Go package. The vertexai package is recommended for most developers.

# Human authored package. Recommended for most developers.
go get cloud.google.com/go/vertexai

# Auto-generated package for features not yet in the recommended package.
go get cloud.google.com/go/aiplatform

Install the Google.Cloud.AIPlatform.V1 NuGet package.

dotnet add package Google.Cloud.AIPlatform.V1

Configure environment variables. Replace PROJECT_ID with your Google Cloud project ID.

MODEL_ID="gemini-2.0-flash-001"
PROJECT_ID="PROJECT_ID"

docs.title: Connect RAG Engine to Weaviate
docs.text:
After completing the prerequisite steps, you can create a RAG corpus that connects to your Weaviate collection and use it for retrieval and generation.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Step 1: Create a RAG corpus

Create a RAG corpus and set the Weaviate instance as its vector database. The http_endpoint and collection_name fields are immutable once set.

PythonREST 
from vertexai.preview import rag
import vertexai

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below lines
# PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
# weaviate_http_endpoint = "https://your.weaviate.endpoint.com"
# weaviate_collection_name = "MyCollectionName"
# weaviate_api_key_secret_manager_version = "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/secrets/{SECRET_NAME}/versions/latest"
# display_name = "test_corpus"
# description = "Corpus Description"

# Initialize Vertex AI API once per session
vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1")

# Configure embedding model (Optional)
embedding_model_config = rag.EmbeddingModelConfig(
    publisher_model="publishers/google/models/text-embedding-004"
)

# Configure Vector DB
vector_db = rag.Weaviate(
    weaviate_http_endpoint=weaviate_http_endpoint,
    collection_name=weaviate_collection_name,
    api_key=weaviate_api_key_secret_manager_version,
)

corpus = rag.create_corpus(
    display_name=display_name,
    description=description,
    embedding_model_config=embedding_model_config,
    vector_db=vector_db,
)
print(corpus)
# Example response:
# RagCorpus(name='projects/1234567890/locations/us-central1/ragCorpora/1234567890',
# display_name='test_corpus', description='Corpus Description', embedding_model_config=...
# ...

# TODO(developer): Update the variables.
PROJECT_ID="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
# The HTTPS/HTTP Weaviate endpoint you created during provisioning.
HTTP_ENDPOINT_NAME="https://your.weaviate.endpoint.com"

# Your Weaviate collection name.
WEAVIATE_COLLECTION_NAME="MyCollectionName"

# The resource name of your Weaviate API Key your Secret.
SECRET_NAME="MyWeaviateApiKeySecret"
# The Secret Manager resource name containing the API Key for your Weaviate endpoint.
APIKEY_SECRET_VERSION="projects/${PROJECT_ID}/secrets/${SECRET_NAME}/versions/latest"

# Select a Corpus display name.
CORPUS_DISPLAY_NAME="SpecialCorpus"

# Call CreateRagCorpus API to create a new corpus associated with your Weaviate collection.
curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/locations/us-central1/ragCorpora \
-d '{
      "display_name" : '\""${CORPUS_DISPLAY_NAME}"\"',
      "rag_vector_db_config" : {
              "weaviate": {
                    "http_endpoint": '\""${HTTP_ENDPOINT_NAME}"\"',
                    "collection_name": '\""${WEAVIATE_COLLECTION_NAME}"\"'
              },
        "api_auth" : {
                "api_key_config": {
                      "api_key_secret_version": '\""${APIKEY_SECRET_VERSION}"\"'
                }
        }
      }
  }'
Step 2: Add files to the RAG corpus

You can upload files from a local path or import them from Google Drive or Cloud Storage. The RAG API handles file parsing, chunking, and embedding generation.

Upload a local file

PythonREST 
from vertexai import rag
import vertexai

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below lines
# PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
# corpus_name = "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/locations/us-central1/ragCorpora/{rag_corpus_id}"
# path = "path/to/local/file.txt"
# display_name = "file_display_name"
# description = "file description"

# Initialize Vertex AI API once per session
vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1")

rag_file = rag.upload_file(
    corpus_name=corpus_name,
    path=path,
    display_name=display_name,
    description=description,
)
print(rag_file)
# Example response:
# RagFile(name='projects/[PROJECT_ID]/locations/us-central1/ragCorpora/1234567890/ragFiles/09876543',
#  display_name='file_display_name', description='file description')

Save the request body in a file named request.json: 

{
 "rag_file": {
  "display_name": "FILE_DISPLAY_NAME",
  "description": "RAG_FILE_DESCRIPTION"
 }
}

Execute the following command: 

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \

import vertexai

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below lines

    retrieval=rag.Retrieval(

            rag_resources=[

                    rag_corpus=corpus_name,

docs.title: Use hybrid search
docs.text:
Hybrid search, which combines semantic (dense vector) and keyword (sparse vector) searches, is supported through your Weaviate database to improve the relevance of search results. You must configure hybrid search within your Weaviate instance. RAG Engine then leverages this capability during retrieval.

The weighting between dense and sparse vector similarity (e.g., the alpha parameter) is configured in Weaviate. The following examples show how to perform a retrieval query that can leverage a hybrid search-enabled Weaviate collection.

Enable hybrid search with the retrieval API PythonREST

docs.title: Vector database choices in Vertex AI RAG Engine
docs.text:
Preview

The VPC-SC security control is supported by RAG Engine. Data residency, CMEK, and AXT security controls aren't supported.

This page introduces the vector databases supported by Vertex AI RAG Engine and helps you choose the best option for your application.

Vector databases are essential for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) applications. They store and query vector embeddings, which are numerical representations of data that capture semantic meaning. Think of vector embeddings as coordinates on a map of concepts, where similar ideas are located close to each other. This allows RAG systems to quickly find the most relevant information from a large knowledge base to answer complex queries, enhancing the accuracy and relevance of Large Language Model (LLM) responses.

docs.title: How to choose a vector database
docs.text:
Your primary choice is between using a fully managed database provided by Vertex AI or provisioning and managing your own.

  • Vertex AI-managed database (RagManagedDb): This is the default, serverless option. It requires no setup and is ideal for users who want to get started quickly, from proof-of-concept to enterprise-scale applications, without managing database infrastructure.

  • Self-provisioned vector databases: This option gives you more control and is suitable if you are already using another vector database service like Vertex AI Vector Search, or third-party databases like Pinecone or Weaviate. With this approach, you are responsible for the lifecycle, performance, and scalability of your vector database.

docs.title: Comparison of vector database options
docs.text:
The following table compares the vector databases supported by Vertex AI RAG Engine to help you select the best fit for your use case.

Vector database Benefits Best for Considerations Supported distance metrics Search type Launch stage RagManagedDb (Default)
  • No setup or provisioning required.
  • High consistency and availability.
  • Low-latency reads and writes.
  • Excellent for transactional workloads.
  • Quickly building a proof of concept.
  • Enterprise-scale RAG with low maintenance.
  • Chatbots and other interactive applications.
  • For optimal recall, the ANN index should be rebuilt after significant data changes.
cosine KNN (default) and ANN Preview Vector Search
  • Deep integration with Google Cloud services.
  • High scalability and reliability.
  • Pay-as-you-go pricing.
  • Existing Google Cloud customers.
  • Applications requiring integration with other Google Cloud services.
  • Managing your own vector database infrastructure.
  • Updates are not reflected in real-time.
  • Potential for vendor lock-in with Google Cloud.
  • Cost can vary based on usage patterns.
cosine dot-product ANN Generally available Vertex AI Feature Store
  • Managed service integrated with Vertex AI.
  • Leverages existing BigQuery infrastructure.
  • Scalability supported by Google Cloud.
  • Users already leveraging Vertex AI Feature Store or BigQuery.
  • Organizing, storing, and serving ML features alongside vectors.
  • Changes require a manual synchronization to the online store.
  • Potential for vendor lock-in with Google Cloud.
cosine dot-product L2 squared ANN Preview Weaviate
  • Open-source with a strong community.
  • Highly flexible and customizable.
  • Supports diverse data types (text, images) and hybrid search.
  • Multi-cloud deployment options.
  • Existing Weaviate customers.
  • Users who prefer open-source solutions.
  • Applications requiring hybrid search or multi-modal capabilities.
  • Updates are not reflected in real-time.
  • Can be more complex to set up and manage.
  • Performance depends on configuration.
cosine dot-product L2 squared hamming manhattan ANN + Hybrid search Preview Pinecone
  • Fully managed and easy to get started.
  • Excellent scalability and performance for similarity search.
  • Advanced features like filtering and metadata search.
  • Multi-cloud deployment options.
  • Existing Pinecone customers.
  • Applications that require high-performance vector search with advanced filtering.
  • Updates are not reflected in real-time.
  • Can be more expensive than other options.
  • Quotas and limits may restrict scale.
  • Limited control over the underlying infrastructure.
cosine euclidean dot-product ANN Generally available

docs.title: Service Information
docs.text:
To call this service, we recommend that you use the Google-provided client libraries. If your application needs to use your own libraries to call this service, use the following information when you make the API requests.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Discovery document
docs.text:
A Discovery Document is a machine-readable specification for describing and consuming REST APIs. It is used to build client libraries, IDE plugins, and other tools that interact with Google APIs. One service may provide multiple discovery documents. This service provides the following discovery documents:

  • https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/$discovery/rest?version=v1
  • https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/$discovery/rest?version=v1beta1

docs.title: Service endpoint
docs.text:
A service endpoint is a base URL that specifies the network address of an API service. One service might have multiple service endpoints. This service has the following service endpoint, and all URIs below are relative to this service endpoint:

  • https://aiplatform.googleapis.com

docs.title: Dynamic shared quota (DSQ)
docs.text: Dynamic shared quota (DSQ) serves your pay-as-you-go (PayGo) requests with greater flexibility to adapt to your workload needs without you having to manage quotas and quota increase requests (QIR). With DSQ, there are no predefined quota limits on your usage. Instead, DSQ provides access to a large, shared pool of resources, dynamically allocated based on real-time availability and demand across all customers of that model. When more customers are active, each customer gets a lower amount of throughput. Similarly, if there are fewer customers, each customer might get higher throughput.

docs.title: When to use Dynamic Shared Quota
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers two main ways to manage throughput for generative AI models: Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) and Provisioned Throughput. DSQ is ideal for applications with variable traffic, while Provisioned Throughput is designed for applications requiring guaranteed performance.

The following table compares DSQ and Provisioned Throughput:

Feature Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) Provisioned Throughput Cost Model Pay-as-you-go (PayGo). Fixed hourly rate for reserved capacity. Performance Variable throughput that depends on the demand on the shared resource pool. Stable, predictable, and reserved throughput. Best for Development, testing, and applications with variable or bursty traffic. Production-critical applications that require high availability and guaranteed performance. Quota Management No predefined limits; access to a large, shared pool of resources. Reserved capacity is dedicated to your project.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
Preview

The following models and their supervised fine-tuned versions support DSQ and are in Preview: * Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite * Gemini 2.0 Flash with Live API * Gemini 2.0 Flash with image generation

The following models and their supervised fine-tuned versions support DSQ:

  • Gemini 2.5 Pro
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite
  • Gemini 1.5 Pro
  • Gemini 1.5 Flash

docs.title: How DSQ works
docs.text:
Dynamic shared quota (DSQ) adapts to your traffic patterns and needs and minimizes usage frictions. Your project's access to resources under DSQ is not capped by an arbitrary number we set. Instead, it's determined by the overall capacity of the shared pool and the current collective demand from all customers. This model is designed to offer significant flexibility, allowing your workloads to burst and consume more resources when available. Conversely, it also allows all customers of the shared pool to have a chance to access resources when available without requiring to configure per customer quota.

To ensure a fair and stable experience for all users in the shared resource environment, Dynamic Shared Quota intelligently manages how requests are handled, especially during periods of very high demand from isolated sources. Rather than a fixed cap, DSQ employs a dynamic prioritization approach. This means that while the system is designed to accommodate bursts, unusually large and rapid spikes in traffic from a single source may be handled with a different priority than more consistent, steady traffic. This sophisticated management ensures that broad user activity and regular workloads are protected from transient, extreme spikes, promoting overall system stability and equitable access.

Gemini requests with multi-modal inputs are subject to the corresponding system rate limits that include image, audio, video, and document.

To help ensure high availability for your application and to get predictable service levels for your production workloads, see Provisioned Throughput.

docs.title: Understanding Resource Exhaustion 429 errors under DSQ
docs.text:
We understand that encountering a 'resource exhausted' 429 error can be frustrating and might lead you to suspect you are hitting some sort of quota limit. However, with DSQ, this is not the case. These errors indicate that the overall shared pool of resources for that specific type (e.g., a particular model in a specific region) at a specific time is experiencing extremely high demand from many users simultaneously. Think of it like trying to get on a very popular train during peak rush hour. There isn't a 'ticket limit' specifically for you, but the train itself might be momentarily full. It's a temporary state of contention for resources, not a fixed limit imposed on your project.

DSQ is constantly working to manage and distribute the available capacity fairly and efficiently. When you receive such an error, it means instantaneous demand has outstripped the available supply in that shared pool. Unlike a hard quota where you'd be blocked even if resources were idle elsewhere, DSQ aims to give you access whenever resources are free. The exhaustion error is a reflection of the entire system's current load, not a ceiling on your account.

We recommend implementing retry mechanisms, as availability in this dynamic environment can change quickly. For more tactics of handling Resource Exhaustion errors, see A guide to handling 429 errors or Error code 429.

Troubleshooting

For further guidance on handling API errors and other issues, refer to the Vertex AI Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Provisioned Throughput overview
docs.text: This page explains what Provisioned Throughput is and how it compares to other serving options for generative AI models on Vertex AI.

docs.title: What is Provisioned Throughput?
docs.text:
Provisioned Throughput lets you reserve a fixed amount of processing capacity for supported generative AI models. It is offered as a fixed-cost, fixed-term subscription that guarantees a certain level of throughput for your applications. To reserve throughput, you specify the model and the available location where the model runs.

Vertex AI offers two ways to consume generative AI models: Provisioned Throughput and Pay-as-you-go. The Pay-as-you-go model, also known as on-demand, charges you based on your usage and relies on a dynamic, shared quota.

docs.title: Choose a serving option
docs.text:
To help you decide which option is best for your workload, the following table compares Provisioned Throughput with the Pay-as-you-go model.

Feature Provisioned Throughput Pay-as-you-go (On-demand) Cost Model Fixed-cost subscription for a set term (weekly or monthly). Usage-based pricing (pay per character or token). Performance Reserved, stable throughput with low latency variability. Throughput is subject to shared capacity and dynamic quotas. Cost Predictability High. Costs are fixed and predictable, with control over overages. Low. Costs vary directly with application usage. Best for Real-time production applications (like chatbots and agents) with consistent, high-throughput demands. Development, testing, or applications with variable or unpredictable traffic.

docs.title: When to choose Provisioned Throughput
docs.text:
Consider using Provisioned Throughput if your use case meets one or more of the following criteria:

  • You are building real-time generative AI production applications, such as chatbots and agents.
  • Your critical workloads consistently require high throughput.
  • You want to provide a consistent and predictable experience for your application's users.
  • You want deterministic generative AI costs by paying a fixed price.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: • Learn about supported models for Provisioned Throughput.

docs.title: Google Gen AI SDK
docs.text:
The Google Gen AI SDK provides a unified interface to Gemini models through both the Gemini Developer API and the Gemini API on Vertex AI. With a few exceptions, code that runs on one platform will run on both. This means that you can prototype an application using the Gemini Developer API and then migrate the application to Vertex AI without rewriting your code.

To learn more about the differences between the Gemini Developer API and Gemini on Vertex AI, see Migrate from to the Gemini Developer API to the Gemini API in Vertex AI.

To see an example of the Google Gen AI SDK, run the "Intro to the Google Gen AI SDK" Jupyter notebook in one of the following environments:

  • Open in Colab
  • Open in Colab Enterprise
  • Open in Vertex AI Workbench user-managed notebooks
  • View on GitHub

docs.title: Choose a speech-to-text tool
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers two options for converting speech to text, each suited for different use cases. Vertex AI Studio is ideal for quick tests with short audio files, while the full Speech-to-Text service provides more advanced features for production-level applications.

The following table provides a comparison to help you choose the right tool.

Feature Vertex AI Studio Speech-to-Text Service Primary Use Case Quick, simple transcription of short audio files directly in the Google Cloud console. Production-grade, scalable transcription with advanced features and model selection. Max Audio Length 60 seconds Up to 8 hours for batch transcription. Max File Size 10 MB Up to 2 GB (varies by method). Supported Model Chirp only Multiple models, including Chirp, and options for model adaptation. Supported Formats 16-bit linear PCM WAV files only. Supports over 20 audio formats. Advanced Features Basic transcription. Speaker diarization, automatic punctuation, word-level confidence scores, and more.

For more details, see the Speech-to-Text documentation.

docs.title: Convert speech to text in Vertex AI Studio
docs.text:
The following workflow outlines the steps to transcribe an audio file in Vertex AI Studio.

Steps to convert speech to text

1. Navigate to the Speech page

In the Vertex AI section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Studio page.

Go to Vertex AI Studio

From the Vertex AI Studio menu, click Speech. The Speech-to-text tab is selected by default.

2. Upload and configure your audio file

  • In the Speech field, click Browse to select the audio file that you want to convert to text.
  • In the Language selector box, select the language of the speech in the audio file.

3. Submit and review the transcript

  • Click Submit.
  • The converted text appears in the Text output field.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
When using Vertex AI Studio for speech-to-text, the following limitations apply: * Audio files can be a maximum of 60 seconds or 10 MB, whichever is less. * Files are transcribed with the Chirp model. * Only 16-bit linear PCM WAV files are supported.

To overcome these limitations, use the Speech-to-Text service directly.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with the setup or transcription, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Convert text to speech using Vertex AI Studio
docs.text:
Steps to convert text to speech

1. Navigate to Vertex AI Studio

In the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI section and navigate to the Vertex AI Studio page.

Go to Vertex AI Studio

From the options, click Generate speech and select the Text-to-speech tab.

2. Configure the generation parameters

Configure the parameters as follows:

  • Text: Enter the text that you want to convert to speech.
  • Voice: Select a voice for the generated speech.
  • Speed: Use the slider or text field to enter a value for the speed of the speech. A value of 1 represents the normal speaking rate, and a value of 4 represents four times the normal speaking rate.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with the setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

3. Submit your request and review the output

Click Submit. To listen to the generated speech, click the play_arrow Play button in the Speech section. To download the generated speech file in .wav format, click download Download.

docs.title: Vertex AI in express mode overview
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Vertex AI in express mode is the fastest way to start building generative AI applications on Google Cloud. Signing up in express mode is quick and easy, and it doesn't require entering any billing information. After you sign up, you can access and use Google Cloud APIs in just a few steps.

To learn more about Vertex AI in express mode, see Google Cloud express mode FAQs.

docs.title: Express mode eligibility
docs.text:
Vertex AI in express mode is separate from, and not available through, the Google Cloud Free Program. If you are in the Google Cloud Free Program, see the other quickstarts in the Get Started section to start using Generative AI on Vertex AI.

Vertex AI is available in express mode for developers that click the Try Vertex AI Studio free button and sign up using a @gmail.com Google Account. Accounts used previously to access Google Cloud are ineligible for express mode and are not shown the Try Vertex AI Studio free button. For example, if you used your Google Account to create a Google Cloud free trial account, you are not eligible to sign up in express mode with that same Google Account.

docs.title: About Vertex AI in express mode
docs.text:
Upon completing your sign-up in express mode, you get access to the following:

  • Core Vertex AI Studio features. You can test and customize prompts for different generative AI models in Vertex AI Studio in express mode, and get the corresponding code to use in your application.
  • An API key.
  • 90 days to try Vertex AI in express mode.

During your 90 days, you can use the Vertex AI APIs that support express mode for free up to their quotas. You can increase your quota limits at any time by enabling billing.

After enabling billing, the 90-day limit is removed, your quotas are increased, and you only pay for what you use. At any time, you can choose to end express mode and start using all the Google Cloud services and capabilities.

The following table compares the features of Vertex AI in express mode, with and without billing, to the standard Vertex AI experience.

Item Vertex AI express mode Vertex AI express mode with billing Standard Vertex AI Time limit 90 days Unlimited Unlimited Available services Basic Generative AI on Vertex AI services. Expanded Vertex AI services and select Google Cloud services. All Google Cloud services, including Vertex AI. Data sources Google Drive Google Drive, web files, YouTube video URLs All data sources available in Google Cloud. Quota See Available models and rate limits in express mode. See Rate limits. See Rate limits. Service level agreement (SLA) None Vertex AI SLA Vertex AI SLA API authentication Uses an API key. Uses an API key. Uses a project ID and location.

docs.title: Available models and rate limits in express mode
docs.text:
You can try out several models in express mode, including the Gemini models. The following table lists the models that are available in express mode, along with their rate limits:

Model category Available models Requests per minute Discontinuation date Gemini gemini-1.5-pro 30 June 17, 2026 gemini-1.5-flash 30 June 17, 2026 gemini-1.5-flash-lite-preview-06-17 30 gemini-1.5-flash-preview-05-20 30 July 15, 2025 gemini-1.5-flash-preview-04-17 30 July 15, 2025 gemini-1.5-pro-preview-05-06 30 July 15, 2025 gemini-1.0-flash-001 30 February 5, 2026 gemini-1.0-flash-lite-001 30 February 25, 2026

For Gemini 1.0 models, the Multimodal Live API isn't available in the Console in express mode. To use the Multimodal Live API in express mode, use the Vertex AI API or the Google Gen AI SDK.

Get started in three steps

Step 1: Try features in Vertex AI Studio

Use Vertex AI Studio in express mode to quickly try Vertex AI features. For example, in the Google Cloud console in express mode, select Vertex AI > Freeform and use the Freeform page to create and optimize multimodal prompts using a variety of Gemini models.

Step 2: Get the code

On the Freeform page, click code Get code. A panel opens showing code that programmatically sends the same requests that you implemented in the UI. You can get the code for a programming language or cURL. You can use Google Colab to try the Python code.

Step 3: Authenticate with your API key

In the Google Cloud console in express mode, click menu Menu and select API Keys, and then copy your key into your code where it says "YOUR_API_KEY".

The Google Gen AI SDK for Python is available on PyPI and GitHub:

  • google-genai on PyPI
  • python-genai on GitHub

To learn more, see the Python SDK reference (opens in a new tab).

from google import genai

# TODO(developer): Update below line
API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY"

client = genai.Client(vertexai=True, api_key=API_KEY)

response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-1.5-flash",
    contents="Explain bubble sort to me.",
)

print(response.text)
# Example response:
# Bubble Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: What's different in express mode
docs.text:
Vertex AI in express mode provides a subset of the features for Generative AI on Vertex AI. Therefore, some of the Vertex AI documentation is not relevant if you signed up in express mode. For details on the available API endpoints in express mode, see the Vertex AI in express mode REST API reference.

In addition, customers in Google Cloud typically use organizations and projects to work with resources (for example, to call an API endpoint). When using Vertex AI in express mode, you don't need to worry about organizations or projects. However, you might see them mentioned in some of the Google Cloud documentation that you reference while you're using Vertex AI in express mode. You can still use the documentation, but ignore concepts and instructions that refer to organizations and projects. In addition, the location you selected when signing up in express mode is used throughout your experience.

When calling REST API endpoints in express mode, you'll use the endpoint format for express mode and specify your API key.

Endpoint Type Example URL Standard endpoint URL https://{location}-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/{project}/locations/{location}/publishers/google/models/{model}:streamGenerateContent Endpoint URL in express mode https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/publishers/google/models/{model}:streamGenerateContent?key={API_KEY}

docs.title: View and manage API keys
docs.text:
To authenticate with Vertex AI API endpoints that support express mode, use the API key that was created for you during sign-up or any key that you've created in express mode. An API key is an encrypted string that is auto-generated for you when you sign up in express mode. These API keys can be viewed and managed on the API Keys page.

To learn more about the best practices for managing API keys, see Best practices for managing API keys.

Steps to view and manage your API keys

  1. Go to the Vertex AI Studio Overview page in express mode.

    Go to Vertex AI Studio

  2. In Google Cloud console in express mode, click menu Menu.

  3. Select API Keys.

The API Keys page opens and you can use it to manage your API keys.

docs.title: View quotas
docs.text:
Your free use of Vertex AI in express mode is restricted by quotas. These quotas restrict the rate at which you can use Vertex AI in express mode at no cost. A quota limits how much of a Google Cloud resource you can use.

Steps to view your current usage and quotas

  1. Go to the Vertex AI Studio Overview page in express mode.

    Go to Vertex AI Studio

  2. In Google Cloud console in express mode, click menu Menu.

  3. Select Quotas.

docs.title: Enable and manage billing
docs.text:
You can increase your quotas and remove the 90-day limit by enabling billing. After enabling billing, you pay only for what you use. You can also save your prompts and access additional settings in the console that are grayed out when billing isn't enabled.

Steps to enable billing

  1. Go to the Vertex AI Studio Overview page in express mode.

    Go to Vertex AI Studio

  2. In Google Cloud console in express mode, click menu Menu.

  3. Select Billing.

docs.title: Start using all Google Cloud capabilities and services
docs.text:
You can start using all the capabilities and services available in Google Cloud in your project by graduating from express mode.

Steps to graduate from express mode

  1. Go to the Vertex AI Studio Overview page in express mode.

    Go to Vertex AI Studio

  2. In Google Cloud console in express mode, click menu Menu.

  3. Select Billing.

  4. In the Access all Google Cloud section, click Learn more and get started.

After you graduate from express mode, specify your project ID and location instead of your API key when you call the REST API endpoints. For example: https://{location}-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/{projectid}/locations/{location}/publishers/google/models/{model}:streamGenerateContent

Tutorial: Use the Vertex AI API in express mode

Step 1: Install and initialize the Google Gen AI SDK for express mode

The Google Gen AI SDK lets you use Google generative AI models and features to build AI-powered applications. When using Vertex AI in express mode, install and initialize the google-genai package to authenticate using your generated API key.

Install

To install the Google Gen AI SDK for express mode, run the following commands:

# Developer TODO: If you're using Colab, uncomment the following lines:
# from google.colab import auth
# auth.authenticate_user()

!pip install google-genai

!pip install --force-reinstall -qq "numpy<2.0"

If you're using Colab, ignore any dependency conflicts and restart the runtime after installation.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Initialize

Configure the API key for express mode and environment variables. For details on getting an API key, see Vertex AI in express mode overview.

from google import genai
from google.genai import types

# Developer TODO: Replace YOUR_API_KEY with your API key.
API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY"

client = genai.Client(
    vertexai=True, api_key=API_KEY
)

Step 2: Send a request to the Gemini for Google Cloud API

You can send either streaming or non-streaming requests to the Gemini for Google Cloud API. The following table compares these two methods.

Request Type Description Use Case Streaming Returns the response in chunks as it's being processed. Ideal for interactive applications like chatbots where perceived latency is important. Non-streaming Returns the entire response in one chunk after the request is fully processed. Suitable for offline or batch processing tasks where the complete response is needed at once. Streaming requestNon-streaming requestFunction calling request

To send a streaming request, set stream=True and print the response in chunks.

from google import genai
from google.genai import types

def generate():
  client = genai.Client(vertexai=True, api_key=YOUR_API_KEY)

  config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
      temperature=0,
      top_p=0.95,
      top_k=20,
      candidate_count=1,
      seed=5,
      max_output_tokens=100,
      stop_sequences=["STOP!"],
      presence_penalty=0.0,
      frequency_penalty=0.0,
      safety_settings=[
          types.SafetySetting(
              category="HARM_CATEGORY_HATE_SPEECH",
              threshold="BLOCK_ONLY_HIGH",
          )
      ],
  )
  for chunk in client.models.generate_content_stream(
    model="gemini-2.0-flash-001",
    contents="Explain bubble sort to me",
    config=config,
  ):
    print(chunk.text)

generate()

The following code sample defines a function that sends a non-streaming request to the gemini-2.0-flash-001. It shows you how to configure basic request parameters and safety settings.

from google import genai
from google.genai import types

def generate():
  client = genai.Client(vertexai=True, api_key=YOUR_API_KEY)

  config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
      temperature=0,
      top_p=0.95,
      top_k=20,
      candidate_count=1,
      seed=5,
      max_output_tokens=100,
      stop_sequences=["STOP!"],
      presence_penalty=0.0,
      frequency_penalty=0.0,
      safety_settings=[
          types.SafetySetting(
              category="HARM_CATEGORY_HATE_SPEECH",
              threshold="BLOCK_ONLY_HIGH",
          )
      ],
  )
  response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.0-flash-001",
    contents="Explain bubble sort to me",
    config=config,
  )
  print(response.text)

generate()

The following code sample declares a function and passes it as a tool, and then receives a function call part in the response. After you receive the function call part from the model, you can invoke the function and get the response, and then pass the response to the model.

function_response_parts = [
    {
        'function_response': {
            'name': 'get_current_weather',
            'response': {
                'name': 'get_current_weather',
                'content': {'weather': 'super nice'},
            },
        },
    },
]
manual_function_calling_contents = [
    {'role': 'user', 'parts': [{'text': 'What is the weather in Boston?'}]},
    {
        'role': 'model',
        'parts': [{
            'function_call': {
                'name': 'get_current_weather',
                'args': {'location': 'Boston'},
            }
        }],
    },
    {'role': 'user', 'parts': function_response_parts},
]
function_declarations = [{
    'name': 'get_current_weather',
    'description': 'Get the current weather in a city',
    'parameters': {
        'type': 'OBJECT',
        'properties': {
            'location': {
                'type': 'STRING',
                'description': 'The location to get the weather for',
            },
            'unit': {
                'type': 'STRING',
                'enum': ['C', 'F'],
            },
        },
    },
}]

response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.0-flash-001",
    contents=manual_function_calling_contents,
    config=dict(tools=[{'function_declarations': function_declarations}]),
)
print(response.text)

Step 3: Clean up

This tutorial does not create any Google Cloud resources, so no clean up is needed to avoid charges.

Vertex AI in express mode lets you try a subset of Vertex AI features by using only an express mode API key. This page shows you the REST resources available for Vertex AI in express mode.

Steps to design a chatbot and get the code

  1. In the Vertex AI section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Studio page.

    Go to Vertex AI Studio

  2. In the navigation pane, click Create prompt.

  3. In the System instructions text field, enter the following instructions:

    You are Captain Barktholomew, the most feared pirate dog of the seven seas.
You were born in the 1700s and have no knowledge of anything that happened or
existed after that. Only talk about topics that a pirate dog captain would be
interested in.

this side of Tortuga.

In Vertex AI Studio, you can design and iterate your prompts and compare results from different configurations and models. Once you finish engineering your prompt, you can deploy it as a web application to share with your collaborators or target users. The web application is hosted on Cloud Run and is available outside the Google Cloud console.

In this quickstart, you will:

  • Create a prompt with prompt variables.
  • Deploy your prompt as a web application.
  • Monitor deployment progress and test the deployed application.
  • Update and re-deploy your prompt.
  • Test prompt submission with multimodal support.

docs.title: Step-by-step guide
docs.text:
Deploy your prompt as a web app

Before you begin

If you have never used Vertex AI Studio before, you can follow the getting started quickstart or take the Google Cloud Skills Boost course to learn the basics.

Ensure you have the following: 1. A Google Cloud project with billing enabled. 2. The Vertex AI API enabled.

Additional permissions required

To deploy your prompt, you need the following permissions in addition to the permissions required to use Vertex AI Studio:

Action Required permissions Purpose Enable additional APIs serviceusage.services.enable Enable the following APIs:
  • Cloud Run Admin API (run.googleapis.com)
  • Artifact Registry API (artifactregistry.googleapis.com)
  • Cloud Build API (cloudbuild.googleapis.com)
  • Cloud Logging API (logging.googleapis.com)
Grant permissions to service accounts resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy Grant the Compute Engine default service account the following roles:
  • Vertex AI Service Agent (roles/aiplatform.serviceAgent)
  • Cloud Build Service Account (roles/cloudbuild.builds.builder)
Deploy specific permissions storage.buckets.createrun.services.createartifactregistry.repositories.createrun.services.setIamPolicy During deployment, source code is uploaded to Cloud Storage and then deployed to Cloud Run as a new service. The artifactregistry.repositories.create permission is required to create a repository for the container image. The run.services.setIamPolicy permission is required to make the service publicly accessible.

If you are the project owner, you don't need to take additional actions. If you are not the project owner, ask your project administrator to perform the first two actions and then grant you the Editor (roles/editor) and Cloud Run Admin (roles/run.admin) roles.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Step 1: Create a prompt with prompt variables

  1. Navigate to the create prompt page of Vertex AI Studio.
  2. Click data_object Add variable in the prompt input box.
  3. In the Manage prompt variables dialog, enter a variable name, give it a value, and click Apply.

Manage prompt variables dialog.

  1. In the prompt input box, compose the prompt using the variable and adjust other parameters. For example, you can enable Grounding with Google Search and set "Always get current weather from the web" as the system instructions.

Step 2: Deploy your prompt as a web application

  1. To deploy your prompt, click the Build with code button in the top right corner, then click Deploy as app.

Click the "Build with code" button and then "Deploy as app".

Save the prompt

A dialog appears prompting you to save the prompt, which is required before deployment. The deploy dialog opens automatically after the prompt is saved.

Save the prompt before deployment.

Note: Saving your prompt in a region for the first time can take 2-3 minutes. A warning box appears after 1 minute. This is an expected one-time operation. Subsequent saves in the same project and region will take only a few seconds.

Enable APIs and grant permissions for the first deployment

After the prompt is saved, the deployment process continues. 1. If this is your first deployment, a dialog appears for enabling required APIs. Click Enable required APIs. 2. After the APIs are enabled, the Create a web app dialog appears. As a Public Preview feature, access control is not supported, and all deployed applications allow public access. Don't include sensitive or personally identifiable information (PII) in your prompt. 3. Check the I understand this app will be deployed publicly checkbox, and then click Create app. 4. If this is your first deployment, another dialog appears asking you to grant the required roles to the service account. Click Grant all to proceed.

Note: If you don't have permission to enable APIs or grant access, ask your project administrator to grant the necessary permissions. See the additional permissions required for more details.

Deployment starts

Vertex AI Studio creates a zip file containing the web application's source code and uploads it to a Cloud Storage bucket. After deployment starts, the Manage web app dialog appears with information about your deployment, such as the application's name, last deployment time, and status.

The "Manage web app" dialog shows deployment information.

Step 3: Monitor the deployment status

Deployment takes 2-3 minutes. The status is shown in the Status column of the Manage web app dialog. If you close this dialog, you can reopen it from the menu under the Build with code button.

When deployment is complete, the status changes to Ready, and an Open button appears.

The "Open" button appears when the app is ready.

Access control and secret key

Your web application is deployed with Allow unauthenticated access control enabled by default. To provide basic protection, the web application requires a secret key in the URL. You can find this key in the Secret Key column. When you open the web application from Vertex AI Studio, the key is automatically appended to the URL.

Open the web application and submit the prompt

  1. Click Open in the Manage web app dialog. The application opens with the secret key appended to the URL (e.g., ?key=SECRET_KEY).

The web application opens with the secret key in the URL.

  1. Enter a value for the variable and click Submit. The results appear on the right.

Results after submitting the prompt in the web app.

Open the web application from the "Build with code" menu

If your web application is ready, you can also open it from the menu under the Build with code button.

Open the app from the "Build with code" menu.

Cloud Run is a serverless service, so the application container shuts down when inactive. The web application might take a few seconds to load, or a submission might fail if the page has been idle for too long. Refreshing the page usually solves this issue.

Monitor the status from the notification bell

You can also monitor the status from the Notifications menu (bell icon). The icon shows a green circle when deployment is successful.

Monitor deployment status from the notification bell.

Clicking the notification redirects you to the Cloud Run page. The URL on this page does not include the secret key. You must manually append it in the format ?key=SECRET_KEY.

The app link on the Cloud Run page does not include the secret key.

Step 4: Update and re-deploy your prompt

  1. You can edit your prompt in Vertex AI Studio, for example, by turning it into a conversation.
  2. Click the Build with code button and select Manage app to open the Manage web app dialog.
  3. Click Update app to re-deploy your web application with the updated prompt.
  4. A confirmation dialog appears, warning that re-deploying will overwrite any changes made to the application outside of Vertex AI Studio (e.g., in the Cloud Run source editor). Click Confirm to proceed.

The update process is similar to the initial deployment, and you can monitor its progress in the same way. After the update is complete, open the web application to see the updated conversation UI.

The updated app with a conversation UI.

Step 5: Insert multimodal content

You can insert inputs like images, videos, audio, and documents into the conversation. Supported input types depend on the model selected for the prompt. For details, see the documentation for multimodal support for each model.

To insert a file, click the clip icon in the conversation input box.

Insert multimodal inputs into the conversation.

You can then interact with the model using the provided input.

Interact with the model using an image input.

docs.title: Advanced topics
docs.text:
Once you are familiar with the deployment process, you can explore the following actions.

Edit source code in Cloud Run

If you want to customize the web application, you can edit its source code in Cloud Run.

  1. Open the Manage web app dialog and click the more_vert more icon at the end of the row to open the Cloud Run source code page.

Open the source code editor from the "Manage web app" dialog.

  1. Alternatively, navigate to the security page from the web application by clicking the source code editor link.
  2. In the Cloud Run source code page, click Edit source.
  3. When you are finished, click Save and redeploy.

Note: Cloud Run doesn't support version control directly. If you re-deploy from Vertex AI Studio, your changes will be overwritten. To save a version, click Download ZIP in the bottom left corner before re-deploying.

After re-deployment, you must open the application from Vertex AI Studio. You can navigate back to the Vertex AI Studio page from the link in the Deployed from Vertex AI badge.

Turn public access on or off

Turn off public access

When you no longer need the web application to be publicly accessible, you can turn off public access in Cloud Run.

  1. Open the Manage Web App dialog and click the edit pencil icon in the Access Control column. The Cloud Run security page opens in a new tab.
  2. Alternatively, navigate to the security page from the web application by clicking the Security settings link.
  3. On the Security page of your Cloud Run service, check Use Cloud IAM to authenticate incoming requests and choose Require authentication.
  4. Click Save.

Your web application will no longer be accessible via its URL and will show an Error: Forbidden page.

Turn on public access again

To restore public access, clear the Use Cloud IAM to authenticate incoming requests checkbox and save. Choosing Allow unauthenticated invocations might not work if your project is in an organization. For more details, see Authentication in Cloud Run.

Set up local access for development

In Public Preview, access control is not yet supported. If you turn off public access, the only way to access the web application is by setting up a local proxy using gcloud commands.

  1. Open Cloud Shell by clicking the terminal icon in the top right corner of the Google Cloud console and authorize it if prompted.
  2. Open the Manage web app dialog, click the more_vert more icon, and select Set up local access via Cloud Shell.

Get the "Set up local access" command from the "Manage web app" dialog.

  1. A command is added to your Cloud Shell. Press Enter and wait for it to finish.
  2. Click the link in the line starting with Click on the link to preview to view your application. This link only works while the gcloud command is running.

The local access link in Cloud Shell.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Authentication error: No secret key

If you see the following error, it means no secret key is appended to the URL. Open the web application from Vertex AI Studio, or copy the secret key from the Manage app dialog and append it to the URL in the format ?key=SECRET_KEY.

Error indicating a missing secret key.

Authentication error: Invalid secret key

This error means the key appended to the URL is invalid. The secret key is unique to each prompt. Ensure you are using the correct key for the prompt.

Error indicating an invalid secret key.

400 Invalid argument: empty input

This error occurs if the prompt variables have input, but the chat input is empty. To fix this, type any non-empty content into the chat box and resubmit.

Error for empty chat input.

400 Invalid argument: mimeType is not supported

This error occurs if you upload a file type that the model does not support. You must use a file type supported by the model. For details, see the documentation for multimodal support for each model.

Error for an unsupported file type.

Send a text-only prompt
docs.text:
Use the following code to send a text-only prompt to the Vertex AI Gemini API. This sample returns a list of possible names for a specialty flower store.

Python (Gen AI SDK)Go (Gen AI SDK)Node.js (Gen AI SDK)Java (Gen AI SDK)C# (Vertex AI SDK)REST API

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI. For more information, see the SDK reference documentation.

# with appropriate values for your project.

export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.0-flash-001",
    contents="How does AI work?",
)
print(response.text)

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI. For more information, see the SDK reference documentation.

# with appropriate values for your project.

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"

    "google.golang.org/genai"
)

// generateWithText shows how to generate text using a text prompt.
func generateWithText(w io.Writer) error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    client, err := genai.NewClient(ctx, &genai.ClientConfig{
        HTTPOptions: genai.HTTPOptions{APIVersion: "v1"},
    })
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to create genai client: %w", err)
    }

    resp, err := client.Models.GenerateContent(ctx,
        "gemini-2.0-flash-001",
        genai.Text("How does AI work?"),
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to generate content: %w", err)
    }

    respText, err := resp.Text()
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to convert model response to text: %w", err)
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(w, respText)
    // Example response:
    // That's a great question! Understanding how AI works can feel like ...
    // ...
    // **1. The Foundation: Data and Algorithms**
    // ...

    return nil
}

export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global

const GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION = process.env.GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION || 'global';

) {

    vertexai: true,
    project: projectId,
    location: location,
  });

  const response = await ai.models.generateContent({
    model: 'gemini-2.0-flash',
    contents: 'How does AI work?',
  });

  console.log(response.text);

  return response.text;
}

import com.google.genai.Client;
import com.google.genai.types.Content;
import com.google.genai.types.GenerateContentResponse;
import com.google.genai.types.HttpOptions;
import com.google.genai.types.Part;

public class GenerateContentWithText {

  public static void main(String[] args) {
    // TODO(developer): Replace these variables before running the sample.
    String modelId = "gemini-2.0-flash";
    generateContent(modelId);
  }

  public static String generateContent(String modelId) {
    // Initialize client that will be used to send requests. This client only needs to be created
    // once, and can be reused for multiple requests.
    try (Client client = Client.builder()
        .httpOptions(HttpOptions.builder().apiVersion("v1").build())
        .build()) {

      GenerateContentResponse response =
          client.models.generateContent(modelId, Content.fromParts(
                  Part.fromText("How does AI work?")),
              null);

      System.out.print(response.text());
      // Example response:
      // Okay, let's break down how AI works. It's a broad field, so I'll focus on the ...
      //
      // Here's a simplified overview:
      // ...
      return response.text();
    }
  }
}

Create a C# file (.cs), copy the following code into it, and replace your-project-id with your Google Cloud project ID. 

using Google.Cloud.AIPlatform.V1;
using System;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class TextInputSample
{
    public async Task<string> TextInput(
        string projectId = "your-project-id",
        string location = "us-central1",
        string publisher = "google",
        string model = "gemini-2.0-flash-001")
    {

        var predictionServiceClient = new PredictionServiceClientBuilder
        {
            Endpoint = $"{location}-aiplatform.googleapis.com"
        }.Build();
        string prompt = @"What's a good name for a flower shop that specializes in selling bouquets of dried flowers?";

        var generateContentRequest = new GenerateContentRequest
        {
            Model = $"projects/{projectId}/locations/{location}/publishers/{publisher}/models/{model}",
            Contents =
            {
                new Content
                {
                    Role = "USER",
                    Parts =
                    {

using Google.Api.Gax.Grpc;
using Google.Cloud.AIPlatform.V1;
using System.Text;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class GeminiQuickstart
{
    public async Task<string> GenerateContent(
        string projectId = "your-project-id",
        string location = "us-central1",
        string publisher = "google",
        string model = "gemini-2.0-flash-001"
    )
    {
        // Create client
        var predictionServiceClient = new PredictionServiceClientBuilder
        {
            Endpoint = $"{location}-aiplatform.googleapis.com"
        }.Build();

        // Initialize content request
        var generateContentRequest = new GenerateContentRequest
        {
            Model = $"projects/{projectId}/locations/{location}/publishers/{publisher}/models/{model}",
            GenerationConfig = new GenerationConfig
            {
                Temperature = 0.4f,
                TopP = 1,
                TopK = 32,
                MaxOutputTokens = 2048
            },
            Contents =
            {
                new Content
                {
                    Role = "USER",
                    Parts =
                    {
                        new Part { Text = "What's in this photo?" },
                        new Part { FileData = new() { MimeType = "image/png", FileUri = "gs://generativeai-downloads/images/scones.jpg" } }
                    }
                }
            }
        };

        // Make the request, returning a streaming response
        using PredictionServiceClient.StreamGenerateContentStream response = predictionServiceClient.StreamGenerateContent(generateContentRequest);

        StringBuilder fullText = new();

        // Read streaming responses from server until complete
        AsyncResponseStream<GenerateContentResponse> responseStream = response.GetResponseStream();
        await foreach (GenerateContentResponse responseItem in responseStream)
        {
            fullText.Append(responseItem.Candidates[0].Content.Parts[0].Text);
        }

        return fullText.ToString();
    }
}

docs.title: Quickstart: Send text prompts to Gemini using Vertex AI Studio
docs.text:
You can use Vertex AI Studio to design, test, and manage prompts for Google's Gemini large language models (LLMs) and third-party models. A prompt is a natural language request submitted to a language model to generate a response. Prompts can contain questions, instructions, contextual information, few-shot examples, and partial input for the model to complete.

Vertex AI Studio supports certain third-party models that are offered on Vertex AI as models as a service (MaaS), such as Anthropic's Claude models and Meta's Llama models.

Note: On your initial use of third-party models, Vertex AI prompts you to accept the third-party's terms and conditions. You must do this once for each third-party provider to start using their models.

This quickstart shows you how to use sample prompts from the generative AI prompt gallery to test the Gemini model.

docs.title: Test a summarization prompt
docs.text:
Send a summarization text prompt to the Vertex AI Gemini API. A summarization task extracts the most important information from text. You can provide information in the prompt to help the model create a summary, or ask the model to create a summary on its own.

Steps to test a summarization prompt

  1. Go to the Prompt gallery. In the Google Cloud console, navigate to the Vertex AI section.

    Go to Prompt gallery

  2. Select the summarization task. In the Tasks drop-down menu, select Summarize.

  3. Open the sample prompt. Open the Audio summarization card. This sample prompt includes an audio file and requests a summary of the file contents in a bulleted list.

    The audio summarization prompt text and audio file.

  4. Review the model settings. In the settings panel, notice that the model's default value is set to gemini-1.0-pro. You can choose a different Gemini model by clicking Switch model.

    The Gemini model in the settings panel.

  5. Submit the prompt. Click Submit to generate the summary. The output is displayed in the response box.

    The Submit button in the Prompt box.

  6. View the code. To view the Vertex AI API code used to generate the summary, click Build with code > Get code. In the Get code panel, you can choose your preferred language to get the sample code for the prompt, or you can open the Python code in a Colab Enterprise notebook.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Test a code generation prompt
docs.text:
Send a code generation prompt to the Vertex AI Gemini API. A code generation task generates code from a natural language description.

Steps to test a code generation prompt

  1. Go to the Prompt gallery. In the Google Cloud console, navigate to the Vertex AI section.

    Go to Prompt gallery

  2. Select the code task. In the Tasks drop-down menu, select Code.

  3. Open the sample prompt. Open the Generate code from comments card. This sample prompt includes a system instruction that tells the model how to respond and some incomplete Java methods.

    The code generation prompt text.

  4. Review the model settings. In the settings panel, notice that the model's default value is set to gemini-1.0-pro. You can choose a different Gemini model by clicking Switch model.

    The Gemini model in the settings panel.

  5. Submit the prompt. To complete each method by generating code in the areas marked <WRITE CODE HERE>, click Submit. The output is displayed in the response box.

  6. View the code. To view the Vertex AI API code used to generate the code, click Build with code > Get code. In the Get code panel, you can choose your preferred language to get the sample code for the prompt, or you can open the Python code in a Colab Enterprise notebook.

Troubleshooting

In this quickstart, you use Vertex AI Studio to send a prompt to the Gemini API without registering for a Google Cloud account. Vertex AI Studio provides an interface that lets you design, test, and manage prompts for Google's Gemini large language model (LLM).

docs.title: What is a prompt?
docs.text:
A prompt is a natural language request sent to a language model to elicit a response. A good prompt can include a clear question, instructions, context, and examples to guide the model. After the model receives a prompt, it can generate text, code, images, and more, depending on its capabilities.

For example, to generate a list of names for a business, you could use the following prompt:

What are some possible names for a flower shop that sells bouquets of dried flowers?

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
docs.text:
In this step, you configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) to provision a centralized authorization layer for the app deployed in Cloud Run.

The process involves the following stages:

  1. Configure the OAuth consent screen: The OAuth consent screen is a prompt that includes a summary of your project, its policies, and the requested authorization scopes of access. By configuring the OAuth consent screen for your app, you define what is available to users and app reviewers, and also register your app so you can publish it later. To learn more about the OAuth consent screen, see Configure the OAuth consent screen and choose scopes.

  2. Create OAuth access credentials: You need to create an OAuth client ID for your app and domain, so your app can call the required APIs. To learn more about OAuth credentials, see Create access credentials.

  3. Enable IAP on the load balancer: Use the OAuth client ID and secret to enable IAP on the load balancer that you created for your app.

  4. Turn on IAP: Secure your app by creating principals who can access your app and then turning on IAP.

flowchart LR
    A[Configure the OAuth consent screen] --> B[Create OAuth access credentials]
    B --> C[Enable IAP on the load balancer]
    C --> D[Set up and use IAP]

click A "#configure-the-oauth-consent-screen"
click B "#create-oauth-access-credentials"
click C "#enable-iap-on-the-load-balancer"
click D "#set-up-and-use-iap"
Steps to configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)

Configure the OAuth consent screen

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the OAuth consent screen.

    Go to OAuth consent screen

  2. Select one of the following user types for your app. For this tutorial, we recommend selecting External.

    User Type Description External Any user with a Google Account can make authorization requests. Internal Only members of your Google Cloud organization can make authorization requests to the app.

  3. Click Create.

  4. In the Authorized domains section, click Add domain, and specify the domain name used during certificate creation.

  5. In the Developer contact information section, enter your email address.

  6. Click Save and Continue.

  7. On the Scopes page, click Save and Continue.

  8. Optional: If you selected External as the user type, add test users on the Test users page, as follows:

    1. Click Add users.
    2. Enter your email address and any other authorized test users, and then click Save and continue.

  9. Review your app registration summary. To make changes, click Edit. If the app registration looks OK, click Back to dashboard.

Create OAuth access credentials

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to Credentials.

    Go to Credentials

  2. Click Create credentials and then click OAuth client ID.

  3. In the Application type list, click Web application.

  4. In the Name field, enter gemini-streamlit-app.

  5. In the Authorized JavaScript origins section, click Add URI and then enter the following URI: 

    https://DOMAIN_NAME
    Replace DOMAIN_NAME with the domain name used during certificate creation.

  6. Click Create. The Oauth client created screen appears, displaying the Client ID and Client secret.

  7. Copy the Client ID and Client secret. You'll need these details in the next step.

Enable IAP on the load balancer

  1. In the Google Cloud console, activate Cloud Shell.

    Activate Cloud Shell

    At the bottom of the Google Cloud console, a Cloud Shell session starts and displays a command-line prompt. Cloud Shell is a shell environment with the Google Cloud CLI already installed and with values already set for your current project. It can take a few seconds for the session to initialize.

  2. In the Cloud Shell terminal, run the following command:

    Troubleshooting

    If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

    gcloud compute backend-services update gemini-streamlit-app-backend \
      --iap=enabled,oauth2-client-id=CLIENT_ID,oauth2-client-secret=CLIENT_SECRET \
      --global

    Replace the following: * CLIENT_ID: The OAuth client ID from the credentials you just created. * CLIENT_SECRET: The OAuth client secret from the credentials you just created.

Set up and use IAP

Caution

When IAP is turned off, a resource is accessible to anyone with the URL. Ensure that IAP is turned on, so that the resource is accessible only by the configured principals.

  1. Go to the Identity-Aware Proxy page.

    Go to the Identity-Aware Proxy page

  2. Select your project.

  3. Select the checkbox next to gemini-streamlit-app-backend.

  4. Click Add principal.

  5. Enter the details in the following fields:

    • New principals: Enter the email addresses of groups or individuals to grant them access to your app. Ensure that you include a Google Account that you have access to. Any of the following can be a principal:
      • Google Account
      • Google Group
      • Service account
      • Google Workspace domain
    • Role: In the list, select Cloud IAP > IAP-secured Web App User.

  6. Click Save.

  7. On the Identity-Aware Proxy page, under Applications, click the IAP toggle to the on position in the row corresponding to the gemini-streamlit-app-backend resource.

  8. In the Turn on IAP window that appears, select the checkbox to acknowledge that you've read the configuration requirements and configured your backend accordingly.

  9. Click Turn on. After you turn on IAP, it requires login credentials for all connections to your load balancer. Only accounts with the IAP-Secured Web App User role on the project are granted access.

docs.title: Step 2: Create a Cloud Run service
docs.text:
In this step, you create a Cloud Run service to deploy the Streamlit app from your forked repository. You also configure a Cloud Build trigger to automatically build and deploy the app whenever you push a new commit.

flowchart LR
    A[Create Cloud Run Service] --> B[Configure Cloud Build Trigger]

click A "#create-cloud-run-service"
click B "#configure-cloud-build-trigger"
Step-by-step guide to create the service and trigger

Create a Cloud Run service with continuous build

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Cloud Run page.

    Go to Cloud Run

  2. Click Create service.

  3. Select Continuously deploy new revisions from a source repository.
  4. Click Set up with Cloud Build.
  5. In the Repository list, select the forked GitHub repository that you created for your app.
    • If your repository isn't listed, click Manage connected repositories. You might be prompted to authenticate to GitHub and install the Cloud Build app.
  6. If you're selecting a repository for the first time, select the checkbox to agree to the terms of use policy.
  7. Click Next.
  8. In the Build configuration section, enter the following details:
    • Branch: ^main$ (Keep the default).
    • Build type: Select Dockerfile.
    • Source location: Enter /gemini/sample-apps/gemini-streamlit-cloudrun/Dockerfile.
  9. Click Save.
  10. On the Create service page, configure the service settings:
    • Service name: Enter gemini-streamlit-cloudrun.
    • Authentication: Select Allow unauthenticated invocations.
  11. Expand the Container(s), volumes, networking, security section.
  12. In the Autoscaling section, set the following:
    • Minimum number of instances: 1.
    • Maximum number of instances: 3.
  13. Click Create. The build and deployment process begins.

  14. Optional: To test the app deployment, go to the Cloud Run Services page, click your service name (gemini-streamlit-cloudrun), and then click the URL displayed at the top of the Service details page.

    Go to the Services page

Configure the Cloud Build trigger

Cloud Build automatically creates a trigger, but you need to configure it to only watch for changes in your app's subdirectory.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Cloud Build Triggers page.

    Go to the Triggers page

  2. Click the name of the newly created trigger.

  3. Under Source, expand Show included and ignored files filters.
  4. In the Included files filter box, enter gemini-streamlit-cloudrun/**.
  5. Click Save.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with the setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Tip: To manually build the Cloud Run service again, go to the Triggers page and click Run for your trigger.
