docs.title: Bounding box detection
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is experimental and is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

The Gemini API can perform object detection and localization within images and video. By identifying and delineating objects with bounding boxes, you can build a wide range of applications.

Key benefits include:

  • Simple integration: Easily add object detection capabilities to your applications, regardless of your computer vision expertise.
  • Customizable detection: Generate bounding boxes based on custom text instructions (e.g., "I want to see bounding boxes of all the green objects in this image") without needing to train a custom model.

To see a complete, runnable example of bounding box detection, you can open the "Spatial understanding with Gemini" notebook in your preferred environment.

Open in Colab Open in Colab Enterprise Open in Vertex AI Workbench View on GitHub

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Bounding Box: A rectangular box used to identify the location of an object in an image or video frame.
  • Object Detection: The process of identifying and locating objects within an image or video.
  • Localization: The task of predicting the precise location of an object, typically represented by a bounding box.
  • Normalized Coordinates: A system where coordinates are scaled to a common range (e.g., 0 to 1000), making them independent of the original image's dimensions.
Set up your environment

Install the SDK

To get started, install the Generative AI SDK for Python.

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Set environment variables

Set environment variables to use the Generative AI SDK with Vertex AI.

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Detect objects with bounding boxes
docs.text:
The following workflow outlines the steps to detect objects and draw bounding boxes using the Python SDK.

flowchart TD
    A[Set up environment] --> B[Define helper functions]
    B --> C[Configure the model]
    C --> D[Generate content and visualize]

click A "#setup-environment"
click B "#define-helper-functions"
click C "#configure-the-model"
click D "#generate-content-and-visualize"
Python SDK

1. Import libraries and define helper functions

First, import the necessary libraries. The following helper code includes a pydantic class to represent a bounding box and a function to draw the boxes on an image using PIL. The model returns bounding boxes in the [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max] format, with coordinate values normalized to 1000.

View the helper code 
import requests
from google import genai
from google.genai.types import (
    GenerateContentConfig,
    HarmBlockThreshold,
    HarmCategory,
    HttpOptions,
    Part,
    SafetySetting,
)
from PIL import Image, ImageColor, ImageDraw
from pydantic import BaseModel

# Helper class to represent a bounding box
class BoundingBox(BaseModel):
    """
    Represents a bounding box with its 2D coordinates and associated label.

    Attributes:
        box_2d (list[int]): A list of integers representing the 2D coordinates of the bounding box,
                            typically in the format [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max].
        label (str): A string representing the label or class associated with the object within the bounding box.
    """

    box_2d: list[int]
    label: str

# Helper function to plot bounding boxes on an image
def plot_bounding_boxes(image_uri: str, bounding_boxes: list[BoundingBox]) -> None:
    """
    Plots bounding boxes on an image with labels, using PIL and normalized coordinates.

    Args:
        image_uri: The URI of the image file.
        bounding_boxes: A list of BoundingBox objects. Each box's coordinates are in
                        normalized [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max] format.
    """
    with Image.open(requests.get(image_uri, stream=True, timeout=10).raw) as im:
        width, height = im.size
        draw = ImageDraw.Draw(im)

        colors = list(ImageColor.colormap.keys())

        for i, bbox in enumerate(bounding_boxes):
            # Scale normalized coordinates to image dimensions
            abs_y_min = int(bbox.box_2d[0] / 1000 * height)
            abs_x_min = int(bbox.box_2d[1] / 1000 * width)
            abs_y_max = int(bbox.box_2d[2] / 1000 * height)
            abs_x_max = int(bbox.box_2d[3] / 1000 * width)

            color = colors[i % len(colors)]

            # Draw the rectangle using the correct (x, y) pairs
            draw.rectangle(
                ((abs_x_min, abs_y_min), (abs_x_max, abs_y_max)),
                outline=color,
                width=4,
            )
            if bbox.label:
                # Position the text at the top-left corner of the box
                draw.text((abs_x_min + 8, abs_y_min + 6), bbox.label, fill=color)

        im.show()

2. Configure the model

Next, configure the model by providing system instructions, generation parameters, and a response schema. By setting response_mime_type to application/json and providing a response_schema, you instruct the model to return a JSON object that conforms to the structure of the BoundingBox class.

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))

config = GenerateContentConfig(
    system_instruction="""
    Return bounding boxes as an array with labels.
    Never return masks. Limit to 25 objects.
    If an object is present multiple times, give each object a unique label
    according to its distinct characteristics (colors, size, position, etc..).
    """,
    temperature=0.5,
    safety_settings=[
        SafetySetting(
            category=HarmCategory.HARM_CATEGORY_DANGEROUS_CONTENT,
            threshold=HarmBlockThreshold.BLOCK_ONLY_HIGH,
        ),
    ],
    response_mime_type="application/json",
    response_schema=list[BoundingBox],
)

3. Generate content and visualize

Finally, call the model with an image and a text prompt. The response will contain the parsed bounding box data, which you can then visualize using the helper function.

image_uri = "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/socks.jpg"

response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents=[
        Part.from_uri(
            file_uri=image_uri,
            mime_type="image/jpeg",
        ),
        "Output the positions of the socks with a face. Label according to position in the image.",
    ],
    config=config,
)
print(response.text)
plot_bounding_boxes(image_uri, response.parsed)

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Example response:

The response.text will contain a JSON string similar to the following:

[
    {"box_2d": [6, 246, 386, 526], "label": "top-left light blue sock with cat face"},
    {"box_2d": [234, 649, 650, 863], "label": "top-right light blue sock with cat face"}
]

docs.title: Control access to Model Garden models
docs.text:
The Model Garden organization policy lets you centrally control which models your users can access and what actions they can take. By default, any principal with permissions to use Vertex AI can use Model Garden to discover, customize, and deploy a wide variety of Google and third-party models.

You can define a policy at the organization, folder, or project level to ensure that your users can only access an approved set of models. For example, you might set a policy to restrict usage to a specific list of Google and third-party models for production environments. A policy applies to all principals within its scope and is not configured on a per-user basis.

For more information, see Introduction to the Organization Policy Service.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Before you begin

Concepts

Concepts
  • Organization Policy: A service for centrally controlling your organization's cloud resources.
  • Model Garden: A curated platform in Vertex AI for discovering, testing, and deploying foundation models.
  • Model ID: The unique identifier for a model in Model Garden, formatted as publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL_NAME.
  • Constraint: A specific type of restriction applied to a Google Cloud service or a list of services.
  • Resource Hierarchy: The organization of Google Cloud resources in a tree-like structure, consisting of an organization, folders, and projects.

Policy evaluation

When a policy is evaluated, all policies that apply to a particular resource are merged. Any explicit deny value takes precedence over any explicit allow value.

For example, if a folder policy denies a specific model and a project policy within that folder allows the same model, access to the model is denied at the project level. The explicit deny at the folder level overrides the allow at the project level. However, if you configure the project policy to override all parent policies, access to the model is allowed.

For more information, see Understanding hierarchy evaluation in the Resource Manager documentation.

Considerations

  • The Model Garden organization policy only applies to models in Model Garden. It does not apply to models registered in the Vertex AI Model Registry.
  • An organization policy can't exceed 500 total allowed and denied values.
  • For a custom policy, you must specify each model and action individually. You cannot allow or deny a group of models with a single rule (for example, denying all third-party models).

docs.title: How Model Garden access control works
docs.text:
This section describes the workflow for controlling access to Model Garden models.

flowchart TD
    A[Understand policy options] --> B[Identify model IDs and actions]
    B --> C[Set the organization policy]
    C --> D[Verify policy enforcement]

click A "#understand-policy-options"
click B "#identify-model-ids-and-actions"
click C "#set-an-organization-policy-for-model-garden"
click D "#verify-the-policy"

docs.title: Understand policy options
docs.text:
When you set a policy, you choose one of the following enforcement approaches. By default, if no policy is set or inherited, all models and actions are allowed.

Policy Option Definition and Use Case Allow all models This is the default behavior. All models and actions in Model Garden are accessible. Use this if you do not need to restrict model access. Deny all models All models and actions in Model Garden are blocked. Use this to completely disable access to Model Garden within a specific organization, folder, or project. Custom allow policy Explicitly lists the models and actions that are permitted. All other models and actions are implicitly denied. Use this for a "deny by default" security posture, where you only want to grant access to a pre-approved list of models. Custom deny policy Explicitly lists the models and actions that are denied. All other models and actions are implicitly allowed. Use this for an "allow by default" posture, where you want to permit access to most models but block a few specific ones.

docs.title: Specify models and actions in a policy
docs.text:
To specify models in a custom policy, use the following format, which combines the model ID and a specific action:

publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL_NAME:ACTION

Replace the following:

  • PUBLISHER: The name of the publisher who owns the model.
  • MODEL_NAME: The name of the model to allow or deny.
  • ACTION: The model action to allow or deny.

For example, to define a policy rule for predictions with the Gemini 1.0 Pro model, you would specify publishers/google/models/gemini-1.0-pro:predict.

The fully qualified ID (publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL_NAME) is also known as the model ID. To find the model ID for a model, go to its model card in Model Garden. For links to model cards, see the list of models in Explore AI models in Model Garden.

Model actions

For each model, you can allow or deny the following actions:

  • predict: Specifies whether users can make online and batch predictions with a model's managed API (model as a service).
  • deploy: For models without a managed API, specifies whether users can deploy models on Google Cloud (for example, using one-click deployment in the Google Cloud console).
  • tune: Specifies whether users can tune models.

docs.title: Set an organization policy for Model Garden
docs.text:
You can set a policy for Model Garden using the Google Cloud console or the Google Cloud CLI. The name of the constraint to use is vertexai.allowedModels.

Google Cloud consoleGoogle Cloud CLI

You can create and manage organization policies directly in the Google Cloud console. When editing the policy, you can select a customization option and add conditional rules to specify the allowed or denied models and actions.

For detailed instructions, see Creating and managing organization policies.

To set a policy with the gcloud CLI, you first create a YAML file that defines your policy rules. Then, you apply the policy to your desired organization, folder, or project.

For detailed instructions, see Using constraints.

docs.title: Policy examples
docs.text:
The following examples are in the YAML format used when setting a policy with the gcloud CLI.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Example: Deny a set of models

The following policy denies specific actions on a list of models and implicitly allows all other models and actions.

name: organizations/ORGANIZATION_ID/policies/vertexai.allowedModels
spec:
  rules:
    - values:
        deniedValues:
        - publishers/meta/models/llama3:deploy
        - publishers/google/models/gemini-1.5-flash-001:tune
        - publishers/hf-google/models/gemma-2b:deploy

Replace ORGANIZATION_ID with the ID of your Google Cloud organization. For more information, see Getting an organization resource.

Example: Allow a set of models

The following policy allows specific actions on a list of models and implicitly denies all other models and actions.

name: organizations/ORGANIZATION_ID/policies/vertexai.allowedModels
spec:
  rules:
    - values:
        allowedValues:
        - publishers/meta/models/llama3:deploy
        - publishers/google/models/gemini-1.5-flash-001:tune
        - publishers/hf-google/models/gemma-2b:deploy

docs.title: Verify the policy
docs.text: After you set and apply the policy, its effects are enforced in the associated organization, folder, or project. Users will only be able to see and use the models and actions permitted by the effective policy in the Model Garden UI and through the API. For example, if a model's deploy action is denied, the Deploy button will be disabled on its model card in the Google Cloud console.

docs.title: Generative AI and zero data retention
docs.text:
Google was the first in the industry to publish an AI/ML Privacy Commitment, which outlines our belief that customers should have the highest level of security and control over their data that is stored in the cloud. That commitment extends to Google Cloud's generative AI products. Google ensures that its teams are following these commitments through robust data governance practices, which include reviews of the data that Google Cloud uses in the development of its products. More details about how Google processes data can also be found in Google's Cloud Data Processing Addendum (CDPA).

Concepts
  • Zero Data Retention: A state where a service does not store or retain any customer data after a request is processed.
  • Data Caching: Temporarily storing user inputs and model outputs to reduce latency for subsequent, similar prompts.
  • Prompt Logging: Recording prompts for the purpose of monitoring and preventing service abuse.
  • Grounding: Using external, verifiable data sources, like Google Search, to improve the factual accuracy of a model's response.
  • Session Resumption: An optional feature that stores session data to allow a user to reconnect to a previous API session.

docs.title: Training restriction
docs.text: As outlined in Section 17 "Training Restriction" in the Service Terms section of Service Specific Terms, Google won't use your data to train or fine-tune any AI/ML models without your prior permission or instruction. This applies to all managed models on Vertex AI, including GA and pre-GA models.

docs.title: Customer data retention and achieving zero data retention
docs.text:
To achieve zero data retention, customers must take specific actions to disable features where customer data is retained for limited periods. The following table outlines these scenarios and the required actions.

Scenario Data Stored Retention Period Action for Zero Retention Data Caching User inputs and model outputs. Up to 24 hours. Disable data caching at the project level. Prompt Logging for Abuse Monitoring Prompts from non-invoiced accounts. Up to 30 days. Request an exception for abuse monitoring. See Abuse monitoring. Grounding with Google Search Prompts, contextual information, and generated output. Up to 30 days. Do not use the Grounding with Google Search feature. Session Resumption for Gemini Live API Text, video, and audio prompt data and model outputs. Up to 24 hours. Do not enable this optional feature in the API request. See Live API.

This applies to all managed models on Vertex AI, including GA and pre-GA models.

docs.title: Enabling and disabling data caching
docs.text:
You can manage data caching for your Google Cloud project by using the following curl commands. To grant the permissions required to manage caching, see Vertex AI access control with IAM.

The following diagram shows the workflow for managing data caching settings.

flowchart TD
    A[Get current cache status] --> B["Disable caching (if enabled)"]
    A --> C["Enable caching (if disabled)"]

click A "#get-current-cache-setting"
click B "#disable-caching"
click C "#enable-caching"

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Get current cache settingDisable cachingEnable caching

Run the following command to determine if caching is enabled or disabled for a project. To run this command, a user must be granted one of the following roles: roles/aiplatform.viewer, roles/aiplatform.user, or roles/aiplatform.admin.

PROJECT_ID=PROJECT_ID
# Setup project_id
$ gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID

# GetCacheConfig
$ curl -X GET -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig

# Response if caching is enabled (caching is enabled by default).
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig"
}

# Response if caching is disabled.
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig"
  "disableCache": true
}

Run the following curl command to disable caching for a Google Cloud project. To run this command, a user must be granted the Vertex AI Administrator role, roles/aiplatform.admin.

PROJECT_ID=PROJECT_ID
# Setup project_id
$ gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID

# Opt-out of caching.
$ curl -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig -d '{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig",
  "disableCache": true
}'

# Response.
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig/operations/${OPERATION_ID}",
  "done": true,
  "response": {
    "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.Empty"
  }
}

If you disabled caching for a Google Cloud project and want to re-enable it, run the following curl command. To run this command, a user must be granted the Vertex AI Administrator role, roles/aiplatform.admin.

PROJECT_ID=PROJECT_ID
# Setup project_id
$ gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID

# Opt in to caching.
$ curl -X PATCH     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig -d '{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig",
  "disableCache": false
}'

# Response.
{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/projects/PROJECT_ID/cacheConfig/operations/${OPERATION_NUMBER}",
  "done": true,
  "response": {
    "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.Empty"
  }
}

docs.title: Dynamic shared quota (DSQ)
docs.text:
Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) serves your pay-as-you-go (PayGo) requests with greater flexibility to adapt to your workload needs without requiring you to manage quotas or submit quota increase requests (QIR). With DSQ, there are no predefined quota limits on your usage. Instead, DSQ provides access to a large, shared pool of resources that are dynamically allocated based on real-time availability and demand across all customers using a specific model.

When more customers are active, each customer might experience lower throughput. Conversely, when fewer customers are active, each customer might achieve higher throughput.

Concepts
  • Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ): A flexible, pay-as-you-go quota model that provides access to a large, shared pool of resources allocated dynamically based on real-time demand.
  • Provisioned Throughput: A service that reserves a specific amount of model processing capacity exclusively for your use, ensuring consistent performance and availability for a fixed cost.

docs.title: When to use Dynamic Shared Quota
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers two primary ways to manage throughput for generative AI models: Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) and Provisioned Throughput. DSQ is ideal for applications with variable traffic, while Provisioned Throughput is designed for applications requiring stable, predictable performance.

The following table compares DSQ and Provisioned Throughput:

Feature Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) Provisioned Throughput Best for Applications with variable or unpredictable traffic, development, and testing. Production applications requiring high, stable throughput and guaranteed availability. Cost Model Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) based on usage. Fixed hourly cost for reserved capacity, with a one-hour minimum commitment. Performance Throughput is dynamic and depends on shared resource availability and overall system demand. Guaranteed, stable, and predictable throughput based on the reserved capacity. Quota Management No predefined limits; access to a large, shared resource pool. Capacity is reserved exclusively for your project.

For workloads that demand high availability and predictable service levels, see Provisioned Throughput.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
The following Gemini models and their supervised fine-tuned versions support DSQ:

Preview

  • Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash with Live API
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash with image generation
  • Gemini 2.5 Pro
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite

The following legacy Gemini models also support DSQ:

  • Gemini 1.5 Pro
  • Gemini 1.5 Flash

docs.title: How DSQ works
docs.text:
DSQ adapts to your traffic patterns by providing access to a large, shared resource pool. Your project's access to this pool is not capped by a predefined limit but is determined by the overall capacity and the collective real-time demand from all customers. This model offers significant flexibility, allowing your workloads to burst and consume more resources when they are available.

To ensure a fair and stable experience, DSQ uses a dynamic prioritization approach to manage requests, especially during periods of high demand. This means that while the system accommodates bursts, unusually large and rapid spikes in traffic from a single source might be handled with a different priority than more consistent traffic. This management approach protects overall system stability and ensures equitable access for all users.

Gemini requests with multi-modal inputs are subject to the corresponding system rate limits for image, audio, video, and document processing.

docs.title: Handling 429 Resource Exhausted errors
docs.text:
With DSQ, a 429 Resource Exhausted error does not mean you have hit a fixed quota limit on your project. Instead, it indicates that the shared resource pool for a specific model in a region is temporarily experiencing demand that exceeds the available capacity. This is a temporary state of contention for resources, not a permanent block on your project.

Think of it like trying to board a popular train during peak rush hour. There isn't a ticket limit specifically for you, but the train itself might be momentarily full.

Because availability in this dynamic environment can change quickly, we recommend implementing exponential backoff and retry mechanisms in your application to handle these errors. For more tactics, see A guide to handling 429 errors.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Enable Data Access audit logs
docs.text:
To monitor the usage of your model endpoints, you can enable Data Access audit logs for Vertex AI. These logs help you track who did what, where, and when. Data Access audit logs include "admin read" operations that read metadata or configuration, and "data read" and "data write" operations that read or write user-provided data.

Before you begin Concepts

Audit Logs: Chronological records of activities that have occurred within a system, which are used for security, compliance, and operational troubleshooting. Data Access audit logs: A type of audit log that records API calls that read, write, or modify user data.

Grant permissions

To view the data_access log stream in the Google Cloud console after enabling the logs, you need the Private Logs Viewer (roles/logging.privateLogViewer) IAM role.

docs.text:
