To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Vertex AI SDK for Python API reference documentation.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

import os

from google.auth import default

import vertexai
from vertexai.preview.language_models import (
    EvaluationTextClassificationSpec,
    TextGenerationModel,
)

PROJECT_ID = os.getenv("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT")


def evaluate_model() -> object:
    """Evaluate the performance of a generative AI model."""

    # Set credentials for the pipeline components used in the evaluation task
    credentials, _ = default(scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"])

    vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1", credentials=credentials)

    # Create a reference to a generative AI model
    model = TextGenerationModel.from_pretrained("text-bison@002")

    # Define the evaluation specification for a text classification task
    task_spec = EvaluationTextClassificationSpec(
        ground_truth_data=[
            "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/llm_classification_bp_input_prompts_with_ground_truth.jsonl"
        ],
        class_names=["nature", "news", "sports", "health", "startups"],
        target_column_name="ground_truth",
    )

    # Evaluate the model
    eval_metrics = model.evaluate(task_spec=task_spec)
    print(eval_metrics)
    # Example response:
    # ...
    # PipelineJob run completed.
    # Resource name: projects/123456789/locations/us-central1/pipelineJobs/evaluation-llm-classification-...
    # EvaluationClassificationMetric(label_name=None, auPrc=0.53833705, auRoc=0.8...

    return eval_metrics

docs.text:
After the evaluation job is complete, you can find the results in the Cloud Storage output directory that you specified when creating the job. The results file is named evaluation_metrics.json.

For tuned models, you can also view evaluation results in the Google Cloud console.

Steps to view results in the Google Cloud console

  1. In the Vertex AI section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Vertex AI Model Registry page.

  2. Click the name of the tuned model to view its evaluation metrics.

  3. In the Evaluate tab, click the name of the evaluation run that you want to view.

docs.title: Configure a judge model
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Model-based metrics provide various approaches to customize and help you generate evaluation metrics based on your criteria and use cases. This page describes how to configure your judge model for your ideal use case.

For the basic evaluation workflow, see the Gen AI evaluation service quickstart. The Advanced judge model customization series includes the following pages:

  1. Evaluate a judge model
  2. Prompting for judge model customization
  3. Configure a judge model (current page)
Concepts
  • Judge model: An LLM used to evaluate the quality of another model's output based on specified criteria.
  • System instructions: A set of directives given to a model to guide its overall behavior, tone, and response style.
  • Response flipping: A technique to reduce positional bias by swapping the order of candidate and baseline model responses during pairwise evaluation.
  • Multi-sampling: The practice of querying the judge model multiple times for the same input to improve the consistency and reliability of its evaluation.
  • Tuned judge model: A judge model that has been fine-tuned on a specific dataset to improve its evaluation accuracy for a particular task.

docs.title: Overview of configuration methods
docs.text:
You can configure your judge model to improve evaluation quality using several methods. The following table provides a high-level comparison to help you choose the right approach for your needs.

Method Description Best for System instructions Provide high-level directives to the judge model to influence its persona, tone, and evaluation style. Setting a consistent evaluation context or persona (e.g., "You are an expert in medical writing"). Response flipping Swaps the order of the baseline and candidate model responses in half of the evaluation calls. Reducing positional bias in pairwise evaluations where the judge model might favor the first or second response. Multi-sampling Calls the judge model multiple times for the same evaluation to average out randomness. Improving the consistency and reliability of evaluation scores, especially when the judge model shows variability. Tuned judge model Uses a fine-tuned LLM as the judge model. Achieving the highest evaluation quality for a specific, well-defined use case with sufficient tuning data.

docs.title: Use system instructions
docs.text:
Gemini models can accept system instructions, which are a set of instructions that guide how the model processes prompts. You can use system instructions to specify roles, personas, contextual information, or a desired explanation style and tone. The judge model typically gives higher importance to system instructions than to input prompts.

For a list of models that support system instructions, see Supported models.

The following example using the Vertex AI SDK adds system_instruction at the metric level for a PointwiseMetric. You can use the same approach with PairwiseMetric.

system_instruction = "You are an expert evaluator."
linguistic_acceptability = PointwiseMetric(
    metric="linguistic_acceptability",
    metric_prompt_template=linguistic_acceptability_metric_prompt_template,
    system_instruction=system_instruction,
)

eval_result = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[linguistic_acceptability]
).evaluate()

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Advanced judge model configurations
docs.text:
You can further customize the judge model for bias reduction, consistency, and accuracy by passing an AutoraterConfig object to your EvalTask.

Enable response flippingConfigure multi-samplingUse a tuned judge model

For PairwiseMetrics, the judge model evaluates which of two responses (one from a baseline model, one from a candidate model) better aligns with the specified criteria. However, the model might be biased toward the response presented first.

To reduce this bias, you can enable response flipping. When enabled, the service flips the baseline and candidate model responses in half of the calls to the judge model.

from vertexai.preview.evaluation import AutoraterConfig

pairwise_relevance_prompt_template = """
    # Instruction
    …

    ### Response A
    {baseline_model_response}

    ### Response B
    {candidate_model_response}
"""

my_pairwise_metric = PairwiseMetric(
    metric="my_pairwise_metric",
    metric_prompt_template=pairwise_relevance_prompt_template,
    candidate_response_field_name = "candidate_model_response",
    baseline_response_field_name = "baseline_model_response"
)


# Define an AutoraterConfig with flip_enabled
my_autorater_config = AutoraterConfig(flip_enabled=True)

# Define an EvalTask with autorater_config
flip_enabled_eval_result = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[my_pairwise_metric],
    autorater_config=my_autorater_config,
).evaluate()

The judge model might show some randomness in its responses. Additional sampling can help negate this randomness and lead to more consistent results, though it increases latency.

You can set the sampling_count to an integer between 1 and 32. The recommended default is 4, which balances consistency and latency.

from vertexai.preview.evaluation import AutoraterConfig

# Define customized sampling count in AutoraterConfig
autorater_config = AutoraterConfig(sampling_count=6)

# Run evaluation with the sampling count.
eval_result = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[METRICS],
    autorater_config=autorater_config
).evaluate()

If you have high-quality tuning data for your evaluation use case, you can tune a Gemini model and use it as your judge model for improved accuracy. You can specify a tuned model as the judge model through AutoraterConfig.

from vertexai.preview.evaluation import {
   AutoraterConfig,
   PairwiseMetric,
   tune_autorater,
   evaluate_autorater,
}

# Tune a model to be the judge model. The tune_autorater helper function returns an AutoraterConfig with the judge model set as the tuned model.
autorater_config: AutoRaterConfig = tune_autorater(
    base_model="gemini-1.0-pro",
    train_dataset=f"{BUCKET_URI}/train/sft_train_samples.jsonl",
    validation_dataset=f"{BUCKET_URI}/val/sft_val_samples.jsonl",
    tuned_model_display_name=tuned_model_display_name,
)

# Alternatively, you can set up the judge model with an existing tuned model endpoint
autorater_config = AutoraterConfig(autorater_model=TUNED_MODEL)

# Use the tuned judge model
eval_result = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[METRICS],
    autorater_config=autorater_config,
).evaluate()

docs.title: Define your evaluation metrics
docs.text: The first step to evaluate your generative models or applications is to identify your evaluation goal and define your evaluation metrics. This page provides an overview of concepts related to defining evaluation metrics for your use case.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Generative AI models can be used to create applications for a wide range of tasks, such as summarizing news articles, responding to customer inquiries, or assisting with code writing. The Gen AI evaluation service in Vertex AI lets you evaluate any model with explainable metrics.

To evaluate your application's performance on a specific task, you must define the criteria you want to measure and the metrics to score them:

  • Criteria: Single or multiple dimensions you would like to evaluate upon, such as conciseness, relevance, correctness, or appropriate choice of words.
  • Metrics: A single score that measures the model output against the defined criteria.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Judge Model: A model used to evaluate the output of another model based on specified criteria.
  • Ground Truth: A dataset of high-quality, reference examples used to evaluate a model's performance with computation-based metrics.
  • ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation): A set of metrics used for evaluating automatic summarization and machine translation by comparing a model's output to a human-created reference.
  • BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy): A metric for evaluating the quality of machine-translated text by measuring its similarity to a set of high-quality reference translations.
  • Chain-of-thought prompting: A technique that encourages a large language model (LLM) to explain its reasoning process step-by-step, which can improve the accuracy of its final answer.
  • Function Calling: The ability of a model to intelligently decide to call external tools or functions to perform actions or retrieve information.

docs.title: Types of evaluation metrics
docs.text:
The Gen AI evaluation service provides two major types of metrics: model-based and computation-based. Use the following table to decide which approach is best for your use case.

Evaluation approach How it works Data requirements Cost and speed Model-based metrics Use a judge model to assess performance based on descriptive evaluation criteria. Ground truth is optional. Slightly more expensive and slower. Computation-based metrics Use mathematical formulas to assess performance by comparing model output to a reference. Ground truth is usually required. Low cost and fast.

To get started after choosing your metrics, see Prepare your dataset and Run evaluation.

docs.title: Define your model-based metrics
docs.text:
Model-based evaluation involves using a machine learning model (a "judge model") to evaluate the outputs of your candidate model. Proprietary Google judge models, such as Gemini, are calibrated with human raters to ensure their quality and are available out of the box.

Model-based evaluation follows this process:

  1. Data preparation: You provide evaluation data in the form of input prompts. The candidate models receive the prompts and generate corresponding responses.
  2. Evaluation: The evaluation metrics and generated responses are sent to the judge model. The judge model evaluates each response individually, providing a row-based assessment.
  3. Aggregation and explanation: The Gen AI evaluation service aggregates these individual assessments into an overall score. The output also includes chain-of-thought explanations for each judgment, outlining the rationale behind the selection.

docs.title: Choose between pointwise and pairwise evaluation
docs.text:
You can measure model-based metrics pointwise or pairwise. Pairwise metrics are only supported with Gemini as a judge model. Use the following table to decide which evaluation method to use.

Evaluation type Definition When to use Example use cases Pointwise evaluation Evaluate one model and generate scores based on the criteria.
  • When you need a score for each model being evaluated.
  • When it is not difficult to define the rubric for each score.
  • Understanding how your model behaves in production.
  • Exploring the strengths and weaknesses of a single model.
  • Identifying which behaviors to focus on when tuning.
  • Getting the baseline performance of a model.
Pairwise evaluation Compare two models against each other, generating a preference based on the criteria.
  • When you want to compare two models and a score is not necessary.
  • When the score rubric for pointwise is difficult to define.
  • Determining which model to put into production.
  • Choosing between model types (e.g., Gemini Pro versus Claude 3).
  • Choosing between different prompts.
  • Determining if tuning improved a baseline model.

docs.title: Set up your model-based metrics
docs.text:
The Gen AI evaluation service offers the following options to set up your model-based metrics with the Vertex AI SDK.

Option Description Best for Use an existing example Use a prebuilt metric prompt template to get started. Common use cases, time-saving. Define metrics with our templated interface Get guided assistance in defining your metrics. Our templated interface provides structure and suggestions. Customization with support. Define metrics from scratch Have complete control over your metric definitions. Ideal for highly specific use cases. Requires more technical expertise and time investment.

As an example, you might want to develop a generative AI application that returns fluent and entertaining responses. For this application, you can define two criteria for evaluation using the templated interface:

  • Fluency: Sentences flow smoothly, avoiding awkward phrasing or run-on sentences. Ideas and sentences connect logically, using transitions effectively where needed.
  • Entertainment: Short, amusing text that incorporates emoji, exclamations, and questions to convey quick and spontaneous communication and diversion.

To turn those two criteria into a metric, you want an overall score ranging from -1 to 1 called custom_text_quality. You can define a metric like this:

# Define a pointwise metric with two criteria: Fluency and Entertaining.
pointwise_metric = PointwiseMetric(
    metric="custom_text_quality",
    metric_prompt_template=PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate(
        criteria={
            "fluency": (
                "Sentences flow smoothly and are easy to read, avoiding awkward"
                " phrasing or run-on sentences. Ideas and sentences connect"
                " logically, using transitions effectively where needed."
            ),
            "entertaining": (
                "Short, amusing text that incorporates emojis, exclamations and"
                " questions to convey quick and spontaneous communication and"
                " diversion."
            ),
        },
        rating_rubric={
            "1": "The response performs well on both criteria.",
            "0": "The response is somewhat aligned with both criteria",
            "-1": "The response falls short on both criteria",
        },
    ),
)

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

For a complete list of metric prompt templates, see Metric prompt templates for evaluation.

docs.title: Evaluate translation models
docs.text:
Preview

This product or feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

The Gen AI evaluation service offers specialized metrics for translation tasks. You can use these to evaluate the quality and accuracy of translation model results, whether they are outputs of NMT, TranslationLLM, or Gemini models. You can also use Gemini as a judge model to evaluate your model for fluency, coherence, verbosity, and text quality in combination with these metrics.

Metric Type Description Scoring MetricX Model-based An error-based metric developed by Google. Available as both reference-based and reference-free (QE). Predicts a score between 0 and 25. A lower score is better. COMET Model-based Employs a reference-based regression approach. Provides scores from 0 to 1. A higher score is better. BLEU Computation-based Indicates how similar the candidate text is to the reference text. Provides scores from 0 to 1. A higher score is better.

Note that BLEU scores are not recommended for comparing across different corpora and languages. Many translation experts have shifted to model-based metric approaches like MetricX and COMET, which have a higher correlation with human ratings and are more granular in identifying error scenarios.

To learn how to run evaluations for translation models, see Evaluate a translation model.

docs.title: Define your computation-based metrics
docs.text:
Computation-based metrics compare whether the LLM-generated results are consistent with a ground-truth dataset of input and output pairs. These metrics can be categorized into the following groups:

  • Lexicon-based metrics: Use math to calculate the string similarities between LLM-generated results and ground truth, such as Exact Match and ROUGE.
  • Count-based metrics: Aggregate the number of rows that hit or miss certain ground-truth labels, such as F1-score, Accuracy, and Tool Name Match.
  • Embedding-based metrics: Calculate the distance between the LLM-generated results and ground truth in the embedding space, reflecting their level of similarity.

In the generative AI evaluation service, you can use computation-based metrics through the Vertex AI SDK for Python.

docs.title: General text generation
docs.text:
The following metrics help you to evaluate the model's ability to ensure the responses are useful, safe, and effective for your users.

Exact match

The exact_match metric computes whether a model response matches a reference exactly.

  • Token limit: None

Evaluation criteria

Not applicable.

Metric input parameters

Input parameter Description response The LLM response. reference The golden LLM response for reference.

Output scores

Value Description 0 Not matched 1 Matched BLEU

The bleu (BiLingual Evaluation Understudy) metric holds the result of an algorithm for evaluating the quality of the response, which has been translated from one natural language to another. The quality of the response is considered to be the correspondence between a response parameter and its reference parameter.

  • Token limit: None

Evaluation criteria

Not applicable.

Metric input parameters

Input parameter Description response The LLM response. reference The golden LLM response for the reference.

Output scores

Value Description A float in the range of [0,1] Higher scores indicate better translations. A score of 1 represents a perfect match to the reference. ROUGE

The ROUGE metric is used to compare the provided response parameter against a reference parameter. All rouge metrics return the F1 score. rouge-l-sum is calculated by default, but you can specify the rouge variant that you want to use.

  • Token limit: None

Evaluation criteria

Not applicable.

Metric input parameters

Input parameter Description response The LLM response. reference The golden LLM response for the reference.

Output scores

Value Description A float in the range of [0,1] A score closer to 0 means poor similarity between response and reference. A score closer to 1 means strong similarity between response and reference.

docs.title: Tool use and function calling
docs.text:
The following metrics help you to evaluate the model's ability to predict a valid tool (function) call.

Tool call valid

The tool_call_valid metric describes the model's ability to predict a valid tool call. Only the first tool call is inspected.

  • Token limit: None

Evaluation criteria

Evaluation criterion Description Validity The model's output contains a valid tool call. Formatting A JSON dictionary contains the name and arguments fields.

Metric input parameters

Input parameter Description prediction The candidate model output, which is a JSON serialized string that contains content and tool_calls keys. The content value is the text output from the model. The tool_calls value is a JSON serialized string of a list of tool calls. Here is an example:{"content": "", "tool_calls": [{"name": "book_tickets", "arguments": {"movie": "Mission Impossible Dead Reckoning Part 1", "theater":"Regal Edwards 14", "location": "Mountain View CA", "showtime": "7:30", "date": "2024-03-30","num_tix": "2"}}]} reference The ground-truth reference prediction, which follows the same format as prediction.

Output scores

Value Description 0 Invalid tool call 1 Valid tool call Tool name match

The tool_name_match metric describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct tool name. Only the first tool call is inspected.

  • Token limit: None

Evaluation criteria

Evaluation criterion Description Name matching The model-predicted tool call matches the reference tool call's name.

Metric input parameters

Input parameter Description prediction The candidate model output, which is a JSON serialized string that contains content and tool_calls keys. The content value is the text output from the model. The tool_call value is a JSON serialized string of a list of tool calls. Here is an example:{"content": "","tool_calls": [{"name": "book_tickets", "arguments": {"movie": "Mission Impossible Dead Reckoning Part 1", "theater":"Regal Edwards 14", "location": "Mountain View CA", "showtime": "7:30", "date": "2024-03-30","num_tix": "2"}}]} reference The ground-truth reference prediction, which follows the same format as the prediction.

Output scores

Value Description 0 Tool call name doesn't match the reference. 1 Tool call name matches the reference. Tool parameter key match

The tool_parameter_key_match metric describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct parameter names.

  • Token limit: None

Evaluation criteria

Evaluation criterion Description Parameter matching ratio The ratio between the number of predicted parameters that match the parameter names of the reference tool call and the total number of parameters.

Metric input parameters

Input parameter Description prediction The candidate model output, which is a JSON serialized string that contains the content and tool_calls keys. The content value is the text output from the model. The tool_call value is a JSON serialized string of a list of tool calls. Here is an example:{"content": "", "tool_calls": [{"name": "book_tickets", "arguments": {"movie": "Mission Impossible Dead Reckoning Part 1", "theater":"Regal Edwards 14", "location": "Mountain View CA", "showtime": "7:30", "date": "2024-03-30","num_tix": "2"}}]} reference The ground-truth reference model prediction, which follows the same format as prediction.

Output scores

Value Description A float in the range of [0,1] The higher score of 1 means more parameters match the reference parameters' names. Tool parameter KV match

The tool_parameter_kv_match metric describes the model's ability to predict a tool call with the correct parameter names and key values.

  • Token limit: None

Evaluation criteria

Evaluation criterion Description Parameter matching ratio The ratio between the number of the predicted parameters that match both the parameter names and values of the reference tool call and the total number of parameters.

Metric input parameters

Input parameter Description prediction The candidate model output, which is a JSON serialized string that contains content and tool_calls keys. The content value is the text output from the model. The tool_call value is a JSON serialized string of a list of tool calls. Here is an example:{"content": "", "tool_calls": [{"name": "book_tickets", "arguments": {"movie": "Mission Impossible Dead Reckoning Part 1", "theater":"Regal Edwards 14", "location": "Mountain View CA", "showtime": "7:30", "date": "2024-03-30","num_tix": "2"}}]} reference The ground-truth reference prediction, which follows the same format as prediction.

Output scores

Value Description A float in the range of [0,1] The higher score of 1 means more parameters match the reference parameters' names and values.

docs.title: Baseline evaluation quality for generative tasks
docs.text: When evaluating the output of generative AI models, note that the evaluation process is inherently subjective, and the quality of evaluation can vary depending on the specific task and evaluation criteria. This subjectivity also applies to human evaluators. For more information about the challenges of achieving consistent evaluation for generative AI models, see Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena and Learning to summarize from human feedback.

docs.title: Evaluate a judge model
docs.text:
Preview

This product or feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

For model-based metrics, the Generative AI evaluation service evaluates your models with a foundational model, such as Gemini, that has been configured and prompted as a judge model.

Using a judge model is a scalable and cost-effective alternative to human evaluation for large language models (LLMs). By default, the evaluation service uses a configured Gemini 1.0 Pro model with customizable prompts to assess your model's performance across various use cases.

This document is the first part of the Advanced judge model customization series, which provides tools to evaluate and configure the judge model for your specific needs.

  • 1. Evaluate a judge model (this page)
  • 2. Prompting for judge model customization
  • 3. Configure a judge model

For the basic evaluation workflow, see the Generative AI evaluation service quickstart.

This document describes the workflow for evaluating a customized judge model. The following diagram shows the high-level steps.

flowchart TD
    A["Prepare the evaluation dataset"] --> B["Review available metrics"]
    B --> C["Evaluate the judge model"]

    click A "#prepare-the-evaluation-dataset"
    click B "#available-metrics"
    click C "#example-evaluate-a-custom-fluency-metric"
Before you begin

Prepare the evaluation dataset

To evaluate model-based metrics, you need an evaluation dataset that includes human ratings as the ground truth. The goal is to compare the scores from the judge model with human ratings to determine if the judge model's quality is sufficient for your use case.

Your dataset must contain a ground truth column that corresponds to the metric you are evaluating:

  • For PointwiseMetric, add a {metric_name}/human_rating column.
  • For PairwiseMetric, add a {metric_name}/human_pairwise_choice column.

Dataset schema

Model-based metric Human rating column PointwiseMetric {metric_name}/human_rating PairwiseMetric {metric_name}/human_pairwise_choice Concepts
  • PointwiseMetric: Evaluates a single model's response on a numeric scale (e.g., rating fluency from 1 to 5).
  • PairwiseMetric: Compares the responses of two models (a candidate and a baseline) and indicates a preference (e.g., Model A is better, Model B is better, or it's a tie).
  • Confusion matrix: A table used to evaluate the performance of a classification model by showing the counts of true positive, true negative, false positive, and false negative predictions.
  • f1 score: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a single score that balances both concerns.
Available metrics

The evaluation service provides different metrics depending on the number of possible outcomes (classes) for your PointwiseMetric or PairwiseMetric.

| Metric Type | Available Metrics ...| | 2-Class(e.g., PointwiseMetric with scores 0/1, or PairwiseMetric with choices A/B) | 2-class balanced accuracy2-class balanced f1 scoreConfusion matrix (to calculate TPR, TNR, FPR, FNR) | | Multi-Class(e.g., PointwiseMetric with scores 1-5, or PairwiseMetric with choices A/B/Tie) | Multiple-class balanced accuracyMultiple-class balanced f1 score - To calculate other metrics, you can use open-source libraries.

Metric calculation details

Formulas

  • 2-class balanced accuracy: ( (1/2)*(True Positive Rate + True Negative Rate) )
  • Multiple-class balanced accuracy: ( (1/n) *∑_{i=1...n}(recall(class_i)) )
  • 2-class / Multiple-class balanced f1 score: ( ∑_{i=0,1} (cnt_i/sum) * f1(class_i) )
    • Where ( f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) )
    • ( precision = True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives) )
    • ( recall = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives) )
    • ( n ) : number of classes
    • ( cnt_i ) : number of ( class_i ) in ground truth data
    • ( sum ): number of elements in ground truth data

Confusion matrix example

The result fields confusion_matrix and confusion_matrix_labels can be used to build a confusion matrix. For example, the following result:

confusion_matrix = [[20, 31, 15],
                    [10, 11,  3],
                    [ 3,  2,  2]]
confusion_matrix_labels = ['BASELINE', 'CANDIDATE', 'TIE']

Translates to the following confusion matrix, where rows represent the predicted label and columns represent the true label:

             BASELINE |  CANDIDATE | TIE
   BASELINE.    20         31        15
   CANDIDATE.   10         11         3
   TIE.         3          2         2
Example: Evaluate a custom fluency metric

The following example shows how to update a model-based metric with a custom definition of fluency and then evaluate the quality of that metric against human ratings.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

from vertexai.preview.evaluation import (
   AutoraterConfig,
   PairwiseMetric,
)
from vertexai.preview.evaluation.autorater_utils import evaluate_autorater


# Step 1: Prepare the evaluation dataset with the human rating data column.
human_rated_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
  "prompt": [PROMPT_1, PROMPT_2],
    "response": [RESPONSE_1, RESPONSE_2],
  "baseline_model_response": [BASELINE_MODEL_RESPONSE_1, BASELINE_MODEL_RESPONSE_2],
    "pairwise_fluency/human_pairwise_choice": ["model_A", "model_B"]
})

# Step 2: Get the results from model-based metric
pairwise_fluency = PairwiseMetric(
    metric="pairwise_fluency",
    metric_prompt_template="please evaluate pairwise fluency..."
)

eval_result = EvalTask(
    dataset=human_rated_dataset,
    metrics=[pairwise_fluency],
).evaluate()

# Step 3: Calibrate model-based metric result and human preferences.
# eval_result contains human evaluation result from human_rated_dataset.
evaluate_autorater_result = evaluate_autorater(
  evaluate_autorater_input=eval_result.metrics_table,
  eval_metrics=[pairwise_fluency]
)

docs.title: Evaluate Gen AI agents
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

After you build and test your generative AI model, you can use it to create an agent, such as a chatbot, that performs tasks. The generative AI evaluation service helps you measure how well your agent completes these tasks and achieves its goals for your specific use case.

This document guides you through the process of evaluating your agent's performance using the Vertex AI SDK.

Concepts
  • Agent: An autonomous system that uses a large language model (LLM) to understand user requests and perform tasks by calling appropriate tools.
  • Trajectory: The sequence of tool calls an agent makes to process a request and arrive at a final response.
  • Tool Call: A specific action or function that an agent invokes, such as calling an API or querying a database.
  • LangChain: An open-source framework for developing applications powered by language models, including agents.
  • Agent Engine: A Google Cloud platform based on LangChain on Vertex AI that lets you deploy and manage agents.

The following diagram shows the workflow for evaluating a generative AI agent.

flowchart TD
    A[Prepare your evaluation dataset] --> B[Define evaluation metrics]
    B --> C[Import your evaluation dataset]
    C --> D[Run the evaluation]
    D --> E[View and interpret results]

    click A "#prepare-your-evaluation-dataset"
    click B "#step-1-define-evaluation-metrics"
    click C "#step-2-import-your-evaluation-dataset"
    click D "#step-3-run-the-evaluation"
    click E "#step-4-view-and-interpret-results"

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: Before you can evaluate your agent, you need to choose a supported agent type and prepare your evaluation dataset.

docs.title: Supported agents
docs.text:
The generative AI evaluation service supports the following types of agents. Choose the one that best fits your development environment and customization needs.

Supported Agent Description Best for... Agent built with Agent Engine's template An agent deployed and managed on Agent Engine (LangChain on Vertex AI), a fully managed Google Cloud platform. Users who want a managed, low-code environment for deploying and managing agents. LangChain agents built using Agent Engine's customizable template An agent built with the open-source LangChain framework and deployed on Agent Engine. Developers who need the flexibility of LangChain combined with the managed services of Agent Engine. Custom agent function A flexible Python function that takes a prompt and returns a response and trajectory in a dictionary format. Users who have a custom-built agent and need maximum flexibility for integration.

docs.title: Prepare your evaluation dataset
docs.text:
Your evaluation dataset provides the ground truth for measuring your agent's performance. The schema for your dataset depends on the evaluation method you choose.

  • Final response evaluation: The data schema is similar to that of model response evaluation.
  • Trajectory evaluation: Your dataset must include the predicted_trajectory and reference_trajectory for each example.
Input Field Description predicted_trajectory The list of tool calls the agent actually used to generate the final response. reference_trajectory The expected or ideal sequence of tool calls the agent should have used to satisfy the query. This is not required for the trajectory_single_tool_use metric.

The following is an example of a Pandas DataFrame for trajectory evaluation.

Note: Example datasets are for demonstration purposes and should not be used in production.

import pandas as pd

reference_trajectory = [
# example 1
[
  {
    "tool_name": "set_device_info",
    "tool_input": {
        "device_id": "device_2",
        "updates": {
            "status": "OFF"
        }
    }
  }
],
# example 2
[
    {
      "tool_name": "get_user_preferences",
      "tool_input": {
          "user_id": "user_y"
      }
  },
  {
      "tool_name": "set_temperature",
      "tool_input": {
          "location": "Living Room",
          "temperature": 23
      }
    },
  ]
]

predicted_trajectory = [
# example 1
[
  {
    "tool_name": "set_device_info",
    "tool_input": {
        "device_id": "device_3",
        "updates": {
            "status": "OFF"
        }
    }
  }
],
# example 2
[
    {
      "tool_name": "get_user_preferences",
      "tool_input": {
          "user_id": "user_z"
      }
    },
    {
      "tool_name": "set_temperature",
      "tool_input": {
          "location": "Living Room",
          "temperature": 23
      }
    },
  ]
]

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
    "predicted_trajectory": predicted_trajectory,
    "reference_trajectory": reference_trajectory,
})

docs.title: How to evaluate an agent
docs.text: Follow these steps to configure and run an agent evaluation job.

docs.title: Step 1: Define evaluation metrics
docs.text:
You can evaluate an agent based on its final output or the path it took to get there.

Evaluation Method Description Final response evaluation Evaluates the quality of the agent's final output, regardless of the steps taken. This determines if the agent achieved its goal. Trajectory evaluation Evaluates the sequence of tool calls (the path) the agent took to reach the final response. This determines if the agent followed the correct process.

With the generative AI evaluation service, you can trigger an agent execution and get metrics for both evaluation methods in a single Vertex AI SDK query.

docs.title: Final response evaluation
docs.text: Final response evaluation follows the same process as model response evaluation. For more information, see Define your evaluation metrics.

docs.title: Trajectory evaluation
docs.text:
The following metrics help you evaluate the model's ability to follow the expected trajectory.

Metric Description trajectory_exact_match Checks if the predicted trajectory is identical to the reference trajectory. trajectory_in_order_match Checks if the predicted trajectory contains all reference tool calls in the same order, allowing for extra calls. trajectory_any_order_match Checks if the predicted trajectory contains all reference tool calls, regardless of order and allowing for extra calls. trajectory_precision Measures the proportion of predicted tool calls that are relevant (i.e., also in the reference trajectory). trajectory_recall Measures the proportion of reference tool calls that were captured in the predicted trajectory. trajectory_single_tool_use Checks if a specific tool was used in the predicted trajectory. View details for trajectory evaluation metrics

trajectory_exact_match

If the predicted trajectory is identical to the reference trajectory, with the exact same tool calls in the exact same order, this metric returns a score of 1; otherwise, it returns 0.

  • Input parameters: predicted_trajectory, reference_trajectory
  • Output scores: 0 (no match), 1 (exact match)

trajectory_in_order_match

If the predicted trajectory contains all the tool calls from the reference trajectory in the same order (and may also have extra tool calls), this metric returns a score of 1; otherwise, it returns 0.

  • Input parameters: predicted_trajectory, reference_trajectory
  • Output scores: 0 (order does not match), 1 (in-order match)

trajectory_any_order_match

If the predicted trajectory contains all the tool calls from the reference trajectory, regardless of order (and may contain extra tool calls), this metric returns a score of 1; otherwise, it returns 0.

  • Input parameters: predicted_trajectory, reference_trajectory
  • Output scores: 0 (does not contain all reference tool calls), 1 (match)

trajectory_precision

This metric measures how many of the tool calls in the predicted trajectory are relevant according to the reference trajectory. It is calculated by dividing the number of matching tool calls by the total number of calls in the predicted trajectory.

  • Input parameters: predicted_trajectory, reference_trajectory
  • Output scores: A float in the range of [0, 1]. A higher score indicates higher precision.

trajectory_recall

This metric measures how many of the essential tool calls from the reference trajectory are captured in the predicted trajectory. It is calculated by dividing the number of matching tool calls by the total number of calls in the reference trajectory.

  • Input parameters: predicted_trajectory, reference_trajectory
  • Output scores: A float in the range of [0, 1]. A higher score indicates better recall.

trajectory_single_tool_use

This metric checks if a specific tool is present in the predicted trajectory. It does not check the order or frequency of tool calls.

  • Input parameters: predicted_trajectory
  • Output scores: 0 (tool is absent), 1 (tool is present)

In addition, the following two agent performance metrics are added to the evaluation results by default. You don't need to specify them in EvalTask.

  • latency: Time taken by the agent to return a response, measured in seconds.
  • failure: Indicates if the agent invocation resulted in an error (1) or succeeded (0).

docs.title: Step 2: Import your evaluation dataset
docs.text:
You can import your dataset from a JSONL or CSV file in Cloud Storage, a BigQuery table, or a Pandas DataFrame.

The generative AI evaluation service provides public datasets to demonstrate agent evaluation. The following code shows how to import an example dataset from a Cloud Storage bucket:

# dataset name to be imported
dataset = "on-device" # Alternatives: "customer-support", "content-creation"

# copy the tools and dataset file
!gcloud storage cp gs://cloud-ai-demo-datasets/agent-eval-datasets/{dataset}/tools.py .
!gcloud storage cp gs://cloud-ai-demo-datasets/agent-eval-datasets/{dataset}/eval_dataset.json .

# load the dataset examples
import json

eval_dataset = json.loads(open('eval_dataset.json').read())

# run the tools file
%run -i tools.py

The dataset variable can be one of the following:

  • "on-device": An On-Device Home Assistant that controls home devices.
  • "customer-support": A Customer Support Agent that handles orders and support tickets.
  • "content-creation": A Marketing Content Creation Agent that manages campaigns.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the evaluation
docs.text:
Run an evaluation job by defining an EvalTask. You can mix final response metrics and trajectory metrics in the same task.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

single_tool_use_metric = TrajectorySingleToolUse(tool_name='tool_name')

eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[
        "rouge_l_sum",
        "bleu",
        custom_trajectory_eval_metric, # custom computation-based metric
        "trajectory_exact_match",
        "trajectory_precision",
        single_tool_use_metric,
        response_follows_trajectory_metric # llm-based metric
    ],
)
eval_result = eval_task.evaluate(
    runnable=RUNNABLE,
)

docs.title: Metric customization
docs.text:
You can customize evaluation metrics to fit your specific needs.

View an example of a custom model-based metric

You can customize a large language model-based metric for trajectory evaluation using a templated interface or from scratch. For more details, see Model-based metrics.

from vertexai.preview.evaluation import PointwiseMetric, PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate

response_follows_trajectory_prompt_template = PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate(
    criteria={
        "Follows trajectory": (
            "Evaluate whether the agent's response logically follows from the "
            "sequence of actions it took. Consider these sub-points:\n"
            "  - Does the response reflect the information gathered during the trajectory?\n"
            "  - Is the response consistent with the goals and constraints of the task?\n"
            "  - Are there any unexpected or illogical jumps in reasoning?\n"
            "Provide specific examples from the trajectory and response to support your evaluation."
        )
    },
    rating_rubric={
        "1": "Follows trajectory",
        "0": "Does not follow trajectory",
    },
    input_variables=["prompt", "predicted_trajectory"],
)

response_follows_trajectory_metric = PointwiseMetric(
    metric="response_follows_trajectory",
    metric_prompt_template=response_follows_trajectory_prompt_template,
)
View an example of a custom computation-based metric

You can also define a custom computation-based metric for trajectory or response evaluation.

from vertexai.preview.evaluation import CustomMetric

def essential_tools_present(instance, required_tools = ["tool1", "tool2"]):
    trajectory = instance["predicted_trajectory"]
    tools_present = [tool_used['tool_name'] for tool_used in trajectory]
    if len(required_tools) == 0:
      return {"essential_tools_present": 1}
    score = 0
    for tool in required_tools:
      if tool in tools_present:
        score += 1
    return {
        "essential_tools_present": score/len(required_tools),
    }

custom_trajectory_eval_metric = CustomMetric(name="essential_tools_present", metric_function=essential_tools_present)

docs.title: Step 4: View and interpret results
docs.text:
The evaluation results are displayed in tables, separating final response metrics from trajectory metrics.

Agent evaluation results tables. Final response metrics

Instance-level results

Column Description response The final response generated by the agent. latency_in_seconds Time taken to generate the response. failure Indicates if a valid response was generated. score The score calculated for the response based on the specified metric. explanation The explanation for the score based on the specified metric.

Aggregate results

Column Description mean The average score across all instances. standard deviation The standard deviation of all scores. Trajectory metrics

Instance-level results

Column Description predicted_trajectory The sequence of tool calls the agent followed. reference_trajectory The expected sequence of tool calls. score The score calculated for the trajectory based on the specified metric. latency_in_seconds Time taken to generate the response. failure Indicates if a valid response was generated.

Aggregate results

Column Description mean The average score across all instances. standard deviation The standard deviation of all scores.

docs.title: Prepare your evaluation dataset
docs.text:
For the Generative AI evaluation service, the evaluation dataset contains the data required to assess your model's performance. This typically includes the model response you want to evaluate, the input prompt used to generate that response, and optionally, a ground truth response for comparison.

This document outlines the required schema for your dataset, the supported import formats, and provides examples for various evaluation scenarios.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Evaluation dataset: A collection of examples used to measure a model's performance, typically containing prompts, model responses, and sometimes ground truth references.
  • Ground truth: The ideal or correct response (often human-verified) against which the model's response is compared for accuracy. It is also referred to as reference.
  • Model-based metrics: Metrics that use another large language model (LLM) as a judge to score a model's response based on criteria like fluency, safety, or summarization quality.
  • Computation-based metrics: Metrics that evaluate a model's response by computing scores based on predefined rules or algorithms, such as BLEU for translation or exact match for question answering.
  • Prompt: The input text or instruction provided to a model to elicit a response.

docs.title: Evaluation dataset schema
docs.text: The structure of your evaluation dataset depends on the metrics you plan to use. The following sections describe the required input fields for different evaluation use cases.

docs.title: General use cases
docs.text:
For most model-based metrics, your dataset needs to provide the following fields:

Input field Contents prompt The user input for the generative AI model or application. This is optional in some cases. response The model's inference response that you want to evaluate. baseline_model_response (Required for pairwise metrics) The baseline model's response used for a side-by-side comparison with your model's response.

If you use the Generative AI Evaluation module of the Vertex AI SDK for Python, the service can automatically generate the response and baseline_model_response fields using the models you specify.

docs.title: Multi-turn or chat
docs.text:
For evaluating conversational models, you need to include the conversation history.

Input field Contents history The history of the conversation between the user and the model before the current turn. prompt The user input for the model in the current turn. response The model's response to be evaluated, based on the history and current prompt. baseline_model_response (Required for pairwise metrics) The baseline model's response, based on the history and current prompt.

docs.title: Computation-based metrics
docs.text:
For computation-based metrics, your dataset must include a ground truth reference to compare against the model's response.

Input field Contents response The model's inference response to be evaluated. reference The ground truth to compare your model's response to.

docs.title: Translation metrics
docs.text:
Preview

This product or feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

For translation tasks, the dataset requires the source text, the translated response, and a ground truth reference translation.

Input field Contents source The source text in the original language that the model translated from. response The model's translated response to be evaluated. reference The ground truth translation to compare your model's response to. This is in the same language as the response.

Depending on your use cases, you can also break down the input user prompt into more granular fields, such as instruction and context, and assemble them for inference by providing a prompt template.

Input field Contents instruction The part of the prompt that contains the instruction for the model (e.g., "Please summarize the following text"). context The part of the prompt that contains the content for the model to process (e.g., the article to be summarized). reference The ground truth to compare your model's response to.

The required inputs for the evaluation dataset must be consistent with your metrics. For more details, see Define your evaluation metrics and Run evaluation and Adapt a metric prompt template to your input data.

docs.title: Supported dataset formats
docs.text:
You can provide your evaluation dataset in one of the following formats. Choose the format that best suits your workflow and data source.

Format Best for JSONL or CSV in Cloud Storage Large, static datasets that are already stored or can be easily uploaded to Cloud Storage. This is a scalable and cost-effective option for production workflows. BigQuery table Very large datasets (terabytes or more) that are already part of your data warehouse in BigQuery. This format is ideal for leveraging existing data infrastructure and complex queries. Pandas DataFrame In-memory datasets used in interactive environments like Jupyter notebooks. This is convenient for experimentation, rapid prototyping, and smaller datasets that fit in memory.

docs.title: Evaluation dataset examples
docs.text:
This section provides dataset examples using the Pandas DataFrame format. While only a few records are shown for illustration, a typical evaluation dataset should contain at least 100 examples for statistically meaningful results.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Pointwise model-basedPairwise model-basedComputation-basedTranslation

The following summarization example demonstrates a sample dataset for pointwise model-based metrics.

import pandas as pd

prompts = [
    # Example 1
    (
        "Summarize the text in one sentence: As part of a comprehensive"
        " initiative to tackle urban congestion and foster sustainable urban"
        " living, a major city has revealed ambitious plans for an extensive"
        " overhaul of its public transportation system. The project aims not"
        " only to improve the efficiency and reliability of public transit but"
        " also to reduce the city's carbon footprint and promote eco-friendly"
        " commuting options. City officials anticipate that this strategic"
        " investment will enhance accessibility for residents and visitors"
        " alike, ushering in a new era of efficient, environmentally conscious"
        " urban transportation."
    ),
    # Example 2
    (
        "Summarize the text such that a five-year-old can understand: A team of"
        " archaeologists has unearthed ancient artifacts shedding light on a"
        " previously unknown civilization. The findings challenge existing"
        " historical narratives and provide valuable insights into human"
        " history."
    ),
]

responses = [
    # Example 1
    (
        "A major city is revamping its public transportation system to fight"
        " congestion, reduce emissions, and make getting around greener and"
        " easier."
    ),
    # Example 2
    (
        "Some people who dig for old things found some very special tools and"
        " objects that tell us about people who lived a long, long time ago!"
        " What they found is like a new puzzle piece that helps us understand"
        " how people used to live."
    ),
]

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
    "prompt": prompts,
    "response": responses,
})

The following open-book question-answering example demonstrates a sample dataset for pairwise model-based metrics, which requires a baseline_model_response for comparison.

import pandas as pd

prompts = [
    # Example 1
    (
        "Based on the context provided, what is the hardest material? Context:"
        " Some might think that steel is the hardest material, or even"
        " titanium. However, diamond is actually the hardest material."
    ),
    # Example 2
    (
        "Based on the context provided, who directed The Godfather? Context:"
        " Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola co-wrote the screenplay for The"
        " Godfather, and the latter directed it as well."
    ),
]

responses = [
    # Example 1
    "Diamond is the hardest material. It is harder than steel or titanium.",
    # Example 2
    "Francis Ford Coppola directed The Godfather.",
]

baseline_model_responses = [
    # Example 1
    "Steel is the hardest material.",
    # Example 2
    "John Smith.",
]

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame(
  {
    "prompt":  prompts,
    "response":  responses,
    "baseline_model_response": baseline_model_responses,
  }
)

For computation-based metrics, a reference (ground truth) field is required.

import pandas as pd

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
  "response": ["The Roman Senate was filled with exuberance due to Pompey's defeat in Asia."],
  "reference": ["The Roman Senate was filled with exuberance due to successes against Catiline."],
})

Tool-use (function calling) metrics

The following example shows input data for computation-based tool-use metrics.

import pandas as pd

json_responses = ["""{
    "content": "",
    "tool_calls":[{
      "name":"get_movie_info",
      "arguments": {"movie":"Mission Impossible", "time": "today 7:30PM"}
    }]
  }"""]

json_references = ["""{
    "content": "",
    "tool_calls":[{
      "name":"book_tickets",
      "arguments":{"movie":"Mission Impossible", "time": "today 7:30PM"}
      }]
  }"""]

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
    "response": json_responses,
    "reference": json_references,
})

Preview

This product or feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

The following example shows input data for translation metrics, which requires source, response, and reference fields.

import pandas as pd

source = [
    "Dem Feuer konnte Einhalt geboten werden",
    "Schulen und Kindergärten wurden eröffnet.",
]

response = [
    "The fire could be stopped",
    "Schools and kindergartens were open",
]

reference = [
    "They were able to control the fire.",
    "Schools and kindergartens opened",
]

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
    "source": source,
    "response": response,
    "reference": reference,
})

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
Follow these best practices when creating your evaluation dataset:

  • Provide representative examples: Your dataset should include examples that reflect the types of inputs your model will process in a production environment.
  • Ensure sufficient size: Your dataset must include at least one evaluation example. We recommend around 100 examples to ensure high-quality aggregated metrics and statistically significant results. A larger dataset helps establish higher confidence in the evaluation results, minimizes the influence of outliers, and ensures that the performance metrics reflect the model's true capabilities. The quality of aggregated metrics tends to plateau when more than 400 examples are provided.

docs.title: Gen AI evaluation service overview
docs.text:
Note: Vertex AI provides model evaluation metrics for both predictive AI and generative AI models. This page provides an overview of the evaluation service for generative AI models. To evaluate a predictive AI model, see Model evaluation in Vertex AI.

The Gen AI evaluation service in Vertex AI lets you evaluate any generative model or application and benchmark the evaluation results against your own judgment, using your own evaluation criteria.

While leaderboards and reports offer insights into overall model performance, they don't reveal how a model handles your specific needs. The Gen AI evaluation service helps you define your own evaluation criteria, ensuring a clear understanding of how well generative AI models and applications align with your unique use case.

Evaluation is important at every step of your Gen AI development process, including model selection, prompt engineering, and model customization. The Gen AI evaluation service is integrated within Vertex AI to help you launch and reuse evaluations as needed.

docs.title: Gen AI evaluation service capabilities
docs.text:
The Gen AI evaluation service can help you with the following tasks:

  • Model selection: Choose the best pre-trained model for your task based on benchmark results and its performance on your specific data.
  • Generation settings: Tweak model parameters (like temperature) to optimize output for your needs.
  • Prompt engineering: Craft effective prompts and prompt templates to guide the model towards your preferred behavior and responses.
  • Improve and safeguard fine-tuning: Fine-tune a model to improve performance for your use case, while avoiding biases or undesirable behaviors.
  • RAG optimization: Select the most effective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture to enhance performance for your application.
  • Migration: Continuously assess and improve the performance of your AI solution by migrating to newer models when they provide a clear advantage for your specific use case.
  • Translation (Preview): Assess the quality of your model's translations.
  • Evaluate agents: Evaluate the performance of your agents using the Gen AI evaluation service.
Concepts
  • EvalTask: A reusable evaluation configuration in Vertex AI that defines the metrics, model, and dataset for an evaluation job.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): A technique that enhances large language model (LLM) responses by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge base and providing it as context to the model.
  • MetricX: A family of model-based evaluation metrics developed by Google for assessing the quality of text generation, including translation.
  • COMET: A neural framework for training multilingual machine translation evaluation models that provides high-quality, human-level assessments.

docs.title: Evaluation process
docs.text:
The Gen AI evaluation service lets you evaluate any Gen AI model or application on your evaluation criteria. The following diagram shows the workflow for using the Gen AI evaluation service.

flowchart TD
    A["Define evaluation metrics"] --> B["Prepare your evaluation dataset"]
    B --> C["Run an evaluation"]
    C --> D["View and interpret your evaluation results"]
    D --> E["(Optional) Evaluate the judge model"]
    E --> F["(Optional) Evaluate generative AI agents"]

    click A "#define-evaluation-metrics"
    click B "#prepare-your-evaluation-dataset"
    click C "#run-an-evaluation"
    click D "#view-and-interpret-your-evaluation-results"
    click E "#evaluate-the-judge-model"
    click F "#evaluate-generative-ai-agents"
Steps in the evaluation process

1. Define evaluation metrics

  • Learn how to tailor model-based metrics to your business criteria.
  • Evaluate a single model (pointwise) or determine the winner when comparing two models (pairwise).
  • Include computation-based metrics for additional insights.

2. Prepare your evaluation dataset

  • Provide a dataset that reflects your specific use case.

3. Run an evaluation

  • Start from scratch, use a template, or adapt existing examples.
  • Define candidate models and create an EvalTask to reuse your evaluation logic through Vertex AI.

4. View and interpret your evaluation results

5. (Optional) Evaluate and improve the quality of the judge model

  • Evaluate the judge model.
  • Use advanced prompt engineering techniques for judge model customization.
  • Use system instructions and judge model configurations to improve evaluation results consistency and reduce judge model bias.

6. (Optional) Evaluate generative AI agents

docs.title: Tutorial: Perform evaluation using the Python SDK
docs.text:
This tutorial shows you how to perform a model-based evaluation with the online evaluation service using the Vertex AI SDK for Python.

You can also run this tutorial as a Jupyter notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab Open in Colab Enterprise Open in Vertex AI Workbench View on GitHub

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • PointwiseMetric: Defines a custom evaluation metric based on specified criteria and a rating rubric.
  • EvalTask: Encapsulates the entire evaluation job, including the dataset, metrics, and experiment details.
  • ExperimentRun: Represents a specific execution of an evaluation task, which is logged as a run within a Vertex AI Experiment.
Prerequisites

  1. Set up your Google Cloud project:

    • Sign in to your Google Cloud account. If you're new to Google Cloud, create an account to evaluate how our products perform in real-world scenarios.
    • In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project. > Note: If you don't plan to keep the resources that you create in this procedure, create a project instead of selecting an existing project. After you finish these steps, you can delete the project, removing all resources associated with the project.
    • Go to project selector
    • Make sure that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.

  2. Install the Vertex AI SDK: Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python with the generative AI evaluation service dependency. 

    !pip install google-cloud-aiplatform[evaluation]

  3. Authenticate to Vertex AI: Set up your credentials. If you are running this quickstart in Colaboratory, run the following command: 

    from google.colab import auth
auth.authenticate_user()
    For other environments, refer to Authenticate to Vertex AI.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Perform evaluation
docs.text:
The following workflow diagram outlines the steps to perform a model evaluation using the Python SDK.

flowchart TD
    A["Import libraries and initialize Vertex AI"] --> B["Set up evaluation metrics"]
    B --> C["Prepare your dataset"]
    C --> D["Run the evaluation and view results"]
    D --> E["Clean up resources"]

click A "#import-libraries"
click B "#set-up-metrics"
click C "#prepare-dataset"
click D "#run-evaluation"
click E "#clean-up"
Tutorial: Evaluate a model with the Python SDK

Import libraries and initialize Vertex AI

Import the necessary libraries and initialize the Vertex AI SDK with your project ID and location. The EXPERIMENT_NAME is used to log the evaluation run.

import pandas as pd

import vertexai
from vertexai.evaluation import EvalTask, PointwiseMetric, PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate
from google.cloud import aiplatform

PROJECT_ID = "PROJECT_ID"
LOCATION = "LOCATION"
EXPERIMENT_NAME = "EXPERIMENT_NAME"

vertexai.init(
    project=PROJECT_ID,
    location=LOCATION,
)
Note that EXPERIMENT_NAME can only contain lowercase alphanumeric characters and hyphens, up to a maximum of 127 characters.

Set up evaluation metrics

Define your evaluation metric based on custom criteria. The following example defines a metric called custom_text_quality that evaluates generated text based on Fluency and Entertaining criteria, with a corresponding rating rubric.

custom_text_quality = PointwiseMetric(
    metric="custom_text_quality",
    metric_prompt_template=PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate(
        criteria={
            "fluency": (
                "Sentences flow smoothly and are easy to read, avoiding awkward"
                " phrasing or run-on sentences. Ideas and sentences connect"
                " logically, using transitions effectively where needed."
            ),
            "entertaining": (
                "Short, amusing text that incorporates emojis, exclamations and"
                " questions to convey quick and spontaneous communication and"
                " diversion."
            ),
        },
        rating_rubric={
            "1": "The response performs well on both criteria.",
            "0": "The response is somewhat aligned with both criteria",
            "-1": "The response falls short on both criteria",
        },
    ),
)

Prepare your dataset

Create a Pandas DataFrame containing the model responses you want to evaluate.

responses = [
    # An example of good custom_text_quality
    "Life is a rollercoaster, full of ups and downs, but it's the thrill that keeps us coming back for more!",
    # An example of medium custom_text_quality
    "The weather is nice today, not too hot, not too cold.",
    # An example of poor custom_text_quality
    "The weather is, you know, whatever.",
]

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
    "response" : responses,
})

Run the evaluation and view results

Create an EvalTask with your dataset and metrics, then run the evaluation.

eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=eval_dataset,
    metrics=[custom_text_quality],
    experiment=EXPERIMENT_NAME
)

pointwise_result = eval_task.evaluate()

View the evaluation results for each response in the metrics_table Pandas DataFrame.

pointwise_result.metrics_table

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Clean up resources

To avoid incurring charges to your Google Cloud account for the resources used in this tutorial, delete the ExperimentRun created by the evaluation.

aiplatform.ExperimentRun(
    run_name=pointwise_result.metadata["experiment_run"],
    experiment=pointwise_result.metadata["experiment"],
).delete()

docs.title: Prepare supervised fine-tuning data for Gemini models
docs.text: This document describes how to prepare and format a supervised fine-tuning dataset for a Gemini model.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts and prerequisites

Concepts

  • Supervised fine-tuning: A process of updating a pre-trained model's weights by providing it with a labeled dataset of examples that are specific to a desired task or domain.
  • JSON Lines (JSONL): A text format for storing structured data where each line is a valid JSON object, separated by newlines.
  • Multi-turn conversation: A conversational exchange that includes multiple back-and-forth messages between a user and a model, maintaining context across turns.
  • System instruction: A directive given to the model to guide its behavior and steer its responses toward a specific style or format.

Prerequisites

  • Ensure you have a Cloud Storage bucket in your Google Cloud project to store your dataset files. For more information, see Create a Cloud Storage bucket.

Limitations

For limitations on datasets, such as maximum input and output tokens, maximum validation dataset size, and maximum training dataset file size, see About supervised fine-tuning for Gemini models.

docs.title: Data preparation workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the workflow for preparing your supervised fine-tuning data.

flowchart TD
    A["Step 1: Understand dataset requirements"] --> B["Step 2: Choose and format your dataset"]
    B --> C["Step 3: Upload the dataset to Cloud Storage"]

    click A "#step-1-understand-dataset-requirements"
    click B "#step-2-choose-and-format-your-dataset"
    click C "#step-3-upload-the-dataset-to-cloud-storage"

docs.title: Step 1: Understand dataset requirements
docs.text:
A supervised fine-tuning dataset is used to teach a pre-trained model a new skill. The dataset consists of examples, where each example demonstrates the desired task.

  • Training dataset: The set of examples used during the tuning process to update the model's weights. For best results, we recommend starting with 100 to 500 examples. The quality of the dataset is more important than the quantity.
  • Validation dataset: An optional but strongly recommended dataset used to measure the model's performance during and after tuning. It helps verify that the model is learning effectively and not overfitting to the training data.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose and format your dataset
docs.text:
You can provide your tuning data in one of two formats. Use the following table to help you decide which format is best for your use case.

Format Description Use Case JSON Lines (JSONL) Each line in the file is a complete JSON object representing a single tuning example. This format is ideal for text-based and conversational tuning tasks. Recommended for most text, chat, and instruction-following tuning tasks due to its simplicity and readability. Vertex AI Multimodal Dataset A managed dataset resource in Vertex AI that can contain various data types, including images, text, and video. Recommended for tuning with non-text data types, such as images. For more information, see Multimodal datasets.

This guide focuses on the JSONL format.

docs.title: Create a JSONL dataset
docs.text:
Each line in your JSONL file must be a JSON object containing a messages array. The messages array holds the conversational exchange for a single example.

  • The messages field consists of an array of role-content pairs.
  • The role can be system, user, or model.
    • The system role is optional and provides high-level instructions or context for the model. It can only appear as the first message in the array.
    • The user and model roles are required and must alternate. A conversation always starts with a user message (after the optional system message) and is followed by a model message.
  • The content field contains the text of the message.

For each example, the maximum token length for all messages combined is 131,072 tokens. Additionally, the content for each model message must not exceed 8,192 tokens.

View a JSONL data example

Here is an example of a JSONL file with two tuning examples. The first example is a simple question-and-answer pair, and the second is a multi-turn conversation.

{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "What is the official name of the Gemini model for enterprise customers?"
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "content": "The official name is Gemini on Vertex AI."
    }
  ]
}
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "system",
      "content": "You are a friendly and helpful chatbot that provides concise and accurate answers."
    },
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "What are the main benefits of using Google Cloud?"
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "content": "Google Cloud offers several benefits, including scalability, a global network, cutting-edge security, and powerful data analytics and machine learning services."
    },
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Can you elaborate on the security benefits?"
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "content": "Certainly. Google Cloud protects your data, applications, and infrastructure with a multi-layered security approach that leverages Google's global infrastructure and security experts. This includes features like data encryption at rest and in transit, identity and access management, and advanced threat detection."
    }
  ]
}

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Follow data creation best practices
docs.text:
To get the best performance from your tuned model, follow these best practices when creating your dataset.

  • Maintain consistency with production data: The examples in your dataset should match the formatting and style of your expected production traffic. For example, if your dataset examples include a question: prefix, your production prompts should also include that prefix.
  • Follow prompt design best practices: The user content in your examples should follow the best practices for prompt design. Provide clear and detailed instructions for the task you want the model to perform. For more information, see Introduction to prompt design.

docs.title: Step 3: Upload the dataset to Cloud Storage
docs.text:
To run a tuning job, you must upload your dataset file to a Cloud Storage bucket. The region of the bucket doesn't matter, but we recommend using a bucket that is in the same Google Cloud project where you plan to tune your model.

After your bucket is ready, upload your JSONL dataset file to the bucket.
