docs.title: Run an evaluation with the Vertex AI SDK
docs.text: To make fair comparisons between generative models, you typically need to repeatedly evaluate various models and prompt templates against a fixed evaluation dataset using specific metrics.

docs.title: Instantiate the EvalTask class
docs.text:
The EvalTask class helps you evaluate models and applications based on specific tasks. It also integrates with Vertex AI Experiments to help you track configurations and results for each evaluation run, empowering you to make informed decisions.

The following example demonstrates how to instantiate the EvalTask class and run an evaluation:

from vertexai.evaluation import (
    EvalTask,
    PairwiseMetric,
    PairwiseMetricPromptTemplate,
    PointwiseMetric,
    PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate,
    MetricPromptTemplateExamples，
)

eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=DATASET,
    metrics=[METRIC_1, METRIC_2, METRIC_3],
    experiment=EXPERIMENT_NAME,
)

eval_result = eval_task.evaluate(
    model=MODEL,
    prompt_template=PROMPT_TEMPLATE,
    experiment_run=EXPERIMENT_RUN,
)

docs.title: Run evaluation with model-based metrics
docs.text:
For model-based metrics, use the PointwiseMetric and PairwiseMetric classes to define metrics tailored to your specific criteria. The following table compares the different methods for defining model-based metrics.

Method Description Best for Use existing examples Use pre-defined metric templates for common use cases like fluency or safety. Quickly evaluating standard text quality attributes without writing custom prompts. Use a templated interface Customize pre-defined templates by providing your own criteria and rating rubrics. Tailoring evaluations to specific needs while leveraging a structured template. Use a free-form interface Define a completely custom metric by writing your own prompt template from scratch. Maximum flexibility for complex or unique evaluation scenarios. Use existing examplesUse a templated interfaceUse a free-form interface

You can directly use the built-in constant Metric Prompt Template Examples within the Vertex AI SDK. Alternatively, you can modify and incorporate them in the free-form metric definition interface. For the full list of Metric Prompt Template Examples, see Metric prompt templates.

ConsoleVertex AI SDK

When you're running evaluations in a Colab Enterprise notebook, you can access metric prompt templates from directly within the Google Cloud console.

  1. Click the link for your preferred Gen AI evaluation service notebook.
  2. The notebook opens in GitHub. Click Open in Colab Enterprise. If a dialog asks you to enable APIs, click Enable.
  3. Click the Gen AI Evaluation icon in the sidebar. A Pre-built metric templates panel opens.
  4. Select Pointwise or Pairwise metrics.
  5. Click the metric you want to use, such as Fluency. The code sample for the metric appears.
  6. Click Copy to copy the code sample. Optionally, click Customize to change pre-set fields for the metric.
  7. Paste the code sample into your notebook.

The following Vertex AI SDK example shows how to use the MetricPromptTemplateExamples class to define your metrics:

# View all the available examples of model-based metrics
MetricPromptTemplateExamples.list_example_metric_names()

# Display the metric prompt template of a specific example metric
print(MetricPromptTemplateExamples.get_prompt_template('fluency'))

# Use the pre-defined model-based metrics directly
eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[MetricPromptTemplateExamples.Pointwise.FLUENCY],
)

eval_result = eval_task.evaluate(
    model=MODEL,
)

Customize your metrics by populating fields like Criteria and Rating Rubrics using the PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate and PairwiseMetricPromptTemplate classes within the Vertex AI SDK. Certain fields, such as Instruction, are assigned a default value if you don't provide input.

Optionally, you can specify input_variables, which is a list of input fields used by the metric prompt template to generate model-based evaluation results. By default, the model's response column is included for pointwise metrics, and both the candidate model's response and baseline_model_response columns are included for pairwise metrics.

For additional information, refer to the "Structure a metric prompt template" section in Metric prompt templates.

# Define a pointwise metric with two custom criteria
custom_text_quality = PointwiseMetric(
    metric="custom_text_quality",
    metric_prompt_template=PointwiseMetricPromptTemplate(
        criteria={
          "fluency": "Sentences flow smoothly and are easy to read, avoiding awkward phrasing or run-on sentences. Ideas and sentences connect logically, using transitions effectively where needed.",
          "entertaining": "Short, amusing text that incorporates emojis, exclamations and questions to convey quick and spontaneous communication and diversion.",
        },
        rating_rubric={
          "1": "The response performs well on both criteria.",
          "0": "The response is somewhat aligned with both criteria",
          "-1": "The response falls short on both criteria",
        },
        input_variables=["prompt"],
    ),
)

# Display the serialized metric prompt template
print(custom_text_quality.metric_prompt_template)

# Run evaluation using the custom_text_quality metric
eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[custom_text_quality],
)
eval_result = eval_task.evaluate(
    model=MODEL,
)

For more flexibility in customizing the metric prompt template, you can define a metric directly using the free-form interface, which accepts a direct string input.

# Define a pointwise multi-turn chat quality metric
pointwise_chat_quality_metric_prompt = """Evaluate the AI's contribution to a meaningful conversation, considering coherence, fluency, groundedness, and conciseness.
 Review the chat history for context. Rate the response on a 1-5 scale, with explanations for each criterion and its overall impact.

# Conversation History
{history}

# Current User Prompt
{prompt}

# AI-generated Response
{response}
"""

freeform_multi_turn_chat_quality_metric = PointwiseMetric(
    metric="multi_turn_chat_quality_metric",
    metric_prompt_template=pointwise_chat_quality_metric_prompt,
)

# Run evaluation using the freeform_multi_turn_chat_quality_metric metric
eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=[freeform_multi_turn_chat_quality_metric],
)
eval_result = eval_task.evaluate(
    model=MODEL,
)

docs.title: Evaluate a translation model (Preview)
docs.text:
Preview

This product or feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

To evaluate your translation model, you can specify BLEU, MetricX, or COMET as evaluation metrics when using the Vertex AI SDK.

#Prepare the dataset for evaluation.
sources = [
    "Dem Feuer konnte Einhalt geboten werden",
    "Schulen und Kindergärten wurden eröffnet.",
]

responses = [
    "The fire could be stopped",
    "Schools and kindergartens were open",
]

references = [
    "They were able to control the fire.",
    "Schools and kindergartens opened",
]

eval_dataset = pd.DataFrame({
    "source": sources,
    "response": responses,
    "reference": references,
})

# Set the metrics.

metrics = [
    "bleu",
    pointwise_metric.Comet(),
    pointwise_metric.MetricX(),
]

eval_task = evaluation.EvalTask(
    dataset=eval_dataset,
    metrics=metrics,
)
eval_result = eval_task.evaluate()

docs.title: Run evaluation with computation-based metrics
docs.text:
You can use computation-based metrics standalone, or together with model-based metrics.

# Combine computation-based metrics "ROUGE" and "BLEU" with model-based metrics
eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=EVAL_DATASET,
    metrics=["rouge_l_sum", "bleu", custom_text_quality],
)
eval_result = eval_task.evaluate(
    model=MODEL,
)

docs.title: Run evaluations at scale with the REST API (Preview)
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

If you have large evaluation datasets or periodically run evaluations in a production environment, you can use the EvaluateDataset API in the Gen AI evaluation service to run evaluations at scale.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_NUMBER: Your project number.
  • DATASET_URI: The Cloud Storage path to a JSONL file that contains evaluation instances. Each line in the file should represent a single instance, with keys corresponding to user-defined input fields in the metric_prompt_template (for model-based metrics) or required input parameters (for computation-based metrics). You can only specify one JSONL file. The following example is a line for a pointwise evaluation instance: {"response": "The Roman Senate was filled with exuberance due to Pompey's defeat in Asia."}
  • METRIC_SPEC: One or more metric specs you are using for evaluation. You can use the following metric specs when running evaluations at scale: "pointwise_metric_spec", "pairwise_metric_spec", "exact_match_spec", "bleu_spec", and "rouge_spec".
  • METRIC_SPEC_FIELD_NAME: The required fields for your chosen metric spec. For example, "metric_prompt_template"
  • METRIC_SPEC_FIELD_CONTENT: The field content for your chosen metric spec. For example, you can use the following field content for a pointwise evaluation: "Evaluate the fluency of this sentence: {response}. Give score from 0 to 1\. 0 - not fluent at all. 1 - very fluent."
  • OUTPUT_BUCKET: The name of the Cloud Storage bucket where you want to store evaluation results.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/us-central1/evaluateDataset

Request JSON body:

{
  "dataset": {
    "gcs_source": {
      "uris": "DATASET_URI"
    }
  },
  "metrics": [
    {
      METRIC_SPEC: {
        METRIC_SPEC_FIELD_NAME: METRIC_SPEC_FIELD_CONTENT
      }
    }
  ],
  "output_config": {
    "gcs_destination": {
      "output_uri_prefix": "OUTPUT_BUCKET"
    }
  }
}

To send your request, choose one of these options:

curlPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login , or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI . You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \  
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \  
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \  
     -d @request.json \  
     "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/us-central1/evaluateDataset"

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login . You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token  
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }  

Invoke-WebRequest `  
    -Method POST `  
    -Headers $headers `  
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `  
    -InFile request.json `  
    -Uri "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/us-central1/evaluateDataset" | Select-Object -Expand Content

You should receive a JSON response similar to the following.

Response

{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/us-central1/operations/OPERATION_ID",
  "metadata": {
    "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.cloud.aiplatform.v1beta1.EvaluateDatasetOperationMetadata",
    "genericMetadata": {
      "createTime": CREATE_TIME,
      "updateTime": UPDATE_TIME
    }
  },
  "done": true,
  "response": {
    "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.cloud.aiplatform.v1beta1.EvaluateDatasetResponse",
    "outputInfo": {
      "gcsOutputDirectory": "gs://OUTPUT_BUCKET/evaluation_GENERATION_TIME"
    }
  }
}

You can use the OPERATION_ID you receive in the response to request the status of the evaluation:

curl -X GET \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer "$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token) \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
  "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/us-central1/operations/OPERATION_ID"

docs.title: Increase rate limits and quota
docs.text:
A single evaluation request for a model-based metric results in multiple underlying requests to the Gemini API in Vertex AI and consumes quota for the judge model. You should set a higher evaluation service rate limit in the following use cases:

  • Increased data volume: If you're processing significantly more data using the model-based metrics, you might hit the default requests per minute (RPM) quota.
  • Faster evaluation: If your application requires quicker turnaround time for evaluations, you might need a higher RPM quota.
  • Complex evaluation tasks: A higher RPM quota ensures you have enough capacity to handle resource-intensive evaluations for complex tasks or large amounts of text.
  • High user concurrency: If you anticipate a large number of users simultaneously requesting model-based evaluations and model inference within your project, a higher model RPM limit is crucial.

If you're using the default judge model of gemini-2.0-flash or newer models, we recommend that you use Provisioned Throughput to manage your quota.

For models older than gemini-2.0-flash, use the following instructions to increase the judge model RPM quota:

View steps to increase judge model RPM quota

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the IAM & Admin Quotas page.

    View Quotas in Console

  2. In the Filter field, specify the Dimension (model identifier) and the Metric (quota identifier for Gemini models): base_model:gemini-2.0-flash and Metric:aiplatform.googleapis.com/generate_content_requests_per_minute_per_project_per_base_model.

  3. For the quota that you want to increase, click the more actions menu more_vert button.
  4. In the drop-down menu, click Edit quota. The Quota changes panel opens.
  5. Under Edit quota , enter a new quota value.
  6. Click Submit request.
  7. A Quota Increase Request (QIR) is confirmed by email and typically takes two business days to process.

To run an evaluation using a new quota, set the evaluation_service_qps parameter as follows:

from vertexai.evaluation import EvalTask

# GEMINI_RPM is the requests per minute (RPM) quota for gemini-2.0-flash-001 in your region
# Evaluation Service QPS limit is equal to (gemini-2.0-flash-001 RPM / 60 sec / default number of samples)
CUSTOM_EVAL_SERVICE_QPS_LIMIT = GEMINI_RPM / 60 / 4

eval_task = EvalTask(
    dataset=DATASET,
    metrics=[METRIC_1, METRIC_2, METRIC_3],
)

eval_result = eval_task.evaluate(
    evaluation_service_qps=CUSTOM_EVAL_SERVICE_QPS_LIMIT,
    # Specify a retry_timeout limit for a more responsive evaluation run
    # the default value is 600 (in seconds, or 10 minutes)
    retry_timeout=RETRY_TIMEOUT,
)

For more information about quotas and limits, see Gen AI evaluation service quotas, and Gen AI evaluation service API.

docs.title: Run AutoSxS pipeline to perform pairwise model-based evaluation
docs.text:
Note: For the most updated pairwise model-based evaluation features, see Define your metrics.

This page introduces how to perform pairwise model-based evaluation using AutoSxS, a tool that runs through the evaluation pipeline service. It explains how to use AutoSxS through the Vertex AI API, the Vertex AI SDK for Python, or the Google Cloud console.

docs.title: What is AutoSxS?
docs.text:
Automatic side-by-side (AutoSxS) is a pairwise model-based evaluation tool that uses an autorater to compare the performance of two generative AI models. You can use AutoSxS to evaluate models in the Vertex AI Model Registry or models with pre-generated predictions. This allows AutoSxS to support Vertex AI foundation models, tuned models, and third-party language models.

The autorater is a powerful language model that acts as a human rater, judging the quality of model responses based on a given prompt and a set of evaluation criteria. It determines which model provides a better response and outputs preferences, explanations, and confidence scores.

At a high level, AutoSxS compares the predictions of Model A and Model B using the autorater.

Figure 1. High-level overview of the AutoSxS workflow.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Pairwise model-based evaluation: A method of comparing two models by having a human or an AI-based "autorater" choose the better of two responses to the same prompt.
  • AutoSxS: An automatic, on-demand implementation of pairwise model-based evaluation that uses an AI-based autorater.
  • Autorater: A language model that judges the quality of model responses based on predefined criteria for a specific task.
  • Evaluation dataset: A set of prompts and optional context that are used to test the models. It can be a BigQuery table or a JSON Lines file in Cloud Storage.
  • Prompt parameters: Templated inputs that allow you to flexibly define how data from your evaluation dataset is used to prompt the models and the autorater.
Set up your project

To run the AutoSxS pipeline, you must grant the necessary Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles to the following service accounts.

Core Service Account Permissions

Service account Default principal Description Roles Vertex AI Service Agent service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com The Vertex AI Service Agent is automatically provisioned for your project. If an organization policy modifies its default permissions, you must manually grant the required role. Vertex AI Service Agent (roles/aiplatform.serviceAgent) Vertex AI Pipelines Service Account PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com The service account that runs the pipeline. The Compute Engine default service account is used by default, but you can specify a custom service account.
  • Vertex AI User (roles/aiplatform.user)
  • Storage Object User (roles/storage.objectUser)

Data Source Permissions

Depending on your input and output data sources, you may also need to grant additional roles to the Vertex AI Pipelines Service Account:

Data source Role(s) to grant Where to grant the role(s) Standard BigQuery table BigQuery Data EditorBigQuery Data Viewer Project running the pipelineProject where the table belongs BigQuery view BigQuery Data EditorBigQuery Data Viewer Project running the pipelineProject where the view and underlying table belong BigQuery external table (with Cloud Storage source) BigQuery Data EditorBigQuery Data ViewerStorage Object Viewer Project running the pipelineProject where the external table belongsProject where the source file belongs Cloud Storage file BigQuery Data Viewer Project running the pipeline

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
AutoSxS supports the evaluation of any model when you provide pre-generated predictions. It also supports automatically generating responses for any text model in the Vertex AI Model Registry that supports batch prediction.

If your text model is not in the Model Registry, you can provide pre-generated predictions stored as a JSONL file in Cloud Storage or in a BigQuery table. For pricing information on response generation, see Text generation pricing.

docs.title: Supported tasks and criteria
docs.text:
AutoSxS supports evaluating models for summarization and question-answering tasks. The evaluation criteria are predefined for each task to make the evaluation more objective and improve response quality.

Summarization

The summarization task has a 4,096 input token limit.

Criteria Description Follows instructions To what extent does the model's response demonstrate an understanding of the instruction from the prompt? Grounded Does the response include only information from the inference context and inference instruction? Comprehensive To what extent does the model capture key details in the summarization? Brief Is the summarization verbose? Does it include flowery language? Is it overly terse?

Question Answering

The question_answering task has a 4,096 input token limit.

Criteria Description Fully answers the question The answer responds to the question completely. Grounded Does the response include only information from the instruction context and inference instruction? Relevance Does the content of the answer relate to the question? Comprehensive To what extent does the model capture key details in the question?

docs.title: Evaluation dataset and predictions
docs.text: This section details the data you should provide in your AutoSxS evaluation dataset and best practices for dataset construction.

docs.title: Dataset format
docs.text:
AutoSxS accepts a single evaluation dataset with a flexible schema. The dataset can be a BigQuery table or stored as JSON Lines in Cloud Storage. Each row represents a single example, and the columns can be one of the following:

  • ID columns: Used to identify each unique example.
  • Data columns: Used to fill out prompt templates.
  • Pre-generated predictions: Responses generated by a model for a given prompt. Using pre-generated predictions saves time and resources.
  • Ground-truth human preferences: Used to benchmark AutoSxS against your ground-truth data.

Here is an example evaluation dataset where context and question are data columns, and model_b_response contains pre-generated predictions for one of the models.

context question model_b_response Some might think that steel is the hardest material or titanium, but diamond is actually the hardest material. What is the hardest material? Diamond is the hardest material. It is harder than steel or titanium.

docs.title: Prompt parameters
docs.text:
Many language models take multiple prompt parameters as input. For example, chat-bison takes messages, examples, and context, while text-bison takes a single prompt parameter. AutoSxS provides flexibility to specify these parameters using templates.

You can map a dataset column directly to a prompt parameter:

{'some_parameter': {'column': 'my_column'}}

Alternatively, you can define a template that uses columns from your dataset as variables:

{'some_parameter': {'template': 'Summarize the following: {{ my_column }}.'}}

You can also use the protected default_instruction keyword, which is replaced with the default instruction for the given task:

model_prompt_parameters = {
        'prompt': {'template': '{{ default_instruction }}: {{ context }}'},
}

Gemini

For Gemini models, the prompt parameter keys are contents (required) and system_instruction (optional), aligning with the Gemini request body schema.

model_a_prompt_parameters={
    'contents': {
        'column': 'context'
    },
    'system_instruction': {'template': '{{ default_instruction }}'},
},

text-bison

For text-bison, the input parameter is prompt and the output is content.

model_a_prompt_parameters={
    'prompt': {
        'template': {
            'Answer the following question from the point of view of a college professor: {{ context }}\n{{ question }}'
        },
    },
},
response_column_a='content',  # Column in Model A response.
response_column_b='model_b_response',  # Column in eval dataset.

docs.title: Autorater parameters
docs.text:
The autorater also requires prompt parameters to perform its evaluation.

Autorater prompt parameter Configurable by user? Description Autorater instruction No A calibrated instruction describing the criteria the autorater should use to judge the responses. Inference instruction Yes A description of the task each candidate model should perform. Inference context Yes Additional context for the task being performed. Responses No (configured via pre-generated responses) A pair of responses to evaluate, one from each candidate model.

Here is a sample configuration for the autorater's prompt parameters:

autorater_prompt_parameters={
    'inference_instruction': {
        'template': 'Answer the following question from the point of view of a college professor: {{ question }}.'
    },
    'inference_context': {
        'column': 'context'
    }
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Provide examples that represent the types of inputs your models will process in production.
  • Your dataset must include at least one example. We recommend around 100 examples for high-quality aggregate metrics. Quality improvements tend to diminish after 400 examples.
  • For guidance on writing effective prompts, see Design text prompts.
  • If you use pre-generated predictions, include them in a column of your evaluation dataset. This is useful for comparing models not in the Vertex AI Model Registry and for reusing responses.

docs.title: Evaluation scenarios
docs.text:
AutoSxS can be configured for different evaluation scenarios depending on whether you are using models from the Vertex AI Model Registry or providing pre-generated predictions.

Scenario Model A Source Model B Source Use Case Compare two models Vertex AI Model Registry Vertex AI Model Registry Evaluate a tuned model against a reference model, with AutoSxS generating responses for both. Compare a model to predictions Vertex AI Model Registry Pre-generated predictions Evaluate a model in the registry against an external model or a previous version by providing its responses in the dataset. Compare two sets of predictions Pre-generated predictions Pre-generated predictions Evaluate two external models or benchmark the autorater against human preferences by providing all responses. Compare two modelsCompare a model to predictionsCompare two sets of predictions (Check alignment)

Figure 2. AutoSxS generates responses for both models and evaluates them.

This scenario evaluates a tuned model against a reference model, both from the Vertex AI Model Registry.

# Evaluation dataset schema:
#   my_question: str
#   my_context: str
parameters = {
    'evaluation_dataset': DATASET,
    'id_columns': ['my_context'],
    'task': 'question_answering',
    'autorater_prompt_parameters': {
      'inference_instruction': {'column': 'my_question'},
      'inference_context': {'column': 'my_context'},
  },
    'model_a': 'publishers/google/models/text-bison@002',
    'model_a_prompt_parameters': {'prompt': {'template': '{{my_question}}\nCONTEXT: {{my_context}}'}},
  'response_column_a': 'content',
    'model_b': 'projects/abc/locations/abc/models/tuned_bison',
    'model_b_prompt_parameters': {'prompt': {'template': '{{my_context}}\n{{my_question}}'}},
  'response_column_b': 'content',
}

Figure 3. AutoSxS generates responses for one model and compares them to pre-generated predictions.

This scenario evaluates a model from the registry against a set of pre-generated predictions.

# Evaluation dataset schema:
#   my_question: str
#   my_context: str
#   response_b: str

parameters = {
    'evaluation_dataset': DATASET,
    'id_columns': ['my_context'],
    'task': 'question_answering',
    'autorater_prompt_parameters': {
        'inference_instruction': {'column': 'my_question'},
        'inference_context': {'column': 'my_context'},
    },
    'model_a': 'publishers/google/models/text-bison@002',
    'model_a_prompt_parameters': {'prompt': {'template': '{{my_question}}\nCONTEXT: {{my_context}}'}},
    'response_column_a': 'content',
    'response_column_b': 'response_b',
}

Figure 4. AutoSxS evaluates two sets of pre-generated predictions without running inference.

This scenario evaluates two sets of pre-generated predictions. It is useful for comparing external models or for benchmarking AutoSxS against human-preference data by providing human judgments in the human_preference_column.

# Evaluation dataset schema:
#  my_question: str
#  my_context: str
#   response_a: str
#   response_b: str
#   actual: str
parameters = {
    'evaluation_dataset': DATASET,
    'id_columns': ['my_context'],
    'task': 'question_answering',
    'autorater_prompt_parameters': {
      'inference_instruction': {'column': 'my_question'},
      'inference_context': {'column': 'my_context'},
  },
  'response_column_a': 'response_a',
  'response_column_b': 'response_b',
  'human_preference_column': 'actual',
}

docs.title: Run an evaluation job
docs.text:
This section walks you through the process of running an AutoSxS evaluation job. You can use the REST API, the Vertex AI SDK for Python, or the Google Cloud console.

The following diagram shows the workflow for running a pairwise model-based evaluation job with AutoSxS.

flowchart TD
    A[Step 1: Prepare Evaluation Dataset] --> B[Step 2: Configure and Run Job]
    B --> C[Step 3: View Evaluation Results]

    click A "#prepare-your-evaluation-dataset"
    click B "#configure-and-run-the-job"
    click C "#view-evaluation-results"
Run an evaluation job

Step 1: Prepare your evaluation dataset

First, create your evaluation dataset as a JSONL file in Cloud Storage or as a BigQuery table. The dataset should contain prompts and any additional data required for your evaluation scenario. For more details, see Evaluation dataset and predictions.

Here is an example of a JSONL dataset for a question-answering task, which includes pre-generated predictions for Model B.

{
  "id": 1,
  "question": "What is the hardest material?",
  "context": "Some might think that steel is the hardest material, or even titanium. However, diamond is actually the hardest material.",
  "model_b_response": "Diamond is the hardest material. It is harder than steel or titanium."
}
{
  "id": 2,
  "question": "What is the highest mountain in the world?",
  "context": "K2 and Everest are the two tallest mountains, with K2 being just over 28k feet and Everest being 29k feet tall.",
  "model_b_response": "Mount Everest is the tallest mountain, with a height of 29k feet."
}
{
  "id": 3,
  "question": "Who directed The Godfather?",
  "context": "Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola co-wrote the screenplay for The Godfather, and the latter directed it as well.",
  "model_b_response": "Francis Ford Coppola directed The Godfather."
}

Step 2: Configure and run the job

Next, configure and submit the AutoSxS pipeline job. Use the following syntax to specify the path to your model:

  • Publisher model: publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL (e.g., publishers/google/models/text-bison)
  • Tuned model: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/models/MODEL@VERSION (e.g., projects/123456789012/locations/us-central1/models/1234567890123456789)

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

REST APIVertex AI SDK for PythonGoogle Cloud console

To create a model evaluation job, send a POST request using the pipelineJobs.create method.

Before using the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PIPELINEJOB_DISPLAYNAME: A display name for the pipelineJob.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • LOCATION: The region to run the pipeline components (e.g., us-central1).
  • OUTPUT_DIR: The Cloud Storage URI to store evaluation output (e.g., my-bucket/output).
  • EVALUATION_DATASET: The BigQuery table or Cloud Storage path(s) to your JSONL dataset.
  • TASK: The evaluation task (summarization or question_answering).
  • ID_COLUMNS: A list of columns that uniquely identify each example.
  • AUTORATER_PROMPT_PARAMETERS: The prompt parameters for the autorater.
  • RESPONSE_COLUMN_A: The column containing Model A's predictions.
  • RESPONSE_COLUMN_B: The column containing Model B's predictions.
  • MODEL_A (Optional): The resource name of Model A if responses are not pre-generated.
  • MODEL_B (Optional): The resource name of Model B if responses are not pre-generated.
  • MODEL_A_PROMPT_PARAMETERS (Optional): The prompt parameters for Model A.
  • MODEL_B_PROMPT_PARAMETERS (Optional): The prompt parameters for Model B.
  • JUDGMENTS_FORMAT (Optional): The format for judgments (jsonl, json, or bigquery).
  • BIGQUERY_DESTINATION_PREFIX (Optional): The BigQuery table for judgments if format is bigquery.

Request JSON body (request.json)

{
  "displayName": "PIPELINEJOB_DISPLAYNAME",
  "runtimeConfig": {
      "gcsOutputDirectory": "gs://OUTPUT_DIR",
      "parameterValues": {
          "evaluation_dataset": "EVALUATION_DATASET",
          "id_columns": ["ID_COLUMNS"],
          "task": "TASK",
          "autorater_prompt_parameters": AUTORATER_PROMPT_PARAMETERS,
          "response_column_a": "RESPONSE_COLUMN_A",
          "response_column_b": "RESPONSE_COLUMN_B",
          "model_a": "MODEL_A",
          "model_a_prompt_parameters": MODEL_A_PROMPT_PARAMETERS,
          "model_b": "MODEL_B",
          "model_b_prompt_parameters": MODEL_B_PROMPT_PARAMETERS,
          "judgments_format": "JUDGMENTS_FORMAT",
          "bigquery_destination_prefix": "BIGQUERY_DESTINATION_PREFIX"
      }
  },
  "templateUri": "https://us-kfp.pkg.dev/ml-pipeline/google-cloud-registry/autosxs-template/default"
}

curl command

curl -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
    -d @request.json \
    "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/pipelineJobs"

To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Vertex AI SDK for Python API reference.

For details on pipeline parameters, see the Google Cloud Pipeline Components reference.

Before running the code, make the following replacements:

  • PIPELINEJOB_DISPLAYNAME: A display name for the pipelineJob.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • LOCATION: The region to run the pipeline components (e.g., us-central1).
  • OUTPUT_DIR: The Cloud Storage URI to store evaluation output (e.g., my-bucket/output).
  • EVALUATION_DATASET: The BigQuery table or Cloud Storage path(s) to your JSONL dataset.
  • TASK: The evaluation task (summarization or question_answering).
  • ID_COLUMNS: A list of columns that uniquely identify each example.
  • AUTORATER_PROMPT_PARAMETERS: The prompt parameters for the autorater.
  • RESPONSE_COLUMN_A: The column containing Model A's predictions.
  • RESPONSE_COLUMN_B: The column containing Model B's predictions.
  • MODEL_A (Optional): The resource name of Model A if responses are not pre-generated.
  • MODEL_B (Optional): The resource name of Model B if responses are not pre-generated.
  • MODEL_A_PROMPT_PARAMETERS (Optional): The prompt parameters for Model A.
  • MODEL_B_PROMPT_PARAMETERS (Optional): The prompt parameters for Model B.
  • JUDGMENTS_FORMAT (Optional): The format for judgments (jsonl, json, or bigquery).
  • BIGQUERY_DESTINATION_PREFIX (Optional): The BigQuery table for judgments if format is bigquery.
import os
from google.cloud import aiplatform

parameters = {
    'evaluation_dataset': 'EVALUATION_DATASET',
    'id_columns': ['ID_COLUMNS'],
    'task': 'TASK',
    'autorater_prompt_parameters': AUTORATER_PROMPT_PARAMETERS,
    'response_column_a': 'RESPONSE_COLUMN_A',
    'response_column_b': 'RESPONSE_COLUMN_B',
    'model_a': 'MODEL_A',
    'model_a_prompt_parameters': MODEL_A_PROMPT_PARAMETERS,
    'model_b': 'MODEL_B',
    'model_b_prompt_parameters': MODEL_B_PROMPT_PARAMETERS,
    'judgments_format': 'JUDGMENTS_FORMAT',
    'bigquery_destination_prefix': BIGQUERY_DESTINATION_PREFIX,
}

aiplatform.init(project='PROJECT_ID', location='LOCATION', staging_bucket='gs://OUTPUT_DIR')

job = aiplatform.PipelineJob(
    display_name='PIPELINEJOB_DISPLAYNAME',
    pipeline_root=os.path.join('gs://OUTPUT_DIR', 'PIPELINEJOB_DISPLAYNAME'),
    template_path=(
      'https://us-kfp.pkg.dev/ml-pipeline/google-cloud-registry/autosxs-template/default'),
    parameter_values=parameters,
)

job.run()

  1. Start the evaluation flow.

    You can start from either Model Garden or the Model Registry.

    • To evaluate a Google foundation model:

      1. Go to the Vertex AI Model Garden and select a model that supports pairwise evaluation, such as text-bison. Go to Model Garden
      2. Click Evaluate.
      3. Select a model version and click Select.
      4. If prompted, save a copy of the model to the Vertex AI Model Registry.
      5. On the Create Evaluation page, for Evaluate Method, select Evaluate this model against another model.
      6. Click Continue.

    • To evaluate an existing model in the Model Registry:

      1. Go to the Vertex AI Model Registry page. Go to Vertex AI Model Registry
      2. Click the name of a model that supports pairwise evaluation.
      3. In the Evaluate tab, click SxS.
      4. Click Create SxS Evaluation.

  2. Configure the evaluation.

    Follow the steps in the evaluation creation wizard:

    1. Evaluation dataset: Select an evaluation objective, a model to compare against, your evaluation dataset, and the ID columns.
    2. Model settings: Specify whether to use pre-generated responses from your dataset or have Vertex AI generate them using batch prediction. Configure the response columns and any necessary prompt parameters.
    3. Autorater settings: Enter your autorater prompt parameters and specify an output location for the evaluation results.

  3. Start the evaluation.

    Click Start Evaluation to run the job.

Step 3: View evaluation results

After the pipeline job completes, you can find the results in Vertex AI Pipelines by inspecting the artifacts produced by the AutoSxS pipeline.

Judgments

Judgments are example-level metrics that help you understand model performance on individual prompts. They can be written to Cloud Storage (JSONL) or a BigQuery table and include inference prompts, model responses, autorater decisions, explanations, and confidence scores.

Column Description id columns Columns that distinguish unique evaluation examples. inference_instruction Instruction used to generate model responses. inference_context Context used to generate model responses. response_a Model A's response. response_b Model B's response. choice The model with the better response (Model A, Model B, or Error). confidence A score from 0 to 1 indicating the autorater's confidence in its choice. explanation The autorater's reason for its choice.

Aggregate metrics

AutoSxS calculates win-rate metrics from the judgments table.

Metric Description AutoRater model A win rate Percentage of times the autorater chose Model A's response as better. AutoRater model B win rate Percentage of times the autorater chose Model B's response as better.

Human-preference alignment metrics

If you provide human-preference data, AutoSxS also calculates alignment metrics to benchmark the autorater against human judgments. These include metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Cohen's Kappa.

To see an example of benchmarking AutoSxS against human preference data, run the following notebook:

Open in Colab Open in Colab Enterprise View on GitHub

docs.title: Prepare supervised fine-tuning data for Translation LLM models
docs.text:
This document describes how to prepare and format a dataset for supervised fine-tuning of a Translation Large Language Model (LLM).

The following workflow shows the steps to prepare your data for model tuning.

Before you begin Concepts
  • Supervised fine-tuning: The process of adapting a pre-trained model to a specific task using a labeled dataset containing many examples of that task.
  • JSON Lines (JSONL): A text format where each line is a separate, valid JSON object, used for structuring tuning data.
  • Training dataset: The data used to teach the model the desired behavior during the tuning process.
  • Validation dataset: A separate dataset used to evaluate the model's performance during tuning to prevent overfitting and measure its effectiveness.
  • Cloud Storage: Google Cloud's object storage service, used to store datasets for model tuning jobs.

Set up your project

  1. In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.
  2. Make sure that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.
  3. Enable the Vertex AI API.
  4. Create a Cloud Storage bucket to store your dataset files. For best performance, the bucket should be in the same Google Cloud project and region (us-central1) where you plan to tune your model.

docs.title: Understand data requirements
docs.text:
Your model tuning dataset must be in the JSON Lines (JSONL) format, where each line contains a single tuning example. A supervised fine-tuning dataset is used to adapt a model to a specific domain. For best results, your dataset should contain at least 100 examples.

The following table shows the requirements for training and validation datasets:

Dataset Type Description Recommendations & Limitations Training The dataset used to tune the model.
  • Recommended size: Start with 100 examples and scale up to thousands if needed. Quality is more important than quantity.
  • Max tokens: 1,000 per example (input + output).
  • Max file size: 1 GB.
Validation (Strongly recommended) The dataset used to measure the effectiveness of the tuning job.
  • Max examples: 1,024.
  • Max tokens: 1,000 per example (input + output).
  • Max file size: 1 GB.

docs.title: Data format schema
docs.text:
Each JSONL object in your dataset represents a single training example and must have a contents field.

  • contents: (Required) An array of Content objects that represent the conversation history.
    • role: (Required) The author of the message. Supported values are:
      • user: The message is from the user.
      • model: The message is a response from the model.
    • parts: (Required) An array of Part objects that make up the message.
      • text: (Required) The text content of the message, such as a prompt or a response.

docs.title: Data format example
docs.text:
The following example shows a single data point in a JSONL file for tuning a translation model.

{
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "English: Hello. Spanish:"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "Hola."
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: About supervised fine-tuning for Translation LLM models
docs.text:
Preview

Supervised fine-tuning for translation-llm-002 is in Preview. While tuning is in Preview, there is no charge to tune a model or to use it for inference.

Supervised fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model for a specific translation task by using a labeled dataset containing input and output examples. This process is highly effective for domain-specific applications where the required translation style, format, or terminology differs significantly from the general-purpose data the base model was trained on.

During tuning, the model's weights are adjusted to minimize the difference between its predictions and the ground-truth labels in your dataset, resulting in a model specialized for your use case.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Supervised fine-tuning: A method to adapt a pre-trained model to a specific task by training it on a dataset of labeled examples.
  • Model weights: Parameters within a neural network that are adjusted during training to minimize the difference between model predictions and actual labels.
  • Adapter size: A parameter that controls the capacity of the Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) layers, affecting the trade-off between specialization and model size.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
The following Translation LLM model supports supervised fine-tuning:

  • translation-llm-002

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Maximum tokens (input and output): 1,000 tokens for serving (approximately 4,000 characters).
  • Validation dataset size: 1,024 examples.
  • Training dataset file size: Up to 1 GB for JSONL files.
  • Training example length: 1,000 tokens (approximately 4,000 characters).
  • Adapter size: For translation-llm-002, the only supported value is 4. Using other values will cause the tuning job to fail.

docs.title: Use cases for supervised fine-tuning
docs.text:
A general pre-trained translation model performs well on common text. To teach a model a niche or domain-specific translation task, consider supervised fine-tuning.

Examples include:

  • Industry-specific jargon: Translating medical reports or financial documents that use specialized terminology.
  • Specific style or tone: Adhering to a company's official style guide for all translated content.
  • Unique formatting: Generating output that follows a specific structure, such as formatted lists or tables.
  • Customized responses: Providing terse or verbose translations based on the input type.

docs.title: Configure a tuning job region
docs.text:
Your data, including the transformed dataset and the tuned model, is stored in the region where the tuning job runs. The only supported region for tuning is us-central1.

You can specify the region using the Vertex AI SDK, the REST API, or the Google Cloud console.

Vertex AI SDKREST APIGoogle Cloud console

If you use the Vertex AI SDK for Python, you can specify the region at initialization.

import vertexai
vertexai.init(project='myproject', location='us-central1')

If you create a tuning job by sending a POST request to the tuningJobs.create method, use the URL to specify the region. Replace PROJECT_ID with your project ID.

https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/us-central1/tuningJobs

If you use the Google Cloud console, you can select the region in the Region drop-down list on the Model details page when you create a tuning job.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Quota
docs.text: Quota is enforced on the number of concurrent tuning jobs per project. Every project has a default quota to run at least one tuning job. This is a global quota shared across all regions. To run more jobs concurrently, you must request additional quota for Global concurrent tuning jobs.

docs.title: Pricing
docs.text: Training tokens are calculated by multiplying the total number of tokens in your training dataset by the number of epochs. For more information, see Generative AI on Vertex AI pricing.

  • Tuning Job: A process that runs on Vertex AI to perform the fine-tuning of your model.

Prepare a supervised fine-tuning dataset

docs.title: Create a tuning job
docs.text:
You can create a supervised fine-tuning job by using the REST API or the Vertex AI SDK for Python.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

REST APIPython

To create a model tuning job, send a POST request using the tuningJobs.create method.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • TUNING_JOB_REGION: The region where the tuning job runs. This is also the default region where the tuned model is uploaded. Supported region: us-central1.
  • BASE_MODEL: Name of the translation model to tune. Supported value: translation-llm-002.
  • TRAINING_DATASET_URI: The Cloud Storage URI of your training dataset (e.g., gs://your-bucket/training-data.jsonl). The dataset must be a JSONL file. For best results, provide at least 100 to 500 examples.
  • VALIDATION_DATASET_URI: (Optional) The Cloud Storage URI of your validation dataset file.
  • TUNED_MODEL_DISPLAYNAME: (Optional) A display name for the tuned model. If not set, a random name is generated.

HTTP method and URL:

POST https://TUNING_JOB_REGION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/TUNING_JOB_REGION/tuningJobs

Request JSON body:

{
  "baseModel": "BASE_MODEL",
  "supervisedTuningSpec" : {
      "trainingDatasetUri": "TRAINING_DATASET_URI",
      "validationDatasetUri": "VALIDATION_DATASET_URI",
  },
  "tunedModelDisplayName": "TUNED_MODEL_DISPLAYNAME"
}

To send your request, choose one of these options:

Show the curl command

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell, which automatically logs you into the gcloud CLI. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://TUNING_JOB_REGION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/TUNING_JOB_REGION/tuningJobs"
Show the PowerShell command

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login. You can check the currently active account by running gcloud auth list.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://TUNING_JOB_REGION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/TUNING_JOB_REGION/tuningJobs" | Select-Object -Expand Content

Response:

You should receive a JSON response similar to the following, which includes the TUNING_JOB_ID for your new job.

{
  "name": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/TUNING_JOB_REGION/tuningJobs/TUNING_JOB_ID",
  "createTime": "CREATE_TIME",
  "updateTime": "UPDATE_TIME",
  "status": "STATUS",
  "supervisedTuningSpec": {
        "trainingDatasetUri": "TRAINING_DATASET_URI",
        "validationDatasetUri": "VALIDATION_DATASET_URI",
    },
  "tunedModelDisplayName": "TUNED_MODEL_DISPLAYNAME"
}
Show an example curl command 
PROJECT_ID=myproject
LOCATION=us-central1
curl \
-X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
"https://${LOCATION}-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/locations/${LOCATION}/tuningJobs" \
-d \
$'{
   "baseModel": "translation-llm-002",
   "supervisedTuningSpec" : {
      "training_dataset_uri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini-2_0/text/sft_train_data.jsonl",
      "validation_dataset_uri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini-2_0/text/sft_validation_data.jsonl"
   },
   "tunedModelDisplayName": "tuned_translation_llm"
}'

import vertexai
from vertexai.tuning import sft

docs.title: View tuning and validation metrics
docs.text:
You can configure a model tuning job to collect and report tuning and evaluation metrics, which can then be visualized in Vertex AI Studio.

  1. Go to the Vertex AI Studio page.

    Go to Vertex AI Studio

  2. In the Tune and Distill table, click the name of the tuned model that you want to view metrics for. The tuning metrics appear under the Monitor tab.

View available metrics

Model tuning metrics

The model tuning job automatically collects the following tuning metrics for translation-llm-002:

  • /train_total_loss: Loss for the tuning dataset at a training step.
  • /train_fraction_of_correct_next_step_preds: The token accuracy at a training step. This metric measures the accuracy of the predicted tokens when compared to the ground truth in the tuning dataset.
  • /train_num_predictions: Number of predicted tokens at a training step.

Model validation metrics

You can configure a model tuning job to collect the following validation metrics for translation-llm-002:

  • /eval_total_loss: Loss for the validation dataset at a validation step.
  • /eval_fraction_of_correct_next_step_preds: The token accuracy at a validation step. This metric measures the accuracy of the predicted tokens when compared to the ground truth in the validation dataset.
  • /eval_num_predictions: Number of predicted tokens at a validation step.

Metrics visualizations are available after the tuning job starts and are updated in real time as tuning progresses. If you don't specify a validation dataset when you create the tuning job, only the visualizations for the tuning metrics are available.

# TUNING_JOB_ID = "your-tuning-job-id"

sft_tuning_job = sft.SupervisedTuningJob(f"projects/{PROJECT_ID}/locations/{TUNING_JOB_REGION}/tuningJobs/{TUNING_JOB_ID}")

# Ensure the job has completed and the endpoint is available
if sft_tuning_job.has_ended and sft_tuning_job.tuned_model_endpoint_name:
    tuned_model = GenerativeModel(sft_tuning_job.tuned_model_endpoint_name)
    content = "English: Hello. Spanish:"
    response = tuned_model.generate_content(content)
    print(response.text)
else:
    print("Tuning job has not completed or endpoint is not available.")

docs.title: Tune text embeddings
docs.text:
This page shows you how to tune text embedding models.

Foundation embedding models are pre-trained on a massive dataset of text, providing a strong baseline for many tasks. For scenarios requiring specialized knowledge or highly tailored performance, model tuning enables you to fine-tune the model's representations using your own relevant data. Tuning is supported for stable versions of textembedding-gecko and textembedding-gecko-multilingual models.

Text embedding models support supervised tuning. Supervised tuning uses labeled examples that demonstrate the type of output you want from your text embedding model during inference.

To learn more about model tuning, see How model tuning works.

docs.title: Expected quality improvement
docs.text:
Vertex AI uses a parameter-efficient tuning method for customization. This methodology shows significant gains in quality of up to 41% (average 12%) on experiments performed on public retrieval benchmark datasets.

To see an example of getting tuned text embeddings, run the "Getting Tuned Text-Embeddings on Vertex AI" Jupyter notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab Open in Colab Enterprise Open in Vertex AI Workbench user-managed notebooks View on GitHub

docs.title: Use case for tuning an embedding model
docs.text: Tuning a text embeddings model can enable your model to adapt to a specific domain or task. This can be useful if the pre-trained embeddings model is not well-suited to your specific needs. For example, you might fine-tune an embeddings model on a dataset of your company's customer support tickets. This could help a chatbot understand the different types of customer support issues your customers typically have and answer their questions more effectively. Without tuning, the model doesn't know the specifics of your customer support tickets or the solutions to specific problems for your product.

docs.text:

docs.title: Before you begin
Create an embedding model tuning job
docs.text:
You can create an embedding model tuning job by using the REST API, the Vertex AI SDK for Python, or the Google Cloud console. You can set custom values for hyperparameters such as batch size, learning rate multiplier, and output embedding dimensionality.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Text embedding tuning also supports the following features: * VPC Service Controls: Can be configured to run within a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) by passing the network parameter when creating the PipelineJob. * Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK): To use CMEK, pass the key to the parameterValues.encryption_spec_key_name pipeline parameter, as well as the encryptionSpec.kmsKeyName parameter when creating the PipelineJob.

RESTVertex AI SDK for PythonJavaNode.jsConsole

To create an embedding model tuning job, use the projects.locations.pipelineJobs.create method.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Vertex AI SDK for Python API reference documentation.

import re

from google.cloud.aiplatform import initializer as aiplatform_init
from vertexai.language_models import TextEmbeddingModel


def tune_embedding_model(
    api_endpoint: str,
    base_model_name: str = "text-embedding-005",
    corpus_path: str = "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/corpus.jsonl",
    queries_path: str = "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/queries.jsonl",
    train_label_path: str = "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/train.tsv",
    test_label_path: str = "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/test.tsv",
):  # noqa: ANN201
    """Tune an embedding model using the specified parameters.
    Args:
        api_endpoint (str): The API endpoint for the Vertex AI service.
        base_model_name (str): The name of the base model to use for tuning.
        corpus_path (str): GCS URI of the JSONL file containing the corpus data.
        queries_path (str): GCS URI of the JSONL file containing the queries data.
        train_label_path (str): GCS URI of the TSV file containing the training labels.
        test_label_path (str): GCS URI of the TSV file containing the test labels.
    """
    match = re.search(r"^(\w+-\w+)", api_endpoint)
    location = match.group(1) if match else "us-central1"
    base_model = TextEmbeddingModel.from_pretrained(base_model_name)
    tuning_job = base_model.tune_model(
        task_type="DEFAULT",
        corpus_data=corpus_path,
        queries_data=queries_path,
        training_data=train_label_path,
        test_data=test_label_path,
        batch_size=128,  # The batch size to use for training.
        train_steps=1000,  # The number of training steps.
        tuned_model_location=location,
        output_dimensionality=768,  # The dimensionality of the output embeddings.
        learning_rate_multiplier=1.0,  # The multiplier for the learning rate.
    )
    return tuning_job

import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.CreatePipelineJobRequest;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.LocationName;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PipelineJob;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PipelineJob.RuntimeConfig;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PipelineServiceClient;
import com.google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PipelineServiceSettings;
import com.google.protobuf.Value;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public class EmbeddingModelTuningSample {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
    // TODO(developer): Replace these variables before running this sample.
    String apiEndpoint = "us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com:443";
    String project = "PROJECT";
    String baseModelVersionId = "BASE_MODEL_VERSION_ID";
    String taskType = "DEFAULT";
    String pipelineJobDisplayName = "PIPELINE_JOB_DISPLAY_NAME";
    String outputDir = "OUTPUT_DIR";
    String queriesPath = "QUERIES_PATH";
    String corpusPath = "CORPUS_PATH";
    String trainLabelPath = "TRAIN_LABEL_PATH";
    String testLabelPath = "TEST_LABEL_PATH";
    double learningRateMultiplier = 1.0;
    int outputDimensionality = 768;
    int batchSize = 128;
    int trainSteps = 1000;

    createEmbeddingModelTuningPipelineJob(
        apiEndpoint,
        project,
        baseModelVersionId,
        taskType,
        pipelineJobDisplayName,
        outputDir,
        queriesPath,
        corpusPath,
        trainLabelPath,
        testLabelPath,
        learningRateMultiplier,
        outputDimensionality,
        batchSize,
        trainSteps);
  }

  public static PipelineJob createEmbeddingModelTuningPipelineJob(
      String apiEndpoint,
      String project,
      String baseModelVersionId,
      String taskType,
      String pipelineJobDisplayName,
      String outputDir,
      String queriesPath,
      String corpusPath,
      String trainLabelPath,
      String testLabelPath,
      double learningRateMultiplier,
      int outputDimensionality,
      int batchSize,
      int trainSteps)
      throws IOException {
    Matcher matcher = Pattern.compile("^(?<Location>\\w+-\\w+)").matcher(apiEndpoint);
    String location = matcher.matches() ? matcher.group("Location") : "us-central1";
    String templateUri =
        "https://us-kfp.pkg.dev/ml-pipeline/llm-text-embedding/tune-text-embedding-model/v1.1.4";
    PipelineServiceSettings settings =
        PipelineServiceSettings.newBuilder().setEndpoint(apiEndpoint).build();
    try (PipelineServiceClient client = PipelineServiceClient.create(settings)) {
      Map<String, Value> parameterValues =
          Map.of(
              "base_model_version_id", valueOf(baseModelVersionId),
              "task_type", valueof(taskType),
              "queries_path", valueOf(queriesPath),
              "corpus_path", valueOf(corpusPath),
              "train_label_path", valueOf(trainLabelPath),
              "test_label_path", valueOf(testLabelPath),
              "learning_rate_multiplier", valueOf(learningRateMultiplier),
              "output_dimensionality", valueOf(outputDimensionality),
              "batch_size", valueOf(batchSize),
              "train_steps", valueOf(trainSteps));
      PipelineJob pipelineJob =
          PipelineJob.newBuilder()
              .setTemplateUri(templateUri)
              .setDisplayName(pipelineJobDisplayName)
              .setRuntimeConfig(
                  RuntimeConfig.newBuilder()
                      .setGcsOutputDirectory(outputDir)
                      .putAllParameterValues(parameterValues)
                      .build())
              .build();
      CreatePipelineJobRequest request =
          CreatePipelineJobRequest.newBuilder()
              .setParent(LocationName.of(project, location).toString())
              .setPipelineJob(pipelineJob)
              .build();
      return client.createPipelineJob(request);
    }
  }

  private static Value valueOf(String s) {
    return Value.newBuilder().setStringValue(s).build();
  }

  private static Value valueOf(int n) {
    return Value.newBuilder().setNumberValue(n).build();
  }

  private static Value valueOf(double n) {
    return Value.newBuilder().setNumberValue(n).build();
  }
}

async function main(
  apiEndpoint,
  project,
  outputDir,
  pipelineJobDisplayName = 'embedding-customization-pipeline-sample',
  baseModelVersionId = 'text-embedding-005',
  taskType = 'DEFAULT',
  corpusPath = 'gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/corpus.jsonl',
  queriesPath = 'gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/queries.jsonl',
  trainLabelPath = 'gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/train.tsv',
  testLabelPath = 'gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/embedding/goog-10k-2024/r11/test.tsv',
  outputDimensionality = 768,
  learningRateMultiplier = 1.0,
  batchSize = 128,
  trainSteps = 1000
) {
  const aiplatform = require('@google-cloud/aiplatform');
  const {PipelineServiceClient} = aiplatform.v1;
  const {helpers} = aiplatform; // helps construct protobuf.Value objects.

  const client = new PipelineServiceClient({apiEndpoint});
  const match = apiEndpoint.match(/(?<L>\w+-\w+)/);
  const location = match ? match.groups.L : 'us-central1';
  const parent = `projects/${project}/locations/${location}`;
  const params = {
    base_model_version_id: baseModelVersionId,
    task_type: taskType,
    queries_path: queriesPath,
    corpus_path: corpusPath,
    train_label_path: trainLabelPath,
    test_label_path: testLabelPath,
    batch_size: batchSize,
    train_steps: trainSteps,
    output_dimensionality: outputDimensionality,
    learning_rate_multiplier: learningRateMultiplier,
  };
  const runtimeConfig = {
    gcsOutputDirectory: outputDir,
    parameterValues: Object.fromEntries(
      Object.entries(params).map(([k, v]) => [k, helpers.toValue(v)])
    ),
  };
  const pipelineJob = {
    templateUri:
      'https://us-kfp.pkg.dev/ml-pipeline/llm-text-embedding/tune-text-embedding-model/v1.1.4',
    displayName: pipelineJobDisplayName,
    runtimeConfig,
  };
  async function createTuneJob() {
    const [response] = await client.createPipelineJob({parent, pipelineJob});
    console.log(`job_name: ${response.name}`);
    console.log(`job_state: ${response.state}`);
  }

  await createTuneJob();
}

docs.title: Tune function calling
docs.text:
Function calling lets you create Gemini-based applications that can interact with real-time information and external services like databases, APIs, and document repositories. This enhances your application's ability to provide relevant and contextual responses.

With supervised fine-tuning, you can use your own tuning dataset to improve the accuracy and reliability of your model's function calling capabilities.

Concepts
  • Function calling: A feature that allows a large language model to call external tools or APIs to retrieve information or perform actions, making its responses more dynamic and connected to real-world data.
  • Supervised fine-tuning: The process of adapting a pre-trained model for a specific task by training it on a labeled dataset containing example inputs and desired outputs.
  • Tuning dataset: A collection of example conversations, including user prompts and the ideal model responses (including function calls), used to guide the model's learning during fine-tuning.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text:
The following Gemini model supports function calling tuning:

  • gemini-1.0-pro-002

docs.title: Tuning dataset format
docs.text:
Your tuning dataset must be in a JSONL file where each line contains a single tuning example. The fileUri for your dataset can be the URI of a file in a Cloud Storage bucket or a publicly available HTTPS URL.

The structure of your tuning examples depends on the function calling scenario you want to improve. The following table compares common scenarios.

Scenario Description Best for... Single-turn response The model makes a single function call to answer a user's query and then stops. Simple, one-off requests where the answer can be retrieved with one tool call. Multi-turn chat The model engages in a conversation, using function calls and their responses to inform subsequent replies. Building conversational agents or chatbots that require back-and-forth interaction to resolve a user's request. Parallel function calls The model makes multiple function calls simultaneously in a single turn to gather information from different tools. Complex queries that require information from multiple independent sources to be resolved efficiently.

The following sections provide examples of tuning datasets for each of these scenarios.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Single-turn responseMulti-turn chatParallel function calls

docs.text:
• To learn how to create a tuning job and test the tuned model, see Tune Gemini models by using supervised fine-tuning.
  • To learn more about model tuning, see Introduction to tuning.
  • To learn more about function calling, see Introduction to function calling.

docs.title: Introduction to tuning
docs.text:
Model tuning adapts Gemini to perform specific tasks with greater precision and accuracy. This process works by providing a model with a training dataset that contains a set of examples for specific downstream tasks.

This page provides an overview of model tuning for Gemini, describes the available tuning options, and helps you determine when to use each option.

Concepts
  • Model tuning: A process of adapting a pre-trained model to perform specific tasks by training it on a dataset of examples.
  • Prompt design: The process of creating effective instructions (prompts) to guide a model's output without changing the model itself.
  • Parameter-efficient tuning (PEFT): A tuning approach that updates only a small subset of a model's parameters, making it resource-efficient.
  • Full fine-tuning: A tuning approach that updates all of a model's parameters, which is computationally intensive but can achieve high quality for complex tasks.
  • Supervised fine-tuning: A tuning method where a model learns a new skill from a dataset containing hundreds of labeled examples that demonstrate the desired input and output.

docs.title: Benefits of model tuning
docs.text:
Model tuning is an effective way to customize large models for your tasks and is a key step to improve a model's quality and efficiency. Model tuning provides the following benefits:

  • Higher quality for your specific tasks.
  • Increased model robustness.
  • Lower inference latency and cost due to shorter prompts.

docs.title: Tuning compared to prompt design
docs.text:
You can customize Gemini models using either prompt design or model tuning.

Feature Prompt Design Model Tuning Primary Goal Guide the model's output for a specific request using detailed instructions in the prompt. Adapt the model's core behavior for a specific task by training it on a dataset. Data Requirement A few examples (few-shot) can be included directly in the prompt. Requires a structured training dataset with at least 100 high-quality examples. Best For Rapid prototyping and tasks that don't require deep domain specialization. Complex, specialized tasks where the model needs to learn new or nuanced behavior. Effort Lower initial effort; involves crafting and refining prompts. Higher initial effort; requires preparing a dataset and running a tuning job.

We recommend starting with prompt design to find the optimal prompt. Then, if required, you can proceed to model tuning to further boost performance or fix recurrent errors. While adding more examples to a training dataset might be beneficial, it is important to evaluate where the model makes mistakes before adding more data. High-quality, well-labeled data is crucial for good performance. The data you use for tuning should reflect the prompt distribution, format, and context the model will encounter in production.

Tuning provides the following benefits over prompt design:

  • Allows deep customization of the model, resulting in better performance on specific tasks.
  • Aligns the model with custom syntax, instructions, and domain-specific semantic rules.
  • Offers more consistent and reliable results.
  • Handles more examples at once than can fit in a prompt.
  • Saves cost at inference by removing few-shot examples and long instructions from prompts.

docs.title: Tuning approaches
docs.text:
Parameter-efficient tuning and full fine-tuning are two approaches to customizing large models. Both methods have their advantages and implications in terms of model quality and resource efficiency.

Feature Parameter-Efficient Tuning (PEFT) Full Fine-Tuning Parameters Updated A small subset of the model's parameters. All parameters of the model. Resource Usage Significantly lower computational resources for training and serving. High computational resources for both training and serving. Use Case Efficiently adapts models to specific tasks. Ideal for multi-task learning without extensive retraining. Adapts models for highly complex tasks where the highest possible quality is required. Cost More cost-effective. Higher overall cost due to greater resource demands.

To understand how Vertex AI supports adapter tuning (a form of PEFT) and serving, see the whitepaper, Adaptation of Large Foundation Models.

docs.title: Supported tuning methods
docs.text: Vertex AI supports supervised fine-tuning to customize foundational models. For Gemini, supervised fine-tuning is implemented using the parameter-efficient tuning (PEFT) approach, which is also known as adapter tuning.

docs.title: Supervised fine-tuning
docs.text:
Supervised fine-tuning improves the performance of a model by teaching it a new skill. Data that contains hundreds of labeled examples is used to teach the model to mimic a desired behavior or task. Each labeled example demonstrates what you want the model to output during inference.

When you run a supervised fine-tuning job, the model learns additional parameters that help it encode the necessary information to perform the desired task or learn the desired behavior. These parameters are used during inference. The output of the tuning job is a new model that combines the newly learned parameters with the original model.

Supervised fine-tuning of a text model is a good option when the output of your model isn't complex and is relatively easy to define. It is recommended for classification, sentiment analysis, entity extraction, summarization of content that's not complex, and writing domain-specific queries. For code models, supervised tuning is the only option.

docs.title: Models that support supervised fine-tuning
docs.text:
The following Gemini models support supervised tuning:

  • Gemini 2.5 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite

For more information on using supervised fine-tuning with different data types, see the following pages: * Tune text data * Tune image data * Tune audio data * Tune document data
