docs.title: Choose a call type
docs.text:
You can send requests to Llama models as either a streaming or a unary (non-streaming) call.

Feature Streaming Call Unary Call Response Time Lower perceived latency, as tokens are returned as they are generated. Higher latency, as the full response must be generated before it is returned. Use Case Ideal for interactive, real-time applications like chatbots where users expect immediate feedback. Suitable for offline or batch processing tasks where the entire output is needed at once. Implementation Requires handling a stream of data chunks and assembling the final response on the client side. Simpler implementation; the client receives a single, complete response object.

docs.title: Send the request
docs.text:
The following samples show how to send a request to the publisher model endpoint for a Llama model using either a streaming or unary call.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • LOCATION: A region that supports Llama models. For more information, see Llama model region availability and quotas.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL: The model name you want to use. For more information, see Available models.
  • ROLE: The role associated with a message. You can specify a user or an assistant. The first message must use the user role. The models operate with alternating user and assistant turns.
  • CONTENT: The content, such as text, of the user or assistant message.
  • MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS: Maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately four characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words.
  • ENABLE_LLAMA_GUARD: A boolean that specifies whether to enable Llama Guard on your inputs and outputs. By default, Llama Guard is enabled.

The HTTP method and URL for the request are:

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints/openapi/chat/completions
Streaming callUnary call

Use a streaming call to receive the response as it is being generated. Set "stream": true in the request body.

Request JSON body

{
  "model": "meta/MODEL",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "ROLE",
      "content": "CONTENT"
    }
  ],
  "max_tokens": MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS,
  "stream": true,
  "extra_body": {
    "google": {
      "model_safety_settings": {
        "enabled": ENABLE_LLAMA_GUARD,
        "llama_guard_settings": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

To send your request, choose one of the following options:

cURLPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints/openapi/chat/completions"

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `
    -Method POST `
    -Headers $headers `
    -ContentType: "application/json; charset=utf-8" `
    -InFile request.json `
    -Uri "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints/openapi/chat/completions" | Select-Object -Expand Content

Response

You should receive a series of JSON objects, each representing a chunk of the streamed response. If Llama Guard flags the response as unsafe, the refusal field will contain the reason.

data: {
  "choices": [
    {
      "delta": {
        "content": "CONTENT",
        "role": "assistant",
        "refusal": "REFUSAL_REASON"
      },
      "index": 0
    }
  ],
  "model": "meta/MODEL_NAME",
  "object": "chat.completion.chunk"
}

data: {
  "choices": [
    {
      "delta": {
        "content": "CONTENT",
        "role": "assistant"
      },
      "finish_reason": "stop",
      "index": 0
    }
  ],
  "model": "meta/MODEL_NAME",
  "object": "chat.completion.chunk",
  "usage": {
    "completion_tokens": 131,
    "prompt_tokens": 14,
    "total_tokens": 145
  }
}

Use a unary call to receive the entire response after it has been generated. Set "stream": false in the request body.

Request JSON body

{
  "model": "meta/MODEL",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "ROLE",
      "content": "CONTENT"
    }
  ],
  "max_tokens": MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS,
  "stream": false,
  "extra_body": {
    "google": {
      "model_safety_settings": {
        "enabled": ENABLE_LLAMA_GUARD,
        "llama_guard_settings": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

To send your request, choose one of the following options:

cURLPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login, or by using Cloud Shell.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d @request.json \
     "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/endpoints/openapi/chat/completions"

Note: The following command assumes that you have logged in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

Invoke-WebRequest `

Response

You should receive a single JSON object containing the complete response. If Llama Guard flags the response as unsafe, the refusal field will contain the reason.

{
  "choices": [

      "finish_reason": "stop",
      "index": 0,

        "content": "CONTENT",

docs.title: Llama Guard flagged responses
docs.text:
By default, Llama Guard is enabled on all predictions that you make with Llama models. Llama Guard helps safeguard responses by checking inputs and outputs against a safety taxonomy. If Llama Guard determines the content is unsafe, it flags the response.

  • For Llama 3.3 and Llama 3.1 models, Llama Guard 3 8B is enabled by default.
  • For Llama 3.2 models, Llama Guard 3 11B vision is enabled by default.

If you want to disable Llama Guard, you can set the enabled field to false in the model_safety_settings of your request.

docs.title: Error code 429
docs.text:
When the number of requests sent to a model exceeds its available processing capacity, Vertex AI returns a 429 Resource Exhausted error. The specific error message and resolution path depend on whether you are using the pay-as-you-go service or have purchased Provisioned Throughput.

This document explains the causes of the 429 error for both service models and provides guidance on how to resolve it.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Pay-as-you-go: A service model where you are billed based on the number of requests you make, using a shared pool of resources without reserved capacity.
  • Provisioned Throughput: A service model where you purchase and reserve a specific amount of model processing capacity (measured in GPUs per second) for your project, ensuring consistent availability.
  • Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ): A quota management system that dynamically allocates capacity from a shared pool to different models and regions based on demand.
  • Truncated exponential backoff: An error handling strategy where a client periodically retries a failed request with increasing delays between retries to avoid overwhelming a service.

docs.title: Causes of 429 errors
docs.text:
The 429 error indicates that your requests have exceeded the available capacity. The table below compares how this error is handled in the pay-as-you-go and Provisioned Throughput service models.

Feature Pay-as-you-go Provisioned Throughput Error Message Resource exhausted, please try again later. Too many requests. Exceeded the Provisioned Throughput. Cause The number of requests exceeds the available capacity in the shared resource pool. The number of requests exceeds your reserved throughput capacity. SLA Impact Requests that receive a 429 error are not counted against your error rate as described in the service level agreement (SLA). Errors for usage below your purchased throughput are returned as 5XX and count against the SLA. Errors for usage above your purchased throughput are treated as pay-as-you-go and don't count against the SLA.

With a Provisioned Throughput subscription, Vertex AI reserves the purchased throughput for your project. If you use less than your purchased amount, errors that might otherwise be 429 are returned as 5XX and count toward the SLA error rate. When you exceed your purchased amount, the additional requests are processed on-demand as pay-as-you-go.

If you don't have a Provisioned Throughput subscription and shared resources are unavailable, you will receive a 429 error. Although you don't have reserved capacity, you can retry your request.

docs.title: Resolve 429 errors
docs.text:
The steps to resolve a 429 error vary depending on your service model. Select the tab that corresponds to your setup.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter other issues with your setup, refer to the Vertex AI Troubleshooting Guide.

Pay-as-you-goProvisioned Throughput

On the pay-as-you-go service model, you have the following options to resolve 429 errors:

  • Use the global endpoint: Whenever possible, use the global endpoint instead of a regional endpoint.
  • Implement a retry strategy: Use truncated exponential backoff to retry requests.
  • Request a quota increase: If your model uses quotas, you can submit a Quota Increase Request (QIR).
  • Smooth traffic: If your model uses Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ), smoothing traffic and reducing large spikes can help. For more information, see Dynamic shared quota.
  • Subscribe to Provisioned Throughput: For a more consistent level of service, subscribe to Provisioned Throughput. For more information, see Provisioned Throughput.

To resolve a 429 error when you have a Provisioned Throughput subscription, you can do the following:

  • Allow on-demand processing: Use the default behavior by not setting a header in your prediction requests. Any overages are processed on-demand and billed as pay-as-you-go.
  • Increase reserved capacity: Increase the number of GSUs in your Provisioned Throughput subscription.

docs.title: Provisioned Throughput for Live API
docs.text:
Preview

For information about access to this release, see the access request page.

This section explains how Provisioned Throughput works with the Live API for token counting and quota enforcement.

The Live API supports low-latency multimodal interactions through sessions. It uses a session memory to retain and recall information from interactions within a session. This lets the model recall previously provided or discussed information. Provisioned Throughput supports the Gemini 1.5 Flash with Live API model. For more information about the Live API, including session limits and capabilities, see the Live API reference.

Concepts

Provisioned Throughput: A service that reserves processing capacity for your models at a fixed cost, ensuring consistent performance. Live API: An API designed for low-latency, multimodal conversations that maintains context across multiple requests within a session. Session Memory: The context and history of a Live API conversation that is stored and used in subsequent requests to maintain conversational flow. Tokens: The basic units of text or data that a large language model processes, including equivalents for images, audio, and video.

docs.title: Calculate throughput for Live API
docs.text:
While using the Live API, the tokens stored in the session memory can be used in subsequent requests to the model. As a result, Provisioned Throughput takes into account the incoming tokens as well as session memory tokens in the same request. This might lead to the number of tokens being processed per request being greater than the tokens sent by the user in the ongoing request.

The Live API has a limit on the total tokens that can be stored in the session memory and also has a metadata field containing the total number of tokens. While calculating how much throughput is needed to serve your requests, you must account for tokens in the session memory. If you've used the Live API with pay-as-you-go (PayGo), you can use these traffic patterns and session tokens to help estimate your Provisioned Throughput needs.

docs.title: Example: Estimate throughput for a Live API session
docs.text:
During a session, all traffic is processed either as Provisioned Throughput or pay-as-you-go. If you reach your Provisioned Throughput quota during a session, you'll receive an error message requesting that you try again later. Once you're within your quota, you can resume sending requests. The session state, including the session memory, are available as long as the session is live.

This example illustrates how two consecutive requests are processed by including the tokens from the session memory.

Request 1 details

  • Duration: 10 seconds
  • Tokens sent (audio): 10 seconds x 25 tokens/second = 250 tokens
  • Tokens sent (video): 10 seconds x 258 tokens/frame per second = 2580 tokens
  • Total tokens processed for Request 1:
    • Tokens sent: Sum of audio and video tokens sent = 2580 + 250 = 2830 tokens
    • Tokens received: 100 (audio)

Request 2 details

  • Duration: 40 seconds
  • Tokens sent (audio): 40 seconds x 1000 tokens
  • Total tokens processed for Request 2:
    • Tokens sent: Tokens sent in Request 2 + session memory tokens from Request 1 = 1000 tokens + 2830 tokens = 3830 tokens
    • Tokens received: 200 (audio)

Calculate the number of tokens processed in the requests

The number of tokens processed during these requests is calculated as follows:

  • Request 1 processes only the input and output tokens from the ongoing request, as there are no additional tokens in the session memory.
  • Request 2 processes the input and output tokens from the ongoing request, but also includes the input tokens from the session memory, consisting of the input tokens from the preceding request (Request 1). The burndown rate for tokens in the session memory is the same as that for standard input tokens (1 input session memory token = 1 input token).

If Request 2 took exactly 1 second to process after you sent it, your tokens are processed and applied to your Provisioned Throughput quota as follows:

  1. Calculate total input tokens: Multiply your inputs by their burndown rates. 2830 (session memory tokens) * 1 + 1000 (input text tokens) * 1 = 3830 input tokens

  2. Calculate total output tokens: Multiply your outputs by their burndown rates. 200 (audio output tokens) * 6 = 1200 output tokens

  3. Calculate total processed tokens: Add the input and output totals. 3830 + 1200 = 5030 total tokens

If your Provisioned Throughput quota is greater than 5,030 tokens per second, then this request can be processed immediately. If it's less, the tokens are processed over time at the rate that you've set for your quota.

docs.text: • Purchase Provisioned Throughput.

docs.title: Calculate Provisioned Throughput requirements
docs.text:
This document explains how to calculate your Provisioned Throughput requirements using generative AI scale units (GSUs) and burndown rates.

Concepts
  • Generative AI Scale Unit (GSU): A measure of throughput for your prompts and responses that specifies how much processing power to provision for a model.
  • Burndown rate: A ratio that converts various input and output units (like tokens, characters, or images) into a standardized throughput measurement.
  • Throughput: The rate at which a model can process input and generate output, typically measured in tokens per second.
  • Queries Per Second (QPS): The number of requests sent to the model every second.

docs.title: GSU and burndown rate
docs.text:
A Generative AI Scale Unit (GSU) is a measure of throughput for your prompts and responses. This amount specifies how much throughput to provision for a model.

A burndown rate is a ratio that converts the input and output units (such as tokens, characters, or images) to a standardized unit of throughput (e.g., input tokens per second). This ratio is used to produce a standard unit of consumption across different models and modalities.

Different models consume throughput at different rates. For information about the minimum GSU purchase amount and increments for each model, see Supported models and burndown rates.

The following equation demonstrates how throughput is calculated:

inputs_per_query = inputs_across_modalities_converted_using_burndown_rates
outputs_per_query = outputs_across_modalities_converted_using_burndown_rates

throughput_per_second = (inputs_per_query + outputs_per_query) * queries_per_second

The calculated throughput per second determines how many GSUs you need for your use case.

docs.title: Important Considerations
docs.text:
To help you plan for your Provisioned Throughput needs, review the following important considerations:

  • Requests are prioritized: Provisioned Throughput customers are prioritized and serviced first before on-demand requests.
  • Throughput doesn't accumulate: Unused throughput doesn't accumulate or carry over to the next month.
  • Throughput is measured in tokens per second, characters per second, or images per second: Provisioned Throughput isn't measured solely based on queries per minute (QPM). It's measured based on the query size for your use case, the response size, and the QPM.
  • Provisioned Throughput is specific to a project, region, model, and version: Provisioned Throughput is assigned to a specific project-region-model-version combination. The same model called from a different region won't count against your Provisioned Throughput quota and won't be prioritized over on-demand requests.

docs.title: Context caching
docs.text:
Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

Provisioned Throughput supports default context caching. However, Provisioned Throughput doesn't support caching requests using the Vertex AI API that include retrieving information about a context cache.

By default, Google automatically caches inputs to reduce cost and latency. For the Gemini 1.5 Flash and Gemini 1.5 Pro models, cached tokens are charged at a 75% discount relative to standard input tokens when a cache hit occurs. For Provisioned Throughput, the discount is applied through a reduced burndown rate.

For example, Gemini 1.5 Pro has the following burndown rates for input text tokens and cached tokens:

  • 1 input text token = 1 token
  • 1 input cached text token = 0.25 tokens

Sending 1,000 input tokens to this model results in a burndown of your Provisioned Throughput by 1,000 input tokens per second. However, if you send 1,000 cached tokens to Gemini 1.5 Pro, this results in a burndown of your Provisioned Throughput by 250 tokens per second.

Note that this can lead to higher throughput for similar queries where the tokens aren't cached and the cache discount isn't applied.

To view the burndown rates for models supported in Provisioned Throughput, see Supported models and burndown rates.

docs.title: Example of estimating your Provisioned Throughput needs
docs.text:
To estimate your Provisioned Throughput needs, you can use the estimation tool in the Google Cloud console or perform the calculation manually.

The following workflow outlines the steps to estimate the amount of Provisioned Throughput for your model. The region isn't considered in the estimation calculations.

flowchart LR
    A[Gather requirements] --> B[Calculate throughput]
    B --> C[Calculate GSUs]

click A "#gather-requirements"
click B "#calculate-throughput"
click C "#calculate-gsus"

This table provides the burndown rates for gemini-1.5-flash that are used in the following example.

Model Throughput per GSU Units Minimum GSU purchase increment Burndown rates Gemini 1.5 Flash 3,360 Tokens 1 1 input text token = 1 token 1 input image token = 1 token 1 input video token = 1 token 1 input audio token = 7 tokens 1 output text token = 4 tokens Example: Estimate your Provisioned Throughput needs

Step 1: Gather your requirements

First, identify your model, required queries per second (QPS), and the size of your inputs and outputs.

In this example, the requirement is to support 10 QPS for a query with the following characteristics: * Model: gemini-1.5-flash * Input: 1,000 text tokens and 500 audio tokens * Output: 300 text tokens

To proceed, you will need the burndown rates for your selected model.

Step 2: Calculate your throughput

  • Calculate total input tokens per query: Multiply your inputs by their respective burndown rates. 1,000 * (1 token per input text token) + 500 * (7 tokens per input audio token) = 4,500 burndown-adjusted input tokens per query

  • Calculate total output tokens per query: Multiply your outputs by their burndown rates. 300 * (4 tokens per output text token) = 1,200 burndown-adjusted output tokens per query

  • Calculate total tokens per query: Add your input and output totals together. 4,500 input tokens + 1,200 output tokens = 5,700 total tokens per query

  • Calculate total throughput per second: Multiply the total tokens per query by the QPS. 5,700 total tokens per query * 10 QPS = 57,000 total tokens per second

Step 3: Calculate your GSUs

  • Calculate the number of GSUs: Divide the total tokens per second by the per-second throughput per GSU from the burndown table. 57,000 total tokens per second ÷ 3,360 per-second throughput per GSU = 16.96 GSUs

  • Round up to the nearest increment: The minimum GSU purchase increment for gemini-1.5-flash is 1, so you must round up. You will need 17 GSUs to support your workload.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with calculations or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Provisioned Throughput overview
docs.text: This page explains what Provisioned Throughput is and helps you decide when to use it compared to the pay-as-you-go option for serving generative AI models on Vertex AI.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Provisioned Throughput: A fixed-cost, fixed-term subscription that reserves a specific amount of processing capacity for a supported generative AI model, ensuring consistent performance.
  • Pay-as-you-go (On-demand): A flexible pricing model where you pay only for the resources you consume, with throughput managed by a dynamic shared quota system.

docs.title: Choose a serving option
docs.text:
Vertex AI offers two ways to consume generative AI models: Provisioned Throughput and pay-as-you-go. Provisioned Throughput reserves throughput for a fixed cost, while pay-as-you-go offers a flexible, consumption-based model.

The following table provides a comparison to help you choose the best option for your workload.

Feature Provisioned Throughput Pay-as-you-go (On-demand) Cost Model Fixed-cost, fixed-term subscription. Pay only for what you use. Performance Reserved throughput provides consistent and predictable latency and capacity. Throughput is subject to dynamic shared quotas, which can lead to variability. Best for... Real-time, production-critical applications (e.g., chatbots, agents) that require consistently high throughput. Development, testing, or applications with variable or unpredictable traffic patterns. Cost Management Deterministic and predictable costs with control over overages. Costs scale directly with usage, which can be less predictable for high-traffic applications.

To reserve your throughput with the provisioned option, you must specify the model and the available locations where the model runs.

docs.title: Purchase Provisioned Throughput
docs.text: This page describes how to purchase and manage Provisioned Throughput. It covers important considerations before you buy, the required permissions, and step-by-step instructions for placing, changing, and viewing your orders.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Provisioned Throughput: A service that provides dedicated, reserved processing capacity for generative AI models at a fixed cost.
  • Generative AI Scale Unit (GSU): A unit of measure for the computational capacity purchased with Provisioned Throughput.
  • Term: The fixed duration (e.g., 1 week, 1 month) for which you commit to a Provisioned Throughput purchase.
  • Auto-renewal: An option to automatically extend your Provisioned Throughput subscription at the end of its term.
  • Overage: Usage that exceeds the purchased Provisioned Throughput capacity, typically billed at pay-as-you-go rates.

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
To help you decide whether to purchase Provisioned Throughput, consider the following:

  • You cannot cancel your order during its term. Your Provisioned Throughput purchase is a commitment. However, you can increase the number of purchased GSUs. If you accidentally purchase a commitment or there's a problem with your configuration, contact your Google Cloud account representative for assistance.

  • You can auto-renew your subscription. When you submit your order, you can choose to auto-renew your subscription at the end of its term. You can cancel the auto-renewal process up to 30 days before the start of the next term. Monthly subscriptions can be configured to renew automatically, but weekly terms do not support automatic renewal. For more information, see Change a Provisioned Throughput order.

  • You can change your order with notice. You can modify your auto-renewal behavior, model, model version, or region by editing your existing order in the Google Cloud console. Changes are processed on a best-effort basis, typically within 10 business days. Model changes are limited to the same publisher (e.g., you can switch between Google's Gemini models, but not from a Google model to an Anthropic model).

  • Overage is billed as pay-as-you-go by default. If your throughput exceeds your purchased capacity, overages are processed and billed as standard pay-as-you-go. You can control overages on a per-request basis. For more information, see Use Provisioned Throughput.

For information about pricing, see Provisioned Throughput pricing.

Provisioned Throughput provides dedicated, high-throughput capacity for your generative AI workloads. It is available for a selection of Google and third-party partner models. This document lists the supported models and provides details on their throughput, purchase units, and consumption rates.

The following tables show the models that support Provisioned Throughput, the throughput for each generative AI scale unit (GSU), and the burndown rates for each model.

Concepts

  • Generative AI Scale Unit (GSU): The unit of compute capacity you purchase for Provisioned Throughput.
  • Burndown Rate: The rate at which your purchased GSUs are consumed based on the type and size of your input and output data (e.g., text, images, audio).

To determine the number of tokens your workload requires, you can use the SDK tokenizer or the countTokens API.

docs.title: Use Provisioned Throughput
docs.text: This page explains how Provisioned Throughput works, how to control overages or bypass Provisioned Throughput, and how to monitor usage.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Provisioned Throughput: A service that provides a reserved amount of model processing capacity for a fixed price.
  • Generative AI Scale Units (GSUs): The unit of measure for the reserved processing capacity you purchase for Provisioned Throughput.
  • Pay-as-you-go: A billing model where you are charged based on the amount of processing capacity you use, without any upfront commitment.
  • Quota enforcement period: The time interval over which your usage is measured against your Provisioned Throughput quota.

docs.title: How Provisioned Throughput works
docs.text: This section explains how Provisioned Throughput works by using quota checking through the quota enforcement period.

docs.title: Provisioned Throughput quota checking
docs.text:
Your Provisioned Throughput maximum quota is a multiple of the number of generative AI scale units (GSUs) purchased and the throughput per GSU. It's checked each time you make a request within your quota enforcement period, which is how frequently the maximum Provisioned Throughput quota is enforced.

At the time a request is received, the true response size is unknown. Because we prioritize speed of response for real-time applications, Provisioned Throughput estimates the output token size. If the initial estimate exceeds the available Provisioned Throughput maximum quota, the request is processed as pay-as-you-go. Otherwise, it is processed as Provisioned Throughput. This is done by comparing the initial estimate to your Provisioned Throughput maximum quota.

When the response is generated and the true output token size is known, actual usage and quota are reconciled by adding the difference between the estimate and the actual usage to your available Provisioned Throughput quota amount.

docs.title: Provisioned Throughput quota enforcement period
docs.text:
For gemini-1.0-pro and gemini-1.5-flash models, the quota enforcement period can take up to 30 seconds and is subject to change. This means that you might temporarily experience prioritized traffic that exceeds your quota amount on a per-second basis in some cases, but you shouldn't exceed your quota on a 30-second basis. These periods are based on the Vertex AI internal clock time and are independent of when requests are made.

For example, if you purchase one GSU of gemini-1.5-flash-001, then you should expect 3,360 tokens per second of always-on throughput. On average, you can't exceed 100,800 tokens on a 30-second basis, which is calculated using the following formula:

3,360 tokens per second * 30 seconds = 100,800 tokens

If, in a day, you submitted only one request that consumed 8,000 tokens in a second, it might still be processed as a Provisioned Throughput request, even though you exceeded your 3,360 tokens per second limit at the time of the request. This is because the request didn't exceed the threshold of 100,800 tokens per 30 seconds.

docs.title: Control overages or bypass Provisioned Throughput
docs.text:
You can use the API to control how your requests are handled when you exceed your purchased throughput or to bypass Provisioned Throughput entirely on a per-request basis. The following table compares the available options.

Option Behavior Use Case How to implement Default (Hybrid) Requests use Provisioned Throughput. Overages are automatically processed as pay-as-you-go. You want to use your reserved capacity but also handle traffic spikes without interruptions. No code changes required after your order is active. Provisioned Throughput only Requests that exceed your provisioned capacity return a 429 error. No overages are processed. You need strict cost control and want to avoid any pay-as-you-go charges. Set the X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Request-Type HTTP header to dedicated. Pay-as-you-go only All requests bypass your Provisioned Throughput commitment and are billed at pay-as-you-go rates. You are running experiments or development workloads that shouldn't consume your provisioned capacity. Set the X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Request-Type HTTP header to shared.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The following examples show how to set the request type header to control throughput behavior.

Gen AI SDK for PythonREST

Install the SDK

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Set environment variables and send a request

Set environment variables to use the Gen AI SDK with Vertex AI.

# Replace the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` values
# with appropriate values for your project.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=us-central1
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=True

The following code sends a request using the shared (pay-as-you-go) setting.

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import HttpOptions

client = genai.Client(
    http_options=HttpOptions(
        api_version="v1",
        headers={
            # Options:
            # - "dedicated": Use Provisioned Throughput only
            # - "shared": Use pay-as-you-go only
            # https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/provisioned-throughput
            "X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Request-Type": "shared"
        },
    )
)
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-1.5-flash-001",
    contents="How does AI work?",
)
print(response.text)
# Example response:
# Okay, let's break down how AI works. It's a broad field, so I'll focus on the ...
#
# Here's a simplified overview:
# ...

After you set up your environment, you can use the following curl command to send a request. The sample sends a request to the publisher model endpoint using the dedicated (Provisioned Throughput only) setting.

curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Request-Type: dedicated" \ # Options: dedicated, shared
  $URL \
  -d '{"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Hello."}]}]}'

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Preview

This feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

You can monitor your Provisioned Throughput usage using a set of metrics available in Cloud Monitoring for the aiplatform.googleapis.com/PublisherModel resource type.

Dimensions

You can filter on metrics using the following dimensions:

Dimension Values type input output request_type dedicated: Traffic is processed using Provisioned Throughput. spillover: Traffic is processed as pay-as-you-go quota after you exceed your Provisioned Throughput quota. shared: If Provisioned Throughput is active, then traffic is processed as pay-as-you-go quota using the shared HTTP header. If Provisioned Throughput isn't active, then traffic is processed as pay-as-you-go, by default.

Path prefix

The path prefix for a metric is aiplatform.googleapis.com/publisher/online_serving. For example, the full path for the /consumed_throughput metric is aiplatform.googleapis.com/publisher/online_serving/consumed_throughput.

Metrics

The following Cloud Monitoring metrics are available on the aiplatform.googleapis.com/PublisherModel resource for the Gemini models. Use the dedicated request type to filter for Provisioned Throughput usage.

Metric Display name Description /dedicated_gsu_limit Limit (GSU) Dedicated limit in GSUs. Use this metric to understand your Provisioned Throughput maximum quota in GSUs. /tokens Tokens Input and output token count distribution. /token_count Token count Accumulated input and output token count. /consumed_token_throughput Token throughput Throughput usage, which accounts for the burndown rate in tokens and incorporates quota reconciliation. See Provisioned Throughput quota checking. Use this metric to understand how your Provisioned Throughput quota was used. /dedicated_token_limit Limit (tokens per second) Dedicated limit in tokens per second. Use this metric to understand your Provisioned Throughput maximum quota for token-based models. /characters Characters Input and output character count distribution. /character_count Character count Accumulated input and output character count. /consumed_throughput Character throughput Throughput usage, which accounts for the burndown rate in characters and incorporates quota reconciliation. See Provisioned Throughput quota checking. Use this metric to understand how your Provisioned Throughput quota was used. For token-based models, this metric is equivalent to the throughput consumed in tokens multiplied by 4. /dedicated_character_limit Limit (characters per second) Dedicated limit in characters per second. Use this metric to understand your Provisioned Throughput maximum quota for character-based models. /model_invocation_count Model invocation count Number of model invocations (prediction requests). /model_invocation_latencies Model invocation latencies Model invocation latencies (prediction latencies). /first_token_latencies First token latencies Duration from request received to first token returned.

Anthropic models also have a filter for Provisioned Throughput but only for tokens/token_count.

Monitor usage and set up alerts

Step 1: View the Utilization summary

Default monitoring dashboards for Provisioned Throughput provide metrics that let you better understand your usage and utilization.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Provisioned Throughput page.

    Go to Provisioned Throughput

  2. To view the Provisioned Throughput utilization of each model across your orders, select the Utilization summary tab.

In the Provisioned Throughput utilization by model table, you can view the following for the selected time range:

  • Total number of GSUs you had.
  • Peak throughput usage in terms of GSUs.
  • The average GSU utilization.
  • The number of times you reached your Provisioned Throughput limit.

Step 2: View model-specific metrics

Select a model from the Provisioned Throughput utilization by model table to see more metrics specific to the selected model.

Step 3: Enable recommended alerts

After alerting is enabled, set default alerts to help you manage your traffic usage.

  1. On the Provisioned Throughput page, select the Utilization summary tab.
  2. Select Recommended alerts, and the following alerts display:
    • Provisioned Throughput Usage Reached Limit
    • Provisioned Throughput Utilization Exceeded 80%
    • Provisioned Throughput Utilization Exceeded 90%
  3. Check the alerts that help you manage your traffic.

Step 4: View alert policy details

To view more information about alerts:

  1. Go to the Integrations page in Cloud Monitoring.

    Go to Integrations

  2. Enter vertex into the Filter field and press Enter. Google Vertex AI appears.

  3. To view more information, click View details. The Google Vertex AI details pane displays.
  4. Select the Alerts tab, where you can select an Alert Policy template.

docs.title: Limitations of the dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard might display unexpected results, especially for fluctuating traffic that's either spiky or infrequent (for example, less than 1 query per second). The following reasons might contribute to those results:

  • Time ranges that are larger than 12 hours can lead to a less accurate representation of the quota enforcement period. Throughput metrics and their derivatives, such as utilization, display averages across alignment periods that are based on the selected time range. When the time range expands, each alignment period also expands. The alignment period expands across the calculation of the average usage. Because quota enforcement is calculated at a sub-minute level, setting the time range to a period of 12 hours or less results in minute-level data that is more comparable to the actual quota enforcement period. For more information on alignment periods, see Alignment: within-series regularization. For more information about time ranges, see Regularizing time intervals.
  • If multiple requests were submitted at the same time, monitoring aggregations might impact your ability to filter down to specific requests.
  • Provisioned Throughput throttles traffic when a request was made but reports usage metrics after the quota is reconciled.
  • Provisioned Throughput quota enforcement periods are independent from and might not align with monitoring aggregation periods or request-or-response periods.
  • If no errors occurred, you might see an error message within the error rate chart. For example, An error occurred requesting data. One or more resources could not be found.

docs.title: Fine-tune RAG transformations
docs.text:
When you use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the quality of the retrieved information heavily depends on how your source documents are processed and indexed. Vertex AI RAG Engine runs a set of transformations on your documents during ingestion to prepare them for efficient retrieval.

You can fine-tune these transformations to better suit your specific use case by adjusting parameters that control how documents are split into chunks.

Note

The VPC-SC security controls and CMEK are supported by Vertex AI RAG Engine. Data residency and AXT security controls aren't supported.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Chunking: The process of splitting large documents into smaller, more manageable pieces of text for processing and indexing.
  • Embeddings: Numerical representations of text, where words and sentences are converted into vectors that capture their semantic meaning.
  • Tokens: The basic units of text, such as words, subwords, or characters, that a model processes.

docs.title: Tune chunking parameters
docs.text:
When a document is ingested, Vertex AI RAG Engine performs transformations to prepare the data for indexing. A key part of this process is chunking, where documents are split into smaller pieces. You can fine-tune this process for your specific use case by adjusting the chunk_size and chunk_overlap parameters.

Parameter Description chunk_size Specifies the size of each text chunk in tokens. The default is 1,024 tokens. chunk_overlap Specifies the number of tokens that overlap between adjacent chunks to maintain context. The default is 200 tokens.

Choosing the right chunk size involves a trade-off between context and precision:

  • Smaller chunk size: Creates more specific and precise embeddings. This can improve retrieval accuracy for queries that target fine-grained details. However, it might lose broader context from the original document.
  • Larger chunk size: Captures more general context in each embedding. This can be useful for broader queries but might dilute specific details within the chunk, as the fixed-size embedding has to represent more information.

For example, if you try to embed a 1,000-token passage into a model optimized for 200-token chunks, important details might be lost during the compression.

docs.title: Example: Configure chunking during index creation
docs.text:
You can specify the chunk_size and chunk_overlap when you create or import data into your RAG index. The following example shows a hypothetical configuration for a data ingestion request where the chunk size is set to 512 tokens and the overlap is set to 100 tokens.

{
  "ragCorpus": "projects/your-project/locations/us-central1/ragCorpora/your-corpus-id",
  "importDataConfig": {
    "ragFileImportConfig": {
      "ragFilesConfig": {
        "gcsSource": {
          "uris": ["gs://your-bucket/your-document.pdf"]
        }
      },
      "vertexRagStoreConfig": {
        "chunkingConfig": {
          "chunkSize": 512,
          "chunkOverlap": 100
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Use Document AI layout parser with Vertex AI RAG Engine
docs.text:
Preview

The VPC-SC security controls and CMEK are supported by Vertex AI RAG Engine. Data residency and AXT security controls aren't supported.

This page explains how to use the Document AI layout parser with Vertex AI RAG Engine to improve document chunking for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

docs.title: Overview of Document AI and the layout parser
docs.text:
Document AI is a document-processing platform that transforms unstructured data from documents into structured data suitable for analysis and consumption. It is built on Vertex AI and uses generative AI to help you create scalable, end-to-end document processing applications without requiring specialized machine learning expertise.

The Document AI layout parser extracts content elements like text, tables, and lists from a document. It then creates context-aware chunks that preserve the document's original structure, which improves semantic coherence and reduces noise during information retrieval. For a list of file types supported by the layout parser, see Layout detection per file type.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • RAG Engine: A Vertex AI feature that connects large language models (LLMs) to your enterprise knowledge bases to provide more factual and up-to-date responses.
  • Corpus: A collection of documents that serves as the knowledge base for your RAG application.
  • Chunking: The process of breaking down large documents into smaller, semantically coherent pieces of text for efficient processing by LLMs.
  • Embedding model: A model that converts text into numerical vectors (embeddings) so that semantic similarity can be measured.
  • Layout Parser: A Document AI tool that analyzes the visual structure of a document to improve the quality of text extraction and chunking.
Prerequisites

1. Enable the Document AI API

You must enable the Document AI API for your project. For more information, see the Service Usage documentation.

Enable the API

2. Create and enable a layout parser

Create and enable a layout parser processor. The processor type name is LAYOUT_PARSER_PROCESSOR.

  • To create the processor, follow the instructions in Create a processor.
  • To enable the processor, follow the instructions in Enable a processor.

3. Prepare your RAG corpus

You need a RAG corpus to import your files into.

  • If you don't have a RAG corpus, create one. For an example, see Create a RAG corpus.
  • If you already have a RAG corpus, note that existing files imported without a layout parser won't be automatically reprocessed. To use the layout parser on these files, you must delete and re-import them. For an example of how to delete a file, see Delete a RAG file.

4. Review limitations

The following limitations apply when using the layout parser with the ImportRagFiles API:

  • Maximum input file size is 20 MB for all file types.
  • Maximum of 500 pages per PDF file.

Standard Document AI quotas and pricing also apply.

docs.title: Import files with the layout parser
docs.text:
You can import files and apply the layout parser using either the Google Cloud console or the API.

Google Cloud consolePython SDKREST API

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the RAG Engine page.

    Go to RAG Engine

  2. Click Create corpus.

  3. Enter a Corpus name and an optional Description.
  4. In the Data section, select the source of your data.
  5. Expand the Advanced options section.
    • Chunking strategy: The following default sizes are recommended:
      • Chunk size: 1024
      • Chunk overlap: 256
    • Layout parser: Select the LLM parser option.
      • From the Model dropdown, select your model.
      • Optional: Enter values for Maximum parsing requests per min and Custom parsing prompt.
    • Click Continue.
  6. On the Configure vector store page, select your Embedding model and Vector database.
  7. Click Create corpus.

To learn how to install or update the Vertex AI SDK for Python, see Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python. For more information, see the Python API reference documentation.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Before running the code sample, replace the following variables:

  • YOUR_PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • rag_corpus_id: The ID of your RAG corpus.
  • paths: A list of Cloud Storage or Google Drive locations. For example: ["gs://my-bucket1", "https://drive.google.com/file/123"].
from vertexai import rag
import vertexai

PROJECT_ID = "YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
# The RAG corpus resource name.
corpus_name = f"projects/{PROJECT_ID}/locations/us-central1/ragCorpora/{rag_corpus_id}"
# A list of Google Drive or Cloud Storage paths.
paths = ["https://drive.google.com/file/123", "gs://my_bucket/my_files_dir"]

# Initialize Vertex AI API once per session
vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1")

response = rag.import_files(
    corpus_name=corpus_name,
    paths=paths,
    transformation_config=rag.TransformationConfig(
        rag.ChunkingConfig(chunk_size=1024, chunk_overlap=256)
    ),
    # Optional: This must be an existing storage bucket folder, and the filename must be unique.
    import_result_sink="gs://sample-existing-folder/sample_import_result_unique.ndjson",
    # Optional: Specify the LLM parser configuration.
    llm_parser=rag.LlmParserConfig(
      model_name="gemini-1.5-pro-preview-0514",
      max_parsing_requests_per_min=100,
    ),
    # Optional
    max_embedding_requests_per_min=900,
)
print(f"Imported {response.imported_rag_files} files.")

The following sample shows how to import Cloud Storage files using the layout parser. For more configuration options, see the ImportRagFilesConfig reference.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Before using the request data, replace the following variables:

  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • LOCATION: The region to process the request (for example, us-central1).
  • RAG_CORPUS_ID: The ID of the RAG corpus resource.
  • GCS_URIS: A list of Cloud Storage URIs. For example: ["gs://my-bucket1", "gs://my-bucket2"].
  • LAYOUT_PARSER_PROCESSOR_NAME: The full resource name of the layout parser processor. For example: "projects/{project}/locations/{location}/processors/{processor_id}".
  • CHUNK_SIZE: Optional: The number of tokens for each chunk.

To import files, send a POST request to the ragFiles.import method.

POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/ragCorpora/RAG_CORPUS_ID/ragFiles:import

Request body:

{
  "importRagFilesConfig": {
    "gcsSource": {
      "uris": GCS_URIS
    },
    "ragFileParsingConfig": {
      "layoutParser": {
        "processorName": "LAYOUT_PARSER_PROCESSOR_NAME"
      }
    },
    "ragFileTransformationConfig": {
      "ragFileChunkingConfig": {
        "fixedLengthChunking": {
          "chunkSize": CHUNK_SIZE
        }
      }
    },
  }
}

To send your request, expand one of these options:

curlPowerShell

Note: The following command assumes that you have signed in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
    -d @request.json \
    "https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/ragCorpora/RAG_CORPUS_ID/ragFiles:import"

Note: The following command assumes that you have signed in to the gcloud CLI with your user account by running gcloud init or gcloud auth login.

Save the request body in a file named request.json, and execute the following command:

$cred = gcloud auth print-access-token
$headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer $cred" }

docs.title: Use the LLM parser
docs.text:
Preview

Some of the RAG features are Preview offerings, subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" of the Google Cloud Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features may have limited support, and changes to Pre-GA products and features may not be compatible with other Pre-GA versions. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions. Further, by using the Gemini API on Vertex AI, you agree to the Generative AI Preview terms and conditions (Preview Terms).

The VPC-SC security controls and CMEK are supported by Vertex AI RAG Engine. Data residency and AXT security controls aren't supported.

This page explains how to use the Vertex AI RAG Engine LLM parser.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Vertex AI RAG Engine uses LLMs for document parsing. LLMs have the ability to effectively process documents in the following ways:

  • Understand and interpret semantic content across various formats.
  • Retrieve relevant document chunks.
  • Extract meaningful information from documents.
  • Identify relevant sections in documents.
  • Accurately summarize complex documents.
  • Understand and interact with visuals.
  • Extract data from charts and diagrams.
  • Describe images.
  • Understand relationships between charts and text.
  • Provide more contextually rich and accurate responses.

The capabilities of the Vertex AI RAG Engine significantly improve the quality of generated responses.

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text: The LLM parser only supports Gemini models. If you have the RAG API enabled, you have access to the supported models. For a list of supported generation models, see Generative models.

docs.title: Supported file types
docs.text:
The following file types are supported by the LLM parser:

  • application/pdf
  • image/png
  • image/jpeg
  • image/webp
  • image/heic
  • image/heif

docs.title: Pricing and quotas
docs.text:
For pricing details, see Vertex AI pricing.

For quotas that apply, see Request quotas.

The LLM parser calls Gemini models to parse your documents. This creates additional costs, which are charged to your project. The cost can be roughly estimated using this formula:

cost = number_of_document_files * average_pages_per_document *
(average_input_tokens * input_token_pricing_of_selected_model +
average_output_tokens * output_token_pricing_of_selected_model)

For example, you have 1,000 PDF files, and each PDF file has 50 pages. The average PDF page has 500 tokens, and we need an additional 100 tokens for prompting. The average output is 100 tokens.

Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite is used in your configuration for parsing, and it costs $0.075 for 1M input tokens and $0.3 for output text tokens.

Note: This example is for an educational purpose on how to estimate your cost. It doesn't reflect the real cost you pay for every indexing request using the LLM parser.

cost = 1,000 * 50 * (600 * 0.075 / 1M + 100 * 0.3 / 1M) = 3.75

The cost is $3.75.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Before you begin Concepts
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): A technique that enhances LLM responses by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge base.
  • Corpus: A collection of documents that the RAG system uses as its knowledge base.
  • LLM (Large Language Model): A type of AI model trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human-like language.
  • Embedding: A numerical representation of text, images, or other data that captures its semantic meaning.
  • Prompt: The input text or instruction given to an LLM to elicit a specific response.

Set up your environment

Replace the values in the following variables used in the code samples:

  • PROJECT_ID: The ID for your Google Cloud project.
  • LOCATION: The region where your request is processed.
  • RAG_CORPUS_RESOURCE: The ID of your corpus.
  • GCS_URI: The Cloud Storage URI of the files you want to import.
  • GOOGLE_DRIVE_URI: The Google Drive URI of the files you want to import.
  • MODEL_NAME: The resource name of the model used for parsing. Format: projects/{project_id}/locations/{location}/publishers/google/models/{model_id}
  • CUSTOM_PARSING_PROMPT: Optional: Custom prompt that is configured by the customer for LLM parser to use for parsing documents.
  • MAX_PARSING_REQUESTS_PER_MIN: Optional: The maximum number of requests the job can make to the Vertex AI model per minute. For more information, see Generative AI on Vertex AI rate limits and the Quotas & System Limits page for your project to set an appropriate value.

from vertexai import rag
import vertexai

PROJECT_ID = "PROJECT_ID"
CORPUS_NAME = "RAG_CORPUS_RESOURCE"
LOCATION = "LOCATION"
MODEL_ID = "MODEL_ID"
MODEL_NAME = "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/locations/{LOCATION}/publishers/google/models/{MODEL_ID}"
MAX_PARSING_REQUESTS_PER_MIN = MAX_PARSING_REQUESTS_PER_MIN # Optional
CUSTOM_PARSING_PROMPT = "Your custom prompt" # Optional

PATHS = ["https://drive.google.com/file/123", "gs://my_bucket/my_files_dir"]

# Initialize Vertex AI API once per session
vertexai.init(project={PROJECT_ID}, location={LOCATION})

transformation_config = rag.TransformationConfig(
    chunking_config=rag.ChunkingConfig(
        chunk_size=1024, # Optional
        chunk_overlap=200, # Optional

)

llm_parser_config = rag.LlmParserConfig(
    model_name = MODEL_NAME,
    max_parsing_requests_per_min=MAX_PARSING_REQUESTS_PER_MIN, # Optional

)

rag.import_files(
    CORPUS_NAME,
    PATHS,
    llm_parser=llm_parser_config,
    transformation_config=transformation_config,
)

docs.title: Prompting
docs.text: The Vertex AI RAG Engine LLM parser uses a predefined and tuned prompt for parsing documents. However, if you have specialized documents that might not be suitable for a general prompt, you have the option to specify your custom parsing prompt when using the API. When requesting Gemini to parse your documents, Vertex AI RAG Engine appends a prompt to your default system prompt.

docs.title: Prompt template table
docs.text:
To help with document parsing, the following table provides a prompt template example to guide you in creating prompts that Vertex AI RAG Engine can use to parse your documents:

Instruction Template statement Example Specify role. You are a/an [Specify the role, such as a factual data extractor or an information retriever]. You are an information retriever. Specify task. Extract [Specify the type of information, such as factual statements, key data, or specific details] from the [Specify the document source, such as a document, text, article, image, table]. Extract key data from the sample.txt file. Explain how you want the LLM to generate the output according to your documents. Present each fact in a [Specify the output format, such as a structured list or text format], and link to its [Specify the source location, such as a page, paragraph, table, or row]. Present each fact in a structured list, and link to its sample page. Highlight what should be the focus of the LLM. Extract [Specify the key data types, such as the names, dates, numbers, attributes, or relationships] exactly as stated. Extract names and dates. Highlight what you want the LLM to avoid. [List the actions to avoid, such as analysis, interpretation, summarizing, inferring, or giving opinions]. Extract only what the document explicitly says. No giving opinions. Extract only what the document explicitly says.

docs.title: General guidance
docs.text:
Follow these guidelines to write your prompt to send to the LLM parser.

  • Specific: Clearly define the task and the type of information to be extracted.
  • Detailed: Provide detailed instructions on output format, source attribution, and handling of different data structures.
  • Constraining: Explicitly state what the AI shouldn't do such as analysis or interpretation.
  • Clear: Use clear and directive language.
  • Structured: Organize instructions logically using numbered lists or bullet points for readability.

docs.title: Parsing quality analysis
docs.text:
This table lists results from scenarios that customers ran using Vertex AI RAG Engine. The feedback shows that the LLM parser improves the quality of parsing documents.

Scenario Result Parsing information across slides and linking sections The LLM parser successfully linked section titles on one slide to the detailed information presented on subsequent slides. Understanding and extracting information from tables The LLM parser correctly related columns and headers within a large table to answer specific questions. Interpreting flowcharts The LLM parser was able to follow the logic of a flowchart and extract the correct sequence of actions and corresponding information. Extracting data from graphs The LLM parser could interpret different types of graphs, such as line graphs, and extract specific data points based on the query. Capturing relationships between headings and text The LLM parser, guided by the prompt, paid attention to heading structures and could retrieve all relevant information associated with a particular topic or section. Potential to overcome embedding limitations with prompt engineering While initially hampered by embedding model limitations in some use cases, additional experiments demonstrated that a well-crafted LLM parser prompt could potentially mitigate these issues and retrieve the correct information even when semantic understanding is challenging for the embedding model alone.

The LLM parser enhances the LLM's ability to understand and reason about the context within a document, which leads to more accurate and comprehensive responses.

Vertex AI RAG Engine overview
docs.text: This page provides an overview of the Vertex AI RAG Engine and how it works.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Vertex AI RAG Engine is a component of the Vertex AI platform that facilitates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It serves as a data framework for developing large language model (LLM) applications that are augmented with your specific data. This process, known as context augmentation, allows an LLM to access and utilize your private data, such as your organization's internal knowledge base.

A common limitation of LLMs is their inability to access private or real-time information. By using RAG Engine, you can ground the LLM with your own data, which helps reduce hallucinations and enables the model to provide more accurate and relevant answers. By combining your knowledge sources with the LLM's existing knowledge, you provide a richer context that enhances the quality of the model's responses.

Concepts
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): A technique that enhances LLM responses by first retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge base and providing it as context to the model.
  • Corpus: A collection of documents that you provide to the RAG Engine for indexing and retrieval.
  • Embedding: A numerical vector representation of text that captures its semantic meaning, allowing for efficient similarity searches.
  • Grounding: The process of connecting an LLM's response to specific, verifiable data sources to improve factual accuracy and trustworthiness.

docs.title: How RAG Engine works
docs.text:
The following diagram illustrates the key stages in the Retrieval-Augmented Generation process managed by RAG Engine.

flowchart TD
    A[Data ingestion] --> B[Data transformation]
    B --> C[Embedding]
    C --> D[Data indexing]
    D --> E[Retrieval]
    E --> F[Generation]

    click A "#data-ingestion"
    click B "#data-transformation"
    click C "#embedding"
    click D "#data-indexing"
    click E "#retrieval"
    click F "#generation"
Figure 1. The Retrieval-Augmented Generation process in Vertex AI RAG Engine.

The RAG process consists of the following steps:

1. Data ingestion

Intake data from various sources. Supported sources include local files, Cloud Storage, and Google Drive.

2. Data transformation

Prepare the raw data for indexing. For example, large documents are automatically split into smaller, more manageable chunks. For more information, see Chunking and transformations for RAG.

3. Embedding

Convert the text chunks into numerical representations (vectors) that capture their semantic meaning. This process allows the system to compare the meaning of a user's query with the meaning of the document chunks. For more information, see Get text embeddings.

4. Data indexing

RAG Engine creates an index, referred to as a corpus, which structures the embedded data for efficient searching. The index acts like a detailed table of contents for your knowledge base.

5. Retrieval

When a user submits a query, the retrieval component searches the index to find the most relevant information from your knowledge base.

6. Generation

The retrieved information is combined with the original user query and passed as context to the LLM. This context helps the model generate a factually grounded and relevant response.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Set up your project and environment Concepts
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): A technique that enhances the accuracy and relevance of large language model (LLM) responses by grounding them in external knowledge sources.
  • RAG Corpus: A collection of documents or files that you provide as a knowledge base for the RAG model.
  • RAG File: An individual document within a RAG corpus.
  • Embedding Model: A model that converts text into numerical representations (vectors) to enable semantic search and retrieval.

Grant IAM roles

To use RAG Engine, your user account needs the roles/aiplatform.user IAM role.

  1. Run the following command to grant the role:

    gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member="user:USER_IDENTIFIER" --role="roles/aiplatform.user"

  2. Replace the following:

    • PROJECT_ID: Your Google Cloud project ID.
    • USER_IDENTIFIER: Your email address (for example, myemail@example.com).

Prepare your environment

  1. Install the Vertex AI SDK for Python: If you haven't already, install the SDK by running the following command: 

    pip install --upgrade google-cloud-aiplatform

  2. Set your project configuration: Run this command in the Google Cloud console to set up your project. 

    gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID
    Replace PROJECT_ID with your Google Cloud project ID.

  3. Authorize your login: Run this command to authorize your session. 

    gcloud auth application-default login

    B --> C[Create a RAG corpus]
    C --> D[Import files into the corpus]
    D --> E[Retrieve context from the corpus]

docs.title: Run the RAG workflow
docs.text:
Follow these steps to use the Vertex AI SDK for Python to run RAG Engine tasks.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with code snippets or setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

Run the RAG workflow with the Vertex AI SDK

1. Initialize Vertex AI and define variables

Initialize the Vertex AI SDK and define the variables for your project ID, corpus display name, and file paths.

from vertexai import rag
from vertexai.generative_models import GenerativeModel, Tool
import vertexai

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below lines
# PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
# display_name = "test_corpus"
# paths = ["https://drive.google.com/file/d/123", "gs://my_bucket/my_files_dir"]  # Supports Google Cloud Storage and Google Drive Links

# Initialize Vertex AI API once per session
vertexai.init(project=PROJECT_ID, location="us-central1")

2. Create a RAG corpus

Create a RagCorpus to store your files. You can configure the embedding model to be used for processing the documents.

# Create RagCorpus
# Configure embedding model, for example "text-embedding-005".
embedding_model_config = rag.RagEmbeddingModelConfig(
    vertex_prediction_endpoint=rag.VertexPredictionEndpoint(
        publisher_model="publishers/google/models/text-embedding-005"
    )
)

rag_corpus = rag.create_corpus(
    display_name=display_name,
    backend_config=rag.RagVectorDbConfig(
        rag_embedding_model_config=embedding_model_config
    ),
)

3. Import files

Import your source files into the RagCorpus. You can specify chunking configurations to control how the documents are processed.

# Import Files to the RagCorpus
rag.import_files(
    rag_corpus.name,
    paths,
    # Optional
    transformation_config=rag.TransformationConfig(
        chunking_config=rag.ChunkingConfig(
            chunk_size=512,
            chunk_overlap=100,
        ),
    ),
    max_embedding_requests_per_min=1000,  # Optional
)

4. Retrieve context

Perform a direct retrieval query on your RagCorpus to find relevant context based on a text query.

# Direct context retrieval
rag_retrieval_config = rag.RagRetrievalConfig(
    top_k=3,  # Optional
    filter=rag.Filter(vector_distance_threshold=0.5),  # Optional
)
response = rag.retrieval_query(
    rag_resources=[
        rag.RagResource(
            rag_corpus=rag_corpus.name,
            # Optional: supply IDs from `rag.list_files()`.
            # rag_file_ids=["rag-file-1", "rag-file-2", ...],
        )
    ],
    text="What is RAG and why it is helpful?",
    rag_retrieval_config=rag_retrieval_config,
)
print(response)

5. Enhance generation with a Gemini model

Use the RagCorpus as a tool for a Gemini model. This allows the model to use the retrieved context to generate a more informed and accurate response.

# Enhance generation
# Create a RAG retrieval tool
rag_retrieval_tool = Tool.from_retrieval(
    retrieval=rag.Retrieval(
        source=rag.VertexRagStore(
            rag_resources=[
                rag.RagResource(
                    rag_corpus=rag_corpus.name,  # Currently only 1 corpus is allowed.
                    # Optional: supply IDs from `rag.list_files()`.
                    # rag_file_ids=["rag-file-1", "rag-file-2", ...],
                )
            ],
            rag_retrieval_config=rag_retrieval_config,
        ),
    )
)

# Create a Gemini model instance
rag_model = GenerativeModel(
    model_name="gemini-1.5-flash-001", tools=[rag_retrieval_tool]
)

# Generate response
response = rag_model.generate_content("What is RAG and why it is helpful?")
print(response.text)
# Example response:
#   RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
#   It's a technique used in AI to enhance the quality of responses
# ...

docs.title: Generative AI on Vertex AI quotas and system limits
docs.text: This page introduces the two ways to consume generative AI services, provides a list of quotas and limits by service, and shows you how to view and edit your quotas in the Google Cloud console.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
There are two ways to consume generative AI services: you can use the on-demand Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) model, or you can reserve capacity in advance using Provisioned Throughput.

The following table provides a comparison of these two options:

Feature Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) Provisioned Throughput Best for Getting started, experimentation, and applications with variable traffic. Production applications requiring guaranteed capacity and predictable performance. Pricing Pay only for what you use. Pay an upfront fee for a reserved period (e.g., per hour). Capacity Shared capacity, subject to availability. Dedicated, reserved capacity for your project. Performance Can fluctuate based on overall system demand. Stable and predictable latency and throughput. Quota System Uses either Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ) or a standard quota system, depending on the model. Not subject to standard quotas; capacity is determined by the reservation.

If you're using the PayGo model, your usage is subject to one of two quota systems:

  • Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ): Newer models use DSQ, which dynamically distributes available capacity among all customers for a specific model and region. This removes the need to set quotas or submit quota increase requests. There are no user-managed quotas with DSQ. For more information, see Dynamic shared quota.
  • Standard Quota: Non-Gemini and earlier Gemini models use a standard quota system. These quotas apply to requests for a given Google Cloud project and supported region to ensure fairness and reduce spikes in resource use.

To learn more about getting predictable service levels for your production workloads, see Provisioned Throughput.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Concepts
  • Pay-as-you-go (PayGo): An on-demand service consumption model where you pay for resources as you use them, with capacity shared among users.
  • Provisioned Throughput: A service consumption model where you reserve a dedicated amount of model serving capacity for a specific period, ensuring predictable performance.
  • Dynamic Shared Quota (DSQ): A quota system for PayGo usage that dynamically allocates available capacity, eliminating the need for manual quota management.
  • Standard Quota: A traditional quota system for PayGo usage that sets fixed limits on requests per minute for a given project and region.

docs.title: Use CMEK with Vertex AI RAG Engine
docs.text:
Vertex AI RAG Engine supports VPC Service Controls security controls and Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) to enhance data security. Data residency and AXT security controls aren't supported.

This page provides an overview of encryption options for RAG Engine and shows you how to use CMEK to protect your data.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Prerequisites Concepts
  • Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK): A data encryption method that lets you use your own cryptographic keys, which you manage through Cloud Key Management Service (KMS), to protect your data at rest in Google Cloud services.
  • Cloud Key Management Service (KMS): A cloud service for creating, managing, and using cryptographic keys.
  • RagManagedDb: A fully managed vector database provided by Vertex AI as part of the RAG Engine, optimized for storing and retrieving embeddings for retrieval-augmented generation.

docs.title: Encryption options for RAG Engine
docs.text:
Vertex AI RAG Engine provides robust options for managing the encryption of your data at rest. By default, all user data within RagManagedDb is encrypted using a Google-owned and Google-managed key. For more control, you can use Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

The following table compares Google-default encryption with CMEK.

Feature Google-default encryption Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) Key Management Keys are owned and managed by Google. You control and manage the keys in Cloud KMS. Configuration No setup required; enabled by default. Requires setup of a Cloud KMS key and granting permissions to the RAG Engine service account. Control Limited control over key rotation and management. Full control over key lifecycle, including creation, rotation, and revocation. Use Case Suitable for users who want a simple, secure, and maintenance-free encryption solution. Ideal for organizations with specific compliance or regulatory requirements that mandate control over encryption keys.

docs.title: Use CMEK with a RAG corpus
docs.text:
To use CMEK, you must specify your KMS key when you create a RAG corpus. The encryption_spec field, which defines the KMS key, is immutable. This means you cannot enable or disable CMEK on a RAG corpus after it has been created.

To set up an encryption key and grant the necessary permissions, follow the steps in Set up your KMS key and grant permissions.

Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues with the setup, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: CMEK limitations for Vertex AI RAG Engine
docs.text:
Vertex AI RAG Engine supports CMEK with the following limitations:

  • A RAG corpus that isn't CMEK-enabled must already exist in the project before a CMEK-enabled RAG corpus can be created.
  • CMEK is only supported on RagVectorDbConfig of type RagManagedDb.
  • The encryption_spec field is immutable, which means that CMEK can't be enabled or disabled after the RAG corpus is created.
  • No more than 50 unique KMS keys can be used to create RAG corpora per project per region.

  • For more information on Vertex AI RAG Engine, see Vertex AI RAG Engine overview.
  • To learn more about data at rest, see Data residency.
